similarly produces new flowers of Anethum. It softens and opens the private parts of women, and is suitable for tremors and the chills that come at the onset of periodic fevers, by warming, and it relieves fatigue and is good for pain in the joints.

On the ointment of Lilies, which they call Susinum. Chapter 48.

The Susinum, which others call the Lily ointment, is made as follows. Take nine pounds and five ounces of oil, five pounds and three ounces of aromatic reed, and five ounces of myrrh. Grind all these things together and macerate them in fragrant wine, then cook them. Once the oil is strained, add three and a half pounds of cardamom that has been pounded and soaked beforehand in rainwater, leave it to macerate inside, then press it out. After this, take three and a half pounds of this thickened oil and pour into a large, shallow basin a thousand stripped lily petals, then mix with hands anointed with honey, and leave to rest for a day and a night; the next morning press out the oil into a vessel. But it must immediately be separated from the water that is pressed out along with it, because oil cannot tolerate water the way rose oil can, since when it heats it boils and spoils. To separate it well, it is frequently transferred from one vessel to another anointed with honey, and coarse salt is sprinkled over it, and the sediment it forms is carefully separated. Beyond this, the fragrant materials left over from the pressing are taken and placed in a basin, the same weight of the same oil is poured over them, ten drams of pounded cardamom are added, and everything is carefully mixed by hand, and in a short time it is pressed, continually purging the oil that is extracted. The same materials are added a third time, along with cardamom and salt, mixed with honey-anointed hands, and pressed. The best is the first pressing, the second is next in quality. The least good is the third. Beyond this, one again takes a thousand stripped lily petals and pours them over the oil that was first pressed, proceeding always as was done from the beginning, adding cardamom and pressing. This should also be done in the second and third pressings. The more times fresh lilies are added, the more the virtue increases. Finally, when it is recognized to be perfect, for each composition seventy-two drams of the finest myrrh are added, seventy-five of cardamom, and ten of saffron. Some, having removed an equal weight of saffron and finely pounded and sifted cinnamon, mix them with water in a vessel and pour over them the oil of the first composition, leave it for a while, then separate it from the water, placing it in small dry vessels dusted all over with myrrh and gum and soaked in water, saffron, and honey, then doing the same in the second and third pressings. Some make it simply with balanine oil, or lily oil, or any other oil they like. The best is that made in Phoenicia and in Egypt. But that which is most praised is the one that most breathes the scent of lilies. It warms, softens, and opens obstructions and inflammations of the womb, and is universally most useful for the ailments of women. It is good for ulcers of the head that weep, for hot swellings, for smallpox, and for dandruff of the scalp. It removes the marks of blows and extinguishes those of scars, restoring the skin to its color. Rubbed in it reduces swelling, and drunk it purges bile downward. It stimulates urine, but nonetheless it is harmful to the stomach and causes great nausea.

Q These ointments — that of Lilies, of Basil, of Southernwood, and of Anethum — their compositions being quite clear, truly have no need of further particular annotations.

On the ointment of Narcissus. Chapter 49.

The ointment of Narcissus is made in this way. Take seventy pounds and five ounces of washed oil, and six pounds and two ounces of aspalathus. Pound the aspalathus and macerate it in as much water as amounts to a third part of all the oil, then cook everything together. Remove the aspalathus, and add five pounds and eight ounces of aromatic reed, and together with a piece of myrrh pound them, sift them, and soak them in old fragrant wine, and having mixed everything together, cook, and co-

A once it has boiled well, it is removed from the fire, and when it is cool the oil is strained. Then a great many Narcissus flowers are taken and placed in a vessel, and the oil is poured over them for two days, as was described for the lily preparation. It is mixed, pressed, and transferred from vessel to vessel so that it is well purified from the sediment, otherwise it spoils. It is useful for softening hardnesses and opening obstructions of the feminine parts, but it causes headache.

T Some texts are found which, in the composition of this ointment, require that the aspalathus be cooked only in a third part of the oil. But the other interpretation seems to me much better. For it would have been superfluous to take seventy pounds of oil for this composition and then wish to use only a third part of it. The use of making the ointment from the Narcissus flower had already fallen into disuse by the time of Pliny, as he himself stated expressly in the first chapter of the thirteenth book of his Natural History.

On the Saffron Ointment. Chapter I.

B To make the saffron ointment, the oil is thickened with equal weight and equal measure of all those things described for the lily ointment, and three and a half pounds of this are taken along with eight drams of saffron, and for five days these are mixed together frequently each day. Then on the sixth day all the pure oil is strained off, and to that same saffron is added an equal weight of oil, and this is mixed for thirteen days; then forty drams of pounded and well-sifted myrrh are added, mixed in a mortar as needed, and set aside. There are some others who make it with oil perfumed with fragrances for making the privet ointment. That one is most praised which breathes most strongly of the scent of saffron, and this one is used more in Medicine. The second is that which breathes more of myrrh. The Saffron ointment has the virtue of warming, it provokes sleep, and therefore anointing the nose of those afflicted with frenzy, and likewise the head, benefits them. It matures abscesses and cleanses ulcers. It benefits obstructions and hardnesses in the intimate parts of women, and malignant ulcers in those places when mixed with wax, saffron, marrow, and double the weight of oil. It matures, softens, moistens, and soothes. It is applied with water to eyes that are changing to a bluish color. Related to this ointment are the butter ointment, the onyx ointment, and that of storax. For although they differ from this one in name, they are nonetheless equal in composition and in virtue.

On the Privet Ointment. Chapter II.

C One takes one part of washed omphacine oil and one and a half parts of rainwater, of which one part is used to wash the oil and the other to macerate the aromatic ingredients that are infused in it. Taking therefore five and a half pounds of aspalathus, six and a half of fragrant calamus, one of myrrh, three, and nine ounces of cardamom, and nine and five ounces of oil, the aspalathus first well pounded is infused in the water and cooked in the oil until the first boil. Then the myrrh is incorporated with the calamus well pounded with old fragrant wine, and then divided into pieces, which are placed in the same oil, having first removed the aspalathus; and when they have boiled, the

D cauldron is removed from the fire, and the oil is strained, into which the pounded cardamom is incorporated, and the rest of the water is well beaten in, always stirring with a spatula without stopping, until it is cold. It is then strained, and taking twenty-eight pounds of it, it is infused with forty-six pounds and eight ounces of privet flower; and when they are well macerated, the oil is pressed out through a basket, and if one wishes it more abundant, an equal weight of fresh flowers is added back to it, and it is pressed again, and this may be done two or three times as one pleases. For by doing so it continually becomes more potent. The best is chosen as that which, when breathed, most fills the nose with its scent. There are some who add cinnamon to it. It has the virtue of warming, softening, and opening, and benefits ailments of the secret parts of women and of the nerves. It is useful for pains in the side and for broken bones, either by itself or compounded with cerate. Beyond this it is used in poultices made for pleurisy, inflammations of the groin, and for the convulsive condition in which the nerves, contracting, twist the head back toward the shoulders; and it is also used in medicines for weariness.

BOOK ONE
On the Iris Ointment. Chapter 52.

Take six pounds and eight ounces of the bark of palm fruits, pound them finely, and steep them in seventy pounds and five ounces of oil, together with ten measures of water; cook this in a copper vessel until it gives off a good smell, then strain it into a basin well greased with honey. The Iris ointment is made first from this aromatic oil by placing within it Iris root macerated in thick oil, as described above. There is also another preparation made in this way: take seventy pounds and five ounces of oil, five pounds and two ounces of pounded balsam wood as noted, cook it, then remove the balsam wood and add nine pounds and ten ounces of sweet flag well pounded together with a piece of myrrh soaked in old fragrant wine. Once this is done, take fourteen pounds of this thick, aromatic oil and mix it with an equal weight of pounded Iris root; let it macerate for two days and two nights, then press it out firmly. To make it stronger, add an equal weight of Iris root two or three times, macerating and pressing each time. The best is that which gives off no other odor than that of the Iris, such as is made in Perga of Pamphilia and in Elis of Achaia. The Iris ointment has the property of warming and softening; it removes scabs from cauterizations, cleanses putrid and filthy ulcers. It is good for disorders of women's private parts, and likewise for inflammations and obstructions thereof. It promotes childbirth and opens the hemorrhoidal veins. Distilled with vinegar, rue, and bitter almonds, it is dripped into the ears for ringing sounds. It is good for catarrhs that descend from the head, and for foul ulcers of the nose, by anointing the nostrils with it. Drunk to the weight of a cyathus it purges the belly, relieves flank pains, and promotes urine. It induces vomiting in those who cannot vomit, by rubbing it on the fingers or another stimulating instrument and placing them in the throat. It is used as a gargle in quinsy with honeyed water, and anointing with it is also good for roughness of the windpipe, and for those who have eaten hemlock, coriander, or harmful mushrooms.

Although this chapter is so clear that it needs no more commentary than I gave to the two preceding ones on saffron and privet ointment, I would nevertheless feel I had left something out if I did not say that in this composition of the Iris ointment, when the Iris is mentioned, it is to be understood (even though Dioscorides does not say so explicitly) as the root and not the flower. For the flower gives off a disagreeable and offensive odor rather than a pleasant one, whereas the opposite is true of the root; and therefore, since ointments ought to give off a sweet and pleasing fragrance, it must be the root of the iris and not the flower that Dioscorides intended. It should further be noted that where this chapter says the best Iris ointment is that made in Elis of Achaia, it likely means Elis of Arcadia, because in the writings of those skilled in geography, Elis is found to be in Arcadia and not in Achaia.

On the Gleucine Ointment, or Must Ointment. Chapter 53.

The Gleucine ointment, or Must ointment, is made simply from omphacine oil, with spikenard, sweet flag, Celtic spikenard, palm spathe, aspalathus, melilot, costus, and grape must; the vessel in which the aromatics, the oil, and the wine are placed together is buried in grape pomace for thirty days, stirring it twice each day. The oil is then pressed out and stored. It warms, softens, and resolves. It is good for trembling and the chills that precede fevers, and is useful for disorders of the nerves and women's private parts, and softens better than any other medicine prepared for fatigue.

It is no wonder that Dioscorides calls this composition of the Gleucine ointment simple. For there are other compositions of it found that are much richer in aromatic simples, as one reads in Columella, Book 1, Chapter 14. Yet even that composition, considering the simples that go into it, cannot but manifestly warm. Although Pliny, in Book 4, Chapter 23, expressly says that Gleucine constricts and cools — which is strong evidence that Pliny's Musteum or Gleucine ointment was of a composition entirely different from that of Dioscorides and Columella, or else that he greatly erred in classifying it among the cold temperaments. He also mentions it in Chapter 7 of Book 15, saying that grape must was put into the Gleucine ointment, and that it was prepared with gentle heat, not over fire like the others, but in grape pomace, stirring it twice a day. This accords quite well with Dioscorides, and so it seems more likely that Pliny erred in calling Gleucine cooling than that anything else is amiss.

On the Ointment Amaracinum. Chapter 54.

The excellent ointment Amaracinum is made in Cyzicus from omphacine oil and oil of the unguentary acorn, first thickened with balsam wood, squinanthus, and fragrant calamus, and aromatized with marjoram, costus, amomum, nard, cassia, carpobalsam, and myrrh. Those who wish to make it more precious add cinnamon, using wine to rinse the vessels and honey to blend the ground aromatics. The Amaracinum warms and promotes sleep, opens, softens, and ripens. It promotes urine. It is useful for fistulas, putrid ulcers, and watery hernias, after surgical operations. It causes the scab of cauteries to fall off, and is beneficial for those ulcers which the Greeks, on account of their malignancy, call theriomata. It helps with retention of urine when applied by anointing the seat, and likewise for inflammations thereof, and for opening the hemorrhoidal veins. Applied beneath the female organs it promotes menstruation, resolves hardnesses and swellings. It benefits wounds of the nerves and muscles when applied with carded wool.

Enough has been said of this above in the chapter on Samsuccus. There is therefore no need to repeat it here. Galen mentioned it in his book on Antidotes, while explaining the Hedichroon of Andromache which is used in Theriaca, saying at length that the unguentmakers of his time, in place of marjoram which was anciently used in Cyzicus, put in Marum, so that it would breathe more fragrance; and that therefore, in order to see what the true Amaracinum was, he had some prepared with marjoram alone, which, though it did not breathe so much of fragrance, was nonetheless but little inferior to the other in virtue.

On the Ointment Megalinum. Chapter 55.

The ointment Megalinum was made in former times, but its composition has since gone up in smoke. Nevertheless, so as not to fail in our historical account, it will not be out of place to bring it back to knowledge. It was made in the same manner as the Amaracinum, except that in addition resin was put in it, and in this alone were the two different from each other; and therefore the difference is slight. Resin is not put into ointments to preserve them, nor to make them fragrant, but to give them body and color. The terebinth resin is cooked until it loses its odor. Of the manner of cooking it, we shall speak when we write of it.

On the Ointment Hedichroon. Chapter 56.

That which they call Hedichroon is usually made in Cos, similar in virtue and composition to the Amaracinum, though much more fragrant.

The great Galen made mention of the composition of the Hedichroon in his book on Antidotes, because all the aromatics of it, kneaded with wine, enter into the composition of the Theriaca of Andromache, and although he affirms that he found several compositions of it, he nevertheless wrote down one of this manner as the best. To make the Hedichroon one takes two drams of marum, and equal parts of asarum, marjoram, aspalathus, squinanthus, fragrant calamus, and more from Pontus, of balsam wood, opobalsam, cinnamon, and costus, three drams each, of myrrh six, and equal parts of malabathrum leaf, Indian nard, saffron, cassia, and double of amomum, and one dram of Chian mastic. Then all these things are well ground with Falernian wine into a paste, from which lozenges are formed, similar to those of squill and vipers. Galen was moved to write this composition because, as he affirms, Andromache had omitted to write it down, and in order to make clear to physicians less experienced in simple and compound medicines what the word Hedichroon meant in the composition of the Theriaca, so that they would not fall into the error which he writes befell a physician in his time in Rome, who, never having been present to see the Theriaca made, and yet wishing to make it himself, went searching through the apothecaries' shops for the Hedichroon, thinking it was some herb, or root, or some other simple medicine. This I myself have seen happen to many modern practitioners in our own time. Avicenna, together with the rest of the Arabic school, in their composition of the Theriaca, called the Hedichroon troches of Andaracaron, putting in various compositions that differ greatly in simples, weights, and measures from the description given by Galen; and therefore in compounding the Theriaca it is no wonder that for so long a time the true composition has not been achieved, having been corrupted both by the Arabs and by composers using various and diverse simples.

On the Unguent Metopio. Chapter 57. A

In Egypt the unguent which is commonly known in that region as Metopio — because of the galbanum it contains — takes its name from the tree that produces galbanum. It is composed of bitter almonds, omphacine oil, cardamom, spikenard, fragrant calamus, honey, wine, myrrh, carpobalsam, galbanum, and resin. The finest quality is that which is thick, of heavy odor, and smells more of cardamom and myrrh than of galbanum. It greatly warms, burns, opens, draws, and cleanses ulcers. Added to corrosive unguents, it is beneficial for cut nerves and muscles, and for watery hernias. It is used in softening plasters and in wax salves. It is useful for trembling and for the chill that precedes fevers, and especially for those in which, the nerves being contracted, the head is turned toward the shoulders. It promotes sweating, opens the natural passages of women, softens their hardnesses, and has a universal virtue of softening.

On the Unguent Mendesio. Chapter 58. B

The Mendesio is composed of Balanine oil, myrrh, cassia, and resin; though some, after these ingredients are weighed (pointlessly, however), add a little cinnamon. For those things that are not cooked together do not yield their virtue to it. It has the same value as the Metopio, but is somewhat less effective.

On the Statte. Chapter 59.

The Statte is the fatty substance drawn from fresh myrrh, pounded and soaked in water and then pressed in a press. This liquor is very fragrant and precious, and by itself forms the unguent called Statte. The finest is that which contains no admixture of oil, and that whose small quantity has great virtue. The Statte warms, corresponding in its proportions to myrrh and to unguents that have the virtue of warming.

C Serapione, and likewise all the other Arabic authors together with the whole crowd of apothecaries, call the Statte liquid storax, of which liquor one finds not only in Venice in great quantity, but universally in all apothecaries' shops that deal in medicinal goods. Serapione distinguishes this as follows: in the chapter on storax calamita, speaking also of the liquid kind, he says that it is drawn from myrrh first soaked in water, and then pressed — agreeing in all other respects with the account written by Dioscorides. This identification is further confirmed by the fact that it (that is, the liquid storax that is unadulterated) is most fragrant and bitter to the taste. But one must note that in our own times little of the genuine article is to be found, as happens with almost every other thing that comes from the Levant. For as such goods pass through the hands of the Moors and the Turks — our mortal enemies as Christians — they think it a kind of sacrifice to deceive us in merchandise and in everything else. But to return to the point: I truly believe that when genuine Statte could be obtained, it could legitimately be used in place of the finest myrrh.

On the Unguent of Cinnamon. Chapter 60.

The unguent of cinnamon is made with the oil of the unguentary acorn, thickened with wood of balsam, spikenard, and fragrant calamus, and made aromatic with cinnamon and carpobalsam, to which is added four times as much myrrh as cinnamon, and enough honey to macerate the whole. The best is that which has not a sharp but a pleasant odor, that breathes of myrrh, is thick in body, fragrant, and very bitter to the taste. For such a one will have received its body not from resin but from myrrh — since resin causes no bitterness and no agreeable scent. In its virtues it is very sharp, hot, and bitter, and by reason of its heat it opens the mouths of the veins, resolves and disperses, draws humors and flatulence. It does, however, burden the head; it benefits the defects of the natural passages of women, when one adds double the amount of oil, of wax, and of marrow — for thus it loses much of its sharpness and becomes emollient. Otherwise it burns and hardens more powerfully than all unguents that have body. It is a most effective remedy against fistulas and putrid ulcers. It benefits watery hernias, carbuncles, and gangrenes, with cardamom added. It is usefully applied for the cold and trembling that precede fevers, for bites of venomous animals, and for the stings of scorpions and of those spiders called phalanges, applied with pounded figs.

On the Ointment of Nard.          Chapter 41.

The Nard ointment is prepared in various ways. For it is made either with Malabathrum leaf or without it. Sometimes it is made with Balan oil, or with omphacine oil, adding Squinanthus to thicken it, and to aromatize it: costus, amomum, nard, myrrh, and balsam. The thin variety is praised, not the sharp one, and that which breathes the scent of dry nard or amomum. It has the virtue of drying, is sharp, warms, purges, cleanses the humors, and rarifies. It is liquid and not viscous, unless resin is added. Apart from this, it is made more simply with omphacine oil, squinanthus, sweet calamus, costus, and nard.

On the Ointment of Malabathrum.          Chapter 62.

The Malabathrum ointment is composed of the same ingredients as the Nard ointment, but with more myrrh added; and therefore it warms more, and its virtues correspond to those of the Amaracine ointment and to the one made with saffron.

On the Ointment of Jasmine.          Chapter 63.

The Jasmine ointment is prepared in Persia from the flowers of white violets, of which two ounces are steeped in an Italian sextarius of sesame oil, exchanging the violets as was described for the lily ointment. The Persians use it at their banquets to produce a pleasant scent, for it is suited to the whole body, being rubbed on in baths, and wherever there is need to warm or soften. It has nonetheless a heavy scent, and for this reason many people do not use it willingly.

This chapter on the Jasmine ointment was not truly to be passed over in silence, as several others above have been; for in those there is nothing, and in this one there is something worth saying. First it is important to know that the word "Jasmine," translated from Greek (according to the opinion of the most learned men of our time), means nothing other than "violet-scented," and it does not seem to me that this can be denied, since — as Dioscorides writes — this ointment being made from white violets, it cannot reasonably be called anything other than a violet ointment, referring however to that kind of white violet which in Arabic is called Keiri, and not the common ones that grow almost everywhere along public roads in the countryside. But some modern authors, trusting in the sound of the word, truly believe that this ointment was made from those most fragrant flowers which we call Jasmines, an opinion shared by Ermolao Barbaro and Marcello Virgilio of Florence, who, in order to confirm his own interpretation, wishes that the ancients, and especially Dioscorides, had described the Jasmine together with this species of violet, and that Dioscorides had understood that species of violet to be the Jasmine, which he affirms to be found of a blue color. I cannot in any way agree with this opinion. For it is not to be supposed — I will not even say believed — that Dioscorides, who in his history of simples and in distinguishing one species from another was most diligent, could have so foolishly and without any distinction understood the Jasmine to be that species of blue violet, given that in its roots, stem, height, thickness, branches, leaves, and in many other parts the Jasmine is far removed from violets of any kind. And furthermore, even if one were to grant what Marcello says — though it ought not to be granted, as will be shown — that the Jasmine ointment is made from the flowers of the Jasmine, which he holds to be the blue violet, how can this be reconciled with Dioscorides himself affirming that the Jasmine ointment is composed of white violets? This is further demonstrated by Serapion, the greatest and most faithful imitator of Dioscorides, who shows that violets and Jasmines are two different things, since he wrote about them separately — Jasmines at chapter 176 and violets at chapter 220 — noting their virtues distinctly. One must therefore conclude that had he known that Dioscorides, Galen, and the others had understood the Jasmine under the chapter on violets, he would not have written about them so distinctly in two separate chapters. But being quite certain that the Greeks, and especially Dioscorides, never knew the Jasmine, he devoted a separate chapter to it solely on the authority of various Arab writers, affirming that they are found white, yellow, and blue. It must therefore be firmly believed that this fragrant plant, having been discovered by the Arabs, who seeing that its flowers and scent closely resembled the white violets, wished to imitate the Greek word and derived the name from violets — that is, "Iasmen" — even though in their own language they call it Zambac or Sambac. This shows that Gualthieri, the German of Strasbourg, is clearly mistaken in his new Dioscorides when he too holds that Dioscorides here meant the common Jasmine. But so that its virtues and properties may come to light — since no further mention of it will be made elsewhere in this book — it seems proper to recount here what Serapion wrote about it. The Jasmine is therefore warm in the beginning of the second degree, and is very well suited to humidity, salt phlegm, and to those of cold constitution

FIRST BOOK. 43

and for pains caused by thick and viscous humors. It is beneficial for skin eruptions and blemishes of the face, applied both dry and fresh. Its oil, which is called by the Arabic name Sambacino, is very useful in winter, even though in those of a warm constitution, smelling it often provokes nosebleeds. Some have been deceived by the similarity of the name, thinking that Sambacino oil and Sambucino oil are the same thing; among those so deceived was Giovanni da Vigo the surgeon, in his treatise on Simples, in the chapter on elderberry. However, it is not so long ago that Jasmines were brought to Italy, and even now both the white and the yellow varieties are commonly found in every garden.

On Myrrh. Chapter 64.

Myrrh is a liquid of a tree that grows in Arabia, similar to the Egyptian thorn-tree; from its wounds it drips down onto certain mats placed beneath it, although some of it also congeals around the trunk of the tree. There is found a variety that is very fatty, called Pediasimos, from which, when pressed, a liquid called stakte distills. Beyond this there is another even fattier kind called Gabirea, which grows in rich soils and exudes stakte most abundantly. The highest rank is held by that called Troglodytica, so named after the country where it grows. This is somewhat green in color, transparent, and sharp to the taste. There is also collected a small variety, which holds second place after the Troglodytica; this one, when handled, yields like bdellium, but exhales a heavier odor, and grows in open sunny places. There is yet another called Caucasian, entirely lacking in scent, black as if it had been roasted. The worst of all is that called Ergasima, musty, not fatty, sharp in taste, and in appearance and virtue similar to gum. The kind called Aminea is condemned. From all types pastilles are made: from the fatty kinds, rich and fragrant ones; from the dry kinds, dry and odorless ones. That Myrrh exhales more fragrance whose pastilles have not been mixed with oil. Myrrh is adulterated with gum soaked in water from its own infusion. Choose it fresh, brittle, light, uniform in color, and that which when broken shows some white, smooth veins resembling fingernails, small-grained, bitter, pungent, and fragrant. That which is very heavy and pitch-colored is worthless. It has the virtue of warming and binding; it promotes sleep, consolidates, and dries. It softens hardnesses and opens obstructions in the natural passages of women, and promotes menstruation and childbirth promptly when applied below with wormwood and an infusion of lupins, or with the juice of rue. It is swallowed in the amount of one bean for old coughs, tightness of breath, pain in the sides and chest, and for fluxes of the body and dysentery. It relieves the chills and shivering that precede fevers when taken in the same quantity with pepper and water two hours before the fever begins. Placed under the tongue and held there until it liquefies, it removes roughness of the throat and hoarseness of the voice. It kills worms in the body. It is chewed to sweeten the breath, and applied with liquid alum for the stench of the armpits; it stabilizes loose teeth and tightens the gums when the mouth is rinsed with wine and oil together; made into a plaster it heals wounds of the head, mends ruptures of the ears, and covers bare bones when applied with the flesh of snails. It is beneficial for ear discharges and their inflammations when introduced inside with castoreum, opium, and glaucium. It is used as an ointment for smallpox with honey and cassia. Applied as a plaster with vinegar it purges skin eruptions; rubbed on together with wine, laudanum, and myrtle oil it stops falling hair. It relieves old catarrhs when the nostrils are anointed with a feather. It fills ulcers of the eyes, removes white spots and likewise cloudiness, and polishes away roughness. The soot of Myrrh is made just as that of Frankincense and is useful for all the same purposes, as we shall teach hereafter. BOEOTIC Myrrh is the root of a tree of Boeotia. The best is that which breathes an odor similar to Myrrh, warms, softens, and resolves, and is usefully employed in fumigations.

The Myrrh which is today brought to us from Alexandria is very different from that which Dioscorides described among the species of the good kind. For the greater part, and indeed almost all of that which we have in common use in apothecary shops, lacks all those good qualities attributed to the best. For as one can plainly see, it is neither green, nor fatty, nor sharp, nor fragrant, nor uniform in color, nor filled with those smooth veins said to resemble human fingernails; and although one may detect in it a certain bitterness when tasting it, it is nevertheless not very notable. Wherefore

PRIMO. 45

pressed and passed through cold water in the manner of vermicelli, and they sell it calling it vermicular Styrax. The ignorant approve of this as the purest, not noticing the difference in the fragrance of its odor, since the pure kind breathes forth a very sharp odor. Styrax warms, softens, and ripens. It is useful for coughs, catarrhs, hoarseness, and difficulty breathing, and for lost voice. It is good for obstructions and hardnesses of women's natural parts. Taken by mouth, and applied externally, it promotes menstruation. It gently softens the body, removing a little with the resin of turpentine in the form of pills. It is used effectively in resolving plasters, and in those prepared for fatigue. When burned, it produces a soot, as is done with Incense, which is equally useful in every way as that. An oil is made from it in Syria, which they call Styracine oil, truly excellent for warming and softening. But it causes headache and heaviness of the head, and promotes sleep.

Styrax is commonly called in the apothecaries' shops Storax Calamite, which name was taken from the book of
C the Antidotes of Galen. For speaking of the Simples that enter into Theriaca, he praised as the best Styrax that which was brought from Pamphilia in canes, from which he took the name Calamite, and therefore, since that of this kind is the best to be found, it has always been the custom of physicians when ordering it to give it the name of Calamite, to show that they mean the best kind. For Galen in the same passage says that this kind of Styrax surpasses all other Styaces in quality as much as Falernian wine surpasses every other wine sold cheaply in taverns. From this reasoning, Manardo of Ferrara was induced to think that where in Dioscorides it reads Catabalite, the text has been corrupted, and that one should therefore read Calamite. But however learned Manardo may have been, I am nonetheless more pleased by the opinion of Marcello the Florentine, who holds that one should read Gabalite, not Catabalite. In testimony of which Pliny at chapter 25 of book 12, speaking of Styrax, says it grows in Syria nearest to Judea around Gabala Marathunta, and at Mount Cassius near Seleucia, with which judgment Hermolaus and Ruellius also agree. Pliny praised, beyond those already mentioned, that which comes from Sidon and Cyprus, condemning that which grows in Crete. Pliny gives the reason why Styrax is almost always powdery, saying that the cause is certain winged little worms that fly about during the dog-days and gnaw it and corrupt it, making it powdery; and according to what he says, it is also adulterated with cedar gum, gum arabic, honey, and bitter almonds, for which reason one must observe in this regard the qualities assigned by Dioscorides to the good kind. GALEN made mention of it in book 7 of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Styrax warms, softens, and digests, and therefore greatly helps coughs, catarrhs, flows of phlegm, and hoarsenesses, which they call corizze and bronchi. It promotes menstruation both drunk and applied. The soot of the burned kind is almost similar to that of incense.

On Bdellium. Chapter 66.

Bdellium is a liquid from a Saracen tree. That is praised which is bitter to the taste, and as transparent as hide glue, fatty within, which when handled becomes soft, that is not mixed with wood or other impurities, and which when burned breathes forth an odor similar to that of fragrant nails. There is brought from India a kind that is black and dirty, in rather large pieces, with the odor of aspalathus. There is also brought from Petra a castle another kind that is dry, stringy, and livid, which holds second place. It is counterfeited by mixing it with gum, but this is not so bitter to the taste nor does it breathe forth in perfumes so good an odor. Bdellium has the virtue of warming and softening. It resolves the goiter of the throat, hardnesses, and watery hernias, applied first with sage on an empty stomach. Applied and likewise used as a fumigant, it opens women's natural parts, and provokes birth, and all other humors. Drunk, it breaks stones and promotes urination. It is given usefully against coughs, and the bites of venomous animals. It is good for ruptures, spasms, pain in the side, and the wandering flatulences of the body. It is placed in most softening plasters, which are made for hardnesses and nodosities of the nerves. It is pounded and steeped in hot water, or in wine, and is thus dissolved.

Of the best and excellent Bdellium, to which Dioscorides gives the greatest praise, which is as transparent as hide glue,
Q which we call Carniccio, bitter, workable in handling, and which when burned breathes the odor of fragrant nails — if it still comes to us in our times in Italy, it is so rare that, as we said concerning Myrrh, it is kept only as a reference sample. Some believe that this common kind found in the apothecaries' shops is partly that black kind brought from India, and partly that dry, gummy kind that comes from Arabia. Which, if it were so, we might content ourselves with having at least the mediocre, since we are prevented from having the excellent. But in truth, to find it in the common kind, and pon-

BOOK ONE. 47

the breasts that become inflamed after childbirth. It is used in medicines for the windpipe and the internal organs of the body. Drunk for spitting blood, it is beneficial. But drunk in good health, it causes madness, and drunk in too large a quantity with wine, it kills. Incense is burned in a clean earthenware vessel, first lighting its grains with a lamp flame, and when it is well smoldering and burning, it is immediately covered with another vessel, until it goes out, so that it does not turn to ash. There are some who, to collect the soot when incense is burned, suspend over the little pot where it burns a hollow copper vessel, pierced in the middle, as we shall discuss further when speaking of the soot of incense. Some others put it in a raw earthenware vessel well sealed with clay, and then place it to calcine in the furnace. It is also burned in a new earthenware vessel over well-ignited coals, until it no longer bubbles, no greasiness remains, and it no longer smokes. That which is not burned is easily ground.

On the Bark of Incense. Chapter 68.

The best bark of incense is that which is fatty, fragrant, fresh, smooth, thick, and not cartilaginous. It is counterfeited with pine bark, or with the shells of its fruit, but fire reveals the deception. For when any other bark is burned as incense, it does not ignite but goes off in smoke without any odor. But the bark of incense burns and produces its smoke with a fragrance. It burns in the same way as incense itself, and has the same virtues. But it is more potent and more astringent, and therefore it is given to those who spit blood, and it is placed in pessaries for fluxes from women's natural passages. It is suitable for scars on the eyes and for hollow and foul ulcers. Burned, it effectively treats roughness of the eyelids.

On the Manna of Incense. Chapter 69.

The best manna of incense is that which is white, pure, and granular. It has the same virtues as incense, but is not so potent. It is counterfeited with sifted pine resin, with powder, and with ground incense bark. Fire is indeed the true test of this. For the counterfeit, when burned, does not produce an even smoke, but a sooty and impure one, and one can smell, mixed in with its pleasant scent, another disagreeable odor.

On the Soot of Incense. Chapter 70.

You shall collect the soot of incense thus. Take the grains of incense one by one with a small pair of tongs, light them at a lamp, and place them thus lit into a hollow new earthenware vessel, then cover it with a clean hollow copper vessel, pierced in the middle, placing between the one and the other vessel, on one side or on both sides, small stones four fingers high, so that one may more easily see inside whether the incense is burning, and so as to have enough open space to add more, and therefore before the first is entirely burned, add more, until you have made as much soot as you need. But you must continually go about with a sponge well soaked in cold water, wetting the rim of the lid. For by thus tempering the heat of the copper, the soot adheres to it more firmly; otherwise, being by its lightness liable to fall, it mixes with the ash of the incense burning below. Then sweep the soot from the lid and do the same again until you have as much as you wish. But each time, remove the ash of the burned incense. The soot of incense soothes inflammations of the eyes, prevents catarrhs that descend into them, cleanses ulcers, fills in cavities, and stops cankers. Those of myrrh, resin, storax, and every other sort of liquid substance are made in the same way, and are all universally good for the same ailments.

A [resin is applied] to the itching of the genital members. It is put into softening plasters, into poultices, and into ointments prepared for weariness; and applied and rubbed on by itself, it is good for pains of the sides.

Of Other Resins. Chapter 74.

The liquid resin that distills from the Pine and the Pitch-tree is brought from France and Tuscany, but in ancient times it was brought from Colophon in Asia, whence it took the name Colophonia. There is also brought from Galatia a liquid kind, which is near the Alps, extracted from the Larch, which the country people call Larigna. This, taken as a compound in an electuary, or by itself alone, is very effective against an old cough. Resins differ among themselves in color, for some are white, some the color of oil, and some of honey, as is the Larigna. The liquid resin from the Cypress also distills and is suitable for all the aforesaid purposes.
B Among the dry varieties there are those from the husks of Pines, from the Fir, from the Pitch-tree, and from the Pine. Among all of these, the best to choose is the one that is most fragrant, transparent, neither dry nor moist, brittle, and resembling wax. Those of the Pitch-tree and Fir surpass all others in excellence, for they smell like incense. The most praised come from Pitiusa, an island off the coast of Spain. Those of the Pine, from pine husks, and from the Cypress are less good and do not match the others in virtue; yet they are used nonetheless in their place. The resin of the Mastic-tree corresponds to that of the Terebinth. All liquid resins are cooked in a vessel that holds four times as much as the liquid placed in it; and so, having put in one congius of resin and two of rainwater, they are cooked over a moderate charcoal fire, always stirring, until their natural odor is lost and they become brittle and dry, so that rubbing them with the fingers they crumble easily. They are then stored cold in an uncoated earthen vessel. They are all made very white if first they are melted over a fire and strained from the dregs. They may also be burnt without boiling in water, over a slow fire until they begin to harden, and then many more coals are added, cooking them without any pause for three continuous days and three nights,
C until they become as described above, and then they are stored as said. The dry ones are cooked in a single day. Cooked resins are useful in fragrant plasters, in remedies for weariness, and for giving color to ointments. Soot is made from them in the same way as from incense, for use in liniments made for the adornment of the eyelashes, for erosions at the corners of the eyes, for the falling of eyelid hairs, and for the flow of tears. Ink for writing is also made from them.

R I find, according to what Theophrastus relates in the fifteenth chapter of the second book of his History of Plants, that among the species of Terebinth there is the male and the female. The male bears no fruit, and in this alone it differs from the female, of which two varieties are found: one produces red fruit, resembling lentils, which is truly indigestible food; and the other produces it green before ripening, then red as it ripens, and finally, when fully mature, black, the size of a bean, and it ripens when grapes ripen. Its outer bark is resinous and sulfurous. On Mount Ida and in Macedonia the Terebinths grow short, twisted, and branchy;
D but in Syria near Damascus they become large, spacious, and beautiful, where it is affirmed for certain that there is a very vast mountain filled with nothing but Terebinths. The wood is tough and pliant. Its roots are very firm and deep, and in all its parts it is solid and incorruptible. It produces a flower in form similar to the elm, but of red color; and its fronds, which are almost similar to those of the Laurel, proceed copiously along its small branches, in the way those of the Sorbus proceed, leaving finally one single one at the tip of the crest without a companion; yet they are less notched than those of the Sorbus, and similar in outline to those of the laurel, and as fat as the fruit. It also produces certain galls like walnuts, in which, as in those of the olive, small creatures like gnats gather together with a certain tenacious, resinous liquid; yet the resin is not collected from these, since it is drawn from the trunk of the tree. The fruit, although tenacious to handle, yields but little liquid. But if first the skin is removed, then everything sticks together; yet when washed, the unripe ones float and the black ones sink to the bottom. There grows in India a species which, though in every part similar to the other Terebinths, nonetheless produces fruit quite different from them, resembling almonds, but much more pleasant and agreeable to the taste; for which reason the inhabitants of those places eat it more willingly than almonds. The black Terebinth grows abundantly at Trento on the hill of Castel Trento, where it was first shown to me by

On the Oil of Pitch. Chapter 76.

B The Oil of Pitch is obtained by first separating all the watery part that floats on top,
as whey floats on milk, and then the pitch, placed suspended in wool, is cooked so as to receive
the vapor that exhales during boiling; when it is well soaked, the oil is pressed out
into a vessel. This is repeated until the pitch is cooked out. It has the same virtues
as liquid pitch. Anointed together with barley flour, it causes fallen hair to grow back.
Liquid pitch does the same. This also heals ulcers and the mange of four-footed animals.

On the Soot of Pitch. Chapter 77.

C The soot of liquid pitch is made in the following manner. The pitch is placed in a new
oil lamp that has its wick, and is then lit, and it is placed under an earthen vessel
that has a concave, rounded lid, made narrower at the top and perforated at the bottom,
as furnaces usually are. The pitch is left to burn this way, and as it is consumed more is added,
until sufficient soot has been produced. It has astringent and sharp properties, and is used in
ointments made for ornamenting the eyebrows, and for restoring hairs to bare eyelids. It is also
beneficial for weak, watery, and ulcerated eyes.

On Dry Pitch. Chapter 78.

Dry pitch, which some call Palimpissa, is made by cooking liquid pitch. It is found
in two varieties: one called Boscas, similar to mistletoe, and the other, which is dry.
The pure, fatty, fragrant, reddish, and resinous kind is praised, such as that of Lycia
and that of Calabria, both of which share the nature of pitch and resin. It warms,
softens hardnesses, ripens, resolves small abscesses and bread-like swellings. It refills ulcers,
and is used in medicaments for wounds.

D On Zopissa. Chapter 79.

Some call Zopissa the resin mixed with wax that is scraped and peeled off
ships, and by many it is called Apochima. This, because it has been steeped in sea salt,
has the virtue of resolving. There are also some who call Zopissa the resin
that drips and is gathered from the Pine.

Q Although Dioscorides wrote about several kinds of pitch, their oil, and their soot in various chapters,
nevertheless, since their histories are in themselves most clear, there is no need here to make any further particular explanation.
But since it may perhaps please some to learn how pitch is made, in order to fulfill my duty and their wishes,
I will briefly recount everything that I have sensibly observed in the Trentino, in the mountains of Rieme.
Those who make the pitch commonly called Nauale — the Pegolotti (as the masters of that craft are called) —
take old pine trees which have entirely become resinous heartwood, and cut them diligently into pieces, as one cuts other
wood to make charcoal, and having then built a floor raised somewhat in the middle, sloping evenly toward its
extremities —

FIRST BOOK. 57

its ends with tenacious clay, so that the liquid that drips from the wood may better descend into a channel that surrounds the whole mass; they then arrange with good craft into a round shape the whole cut Theda, following the same order observed in making charcoal. Once the structure is closed and covered, first wrapping the whole mass with well-leafed fir branches and pieces of wood, and then with earth so that no air can escape, they set it alight following the same order and manner used in burning charcoal. This causes the Theda, feeling the great heat of the fire and having no outlet for the flame, to melt and distill the Pitch into the bottom of the channel that surrounds it, whence it flows through other well-arranged channels into certain large vats made of thick planks, well positioned, where it is then loaded into barrels. One knows the work is finished when the mass collapses and stops yielding liquid. Concerning Pitch, GALEN wrote in book vii of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Dry pitch truly heats and dries in the second degree, though it may dry more than it heats. The liquid kind does entirely the opposite, that is, it heats more than it dries, and has in itself and in its parts something subtle, and therefore it is helpful to asthmatics and to those who spit phlegm. For this it suffices to swallow it by licking it together with honey in the measure of one cyathus. Beyond this, Pitches have the virtue of cleansing, ripening, and digesting; and in tasting them there is a slight bitterness and sharpness. Mixed with wax they remove scabby nails and extinguish flying ringworm. Applied in poultices they ripen all hard and raw swellings. In these respects the liquid kind is more potent than the dry. But though it is less good in such matters, it is nonetheless much more powerful in consolidating wounds. For these reasons it is truly clear that liquid Pitch contains within itself a warm moisture. Galen likewise wrote in book vii about the soot of Pitch, among other soots, saying thus: All soot is desiccative, and therefore is of earthy essence, retaining also some remnants of the fire that burned the material from which it was made, and thus it is entirely of earthy nature and fine parts. But if any special quality is found in soots, this derives from nothing other than the material from which they are made; for those made from sharper and hotter materials are likewise such themselves, and the same applies to those made from milder materials. Soot of incense is used primarily in medicines for the eyes, and is found most effective in those made for their inflammations, for the catarrhes that descend into them, and for the ulcerations that form in them, since it modifies and heals them. It is also used as an ornament for the eyelashes and eyelids. That which comes from turpentine and myrrh is pre-eminent for every ailment, no different from that of incense. But that of storax is more powerful and sharper, though still more so is that of liquid Pitch, and more than that is what is made from cedar resin. The sharper kinds are used for defects of the eyelashes and for erosions of the eye's corners, and likewise for tearing eyes, provided they are not inflamed; the milder kinds are used for all the aforementioned conditions, though they are used most in those ailments for which we said above the soot of incense is appropriate.

On Bitumen, or Asphalt. Chapter 80.

The Asphalt that is brought from Judea is considered the finest, and the most praised is that which shines with a deep purple color and has a strong odor. The black and dirty kind is disparaged. It is counterfeited with pitch. It is found in Phoenicia, in Sidon, in Babylon, and on the island of Zakynthos. A liquid form is also found in Sicily in the territory of Agrigento, where it floats upon certain springs, and the people there use it in place of oil for their lamps. Those who call it Sicilian oil are plainly mistaken, for it is nothing other than a kind of Bitumen.

On Pissasphalt. Chapter 81.

Pissasphalt originates in the territory of Apollonia in Epirus; carried down by rivers from the Ceraunian mountains, it is found gathered in lumps along the shores, with an odor mixed of pitch and bitumen.

On the Bitumen called Naphtha. Chapter 82.

The people of Babylon call Naphtha a bituminous liquid that is white, though a black variety is also found. It has such virtue and property of attracting fire to itself that even if fire is placed some distance away it leaps toward it. It is useful for cloudiness and suffusions of the eyes. It extinguishes all Bitumen inflammations, consolidates, dissolves, and softens. Applied, given as fumes, or smelled, it is useful for suffocations and relaxations of the womb. It reveals the falling sickness by giving the patients its fumes, just as the Gagate stone does. It is drunk usefully to bring on the menses with wine and castoreum. It is helpful for chronic coughs, for difficulties of breathing, for snakebite, for sciatica,

PRIMO. 59

to those far from Judea. For this reason I would not affirm that the common Mummy could canonically be used in place of Bitumen, because beyond the fact that genuine Bitumen is first mixed with Pitch, it is further mixed with the moisture and humor that continually seeps from the flesh of human bodies in their tombs. Which one must believe considerably diminishes its own proper and native nature. It would be better to follow Galen sooner, who in the Succedanea places liquid Pitch in place of Asphalt. Furthermore it is to be noted that although Serapion substitutes for Mummy the Pissasphalt of Dioscorides, he does so to commemorate it among its species, knowing certainly that the bodies of such material were embalmed in Syria, just as those are still embalmed today that afterward become the true Mummy of myrrh, aloe, and saffron, of which he made mention at the beginning of the chapter, saying thus: The Mummy of tombs is made of Myrrh, Aloe, and other things mixed with them, and of that moisture which seeps from human bodies. But is such a mixture not brought to Italy in our times? Because in Syria only nobles and the wealthy use such a mixture, as these are things of great value, and such persons have their tombs very well ordered and sealed, and thus Christian merchants who travel in that country cannot so easily steal the bodies from them, as they can with less difficulty take those of poor persons, whose bodies they fill with gold mixed with Pitch. This is true proof that genuine Mummy is not brought from Syria. For this reason those persons manifestly err who by Mummy understand the flesh of such dried bodies, and not their embalming mixture, as do some Apothecaries who pound the flesh and bones, and then put them into all the medicines that call for Mummy in their compositions. It would therefore be necessary for one who wished to have true Mummy to have the bodies of Christians who die in hospitals filled with that mixture of Aloe, Myrrh, and Saffron, and at the proper time to remove it afterward, because (as the Arabs write) Mummy has very many virtues. It is warm and dry in the second degree, is good for headaches caused by a cold cause without present matter. It helps migraine, paralysis, contortion of the mouth, epilepsy, and vertigo, drawing it up through the nose together with marjoram water. For earache it is worth one grain dissolved in oil of white violets or jasmine, and then infusing such liquid into the aching ears. Dissolved to the weight of one carat with a decoction of savory, it helps throat pains. Drunk with a decoction of jujubes, barley, and sebesten for three days it is useful for coughs. Taking one carat with mint water it is useful for heart ailments, and with water of cumin, ameos, and caraway for flatulence of the body. Take one carat with ten grains of Armenian bole and five of saffron together with solvent cassia for falls from a height onto the abdomen, and likewise for blows to the same and to the liver. For hiccups take one grain with a decoction of parsley seed and cumin. A nasal purge is made with musk, castoreum, camphor, and oil of ben for the ancient headache, and especially when it does not easily resolve with other remedies. It is gargled to the weight of one carat with honey vinegar for quinsy. It relieves pains of the spleen at one carat with caraway water, and taken internally with a decoction of martyr's thistle and asafoetida for deadly internal ulcers. For scorpion stings, drink one carat with pure wine, and apply it with fresh cow's butter to the sting. Mummy applied externally stops flows of blood, and drunk when blood comes from the inner parts, it is usefully employed for spitting of blood. It helps ulcers of the channel, of the penis, and of the bladder, and drunk in a carat of milk for those who cannot retain urine. It has been the opinion of many that the bones of dead persons drunk in powder are beneficial for various infirmities of the body, as is the case with Apollonius, and in many other places in the waters that spring spontaneously from the earth, where it is found floating on top, and while it sits on the water it is liquid. But when it is lifted out and dries it becomes harder than dry Pitch. The best is that which originates in that lake of lower Syria which they call the Dead Sea, whose properties have the power to warm and dry in the second degree, and therefore it is justifiably used to consolidate fresh wounds, and in all other cases that require some drying, with a degree of warmth.

Of the Cypress. Chapter 83.

The Cypress has cold and astringent virtue. Its fronds are drunk against fluxes descending to the bladder with raisin wine and a little myrrh, and likewise for retention of urine. With wine its berries are also drunk ground for spitting of blood, for bodily fluxes, dysentery, constriction of breath, asthma, and cough, and their decoction does the same. Ground with dried figs they soften hardnesses and heal polyps of the nose. Cooked in vinegar and ground with lupins they cause rough corns to fall off. Applied they consolidate intestinal hernias. The leaves have the same virtue. It is believed that mosquitoes are driven away by fumigating with the nuts of the Cypress and with the ci-

A He affirms that the plant is very similar to Savin. The priests of the Gauls used Selagine in ancient times against every misfortune and every defect of sight, making certain fumigations with it. But so great was the superstition of those times — which is still observed not a little in our own day — that they would never gather Selagine without first making sacrifice to their gods, and they valued it as worthless unless it was gathered with the right hand alone and with bare feet. Galen wrote of Savin in his sixth book on the faculties of simples, saying thus: Savin is among those things that powerfully dry out, and this for three qualities, which are demonstrated when one tastes it, similar to Cypress, except that this plant is more sharp and more aromatic. It thus partakes of the aforesaid qualities, namely sharpness situated in its warm temperament, and bitterness, and an astringent virtue lesser than that of Cypress, and therefore it is all the more digestive in proportion to how much the Cypress surpasses it in sharpness. This is why it cannot heal wounds, being hot and dry. For it partakes so much of both these qualities together that it causes inflammation. But in putrid ulcers it can be used like Cypress, and especially in malignant and stubborn ones of long standing, for these can tolerate it without any worsening, since it purges, when combined with honey, black and foul ulcers. It resolves carbuncles. Beyond this, through the great subtlety of its essence, it provokes menstruation more than almost anything else, and causes blood in the urine; it also kills the child in the womb and brings it forth when dead. Savin is hot and dry in the third degree, and is among those medicines that are most subtile in their parts. For this reason it is put into scented ointments, especially Gleucinum, and likewise into many antidotes. There are some who put two parts of Savin in medicines in place of Cinnamon. It is truly a medicine that, taken as a drink, can thin and likewise digest thick humors.

On the Cedar. Chapter LXXXVI.

The Cedar is a large tree from which resin is gathered, which they call Cedria. Its fruit is similar to that of the Juniper, but larger and rounder, like that of the Myrtle. The most praised liquor of Cedar is that which is thicker and transparent, of heavy odor, and which when dripped maintains its drops united together. This liquor has the virtue of corrupting living bodies and of preserving the dead, and therefore some called it the life of the dead. It corrupts clothing and hides on account of its excessive heat and dryness. It is useful for clarifying sight, for it removes scars and cloudiness from the eyes. It kills worms in the ears when dripped in with vinegar and with a decoction of Hyssop, and likewise removes ringing and buzzing sounds. Placed in the cavities of teeth it breaks them and relieves the pain. It does the same when one rinses the mouth with it and vinegar. Anointing the genitals with it before intercourse prevents conception; it is applied to inflammations of the throat and in cases of quinsy. It kills lice and likewise nits when applied. It is beneficial when applied with salt to the bite of the cerastes serpent, and is usefully drunk with sweet wine against the poison of the sea-hare. It is applied in cases of elephantiasis, and swallowed by licking with equal benefit. Drunk to the weight of a cyathus it purges and consolidates ulcers of the lungs. Applied in enemas it kills worms of the body and expels a dead fetus. From the liquor of Cedar an oil is made by suspending it over wool, as was said of that made from pitch; it is useful for everything that the same liquor is, but particularly it heals mange in dogs, oxen, and other quadrupeds. It kills their ticks and heals the wounds made by shearing them. Its fruits are called Cedrides, and are by their nature hot; they are harmful to the stomach and helpful for coughs, spasms, ruptures, and urinary distillations. Drunk with ground pepper they provoke menstruation, and with wine they counteract the poison of the sea-hare. Anointing the body with them together with deer fat, or with bone marrow, keeps serpents away. They are also put into antidotes. From the liquor of Cedar a soot is made in the manner of that from pitch, with the same virtues as that.

The Cedar, although it is a tree of notable height, nonetheless has few and shallow roots, not deep, but spread across the uppermost surface of the ground. It resembles the Juniper, for it too produces long, narrow, hard, and sharp-pointed leaves. The Cedar is very dense with branches, and its trunk is entirely knotted and full of cavities where the thickest of its branches joins the trunk. The inner pith is fragrant and reddish, as is that of the Larch. It produces fruit similar to that of the Juniper, but as large as that of the Myrtle, red, bright, fragrant, and good to eat. It ripens in autumn, but always before it ripens it produces new fruits, so that at that time both new and old fruits can be seen on the Cedar. The Cedar thrives in cold and rocky places and loves the mountains more than any other situation. It is always green and never loses its leaves in any season. It is among those plants that, when their top is cut off, die and never sprout again, as do the Cypresses, the Pines, the La-

Nor do I know of any bark among those that are aromatic, which we use in our apothecaries' shops, that could be conjectured to be the Macero. On the Elm. Chapter 93.

The leaves, the bark, and the branches of the Elm have astringent properties. The leaves, ground up and applied with vinegar, cure scabies and heal wounds. This is done even better by that thinner part of the inner bark, wound and wrapped around like a bandage, since it bends as easily as if it were leather. The thickest part of the bark, drunk at the weight of one ounce with wine or cold water, dissolves phlegm. The decoction of the leaves and likewise of the root bark, applied as a fomentation, quickly consolidates broken bones. The moisture found in the first budding leaves, in their little blisters, beautifies the skin and makes the complexion more brilliant. But as it dries it turns into certain tiny creatures almost similar to gnats. Some people cook the leaves in food, just as they cook other garden herbs.

Elm trees are very well known plants in Italy, and therefore there is no need to relate any further history here. But I will say that the liquid which forms in its blisters, beyond the virtues attributed to it by Dioscorides, is truly a most powerful remedy (as I myself have tested many times) for intestinal ruptures in small children, applied with linen cloths under the truss firmly fixed over the rupture. Galen made mention of the Elm in book 7 of On the Properties of Simples, saying thus: I have sometimes healed fresh wounds with the leaves of the Elm alone, relying on their astringent and binding virtue which they possess. The bark is more bitter and more astringent; for which reason it heals scabies when applied with vinegar, and besides this, bound fresh in the manner of a bandage over wounds, it can equally well close them. The roots have the same virtue, and therefore some make washes from their decoction to quickly form a callus where fractures are healed.

On Wood-Dust. Chapter 94.

The wood-dust gathered from old and decayed timbers and trunks, sprinkled like flour over ulcers, cleanses and consolidates them. Soaked first with anise in wine and applied on top with linen cloths, it arrests spreading ulcers.

The wood-dust from old and rotten timbers is truly not to be despised, since it possesses so great a virtue for healing and cleansing ulcers and likewise for arresting the malignant corrosive ones. It is all the more effective when gathered from the timber of trees which have the property of contracting and cleansing. This is clearly demonstrated by that (though little of it is found) which is gathered from Guaiacum wood, which is brought to us from India for the cure of the French disease; for it dries up and consolidates not only ordinary ulcers but those of the same French disease itself, and extinguishes with speed the condylomas of the member. Galen made mention of it, having particular attention also to the trees from which it is gathered, in book 7 of On Simples, saying thus: The dust of old timbers, and especially that which partakes of astringency and binding, such as the elm, cleanses and fills in moist ulcers.

On the Reed. Chapter 95.

Among the species of Reeds there is one called Nastos, from which arrows are made, and a female one, from which the tongues of pipes are made. Besides these there is another called Siringa, fleshy, ringed with strong nodes, suitable for writing. Another species grows near water, called by some Donace and by others Cipria. And there is also found another, thin and white, called Phragmite, and Vallatoria, well known to everyone. Its root, applied by itself alone, and likewise with bulbs, draws out thorns and arrow-heads from wounds, and with vinegar it eases dislocations and pains in the loins. Furthermore, its fresh green leaves, ground up and applied, cure erysipelas and other inflammations. The ash of its bark, smeared on with vinegar, cures alopecia. The down of its tassels, put into the ears, causes deafness. The one called Cipria produces the same effects.

On the Tamarisk, or Tamarigio. Chapter 97.

The Tamarisk is commonly known. It grows near marshes and still waters. It produces a mossy fruit, as does its flower. In Egypt and in Syria a domestic variety grows that is in every way similar to the wild, except that its fruit, which it produces resembling a gall, is unevenly astringent in taste. It is used in place of gall in medicines for the eyes and the mouth. It is given as a drink for spitting of blood, and likewise for stomach fluxes, for women's fluxes, for overflow of bile, and for the bites of those spiders called Phalangi. Applied as a poultice it disperses abscesses. Its bark has the same virtue as the fruit. Wine made from the decoction of the leaves, when drunk, reduces the spleen; and held in the mouth and used as a rinse, it relieves toothache. Sitting in its decoction stops women's fluxes, and rinsing with it kills lice and likewise nits. The ash of the wood, applied, stops women's fluxes. Cups are made from the wood of the Tamarisk for the use of those who suffer from ailments of the spleen, for it is believed that it greatly benefits them.

The domestic Tamarisk does not grow, as far as I know, in Italy as it does in Egypt and Syria; and if it is found in some garden as a domestic variety, it is nothing other than a wild plant transplanted into a domestic setting, as is clearly shown by its fruit and flower, which it produces entirely similar to the wild, and not similar to a gall, as is the case with the domestic variety. I recall having rested many times in the summer in the shade of a plant of remarkable height, along the bank of the Tiber in a garden of the Hospital of Santo Spirito in Rome, which, although it was kept as a domestic plant, nonetheless produced fruit and flower similar to the wild, of which throughout all of Italy an abundance is found along running rivers. For which reason I could not help but marvel at Dioscorides, who says that the Tamarisk grows only near marshes and ponds; for we see in Italy quite the opposite to be the case. This has many times led me to believe either that the text of Dioscorides is corrupt, or that in Greece it grows differently than in Italy, near marshes and ponds. Columella reports that water kept in channels made from the trunk of the Tamarisk, when pigs are allowed to drink from it, cures them of the ailment of the spleen, which they contract during great dry spells by eating too greedily the fruits of trees that fall to the ground when dried out by the drought. The ash of the Tamarisk (as Serapion recounts) powerfully desiccates all ulcers, and especially those caused by burns. The leaves together with the whole plant applied as a fomentation dissolve cold abscesses. Two women were cured of leprosy (as the Arab Alcanzi testifies) by the long use of drinking the decoction of the roots of the Tamarisk with raisins. This has many times led me to believe that in cases of the French disease it could easily take the place of the Indian wood. For some time it used to be sold in place of fragrant Cassia. But once this fraud was discovered, the trickery was abandoned. Galen makes mention of the Tamarisk at the end of the seventh book of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, speaking thus: the Tamarisk is cleansing and incisive, and without having too much apparent desiccating power, it has somewhat of an astringent virtue; by reason of which faculties and qualities it benefits the hardness of the spleen, by cooking the root or the leaves or the outermost small branches in vinegar or in wine. It also heals toothache. The fruit and the bark have not a little of the astringent quality, so that they are almost equal to unripe galls, but in galls there is a manifest harshness, whereas in the fruit of the Tamarisk there is an uneven temperature; for it is mixed with its natural refined subtlety of parts and cleansing virtue. This is truly not found in galls; nonetheless, where galls are not to be found, it is permitted to use the fruit of the Tamarisk in their place, and likewise the bark. Beyond this, the ash of the burned plant is powerfully desiccating and cleansing, though only slightly astringent.

On the Erica. Chapter 98.

The Erica is a small branchy shrub similar to the Tamarisk, but much smaller. The honey made by bees that feed on its flower is considered bad. Its leaves, and likewise its flowers, applied as a poultice, heal the bites of Serpents.

The Erica is a small tree native to Asia and Greece; and according to writers it flowers twice a year, and it is therefore said that of all wild plants the Erica is both the first and the last to flower. Writing of it, Pliny in the ninth chapter of the twenty-fourth book says that the Erica resembles rosemary both in color and in its leaves.
But that it is found in Italy I dare not affirm, although Hermolao says that it grows in the mountains of Padua, and

Of the plant that Ermolao intends, all the mountains of Trentino are still full. But truly it does not seem to me to correspond to it very well. On Acacalide. Chapter 99.

The Acacalide is a seed of a small Egyptian tree, almost similar to that of the tamarisk, whose infusion is used in collyria made to clarify the sight.
The Acacalide, as far as I have been able to investigate, I do not truly believe is brought into Italy; because I have found no seed among those brought here from other countries that resembles it in any way.

B On the Rhamnus. Chapter 100.

The Rhamnus is a small shrub that grows in hedges, and produces its branches straight and thorny, with thorns similar to those of the sharp thorn. It produces small leaves, tender, somewhat long, and a little fleshy. Besides this there is another species of whiter color, and likewise a third species that produces darker leaves, somewhat reddish. It produces branches about five cubits long, and although they are much thornier, nonetheless its thorns are not very firm nor very sharp. Its fruit is broad, white, thin, in the shape of a follicle, like a spindle-whorl. The leaves of all these species, applied as a liniment, are beneficial for erysipelas and for creeping ulcers. It is said that if its branches are placed at doorways and windows of houses, evil spells are driven away.

The Rhamnus, both white and black, is most abundantly found throughout Tuscany precisely in hedges, and especially the white, and both are commonly called marruche; and the true white one is that which produces thorns similar to the sharp thorn, with long, olive-colored, smooth, and fleshy leaves; and the black one, as Dioscorides says, grows to about five cubits in height, has weaker thorns, and produces a follicular, thin, round fruit similar to a spindle-whorl used by women for spinning. It therefore seems to me that Ruellio greatly errs here, believing the Rhamnus to be what we in Italy commonly call Spino merlo, and in Lombardy Spino cervino; because that shrub produces leaves nearly as broad as a pear tree, and bears its fruit as black berries, like those of privet, which painters and miniaturists use to make a very beautiful green, having nothing to do with any Rhamnus. Ruellio likewise errs in citing Theophrastus in this passage, because he unwittingly attributes to the fruit of the Rhamnus everything that Theophrastus immediately after writing of the Rhamnus wrote about the Paliurus. Galen mentions the Rhamnus in Book VIII of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The Rhamnus dries and digests in the second degree, and cools at the end of the first or beginning of the second degree, and therefore it heals erysipelas and herpes, that is, those that are not excessively hot. For this reason one should use the leaves when they are tender.

On the Alimus. Chapter 101.

D The Alimus is a small shrub that grows in hedges, similar to the Rhamnus but without thorns. It produces leaves similar to the olive but broader. It grows in coastal marshes. Its leaves are cooked like other herbs in food. The root drunk with honeyed water at the weight of one dram is good for bodily pains, for spasms, for ruptures, and increases milk in women's breasts.
