On the Dog Briar. Chapter 104.

The Dog Briar is a shrub that grows into a tree considerably larger than the Briar, whose leaves are much broader than those of the myrtle. Around its branches it has firm, stout thorns. It produces a white flower, and a somewhat elongated fruit, resembling the pit of an olive, which as it ripens turns red, and has inside a certain down. The fruit, dried and cooked in wine, and the decoction drunk, stops fluxes of the body: but one must first remove that down of its, because it harms the windpipe of the lung.

I It does not seem to me that the Dog Briar is truly that species of wild rose which produces flowers rather similar to those roses called Musk roses, and fruit similar to that of the rose-bush, as some believe; for it would have sufficed to tell Dioscorides that it resembled the rose-bush, without saying that it grew into a tree much larger than the Briar, and that its leaves were similar to those of the myrtle, from which this wild Rosaio differs greatly, and the fruits are truly much larger than olive pits. In this belief I have since been confirmed by Pliny; for he calls the wild rose-bush particularly Cynorhodon, that is Dog Rose; praising its root wonderfully for the bite of rabid dogs in book 8, chapter 41, and likewise in book 25, chapter 2, where he says that the ancients understood by Dog Rose only those sponges that grow on it; and then writing of the Cynosbatos, that is Dog Briar, he made it into two species very different from the wild rose-bush, as one sees in chapter 24 of book 24, saying that one species has leaves like the sole of a man's foot, and the other like those of the caper. I am further moved, beyond this, by the history written of it by Theophrastus in chapter 17 of book 3, saying thus: The Dog Briar produces red fruit similar to the Pomegranate, and in size is midway between the shrubs and the Pomegranate tree. Its leaves are similar to those of the Vitex. Which shows there is no small difference between the Dog Briar and the wild Roses, of which he later wrote a particular history in chapter 6 of the sixth book, having first spoken at length of the domestic ones, saying thus: The small trees of the wild roses have branches and leaves rougher and more coarse than the domestic ones, and the flowers less colorful and less fragrant, and they are not as large as the domestic ones. Which shows that the wild rose-bush, which they call Cynorhodon, is one thing, and the Dog Briar, called by the Greeks Cynosbatos, is another; and therefore Marcello Vergilio of Florence is manifestly wrong in believing them to be one and the same thing, not perceiving how differently one writes from the other, his most familiar Pliny. To which point the venerable Fathers who have commented on the antidotary of Mesue, not having paid attention, say erroneously that the wild Roses are that plant which the Greeks call Cynosbatos. GALEN wrote of it in book 7 on the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The fruit of this plant is somewhat astringent, but the leaves moderately so, and therefore its particular use is known to everyone. One must truly beware of that which has inside a kind of wool, which harms the windpipe of the lung.

On the Privet. Chapter 105.

The Privet is a tree that produces around its branches leaves similar to those of the olive, but broader, more tender, and greener, and white flowers, mossy and fragrant. Its fruit is black, similar to that of the elderberry. The finest grows in Ascalon and in Canopus. The leaves are astringent, and therefore when chewed they help ulcers of the mouth, and when used as a poultice they help carbuncles and the most violent inflammations. The decoction applied to burns from fire is useful. Ground and infused in the juice of the herb lanaria, they make the hair red. The flower, ground and applied with vinegar to the forehead, eases headache. The Ligustinum ointment mixed with warm things warms and softens the nerves.

We in Tuscany call the Privet Giustrico; others call it Olivetta, others Oluella, and others Chambrosene.
The Arabs call it Alcanna. It grows abundantly along hedgerows beside the public roads throughout Italy, and flowers at the end of Spring and the beginning of Summer. Some believe the Privet to be a certain species of bindweed, which winds itself along hedges around the shrubs, producing its white flowers similar to Bellflowers. In this opinion Servius the grammarian, commentator of Virgil, let himself be carried away, being little truly curious to learn its true history from Pliny or another authentic author. Others have believed the Privet to be the Caprifolium of the Arabs, which is the Ptxiacantha of Dioscorides, and not the Peryclimenum, as Ruellius thinks; but these too have been greatly mistaken. Galen wrote of it in book 7 on the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Of the Privet the leaves and the tender tips are used, and they are of a mixed nature both in their faculties and in their qualities. For they have something digestive together with a watery substance, somewhat warm, and they have something astringent from a cold and earthy substance. For which reason some make a bath of their decoction for burns from fire, and beyond this use it also against many fiery inflammations, and likewise against carbuncles. For they dry without any irritation or sharpness. They are likewise useful when chewed for ulcers that arise on their own in the mouth.

On the Phillirea. Chapter 106.

The Phillirea is a tree the size of the Privet, and its leaves are similar to those of the olive, though broader and darker; its fruit resembles that of the Lentisk, being black, sweetish, and growing in clusters. It grows in rough places. Its leaves are astringent and as useful as those of the wild olive where there is need of binding. Chewed, they are good for ulcers of the mouth, or used as a wash with their decoction. Drunk, they provoke urine, and likewise the menses.

All the modern interpreters of Dioscorides — namely Hermolaus, Ruellius, and Marcello Fiorentino — have believed that the Phillirea described by Dioscorides is truly the tree called Tilia, being deceived by the similarity of the name, since in Greek the Tilia is called Phillira, and not Phillirea. None of these so-called learned men, following one another's footsteps, having discerned this, called the Phillirea "Tilia" in their Latin interpretations. This led many to believe that Dioscorides did not know the Phillirea, since in every respect the Phillirea differs from the Tilia. This shows that these interpreters, besides having erred in translation, did not know what the true Tilia is; for had they had knowledge of it, they would easily have recognized their manifest error. Theophrastus wrote of the Phillira — that is, the true Tilia — in the tenth chapter of the fourth book, saying thus: Among the species of the Tilia, the male and female differ from each other in material, form, and in bearing or not bearing fruit. The wood of the male is hard, knotty, and yellow; the contrary is true of the female, which is white. The bark of the male is thicker, smoother, and harder, and therefore less flexible and tractable than that of the female. The male is sterile, while the female produces abundance of both flowers and fruits. The flower, enclosed in its bud, hangs besides the small stalk of the leaf produced for its support, fastened by another small stalk. It remains green while still closed, but upon opening turns somewhat yellow. The Tilia flowers together with the cultivated trees, and bears a round fruit, somewhat elongated, about the size of a bean, divided by five prominent ribs, inside which is a tiny seed resembling that of the Orache. The leaves are similar to those of Ivy, but more rounded near the stalk and pointed from the middle onward. They are slightly curled at the edges, all notched, and sweet and satisfying to the taste, and therefore much sought after by livestock for grazing. The contrary is seen in the fruit, which is never eaten by any animal. The trunk has little pith and is slightly softer than its wood, since the rest of the wood is soft and sweet. All these features Theophrastus gave for the Tilia, and they are found fully realized in our Tilia. But in my judgment they are not found in the Phillirea of Dioscorides, since the latter bears leaves like the olive, and the former like the Ivy. The Phillirea bears fruit like the Lentisk — a small, reddish berry resembling millet — while the Tilia produces a fruit the size of a bean, green and divided into sections by five ribs, with a seed inside similar to that of the Orache. This clearly demonstrates the difference between them. Furthermore, the height of our common Tilia and the breadth occupied by its dense branches confirms this, since the Phillirea of Dioscorides is a small shrub resembling the Privet. And if Pliny says that the Tilia is a rather low tree, while our experience shows the contrary, one must think that he was deceived by the similarity of the word into confusing the text of Theophrastus — from whom he drew the history — with that of Dioscorides. This leads me further to believe, seeing that he assigns to a single species — namely our common one — in chapter eight of book twenty-four, the virtues that Dioscorides attributes to the Phillirea, besides many others proper to it, as Ruellius has since done following him. The Phillirea then is a tree very different from the Tilia, but is not known in Italy in our times. The bark of the true Tilia, chewed and then applied as a plaster, consolidates fresh wounds; its leaves, ground up, resolve swellings of the feet; and the liquid that drips from it when it is cut to the pith causes hair to grow again and prevents the rest from falling out.

On the Cistus. Chapter 107.

The Cistus, which some call Citharus or Cissarus, grows in rocky places, and is a branchy, leafy shrub, not very large. It produces round, rough, and hairy leaves. The male bears flowers resembling those of the pomegranate, and the female bears white flowers. It has astringent virtue, and therefore its flowers, first ground and then drunk twice a day in harsh wine, are good in dysenteric fluxes. Applied as a liniment they stop creeping ulcers, and mixed with wax they help burns from fire and old ulcers.

Three distinct varieties are found, of three different colors: red, green, and white. Its juice is extracted as from the acacia. Some, having taken the dry Hypocistis and ground it, infuse it...

For without the true Hypocistis one cannot compound the Theriac, nor many other medicines necessary for daily use. What is commonly in use is truly a counterfeit mixture, made from the thickened juice dried in the Sun of that root which we in Tuscany call Safsfrica, or Barba di becco, and which Dioscorides calls Tragopogon, and this manifest error has arisen because the Arabs call the Cistus "barba di becco," and from this it comes that those who make the common Hypocistis in the apothecary shops, believing that the above-mentioned barba di becco is what the Arabs mean, press out its juice and then condense it in the Sun, and so they deceive themselves, and then all those who use it, in place of which it would be far less harmful to use Acacia, if only that too were brought to us pure. Galen made mention of the Cistus in book seven of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The Cistus, or Cistarus, is a small shrub, and in taste and in all its particular operations it is astringent; nonetheless its leaves and tender shoots, when pounded and applied, are so drying and astringent that they can consolidate wounds quite well. Their virtue is truly not a little astringent, so that they may be placed in the second order. The Cistus is not so cold as to lack a certain gentle warmth. That which is called Hypocistis is much more astringent than the leaves, and is therefore a most valuable remedy for all fluxes, such as spitting of blood, women's menstrual flows, stomach ailments, and dysentery. It strengthens and fortifies all the members of the body weakened by excessive moisture, and therefore he usefully puts it in stomach and liver epithymes, and it is placed in the Theriac for no other reason than to fortify and strengthen the body.

Ladanum is commonly called, by some Laudano, and by others Odano, of which, although much counterfeit, sophisticated, and of little value is to be found, I have nonetheless always found the finest quality in Venice at several perfumers, and especially at the perfume shop of the Moro on the Rialto bridge. The roses that belong to Medicine are of several kinds; but those most common in Italy are the red ones,
L the incarnate, and the white. The red are held to be the most excellent, and after these the incarnate, and therefore the white ones common among us are considered the least good, not counting among these that kind of very fragrant white roses which in Tuscany are properly called Damaschine, and in other places Moschette; for these are
C the most laxative of all, and the most fragrant. Roses are composed of diverse substances, which is why they contain, according to their more superficial and more intrinsic parts, diverse temperaments. They have primarily from their earthy and watery parts, which they possess moderately, substance and astringency. From the airy parts somewhat sweetness and aroma, and from those following the nature of fire, warmth and subtlety, bitterness, and the red color in those that are red. In the fresh ones the bitterness overcomes the astringency, and therefore because the first laxative action, which the ancient Greeks did not recognize, proceeds from the bitterness; the fresh ones loosen the body, and not the dried ones. The excellent juice for compounding various medicines is made from the roses, and also from the incarnate ones, although it is not so useful. The infusions made for the laxative rose syrup are made mostly from the incarnate ones; but better and more laxative are the Moschette, which we call Damaschine, when one can obtain a supply; for if one eats twenty or twenty-five of their most fragrant petals before meals, they comfortably loosen the body without any discomfort. The juice of roses is aperitive, resolvent, cleansing, and laxative, and therefore it purges bile and cleanses the blood of it. It is good for overflow of bile, and for obstructions of the stomach and liver. It comforts the heart, helps its trembling, and drives out the humors that cause it. It is good for bilious fevers, such as tertian fevers of all kinds. Modern physicians count among the blessed medicines the infusion of roses, from which the laxative syrup is made; for without discomfort and without any detriment to nature it loosens the body and purges bile. White roses common among us (I do not mean the Damaschine Moschette) are used for nothing other than making water; for in these there is not that lively laxative virtue as in the red ones and the incarnate ones, and therefore it seems to me that Manardo of Ferrara is wrong to criticize Mesue in this matter; for although in the Moschette, which are white, more laxative virtue is found than in all the others, nevertheless one must think that Mesue did not mean these, as something unknown to him, but only the common ordinary white ones, which is easily verified by our knowledge that the Moschette are new in Italy, nor is it found that they were known to the ancients. Roses are truly to be esteemed and held dear, not only for the ornament of gardens, and for the joyful spectacle they present in Spring, but much more for the great usefulness they have with various and diverse medicines important to human life. Wild roses are considerably more astringent and constringent than the domestic ones, but less fragrant, nor is any laxative virtue found in them, as Theophrastus noted at chapter 6 of book 6. On the Willow. Chapter 116.

The Willow is a common tree, whose leaves, seed, bark, and sap all have astringent properties. The leaves ground and drunk with a little wine and pepper help with pains in the sides, and taken alone with water they prevent women from conceiving. The seed drunk stanches the spitting of blood. The bark does the same. Its ash macerated in vinegar cures warts and calluses when applied as a poultice. The juice of the leaves and bark cooked with rose oil in a pomegranate rind helps with earaches. A decoction of both is useful as a fomentation for gout, and
D it cleanses dandruff. The sap is collected by cutting into the bark when the tree produces its flower, and it is later found congealed in the cuts; it is useful for all impediments that cloud the sight.

Although Dioscorides treated the Willow under only one kind, there are nonetheless (as we learn from Theophrastus in book 3, chapter 13, and from Pliny in book 16, chapter 37) willows of many and diverse kinds, such as those throughout Lombardy from which poles and stakes for vineyards are made; those of fine yellow color that are split to make barrel hoops; those from which coarse baskets for farm use are made; and those which are the finest of all, called in Tuscany Venchi, from which baskets are woven. Three kinds of sap from the Willow are described by Pliny, although Dioscorides mentioned only one: the first exudes by itself from the trunk like gum, the second comes from cutting the bark, and the third drips from the trunks when the branches are cut in autumn. No one has described its white foam, which after flowering can be seen hanging in large tufts from its small branches, and is then carried through the air by the wind like feathers. The Willow is a tree that never ages, and from its wood, which is very tough, strong, and light, shields and bucklers are made.

Since olive trees, olives, olive oil, olive gum, and olive lees are all one and the same plant and its fruits, it did not seem to me out of place to write about them all together, and thus satisfy the needs of each subject. Wild olive trees grow in the countryside around Siena, and in various other places in Tuscany very abundantly, and are much smaller than the cultivated ones, thorny, and with shorter leaves. Their olives, of which enormous quantities are gathered, are much smaller than the cultivated ones, but in taste far more flavorful. The thrushes, blackbirds, and starlings bear clear witness to this, since they eagerly prefer the wild ones to the cultivated. Our countrymen who delight in fowling carefully watch these wild olives for birds with great skill, until all the cultivated olives have been fully harvested; and thereafter with birdlime they catch an infinite number of blackbirds and thrushes throughout the entire month of December and January. There are few in Tuscany who gather the wild olives to make oil, because the abundance of the cultivated kind means the wild ones are little valued. I find recorded among the ancients ten varieties of olive: namely the Pausiae, Algianae, Licinianae, Sergiae, Netiae, Calminae, Orchiae, Regiae, Circitae, and Murteae. Although Virgil wrote of only three varieties, so too in our own time no more than three kinds are seen in Tuscany, especially around Siena. Of these, those of the first kind, though they come from the smallest trees, are nevertheless beautiful and of notable size, similar to those of Bologna. They are eaten pickled in brine in foods; for making oil they are entirely useless. The second kind, beautiful in size and color (though considerably smaller than the first), are the best for making oil, producing it golden, sweet, clear, and of the most excellent flavor. The olive trees that bear them are commonly called "olivastre," and are trees of the greatest height, with their branches spreading widely. The third kind are those common throughout all Italy. The finest ones preserved in brine are sent to Rome and to other places in Italy and Spain, where the most lavish tables are to be found. Between the olive and the oak there is (according to the ancient writers) a mortal enmity, so that when olive trees are planted near oaks they soon perish. Olive trees become sterile when browsed by goats during their first sprouting, for which no remedy has been found. But if for any other reason olive trees fail to bear fruit, a proven and effective remedy is to uncover their roots throughout the entire winter season. The gum of the wild, or Ethiopian, olive, although it is useful for many things, is nonetheless in our times not in use in apothecaries, nor do I know that it is gathered. Some have supposed (as we said above in the chapter on Acacia) that it is the Gum Arabic used in apothecaries, and others that it is Elemi gum. But it is truly shown that the gum of the Ethiopian olive is neither Elemi nor Arabic gum, since none of the latter two are found to be sharp and ulcerative to the taste; and because what we commonly call Elemi gum in apothecaries is rather a resin, or liquid produced from some tree unknown to us, perhaps similar to the pine, fir, or spruce, rather than any sort of gum. For at fire, just as other resins do, it immediately melts and becomes entirely liquid like wax, which no kind of true gum does. Although we do not have in our own time any certainty as to which plant Elemi gum comes from, nevertheless, from what the physicians of our time have experienced, and especially surgeons, it is the most excellent of all kinds of resins for healing wounds of the head. Of the great usefulness of olive lees there remains nothing more to say, except that as Cato writes, it is useful to mix it with lime for coating warehouses and shops for cloth and silk fabrics; because it keeps away spiders, moths, and other small worms and harmful creatures, and moreover the moisture that seeps from walls.

The domestic ones shell easily, and the most prized of these are those called Marroni, being much larger and much finer than the others. In the mountains where little grain is grown, they are dried on racks over smoke, then shelled and made into flour, which admirably serves in place of bread. The trees are useful for building houses, for making beams, joists, planks, staves, and barrel hoops. But as firewood they are entirely useless. Chestnut trees love the mountains far more than the plains, because by their nature they enjoy the cold, and for this reason they are seen to thrive much more to the north and in shaded places than elsewhere. Chestnuts, especially the dried ones, powerfully stop fluxes of the stomach and of the body, and are good for spitting of blood. Ground with honey and salt they are usefully applied to the bite of a mad dog. They dissolve hardnesses of the breasts when plastered on with vinegar and barley flour. They provoke lust because they are very flatulent. Eaten abundantly at meals they cause headache, generate wind, constipate the body, and are hard to digest. But those roasted under the ashes are much less harmful when eaten afterwards with pepper and salt, or with sugar.

On Galls. Chapter 134.

The gall is the fruit of the Oak, of which there are two kinds: one called Omphacite, small but rough, knotted like the joints of fingers, firm and not pierced; and the other smooth, light, and pierced. The Omphacite is praised as the better, because it is the more efficacious. Both have a strongly astringent virtue. Ground to powder they dissolve superfluities of the flesh, stop fluxes of the gums and uvula, and heal ulcers of the mouth. Their kernel placed in the cavities of teeth relieves toothache. Burned on coals until thoroughly ignited, then quenched with wine, or vinegar, or sour brine, they stop bleeding. Sitting in their decoction is an efficacious remedy for repositioning a prolapsed womb and stopping its fluxes. Steeped in vinegar or water they turn the hair black. Applied ground with wine, or water, in the form of a liniment, or drunk, they benefit dysenteric and stomach fluxes. These should be mixed with foods, or cooked whole in water, together with some other suitable thing for similar ailments. In sum, the Galls are to be used for binding and drying wherever needed.

Galls are very well known and common, and are produced, as Pliny says, by all plants that produce acorns. They grow when the Sun leaves the sign of Gemini; and when touched by too much heat, they dry out and become hollow. The oak trees produce them in addition to acorns, in larger and smaller forms called Omphaciti. The larger ones possess this particular virtue, that each year with their fruiting they foretell the goodness or badness of the coming year; for if, when those gathered in March that are dry and not pierced are broken open, flies are found inside, it signifies abundance; spiders, famine; and worms, mortality. Let no one marvel that these animals are born from galls, for I myself have seen it many very many times, and few, or almost none, can be found that are not pierced and from which the animal born inside has not already emerged, but that are found pregnant with one of these three animals; and therefore one may say that the Oak produces both fruit and animal. Knowing this, our ancient fathers not without reason said that the Oak was sacred to Jove. Galen wrote of Galls in book seven of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The Gall called Omphacite is a notably acrid medicine, and for the most part earthy and cold, by which it dries and represses fluxes, and moreover binds and brings together all relaxed and languid members, and powerfully resists all fluxes. For which reason one may say it is dry in the third degree and cold in the second. But the other, which is large, pale, and light, is also desiccative, but so much less than the other as it partakes less of that acrid quality, and therefore cooked by itself and applied as a plaster it is a not inconsiderable medicine for inflammations and relaxations of the anus. It is cooked where there is need to bind only a little in water, and where much, in wine. And it grows so much the stronger as the wine is more austere. Moreover, galls that are burned acquire the virtue of stopping blood, from which they take on warmth and sharpness, and therefore are more subtle and more desiccative than the raw ones. Wishing therefore to use them...

FIRST BOOK. 91

that you prepare to stanch blood, place them in the fire of live coals, and when they are thoroughly heated, quench them in water or vinegar.

On Rhu. Chapter 125.

The Rhu, which is placed on food and called Erithro by some, is a seed of a small tree good for tanning leather, so called because those who tan leather use it to thicken the hides. This small tree grows among rocks to the height of two cubits. Its leaves are rather long, reddish, and toothed all around. It produces a clustered fruit, dense, of the size of that of the Terebinth, but somewhat flattened, whose bark is very useful. Its leaves have an astringent property and produce all the effects of Acacia. Their decoction makes hair black, and it is used for dysentery in clysters, in baths for sitting in, and in beverages. It is instilled into ears that are moist. The leaves applied with honey or with vinegar cure cracked skin and pterygium of the fingers. The decoction of dried leaves, pressed out and then boiled down to the consistency of honey, is worth as much as lye. The seed produces the same effects. It is conveniently put into the food of those who suffer from dysenteric or stomach fluxes. Applied in liniments with water it prevents inflammations and abscesses, in fractures of bones, in bruises from blows, and in abrasions. It removes roughness of the tongue when rubbed on with honey. It stanches white discharges in women, and cures hemorrhoids when applied with powdered oak charcoal. The water in which this seed has first been steeped, then cooked and concentrated, is more efficacious than the seed itself. This small tree produces a gum which, placed in the hollow of aching teeth, relieves the pain.

The Rhu of the Greeks is so called, and according to Pliny in book eleven, chapter twenty-four, it has no name in Latin, but is commonly known in apothecary shops as Somacho, a word drawn from the Arabs, as are very many of the other names already mentioned above. For Serapion and all other Arab writers call the Rhu Sumach. The ancients used Rhu in place of salt as a seasoning for their food, and therefore Dioscorides at the beginning of the chapter calls it Rhu, which is placed on food. This custom is observed, as far as I have heard to this day, in Syria and in Egypt, where the finest Rhu grows. It also grows in Italy in many places in the Apennines with all the characteristics that Dioscorides assigns to it. The hides of those excellent Cordovan leathers are tanned with its leaves, which are called Somachi after the name of these leaves, by which they are thickened and curried. Pietro Crinito of Florence thought, as one reads in chapter seven of his book on honorable learning, that the Rhu, which in Cornelius Celsus is also written as Rhos Syriacus, was Manna, thinking that Rhos meant dew, since Manna is nothing other than dew. For this error he was sharply rebuked by Manardo of Ferrara, as may be fully read and seen in his Epistles, in the fifth of the first book addressed to the same Crinito. Ruellio, not knowing what the Fluida of Theophrastus was, which he wrote about in chapter eighteen of the History of Plants, thought that Theophrastus had written of Somacho under that name, not realizing that the Fluida of Theophrastus is none other than the plant from whose roots mistletoe is made, which Ruellio calls Lantana, as it is commonly called in many parts of Italy. Galen wrote of Rhu in book seven of the Properties of Simples, saying thus: The Rhu plant, which is branching, has astringent and desiccant properties, and therefore tanners use it to tighten and dry out hides, from which effect it is called the leather-plant. Besides this, its fruits are primarily used by physicians, and its juice, which is truly very austere, and therefore this medicine is among those that dry in the third degree and cool in the second.

On the Palm and on Dates. Chapter 126.

The Palm grows in Egypt, and its usual time for bearing fruit is somewhat before Autumn, when it ripens. It resembles the Mirabolano of Arabia, and is called a fruit, green in color and with the scent of quince. But when it is left to ripen fully there it is called Phenicobalano. That which is gathered half-ripe is unripe and astringent, and therefore it is drunk in austere wine for fluxes of the body and of women. It stops hemorrhoids, and applied as a plaster it consolidates ulcers. Fresh Phenicobalani are more astringent than dried ones; they cause headache, and if too many are eaten they cause intoxication. The use of dried ones in food is beneficial for spitting of blood, for vomiting of food, and for dysentery. Applied as a plaster with quince honey and Enantine cerate they help with bladder ailments. Those called Cariote, when eaten, heal roughness of the throat. The decoction of the Thebaici, when drunk, extinguishes the fever heat in continuous fevers called Causoni, and drunk with old honeyed water it restores strength. They produce the same effect when eaten in food. A wine is made from these for all the afore-

PRIMO 97

I will pass over those mentioned by Theophrastus and Pliny, since they are unknown in Italy and of no importance. Galen, in book two on the properties of foods, will criticize the use of silique (pods) as food, saying that since they are so woody they are necessarily very hard to digest, and that it would have been better to leave them in the East rather than bring them to our lands.

On All Apples. Chapter 132.

The leaves of all apple trees are astringent, as are their flowers and tips, and especially those of the quince. Apples are astringent when unripe, but ripe ones are otherwise. Those that ripen in spring increase choler, harm all the nerves, and produce flatulence. Quinces are beneficial to the stomach and promote urination. When roasted in the fire they become both more tender and more digestible. They are helpful for stomach and dysenteric fluxes, for spitting of phlegm, and for choleric complaints, and especially when raw. Their infusion is usefully drunk for fluxes of the body and stomach. The juice of the raw fruit is good for difficulty of breathing and tightness of the chest. Their decoction is useful for relaxations of the womb and likewise of the lower bowel. Those preserved in honey promote urination, and the honey used in the preparation, having drawn the virtue of the fruit to itself, becomes astringent and thickening. Quinces cooked in honey are useful to the stomach and very pleasant to the taste, though less binding. They are applied raw in poultices made to check bodily fluxes, for vomiting, for inflammations of the stomach, for inflammations of the breasts, hardness of the spleen, and abscesses of the lower bowel. A wine of quinces is made by first pounding and then pressing them, and to preserve it one adds one sextarius of honey to every sixteen sextarii, for otherwise it turns to vinegar; it is useful for all the aforementioned purposes. From quinces is also prepared an ointment called Melino, which is used wherever an astringent oil is needed. One should choose the true quinces, which are the ones that are small, round, and very fragrant, for those called Struthian, which are large, are considerably inferior. The green and dry flowers are useful in astringent poultices and for inflammations of the eyes and spitting of blood. Drunk with wine they help fluxes of the body and of women. Those apples which, from the taste of honey, are called Melimele lubricate the body and drive out worms, but they are harmful to the stomach and cause thirst. Some call these sweet apples. Those called Epirotic from Epirus, and Orbiculate by the Latins, are agreeable to the stomach. They bind the body and promote urination, but are less potent than quinces. The wild ones resemble the spring apples and are astringent; for this use all those that are unripe and sour are needed. Peaches are good for the stomach and lubricate the body, but the unripe ones are binding, and the dried ones have even greater power to bind. The decoction of dried ones, when drunk, checks fluxes of the stomach and body. Apricots, which the Latins call Precoce, are smaller than these and better for the stomach. The Apples of Media, or Cedromele, which the Latins call Cedri, known to everyone, have their trees, which at every time of the year bear fruit, one crop succeeding another. This fruit is longer than it is round, wrinkled, golden in color, and strongly fragrant. Its seeds resemble those of the pear, and drunk in wine they counteract poisons and move the bowels. The decoction of the fruits, or the juice held in the mouth, sweetens the breath. Cedars are harmful for pregnant women to eat, especially in that condition which the Greeks call Cissa. It is believed that if they are kept in chests or wardrobes they prevent moths from attacking clothes.

Dioscorides wrote of eight species of apples in a single chapter, because they are similar in appearance to peaches, quinces, and cedars. But coming first to common apples, I note (according to what Galen writes in book two on the properties of foods) that there are apples of various flavors and consequently of various effects. For some are austere, some sour, some sweet, some sweet-and-sour, some sour-and-tart, and some sweet, sour, and tart all together. Nevertheless, to a greater or lesser degree all apples are astringent, cold, and earthy, but particularly the sour ones produce cold and thin nourishment. The moderately sweet ones are temperate, inclining however somewhat toward a warm nature. The insipid ones, following the nature of water (although they may seem sweeter than others), are altogether

100 LIBRO

A As was said also of pomegranates, oranges in Italy are of three kinds — that is, sour, medium, and sweet. The sweet ones are warm throughout, and the others are cold in their juice, the more or less so depending on how sour or sweet they are; and therefore in hot fevers the sour and medium kinds are appropriate, but not the sweet. From the juice of lemons, just as from citrons, one makes a syrup useful for quenching the heat of cholera, and in contagious and pestilential fevers. The water distilled from lemons through a glass alembic, besides being used by women to polish their skin, cures skin eruptions wherever they appear on the person, as well as lice. Given to drink to children, it kills the worms of the body; fresh juice squeezed from the fruit does the same, at the quantity of one ounce more or less, depending on whether the children are small or large. Brassavola labored greatly in the preface of his book wishing to explain where the word Aranci was derived, and although he gathered many derivations, in my opinion they hardly fit, since he could not discover that Aranci means nothing other than Aurantia poma, which signifies nothing other than golden apples, or apples of the color of gold.

Of Pears. Chapter 43.

B The species of pears are many, but they are all astringent. For this reason they are usefully employed in repercussive plasters. The decoction of dried pears, and the pears themselves eaten raw, restrain the body. Eaten on an empty stomach they are harmful. Those called Acras are a kind of wild pear that ripens very late. They are astringent, but much more so than the domestic kinds; they serve for all the purposes for which domestic pears are used. Their leaves are also astringent. The ash of the pear tree's wood, taken as a drink, evidently helps those who have eaten harmful mushrooms. Some say that cooking mushrooms together with wild pears makes them harmless and safe to eat.

V Pears are very common fruits in Italy, and therefore it would be quite superfluous to describe how the trees that produce them are cultivated. Many varieties are found, just as in antiquity there were the Superbe, Falerne, Decimane, Dolobelliane, Pompeiane, Liceriane, Seucriane, Tiraniane, Rauoniane, Lateriane, Anitiane, Tiberiane, Neuiane, Turaniane, Amerine, Picentine, Numentine, Alessandrine, Tarentine, Segnine, Porporee, Sementine, Laurine, Amphorine, Coriolane, Cucurbitine, and many others of diverse kinds. All these names are derived either from the men who put them into use, or from the places they came from, or from their resemblance to other fruits, or from their color, or from the seasons in which they ripen. Following this same custom we call our Tuscan pears Moscadelle, Giugnole, Ciampoline, Roggie, Ghiacciuole, Spinose, Quadrane, Carouelle, Papali, San Niccolo, Durelle, Zuccate, Campane, Vernareccie, Gentili, Porcine, Sementine, and many other names. But whoever wished truly to match our pears with the ancient species would need each variety to have a particular and very clear description, since by simple names alone it would be impossible to identify them. Speaking generally, however, as we also said of apples, the properties of pears are known by the taste they leave on the palate — the sweet ones having a different nature from the rough and astringent ones, and from those that combine different flavors — and vice versa. Pears, according to what Galen wrote in book five of the Properties of Simples, are agreeable to the stomach and drying. The wild ones are much more astringent, and therefore more useful in cases of flux than the domestic kinds.

Of the Medlar. Chapter 134.

D The medlar, which is called by some Aronia, is a thorny tree with leaves resembling the oxiacantha. It produces a soft, small fruit with three small stones inside. For this reason some call it Tricocco. It ripens late, and when eaten it is constringent; it is agreeable to the stomach and tightens the bowels. Another species grows in Italy, which some call Setanso and others Epimelida, whose tree produces leaves resembling the apple tree's, though somewhat smaller. It produces a round fruit with a broad navel, good to eat; it is astringent and ripens late.
The two species of medlar written about here by Dioscorides — the first of which, with leaves resembling the Oxiacantha, does not in any way correspond to our Italian medlars. For, as one can sensibly see, our medlars do not have notched leaves similar to the Oxiacantha, their fruit is not soft but rather tart, and they have all five small stones, not three as Dioscorides says this first species of medlar has. But if any fruit found in Italy can be said to be this first species of medlar, it would truly be what is called Azzarolo in Naples, where it is seen in infinite numbers in orchards and gardens. The tree that produces these fruits I myself saw in Naples, going toward Piedigrotta, planted in many places in a very large garden that once belonged to the happy memory of Lord Pompeo, Cardinal Colonna. It is not very unlike the plum tree, but is quite thorny and of medium height. Its leaves are somewhat elongated and notched, almost similar to those of the

102 BOOK

A In Italy, Holly — from whose bark, as from Birdlime, some people make a sticky substance to catch birds — is a plant quite unlike what is described in the history of Lotus found in Theophrastus and Pliny, because Holly has perpetual and very spiny leaves, is small in size, and green-barked, which is entirely contrary to the nature of Lotus. Galen wrote about Lotus in book seven of his work on Simple Medicines, saying: The Lotus does not greatly partake of astringent qualities, but is composed of subtle and drying parts, and therefore the powder of its wood is good for menstrual fluxes, dysentery, and stomach fluxes. It is cooked for this purpose either in water or in wine, according to need, and one does not only use it as an enema, but it is also drunk as a decoction. Moreover, since it visibly prevents hair from falling out, this is sufficient sign that it has some astringent and moderately drying virtue; because (as was said in the chapter on Ladanum) such must be the nature of medicines that prevent the falling of body hair and head hair.

Of the Cornelian Cherry. Chapter 136.

B The Cornelian cherry is a hard tree. It produces a somewhat elongated fruit, nearly similar to olives, which is first green, then wax-colored as it ripens, and finally red when fully ripe. Eaten as food it is astringent. It restrains bodily fluxes and dysentery, taken in food or with grape syrup. It is preserved for use in food with brine, like olives. The humor that sweats out of the branches when burned is useful, applied as an ointment, for skin eruptions.
The Cornelian cherry is a very well-known tree. But as Theophrastus reports in chapter twelve of the third book of his History of Plants, there are both male and female forms, and one can distinguish one from the other: the male has a thicker trunk and branches and is much harder to strip of its bark. The material of its wood is very hard and firm like horn, from which it takes its name. It grows to the height of twelve cubits, with leaves rather similar to those of the Almond tree, but somewhat thicker and more veined. The female, although it makes little trunk, produces quite a number of shoots similar to those of the Chaste tree, and these are much more flexible and less firm than those of the male. On Mount Ida in Troy the male bears no fruit. But in Macedonia (and likewise in Italy) both male and female produce fruits. The wood of the male has no pith and is therefore better and stronger than that of the female. The male produces and ripens its fruit in summer, and the female at the end of autumn, producing fruit considerably inferior to that of the male. It should be noted that they should not be planted or left near the places of bees, because if bees eat their flowers they die. From the pulp of their fruits is made a mixture similar to quince paste, and from their decoction a jelly with sugar, which beyond being very pleasing to the taste, is good for dysenteric fluxes and for those of women when too abundant. Galen reports in book seven of his work on Simple Medicines that their leaves and young shoots very powerfully dry, and therefore consolidate large wounds, especially in firm bodies; but in soft bodies and in small wounds he says they tend rather to be harmful and injurious, because they dry more than is needed.

Of Sorbs. Chapter 137.

C Sorbs, when they are still red and not yet ripe, if sliced and dried in the sun and eaten, constrict the body. Ground at the mill and eaten like polenta they have the same effect. The same is achieved by drinking their decoction.
Sorbs are very common fruits in Italy, known to everyone. Nevertheless I will not fail to mention, following the history that Theophrastus recounts in book twelve of his third book, that among Sorb trees there is a male and a female, and from clear observation one of them is sterile and the other fruit-bearing. Furthermore, sorbs are of two kinds: one with rounder, sweeter, milder, and more flavorsome fruits, and the other with more elongated ones, like small pears, much rougher and coarser than the first. There are also wild ones found, agreeable to the taste and more astringent when dried unripe. Sorbs, as Galen reports in book eight of his work on Simple Medicines and in book two on Foods, are astringent, but much less so than Medlars. Both are more suited to use in medicine than as common food.

Of the Plum, or Prune. Chapter 138.

D The Plum is a very well-known tree. Its fruits are eaten, but they harm the stomach and loosen the bowels. Prunes from Syria, and especially dried Damascus plums, are beneficial to the stomach and constipate the body. The decoction of its leaves, used as a gargle in wine and to wash the mouth, is good for catarrh that descends to the uvula, the gums, and the throat. Likewise the fruits of wild plums, dried after they are ripe, but cooked in grape syrup, are more beneficial to the stomach and better suited to restraining the body. The gum of the Plum is adhesive and, drunk with wine, causes kidney stones to break. It is applied with vinegar to cure skin eruptions in children.

110 BOOK

A of women. A decoction of them made with rue is usefully administered as an enema for pains of the body. Dried figs cooked, then pounded and applied as a poultice dissolve hardnesses, scrofulas, boils, and abscesses that arise behind the ears. They ripen bread, but even more so when iris, or nitre, or lime is added. The same things pounded raw, together with the aforementioned substances, do the same. Together with the unripe rinds of pomegranates they purge hangnails of the fingers, and with cobbler's dye they heal ulcers of the legs that are incurable from continual discharge, and those that heal with difficulty. Cooked in wine with wormwood and barley flour they are usefully applied as a poultice to the bodies of dropsical persons. Roasted and combined with wax they cure swellings. Pounded raw together with mustard of sinape and distilled into the ears they quiet the ringing that is felt there, and likewise the itching. The milk of the fig, both domestic and wild, makes milk curdle just as rennet does, and on the contrary when applied to curdled milk it dissolves it like vinegar. The milk of the fig is ulcerative and aperitive, and loosens the body. Drunk together with ground almonds it opens obstructions of the womb, and applied mixed with egg yolk,

B or with Tuscan wax, it provokes the menses; it is useful in poultices for gout with vinegar and fenugreek flour. It cleanses scab, heals ringworm, vitiligo, blemishes of the face, mange, and ulcers of the head that run, when applied with polenta. It is effective against the stings of scorpions, and the bites of dogs and all venomous animals when applied to them. It heals pains of the teeth by soaking wool in it and placing it in their cavities. It causes those kinds of ants to fall off that resemble warts, by anointing the flesh around them together with grease. The same properties are found in the juice taken from the tender branches of wild figs, full of milk before the buds appear. These are pounded and the juice pressed out, which is then dried in the shade and stored. Both the milk and the juice are used in ulcerative medicines. The tops of the wild fig placed to boil together with beef quickly cook the meat. Mixing the milk when it boils with a fig branch instead of a spoon makes it more laxative. The large early figs, which some call Erinei, soften when applied cooked to hardnesses and scrofulas, and when raw cause warts, corns, and likewise thymi to fall off when applied with flour and nitre.

C The leaves also do the same, which mixed with vinegar and nitre and applied as a liniment cure ulcers of the head that suppurate, dandruff, and epinictides. These are rubbed on fig-like growths and roughnesses of the eyelids. A liniment of the leaves and tops of black figs is made for white vitiligo. These applied as a poultice with honey are good for dog bites and favus ulcers. Large figs together with leaves of wild poppy draw out broken bones, and with wax dissolve boils. They are usefully applied with bitter vetch and wine for the bite of the spider and the scolopendra. A lye is made from the ashes of the branches of both the domestic and the wild fig, repeatedly renewing it through the ashes to make it stronger, and letting it steep and age well; it is suitable for ulcerating and burning wherever there is need, and especially in cancers: for it consumes and burns away all the bad parts that are in excess. It is used in places where needed, by soaking a sponge in it and then applying it to the ailment. Sometimes it is necessary to administer it as an enema in dysentery, chronic fluxes of the body, and ulcers that are deep, cavernous, and

D large: for it cleanses, fills in, and consolidates them, and heals no less than those poultices used to close fresh wounds. It is drunk to liquefy blood congealed in the stomach. The fresh strained liquid, drunk with a cup of water and a little oil, is good for those with ruptures, spasms, and those who have fallen from a height. Drunk alone at the weight of a cup it is good for stomach and dysenteric fluxes. Beyond this it is usefully rubbed with oil on spasms and pains of the nerves: for it provokes sweating. It is given to those who have swallowed gypsum, and it is effective against the bite of the spiders called Phalangi. All the other lyes do the same, especially that made from oak ash, and all have astringent properties.

Figs are the most well-known and common fruits throughout all Italy, and although they are found in both white and black varieties of many kinds, since everyone knows them from the abundance in which they are eaten in autumn, it is not necessary to say which are the best; for taste has well taught everyone that those which are well ripened, plump, and flavorful are the most excellent. But so that one may know, beyond what Dioscorides wrote of their nature and

PRIMO. III

Their qualities, the nourishment they provide, the benefits and harms they can cause — I will report here what I find written by Galen in book two of On the Properties of Foods, where he writes about them in this manner. Figs, although they do not generate as many bad humors as the other fruits of Autumn and Summer, are nevertheless not without their faults and harms. But they have this advantage over those others: they are quickly digested and easily penetrate throughout the entire body. They are manifestly cleansing, as is confirmed by the fact that when eaten by those suffering from kidney stones, they drive them out through the urine. And although all autumnal foods provide little nourishment to the body, figs provide no less than the others, yet the flesh generated from their nourishment is not firm and solid like that produced by bread and pork, but rather soft and loose, for they too are gassy. They would not be eaten without some discomfort to the body were it not for their quick departure from the stomach; since they do not remain there long, they cannot bloat the body too much with wind, and thus are not as harmful as other autumnal fruits. Ripe ones are by far better than unripe ones, as is likewise the case with other fruits, though the difference matters somewhat less here than with other fruits. Well-ripened figs lack little of being free from all harm. Dried figs likewise, although praised for many virtues, nevertheless cause discomfort to those who eat them frequently and in large quantities, since they do not generate very good blood — as is evidenced by the number of lice they produce. They have an attenuating and incisive virtue, by which they loosen the body and purge the kidneys. They are harmful to the liver and spleen when inflamed, as is the common nature of all sweet foods, not that this is peculiar to figs alone; but also to those organs when obstructed and congested. Though dried figs on their own neither benefit nor harm, when combined and eaten with incisive, attenuating, and cleansing substances they are very useful, and therefore some physicians in diseases of the liver and spleen have patients eat them well before a meal, with thyme, or pepper, or ginger, or pennyroyal, or savory, or calamint, or oregano, or hyssop. Doing this can be not only very beneficial to the sick but also to the healthy, since protecting oneself from obstruction of the liver is no less useful for the healthy than for the sick. On the other hand, when dried figs are eaten with foods contrary to the above — those that generate thick humors — they are greatly harmful. And in book two on the properties of simples, Galen said the same: dried figs heat at the end of the first degree or the beginning of the second, and have subtlety in their parts, and are therefore useful for ripening and digesting small abscesses of the body; those best for this purpose are the fattiest, and accordingly those that are sharp in taste are more cleansing. Fresh and dried figs both loosen the body; but fresh ones nourish less, due to the moisture they contain. The fig tree is hot and of subtle substance, as the sap and juice of its leaves clearly demonstrate: for both are powerfully hot in their properties, and show this not only in being cleansing but also in ulcerating and opening the mouths of veins, and in eradicating warts, corns, and similar growths from the limbs. The wild fig tree is much more potent in all these properties, its tips being so hot and subtle in their parts that when boiled with even the toughest beef, they tenderize it wonderfully. By anointing fig trees with oil and pigeon dung (according to Democritus) one produces early figs, and conversely one may delay them greatly by removing the first figs when they are as large as beans. It is held for certain that lightning bolts descending from the sky have the same respect for fig trees as for the laurel.

On the Persea Tree. Chapter 147.

The Persea is a tree of Egypt. It produces a fruit that is good to eat and pleasant to the stomach, in which are found certain spiders called Cranocolatti, especially in the Thebaid; its dried leaves, when applied, staunch flows of blood. Some have said that this tree is poisonous and deadly in Persia, but that when transplanted to Egypt it changed its nature and became healthful and good to eat.

As we said above in the chapter on all Apples, the Persea of Egypt is not (as Marcello Virgilio of Florence imagined) our Italian Peach tree; it is a plant quite different from ours, as can be understood from Dioscorides and from Galen, since both wrote about them in separate chapters. This tree, according to Theophrastus in chapter two of book four of his History of Plants, is a tree of Egypt of great and beautiful stature in its branches, leaves, flowers, and in every other part very similar to the Pear tree, except that it never loses its leaves. It produces fruit in great abundance, and at all times bears both old ripe fruit and young fruit still maturing. The fruits take a year to ripen, and so nature has provided that the young ones grow beneath the old ones. When ripe they are the size of pears, long in the manner of almonds, and green in color. They have a stone like that of plums, but much smaller and softer. The flesh of the fruit is sweet and pleasant in taste, easy to digest, and even when eaten in large quantities is not found to cause any harm. The tree roots very well; for besides being plentiful, the roots are thick and deep. The wood is robust, hard, and beautiful to look upon; and from it are made statues, beds, dining tables, and other honored instruments. Considering all these characteristics, it is plainly evident that these plants are quite different from our Italian Peach trees. Galen, speaking of these

On Iberis. Chapter 148.

Iberis, or Cardamatica, has leaves similar to Nasturtium, but in Spring they are greener than those of Nasturtium. It is a plant a cubit long, and sometimes smaller. It grows in uncultivated places. In summer it produces a milk-colored flower, at which time it is most effective. Beyond this it has two roots similar to Nasturtium, which are hot and ulcerative. For this reason it is praised for sciatica: it is applied to the affected parts, ground up with salted fat in the form of a plaster, for four hours, with the understanding that afterward the patient should enter the bath and have the area anointed with oil on a piece of wool.

B The most excellent Messer Giulio Alessandrino, a very noble physician from Trento, outside the walls of the city of Trento, in a place called "alle Leste," showed me the Iberis clearly — for I had never seen it before — and it was in no way unlike the description written of it by Dioscorides and by several other Greek authors. Galen did not devote any separate chapter to this plant in his books on the properties of simples; but he did say that between this plant and Lepidium there was no other difference than the name alone. And at the end of book ten of his Compositions of Medicines by Location, treating the cure of sciatica as written by Damocrates, affirming the same thing, he said as follows: There is found a small book by Damocrates called the Clinicus, written in iambic verse, as he was wont to do, in which he wrote of three kinds of medicines. The first concerns that herb which he calls Iberis, which he praised for the cure of sciatica, saying that with this herb a certain physician friend of his was cured in a province called Iberia. This herb (as I have said) Damocrates called Iberis, having recognized it only by sight without knowing any name for it, just as the man who taught him its use did not know its name either; but from the signs he describes of it, it appears he is calling Iberis that which the Greeks call Lepidium, naming it thus after the region where his friend was cured. He therefore describes its characteristics in these verses:

This herb grows abundantly in every place,          The green leaves hang until winter comes,
C Near ancient and old tombs,                           The stem grows hard like a vine-shoot,
And along public and well-trodden walls,            And frost dries it, breaks it, and consumes it.
Where no plowman ever                                  In summer it produces a small flower,
Drew his plow across the fields.                       Varied, and white as milk,
It stays green at all hours, producing leaves        After which follows a seed so tiny
Like Nasturtium, but larger,                           It deceives the eye and is scarcely visible.
In Spring, from which the stem then rises,          Its root has companions alongside it,
A cubit high, and often less,                          Most sharp to the taste, whose flavor
And sometimes taller, so that in summer            Much resembles that of Nasturtium.

From this doctrine, I believe one can safely say that among the Greeks Iberis and Lepidium are one and the same thing. This clearly demonstrates that this chapter on Iberis was added to Dioscorides in this place by some overly zealous scribe. Beyond the reasons already given, manifest evidence of this is that we see the end of this first book is in no way a suitable place to treat the history of Iberis; for Dioscorides treated such herbs in an orderly fashion in the second book, where he devoted a separate chapter to Lepidium, which is nothing other than the Iberis of Damocrates. Thus Paul of Aegina rightly said: Lepidium, which we call Iberis, is hot in the third degree, similar to Nasturtium. And in chapter seventy-seven of that same third book, treating the cure of sciatica, he said: The use of the herb Iberis, which is called Lepidium, completely restores to health those who suffer from sciatica. Beyond this, it is also apparent that Paul of Aegina, in addition to the aforementioned Iberis, used in treating sciatica another species quite different from that of Damocrates. This is evident when, in the last passage cited, having first spoken of the true Iberis, he says: But that which grows among us with many branches and leaves like laurel, though larger, many experiments confirm it corresponds to this — not only in sciatica but in many other old and longstanding illnesses. Indeed, the Lepidium described by Pliny at chapter eight of book nineteen, where he writes: Lepidium grows to the height of a cubit, with laurel-like leaves — these characteristics give very good grounds for believing that this second species of Iberis, or if we prefer to call it Lepidium, which produces laurel-like leaves, is that which today is found in all gardens, called by some Piperitis on account of its very sharp taste, and by others Piperella. Thus Hermolao and Ruellius were manifestly wrong in believing that Lepidium was what is commonly called Raphano. For truly the very large leaves produced by Raphano, larger than those of Verbascum and equal to those of Elecampane, demonstrate that those men did not recognize Lepidium.

In the first book, dearest Arso, which we composed on Medical Material, we spoke of all Aromatic things, Oils, Ointments, Trees, and all things that come from them, such as juices, liquors, and fruits. But in this Second book we will speak of animals, honey, milk, fats, varieties of grain, and garden herbs, adding to these the vegetables of sharp taste, since they are related to those others, as if by family lineage, such as Garlic, Onions, and Mustard. On the Sea Urchin.          Chapter One.

The sea urchin is beneficial to the stomach. It loosens the bowels and provokes urine. Its shell, burnt raw, is mixed with preparations used to drive away mange, and the ash of the burnt shells cleanses foul ulcers and reduces superfluous flesh.

The Sea Urchin is a very well known creature, especially to those who live in Italy along the shores of the entire Tyrrhenian Sea and also the Adriatic, since they are found almost everywhere in these seas. I myself have seen great quantities of them when the sea was calm, on the bottom of the great harbor of Civitavecchia and in other places. This animal in its appearance is entirely similar to the chestnut burr — spiny, round, and of similar size — except that its spines are somewhat similar in color to those of the land hedgehog, though somewhat darker and finer. Beneath the spines it has a shell very similar in substance to that of snails, and within its hollow the flesh is found, which is partly yellow and partly dark. They are used as food and are not unpleasant to the taste when properly prepared. This animal uses its spines as feet to move about, and it always moves by rolling around, and thus many are found whose spines have been blunted by long rolling, and others that are entirely filled with seaweed and sea mud. There is a species of considerably greater size, caught in the open sea, called Echinometres, which Aristotle praised (says Paolo Giovio) in the fourth book of his History of Animals as a marvelous remedy for distillations of urine. However, Giovio errs here, because Aristotle did not praise the Echinometra in that context, but rather a certain other small-bodied creature, covered with very fine and long spines, which he said was found in the deepest sea. This shows that Giovio misunderstood Aristotle in this passage. Galen wrote about both the Sea and the Land Urchin in book eleven of his work on the Faculties of Simple Medicines, in a single chapter, saying thus: The ash of the urchin, whether sea or land, is cleansing, digestive, and astringent. For which reason some use it to reduce superfluous flesh and for foul ulcers.

The skin of the land hedgehog, burnt and mixed with liquid pitch, causes hair to regrow that has fallen out due to alopecia. The flesh, dried and drunk with honeyed vinegar, is good for disorders of the kidneys. It benefits those with dropsy and those with elephantiasis, for spasms of the nerves, and for those in a wasting condition, and it dries up internal fluxes. It is stored dried on a tile in the sun, and given in the same manner it produces the same benefits.

The land hedgehogs are well known in Italy and quite common, and are found in both the dog-nosed and pig-nosed varieties, as are also the badgers. This is recognized by their snout, which in some resembles that of dogs, and in others resembles [continues below]

On the Hippocampus. Chapter III.

B The Hippocampus is a small sea creature. Its ashes, mixed with liquid pitch, or grease, or with Amaracine ointment, and applied, cause hair that has fallen out through mange to grow back.

How the Hippocampus came to have its name I find no particular account of, either among the ancients or among

C the modern writers, although all of them count it among the species of sea locusts. One may readily believe that it took its name from the caterpillars that feed on herbs in the fields and gardens, which the Greeks call Campe, perhaps because it resembles them in appearance. And although Dioscorides says the Hippocampus is a small sea creature, the force of the word itself shows quite the opposite. For the term Hippo, joined to other words, generally signifies something large, as we see in Hipposelinum, Hippolapathum, and Hippomarathrum. But this should not be grounds for condemning Dioscorides and the others who used the name before him. For although compared to large sea fish it is a small creature, it is nonetheless large compared to the type of caterpillar it resembles and from which it took its name. I have seen this creature many times in the fish markets among the fish offal; its body and shape are similar to a medium-sized shrimp, but it does not have forked gills, and it has a rather long neck with a somewhat elongated head, and many legs, and is thus altogether similar to those hairy caterpillars, reddish-black in color, that are found underground in gardens and fields, of similar shape, feeding on the roots of herbs and grain. In Trento these are called Cagne, and in the Val d'Anania, because of their hairiness, Orsolane; and Columella very aptly called them hirsute. These animals are very plentiful in the Trentino region, and they come out of the ground when it rains, and so those who find them troublesome in their gardens often water the ground to bring them out in order to kill them.

On Purpura and Buccinae (sea snails). Chapter IV.

The ash of burnt Purpura desiccates, cleans the teeth, consumes superfluous flesh, purifies and consolidates ulcers. The ash of Buccinae does the same, but burns more powerfully. Whoever burns a Buccina filled with salt in an unglazed earthen vessel will produce a most useful powder for rubbing the teeth. It is usefully sprinkled over burns from fire, and is left in place until it hardens; for as the ulcer is dried, it then falls away by itself. Moreover, a lime is made from Buccinae, as we shall describe when we speak of lime. Those parts in the middle of the Buccinae and Purpura,
D around which their shells wind, are called Ciones. These too are burnt in the same way, and are more efficacious because they have more astringent virtue. The flesh of Buccinae is pleasant and agreeable to the taste, and suitable for the stomach, but does not soften the body.

The Purpura are marine animals covered with a hard shell, and according to Pliny in his ninth book, they contain
S that liquid of great value which is properly called Tyrian purple, used to dye the splendid garments of kings and emperors. These small animals carry this liquid in their throat, in a rather pale vein; it is not found in dead ones, because it dissolves along with their vital spirit, and so fishermen always try to catch them alive. They hide for thirty days during the dog days of summer, and in spring they come together, and rubbing against one another they produce a thick saliva like wax. The Purpura has a tongue as long as a man's finger, and of such hardness that with it they bore through oysters, clams, and every other kind of shellfish on which they feed; knowing this well, fishermen who catch them, finding certain shells with sharp-edged husks scattered along the sea sand,

They weave them between cords, withes, and reeds, in the manner of fish-traps, and then hang them on long ropes and throw them into the sea. Thus it happens that these shellfish, being somewhat restless and half-dead, as soon as they feel the water open up, and the Murexes, running in to feed on them, put in their two tongues — but these, as soon as they feel the sting, close again and grip them between both walls of their shells, and hold them prisoner, and so they are afterward pulled out by the fishermen. The Murexes live out of water for fifty days, feeding only on their own saliva, but die immediately when placed in fresh water. They grow in one year to their full size, as do the other kinds of Oysters and Gongoles. The BUCCINES are also a species of Murex, and are called Buccines because they resemble a horn to blow, and because they have a mouthpiece very apt for putting to the mouth. Larger than these are the Murexes, which have a long beak like a channel through which they extend their tongue, entirely composed of fine rings, which is not found in the Buccines. Both have as many rings on their backs as they have lived years. The Buccines do not attach themselves except to rocks, and therefore are found only among the cliffs. The Murexes and Buccines, together with all the other kinds of Shellfish, were celebrated at length by Athenaeus, to whom those who wish to know more may turn. But since PEARLS, which today, both for luxury and for their virtues, are prized throughout the whole world, are produced by a marine animal also numbered among these kinds of shellfish, and since nothing has been written about them by Dioscorides or Galen, and since the subject I am treating has now brought them to my attention, I have not wished to let their praise and their fair name pass unmentioned. The animals that produce them are born, as Pliny relates in the thirty-fifth chapter of the ninth book, in the Indian Ocean, and in that which surrounds the island of Taprobana, Toide, and Perimola, a promontory of India. But the finest and most esteemed Pearls are those found in the Red Sea of Arabia. The animals that produce them are, as the MOTHER-OF-PEARL shells that are brought to us truly demonstrate, very unlike Oysters, and they have this property: that when the season of the year urges them to generate, they open at night, filling themselves and nourishing themselves with the generative dew, and becoming heavy with this, they afterward bring forth Pearls that are clear or cloudy, according to the quality of the dew they have gathered. If when they are swelling it is cloudy weather, they produce pale and murky Pearls. They make them large when they feed abundantly, and they become small when they do not take in enough dew, which is prevented by lightning flashes, because when lightning strikes as they are swelling, they are frightened and close up before they are full of dew. They also close at the sound of thunder. And thus they afterward generate hollow Pearls, without any substance, full of wind. In water, Pearls are soft; but as soon as they are taken out, they harden. Some say that the Mother-of-Pearl shells go in schools, and that they have a King whose body is much larger than the others, just as the Bees that make honey have a queen, and therefore the Fishermen take no little trouble to catch their King, because once they have taken him, they lead the others more easily into the nets. If they become aware, when open, of the hand of the Fisherman who wishes to take them, they close so tightly as to cut off his fingers cruelly, taking their own revenge. Those that are caught are put in certain earthen vessels with much salt. For as the flesh thus wastes away, the Pearls remain clean at the bottom of the vessel. The most esteemed are the large, lucid, round, and heavy ones, things that are rarely found in a single pearl. Juba writes that the Mother-of-Pearl shells of Arabia are like a comb, spiny like the Sea-urchin, behind which the Pearls are found resembling hailstones. Pliny writes that no more than four or five Pearls are found per animal. But Amerigo Vespucci, in his second voyage, which he made through the Atlantic Ocean beneath the sign of the Equinox toward the South, affirms that he obtained a Mother-of-Pearl shell in which one hundred and thirty were found inside. And others who after him have sailed to the New Indies speak of many more, and recount histories very different from what Pliny wrote. They are also fished in the western Ocean toward the north near Scotland and England, but small and of not very praiseworthy color, and from these was made that breastplate which Julius Caesar dedicated to the temple of Diana. Pearls, in the practice of Medicine, according to Serapion the Arab, and likewise Avicenna, are very useful for tremors and weaknesses of the heart, and in collyria for clarifying sight, and for drying up the water and humidity that descends into the eyes.

The dried and ground testicles of the Hippopotamus are drunk against the bite of Serpents.

The Hippopotamus (according to Pliny in the 25th and 26th chapters of his eighth book) is a beast of the Nile considerably larger than the Crocodile, having two hooves on its feet like oxen. It has the back, the mane, and the neigh of a horse, a raised snout, a curved tail, and teeth like a wild boar, though not so harmful. But Aristotle, in the sixth chapter of the third book on the nature of animals, did not say that the teeth, although they protrude from the mouth, are those of a wild boar, but rather that the tail of the Hippopotamus is like that of a boar, and the whole body is no larger than a donkey. Its hide cannot be pierced by any pointed weapon unless it is first soaked, and so shields, helmets, and bucklers are made from it. This animal is so cunning that when it enters fields of grain to graze, it enters backwards so as to appear to have come out, so as not to be caught there. One was brought to Rome alive along with six Crocodiles by Marcus Scaurus the Aedile, who staged a spectacle with them in his games. The Hippopotamus has this nature: when it feels burdened and too full, it goes into the reed beds, where it finds a stump of reed already cut, and rubs only the vein against it until it draws blood, letting out as much as it deems sufficient for itself, and then closes the wound with clay or mud. The ash of its hide mixed with water heals swellings called "pani." Its fat lightens the cold that comes before fevers, and similarly its dung, rubbed on the teeth of the left jaw at the gums until blood comes out, cures toothache. The hide of the left part of the forehead, tied near the groin, prevents coition.

On Castoreum. Chapter 23.

The Beaver is an ambiguous animal, living equally on land and in water, but much more in water, where it feeds on fish and crabs. Its testicles have virtue against serpent venoms. They cause sneezing and are used universally in many ways. Taken with pennyroyal at the weight of two drams, they promote menstruation, expel the afterbirth, and expel creatures from the body. Taken with vinegar they help against flatulence, bodily pain, hiccups, deadly poisons, and Ixia. Administered in clysters they awaken the lethargic, the drowsy, and those stupefied for whatever cause. Dissolved in vinegar and rosewater and smelled, or used as a fumigation, they do the same. Taken as drink and applied in the form of a

D liniment they help the cramped, those with trembling limbs, and all defects of the nerves. They universally have the virtue of warming. Those considered best come from the same source (for it is impossible to find two sacs enclosed in a single membrane), having inside a waxy liquid of heavy and unpleasant smell, strong, biting in taste, and fragile; surrounded by several natural membranes. Some counterfeiters adulterate them by mixing Ammoniac gum with the blood of this animal and the testicles themselves, then packing everything back into the sacs to dry. It is truly false what is said, that when the animal is chased by hunters, it tears off its own testicles in flight with its teeth: for it cannot reach them since they are retracted, as are those of the pig. When removing them, it is necessary to split the hide and preserve that honey-like liquid together with the sac in which it is contained, and to give it to drink after it has dried.

C As may be seen throughout lower Germany wherever the Rhine flows, and through Austria and Hungary wherever the Danube passes, Beavers (as Dioscorides says) are truly animals common to both water and land, being seen
