A On Frogs. Chapter 25.

Frogs boiled and cooked with oil and salt, and eaten, serve as a Theriaca against the bites of all serpents, and their broth drunk does the same. They are also useful against old swellings of the tendons. The ash of burned frogs, sprinkled, stops the flow of blood, and is usefully made into a liniment with pitch to restore hair that is falling out. The blood of green frogs prevents regrowth of hairs that have been removed from the eyelids, when dripped on the places from which they were pulled. Rinsing the mouth with a decoction of frogs made with water and vinegar is beneficial for toothache.

Frogs are found in Italy, and especially in Lombardy, in the greatest abundance, and are common; yet they are not all of one species, one color, or one nature. For there are some that are born from putrefaction, in the dampening that summer rains bring to the dust of the ground, and these have a short life and are not used for anything. Beyond these there are others born by legitimate order of nature in the seas, in rivers, in marshes, and in lakes. There are also land ones, which we in Tuscany call Botte, and others call Rospi (toads), and those which particularly, because they stay in the reeds, are called Calamite; but both of these last are venomous and deadly. In rivers, marshes, and lakes live those that are eaten, of green and gray color, though there too some are found that cannot be eaten with full safety. Frogs give birth (as Pliny said in Book 10, and as we continually observe with good sense) to small dark bits of flesh, which are nothing but eyes and tail, from which the legs then grow, the tail dividing into the hind legs. They live (said Pliny) only six months, and then without being seen they turn to mud, and in Spring those same ones that were first born are reborn from the waters; the reason why nature acts thus in them being hidden. Against this, experience shows that they are seen in Winter in the marshes of the Maremma, which do not freeze, where they are found at all times. And so it must be said that if Pliny's opinion is at all true, it applies only to those mentioned above, which are born from the putrefaction of earth and water.

On the Silurus fish. Chapter 26.

C Eaten fresh, the Silurus nourishes and softens the body; but salted, it gives very little nourishment. It purges the throat and clears the voice. The flesh of the salted fish, applied as a plaster, draws out thorns, arrows, and anything else lodged in the members of the body. Used as a sitting bath in its brine it helps those with dysentery, since it draws out fluxes through the skin. Applied in clysters it cures the pains of sciatica.

I cannot but agree with the well-argued opinion of Paolo Giovio, believing myself too that the fish formerly called Silurus by the ancients is the same as what is today called Sturgeon; just as on the other hand I cannot
N in any way align myself with the very distorted opinions of certain others, of whom some would have the Sturgeon be the Lupo, some the Attilo, and some the Hucca; for, as is shown by the fine and strong arguments put forward by Giovio, it has been plainly proven that the Silurus of the ancients was none other than the Sturgeon of the Moderns, which, abandoning its ancient name from Asturia, a place in Spain where this fish is found most excellent in all of Europe, was thereafter commonly called Storione. These are caught in many places in Italy, and when small they are called Porcellette; and although Sturgeons are best caught in rivers, such as the Tiber, the Po, and others that flow into the Sea, they are nonetheless sea fish. On the Tuna. Chapter 30.

They call Omotaricho the salted flesh of the Tuna, which when eaten and washed down with much wine so as to provoke vomiting by drinking heavily, is useful against the bite of those kinds of vipers called Presteri; and it is likewise useful to cause vomiting of foods that disturb the stomach. Applied externally it is useful against the bites of dogs.

Tunas, from which Tonnina is made, large and fleshy fish similar to pigs, are well known in every seaport, especially in the Tyrrhenian Sea rather than the Adriatic; for at the time of May these fish come from the Ocean and enter through the Strait of Gibraltar between the Pillars of Hercules, moving in enormous schools into this our Sea of Italy, called the Tyrrhenian and the Mediterranean, where then some schools also enter the Adriatic, though in considerably fewer numbers. These fish (according to some writers) are hunted by a very large fish, commonly called the Swordfish, because it has on its snout a very hard and sharp bone, like a sword, with which (as Pliny says in book thirty-two, and mariners who sail the Ocean also report) it pierces and runs through ships. Tunas, being very simple and timid fish, allow themselves to be chased by this Swordfish, like a flock of sheep by a wolf, and thus leaving the Ocean they come into our Italian seas. Not without great excitement among the spectators, they are caught in May and June at the Island of Gades, where the whole population gathers for this fishery with great noise, with voices, drums, and the firing of arquebuses. This is very useful for fishing these fish; because owing to their timidity and foolishness, frightened by the shouting and the great noise, they gather in certain shallows near the shore, where they can then easily be caught in great nets, a whole school at a time, and once divided into pieces and salted in barrels, the Tonnina is made from them. Tunas have different names according to whether they are younger or older: when they are very small and newly born they are called Cordille, and when somewhat larger Limarie, and growing further Palamie, and those that have grown more than a foot are then called Tonni. Pliny holds, and likewise Athenaeus, that Tunas live a long time and grow to enormous fish. Tunas are tormented in the great heat, stung by a certain small worm, just as oxen are tormented by gadflies and horseflies. For this reason, driven by pain, they frequently leap out of the water as if flying, onto ships, at which time they are harmful as food, being quite injurious. Their bellies, although they please the palate greatly, afterward harm the stomach all the more. The leaner parts do the opposite: if they do not please the palate quite as well, they are far less troublesome to the stomach. Though according to Galen in the third book on the properties of foods, all these large fish have hard flesh, difficult to digest, of little nourishment, and producing much waste matter; and therefore these fish are better eaten salted than fresh, since salt is a good means of breaking down their toughness and viscosity.

This was afterward made similarly from mackerel, and this seasoning was used in kitchens with great ceremony, as a condiment for various foods. C I Among all the nocturnal enemies that so often break our sweet rest in sleep, there are truly none more cruel than bedbugs: for besides biting us, breaking our sleep, and sucking our blood, they leave behind such a stench that it offends the senses and spirits far more than all the burning bites they inflict on every limb of the body. And although they are such most troublesome and filthy animals, nature did not wish to deprive them entirely of some useful faculty. Fresh locusts are usefully drunk with wine against scorpion bites. People eat them as food until they are satisfied — those who inhabit Lepti, a region of Africa.

Locusts are called in Tuscany, and in other parts of Italy, by various names: namely grilli, saltelli, caualette, saiuppi, and still other names, according to the customs and variety of the regions. They are very well-known animals, though quite harmful to herbs and to grain. According to what Aristotle wrote in chapter twenty-eight of the sixth book on the nature of animals, the males are considerably larger than the females. The females lay their eggs by thrusting their tails into the ground, from which are born certain powdery little worms covered with a thin skin; when this skin breaks open, locusts are generated from them. In mountainous and cold places very few are found, while on the contrary many are seen on plains and in places where the ground cracks from intense heat. Locusts travel flying across very long stretches of sea, and sometimes have crossed from Africa into Italy — as Pliny said — in such quantities that their swarms darkened the Sun as clouds do, causing no small astonishment among men and fear that, settling in their lands, they would lay them waste; for they ruin much and make barren the places where they alight, eating up the grain and herbs down to the very roots. Of this, in our own times, in the year 1542, the innumerable swarms testified, which coming from the Maeotic Marshes covered not only all of Hungary and the greatest part of Germany, but also all of Italy, where they caused immense damage to small grains and to the herbs of the meadows, eating up legumes, millet, panic grass, and beech-mast down to the roots. The Parthians eat them as food, and so it is no wonder that in Holy Scripture (as one reads in chapter eleven of Leviticus) Moses praised them as food for his Hebrew people, nor that Saint John the Baptist ate them together with wild honey in the desert — although there are some commentators who wish to interpret "locusts" as certain roots, and others as certain treetops. Not agreeing with them, I hold it for true that, being Hebrew and a great observer of the Mosaic law, he truly ate these locusts as animals. In some places, such as the region of Cyrenaica, on the island of Lemnos, and in Syria, people go out in great numbers two or three times a year into the countryside to destroy their nests, and then to kill them once they have hatched, as if they were going to fight against great armies. It is said that in India there are some that are three feet long and very fierce biters.

When the Eagle drives her chicks from the nest before they are fully grown and finished being reared, in order to see them compete among themselves for the food she brings them, the Ossifrage takes them in and finishes rearing them. A On the Salamander. Chapter 55.

The Salamander is a sluggish animal of varied color, and is counted among the lizard family. It is foolishness to believe that it does not burn in fire. Its properties are to eat away, heat, and ulcerate the flesh. It is used in ulcerating medicines and in treatments for leprosy, applied as one applies cantharides, and preserved in the same way. The Salamander dissolved in oil causes hair to fall out; and it is preserved in honey, after first removing its internal organs and then cutting off its head and feet, for the same use.

Salamanders are seen in the forest along every road in the valley of Anania, and in every other part of the Trentino, especially during times of heavy rain in Spring and in Autumn. But in Summer, due to the heat, and in Winter due to the great cold, they very rarely come out from underground. They are animals of body and size similar to green lizards, but with a thicker head, larger body, higher legs, and shorter tail. The latter are very swift, while salamanders are extremely slow in movement. They are all spotted in color, black and yellow, both very vivid colors, and so bright as if they had been burnished by art. They are repulsive and abominable to look at. Writing about them, Pliny at chapter 67 of book 10, said that the Salamander is only seen in rainy weather, and that its nature is so cold that it extinguishes fire by touching it. It also does well, as I have proven, placed on coals, as does the raw flesh of any animal. But thrown into a fire where there is great force of flame, it is a melancholy delusion to believe it does not burn, and that it lives on fire as the Chameleon lives on air. According to Pliny, there is no difference among Salamanders; for they are neither male nor female, and they generate no offspring, but are born of putrefaction. Their bite is venomous like that of serpents, and when they touch fruits or herbs with their mouths, they leave a certain secretion that is truly deadly poison, by which some people have been unwittingly poisoned by eating such fruits or herbs contaminated by them.

On Spiders. Chapter 56.

C The spider called the Wolf Spider, rubbed onto a linen cloth or a thread bandage and applied to the temples or forehead, cures the tertian fever. Its web, spread as a plaster over a wound, stops bleeding and prevents inflammation in wounds that are between flesh and skin. There is another kind that makes white, fine, and thick webs, which, bound in leather (as they say) and attached to the arm, cures the quartan fever. Oil of roses in which this spider has been cooked is good for pains in the ears when dropped in.

Spiders are (according to Aristotle at chapter 39 of book 9) of two kinds, that is, venomous and very harmful, and non-venomous, harmless to anyone. The venomous ones are of two sorts: one similar to the non-biting one called the Wolf Spider, named the Flea Spider, which is small, varied in color, biting, and lascivious; the other is larger, black, with similarly black front legs, slow in movement and very weak, and therefore does not jump as the other does. Among those that do not harm is the Wolf Spider, which is also of two kinds, large and small. This one does not spin a web, whereas the larger one spins a small, rough web close to the ground and along hedges. Of this same kind are also those that make large webs, called the Wise Spiders, among which there are also large and small ones, and these are the ones that weave in our houses, and it is these two kinds that Dioscorides wrote about. Pliny calls those that leave venom with their bite Phalangi; but he says these are not found in Italy, and according to his account in chapter 4 of book 29, these are of far more kinds than Aristotle wrote, and similarly each is called by its own particular name. These cause various accidents when they bite, according to their diverse form and nature; for some cause painful stings similar to those of wasps; others like those of scorpions; others contaminate the knees; others emaciate the body; others cause the mouth to swell; others cause loss of appetite, and others vomiting, and urinating substances similar to spider webs, in the way that some people bitten by rabid dogs urinate with great pain small lumps of flesh the size of a wasp. But even though (as Pliny said) these species of Phalangi are not found in Italy, another species of the most terrible kind is found there, which from Taranto, a city in the kingdom of Naples where they are born in great numbers, are called Tarantulas, which truly cause diverse and strange accidents in the people they bite; for some of those bitten sing, some laugh, some weep, some shout, some vomit, some sleep, some stay awake, some jump, some tremble, some sweat, and some suffer various other accidents, and act madly as if they were possessed. These effects cannot be explained except as proceeding from the diverse natures of these animals, although some hold that Tarantulas produce these different effects according to the day on which they bite, and also according to the hour. These are found in many places in our marshlands of Siena and in the Patrimony; but they are most abundant universally in Puglia, where they hide in the grain fields underground, where they often sting the harvesters who, not knowing

SECOND 139

Because of their "Pufanza," they do not have little boots on their legs. Of these I recall having seen some suffer greatly from the aforementioned accidents. But it is a remarkable thing that the venom of these animals is universally mitigated and overcome by musical sounds; for I have seen three or four of those attacked by various of these accidents be carried to where various instruments for dancing were being played, and immediately their afflictions would subside, and they too would dance most vigorously, so that no one would have thought them to be those who had been bitten by Tarantulas. But when the music stopped, they would return to their former state and fall back into the same accidents little by little. And so it is customary to have music played day and night continuously until they recover: for the prolonged sound ultimately overcomes the malice of the venom of these animals, even as in the meantime, while the music plays, they are given Theriac, Mithridate, and other things universally used against the bites of serpents and asps.

On Lizards. Chapter 58.

The head of the lizard, pounded and applied to the skin, draws out thorns, splinters, and everything else lodged in the members of the body. It draws out warts, calluses, and those kinds of hanging growths. The liver placed in the cavities of the teeth removes the pain. The whole lizard, opened and laid upon the stings of scorpions, eases the pain.

On the Sepa. Chapter 58.

The Sepa, which some call the Chalcidic lizard, drunk in wine, is a remedy against its own bite.

Lizards, very well-known animals, also lay eggs as serpents do, and are the greatest enemies of snails. In Arabia they are one cubit long, as Pliny wrote in the thirty-ninth chapter of his thirteenth book, and in India on Mount Nisa some are found to be twenty-four feet long, of colors ranging from rose to yellow and sky-blue. They are also found, as he wrote in the sixth book, on the Island of Capraria, which is one of the Fortunate Islands, in very large numbers and of great size. The Chalcidic lizards are not found in Italy, but according to report they are born in Libya and in Cyprus, where they live mostly among rocks. Regarding their form, he found various opinions; for some maintain they resemble our common lizards, and others that they are a species of serpent called Cerastes, or very similar to them. Nicander in this agrees with Dioscorides, that they resemble our lizards, and therefore wrote in his Theriaca: Beware of the Sepa, that is the Chalcidic lizard, an animal truly resembling the lizard. But Aetius in book thirteen wrote: the serpent called the Sepa is two cubits long, and being thick in front gradually tapers toward the tail, moves slowly, has a broad head and a pointed mouth, and is entirely spotted and checkered with white, and when it bites it kills in three or four days. Pausanias later, speaking of a certain prince of Arcadia, says that while he was hunting he was bitten by a Sepa, a serpent resembling a small viper, ash-colored and variously spotted, with a broad head, thin neck, thick body, and short tail: which always moves sideways like a crab. This is characteristic of the Cerastes. And so it is necessary to say either that some of these writers were mistaken, or that the Sepa is of two different kinds, and that some wrote of one and some of the other. But I will not fail to mention that in the region of Rome there is found a certain species of lizard all spotted on the back, called Terrantole because they live underground; which, being very venomous, I have more than once thought to be the Chalcidic lizards of Dioscorides.

On the Skink. Chapter 59.

The Skink is found in Egypt, in India, in the Red Sea, and in Lydia of Mauritania. The Skink is the terrestrial Crocodile of its own proper kind. Preserved in salt and nasturtium, they say that the flesh of its kidneys, drunk to the weight of a dram in wine, greatly inflames the desires of Venus. But drunk with a decoction of lentils and honey, or with lettuce seed and water, it has the opposite effect. Beyond this, the Skink is added to antidotes.

Although Dioscorides calls the Skink a terrestrial Crocodile, nevertheless those that are brought to Venice are marine ones from the Red Sea, and those of Egypt from the Nile, and although they resemble Crocodiles in shape, those brought to us are no larger than the largest lizards, and have white scales tending toward yellow, with a brownish stripe from head to tail. This the Crocodiles do not have, being by nature entirely black on their backs. Writing of Skinks, Pausanias said that some were found in Libya two cubits long. In the area of Vicenza there are a kind of small, black ones, which apothecaries often use in place of the marine ones when they cannot obtain others. But in truth I think they are of little value for the effects that the marine ones produce. He wrote of the Skin-

A — Pliny, in the eighth chapter of the twenty-eighth book, says that those from India are much larger than the ones brought to us from Arabia, and beyond praising their kidneys for aphrodisiac uses, he likewise praised the snout and feet, and their entire body when drunk as a remedy against arrow-wound poison. But the Skinks having called crocodiles to my mind — those aquatic creatures particular to the Nile — I say that they are very large and very wicked beasts, and greatly hostile to men. They grow (according to Aristotle in his books on the nature of animals) to a length of fifteen cubits, though Pliny says eighteen. The crocodile has no tongue, and alone among all animals it moves only its upper jaw, keeping the lower fixed. It has the eyes of a pig, teeth most cruel, which jut out from its mouth, very sharp claws on its forefeet, and skin so hard it resists every blow. By day it spends most of its time on land, and by night almost always in the water. Pliny writes, in the eighth chapter of the twenty-eighth book, that there are two kinds, the larger and the smaller. The larger is the kind already described here; the smaller are those he describes as always living on land among herbs and fragrant flowers. According to him, the teeth of the right jaw of the larger kind, tied to the right arm, are useful in aphrodisiac matters. The intestines of the smaller kind, which are very fragrant, are used to make a certain medicine called Crocodileo, very useful for ailments of the eyes. Mixed with water it clears away all blemishes of the face, such as freckles, pimples, discolorations, and similar conditions, making the skin very beautiful. They say that its bile surpasses all medicines for removing cataracts from the eyes and other humors that have thickened there, clouding the sight. The ash of the hide of both kinds, plastered with vinegar on limbs that must be cut or sawed, so deadens feeling that patients feel no pain at all during surgery with iron. The blood of one and the other, smeared on the eyes, brightens the sight. The heart of the crocodile (it is said) wrapped in the wool of a completely black sheep without any spot of another color, and carried on the person, cures quartan fever. The body of the crocodile, with the head and feet removed first and then boiled and eaten, cures sciatica.

Of Earth Worms. Chapter 60.

C — Earth worms, cut into small pieces and applied, heal wounds of the sinews. They cure tertian fever; and distilled usefully in ailments of the ears when cooked in goose fat. The oil of their decoction, dripped into the ear on the side opposite the pain, relieves toothache. Ground up and drunk with raisin wine, they provoke urination.

In Tuscany, earth worms are called Lobrichi, and are much used by modern physicians, cooked in oil, to ease pains in the nerves and joints. However, many apothecaries err in preparing their oil, for they put them to boil in copper pans over a charcoal fire, and in this way they quickly burn the oil and roast the worms. The true method is to make it in a water bath, in a well-sealed glass vessel, because in this way the humor and virtue are extracted without burning or roasting either the oil or the worms. With this method, when done with proper care, I have found it to be wonderfully effective against the pains of hot gout, first anointing the painful area with the oil, and then plastering over it the worms already cooked, pounded, and incorporated with an equal weight of litharge plaster, commonly called triapharmacon. For the same purpose, Pliny praises in the ninth chapter of the thirtieth book their ash plastered with honey and applied for three consecutive days, and likewise their juice when cooked with old oil. Furthermore, taking earthworms and washing them well with wine, then placing them in a well-sealed glass vessel in a water bath for a full day, they turn into a certain viscous liquid which by itself alone consolidates wounds of the sinews and intestines. But it works much more excellently when combined with artificial Balsam, described above in the first book in the chapter on true Balsam, or in its place with oil of larch resin or oil of dwarf pine; for in this way it marvelously consolidates in a short time all fresh wounds in whatever part of the body, except those of the head. Burned earthworms, powdered fine, are usefully given to drink with horehound water or wormwood water; or for those whose bile has overflowed, or composed in some confection with other appropriate things.

Of the Shrew Mouse. Chapter 61.

D — The shrew mouse, cut into pieces and placed over the wound, is a remedy for its own bite.

The shrew mouse (as Aetio relates) is similar in color to the weasel, but in size similar to common mice, and has a pointed snout like the mole, in which it has two rows of teeth both above and below, one set within the other, fine and pointed; and its tail is much shorter than that of common mice. Mention was likewise made of it

Nicander in his Theriaca says that if the Topo agno (shrew-mouse) passes over the track left by cart-wheels it immediately dies, and therefore the earth found clinging to cart-wheels is very useful against its bites. Of these animals, although they are found throughout all Italy, I myself have seen quite a number in the Anania valley within the jurisdiction of Trento. But there I never heard that their bites are venomous, as many ancient writers report. This perhaps occurs because of the nature of the place, as happens with Scorpions, which likewise do not harm you there, even though they do sting people, as has been discussed at length above in their own chapter.

On Mice. Chapter 62.

It is a most certain thing that mice, when they are kept in houses, cut up finely and applied as a plaster, cure the stings of scorpions; and that when roasted and given to children in their food, they dry up the excess saliva that flows in their mouths.

Mice are of various kinds, for they are found large, small, and medium; domestic, wild, and mountain. But speaking first of those that live in houses, and of those that frequent the fields, according to what Aristotle recounts in the last chapter of the sixth book on the nature of animals, these produce more offspring than any other kind of four-footed animal. He says a female of theirs gave proof of this: for having been shut up pregnant in a store of millet, upon opening the place thereafter, one hundred and twenty young mice were found together with the mother. For this reason, in some places they multiply so enormously in the fields without warning, that men who thought they would harvest the grain the next day have found it all eaten in a single night by mice. And indeed, were it not that in the countryside the rains drown great numbers of them in their burrows, and that pigs kill many of them, and foxes, wild cats, and serpents destroy many more, these animals would multiply so greatly as to drive people out of their houses, as they once forced certain peoples of Phrygia to abandon their cities. So great is nature's drive to reproduce in these animals that, as Aristotle also said, in a certain place in Persia, upon a pregnant female being opened by chance, young were found inside the bodies of the other female fetuses, before they had even been born. Some affirmed, as he also said, as a certain fact, that females become pregnant simply by tasting salt. The mice of Egypt are spiny, like our hedgehogs. A species of mice are also the Dormice, and therefore (as Pliny reports in the first chapter of the 36th book) Roman law forbade dormice to be eaten at dinner. But in our times they have been put to use as food, since men felt it would be a wrong to the palate and throat to let such fat animals go to waste, without considering that on account of their fattiness they ruin the appetite, generate gross and cold humors, and are hard to digest. Their flesh is useful medicinally when they are well fattened, for those who suffer from ravenous hunger, which physicians call bulimia. Mountain mice are finally large in body, like rabbits and sometimes larger, but lower in the leg. They have a head like a hare, but with such short ears that they can scarcely be seen to poke out from the head. They have fur almost like a badger, a short tail, and short legs, with grey forepaws armed with very sharp claws. These animals grow more in bulk than in length, and become marvelously fat. In the Trentino, in whose mountains, and especially on the Tonale, many of them are seen, they are called Marmotane, which word, corrected, means nothing other than Mus montanus (mountain mouse). These animals like to stand upright, as bears do, and often use their front paws in place of hands for eating. They have four very sharp front teeth, with which they bite cruelly anyone who displeases them. Kept in houses, even though their origin is in the peaks of the highest wild mountains, they nevertheless become quite tame, but they are very harmful, for they gnaw clothing and everything else left in the wrong place. In winter they willingly retreat into haystacks and straw, where they sleep for whole months, as dormice do. When frightened they cry out with thin, hissing shrieks, so that their voice sounds more like a whistle than anything else. Their meat is better eaten salted than fresh, because the salt, besides preparing their excessive moisture, removes much of the wild smell they give off. But whether salted or fresh, their meat is very hard to digest, weighs on the stomach, and stirs up excessive heat throughout the body; their fat, however, is praised for softening the nerves and joints of contracted limbs.

On Milk. Chapter 63.

Every milk generally produces good humors, provides good nourishment, and softens the body, even though it causes wind in the stomach and bowels. That of spring is more watery than that of summer, and that generated from green grass softens the body more. The white and uniformly thick kind is praised, as is that which, when dropped onto the fingernail, stays gathered on it and does not spread. Goat's milk is less laxative than the others, because goats for the most part feed on binding pasture, such as

A the oaks, the mastic trees, the olives, and the terebinths. Whence their milk is useful for the stomach. That of the Sheep is thick, sweet, and very fatty, and therefore not so suitable for the stomach. Cow's milk, Ass's milk, and Horse's milk are better for the body. Any milk produced from pastures where there is Scammony, Hellebore, Mercury plant, and Bindweed (as has been written of those of the mountains of Giustini) upsets the stomach and the body: and therefore the Goats that feed there on the leaves of white Hellebore, which newly spring from the ground, first vomit themselves, and then yield milk which, when drunk, causes vomiting and upsets the stomach. Any milk that is cooked restrains the body, and especially that in which heated marine stones have been extinguished. Milk commonly benefits all ulcers of the interior organs, and especially those of the throat, lungs, bowels, kidneys, and bladder. Fresh milk is given with raw honey, water, and a little salt for itching of the skin, for ulcerated pustules, and other bad humors. That which is cooked once is less windy. Cooked with heated stones until it reduces by half, it heals the ulcers of the bowels in cases of flux. Every milk has its Whey, which when

B separated is more effective for loosening the body. It is given in illnesses that we wish to purge without harsh or biting things, such as melancholic humors, epilepsy, leprosy, scabies, and pustules that appear all over the body. From any milk is made what the Greeks call Schiston: by boiling it in a new pot and mixing it with a branch taken green from the fig tree, and adding, once it has boiled three or four times, for every hemina of milk, one cyathus of honey-vinegar: for in this way the whey is separated from the milk. But it is necessary, so that while it cooks it does not overflow out of the vessel, to continuously wet the rim of the pot's mouth with a sponge full of cold water, and to submerge in it a silver setarius full of cold water. This Whey is then given to drink up to five mines, walking a little between each mina while drinking it. Beyond what has already been said, every fresh milk is good against all corrosive and burning poisons, such as blister beetles, pine caterpillars, salamanders, buprestis beetles, henbane, aconite, dorycnium, and ephemeron. For this purpose cow's milk is particularly valuable. Milk used as a gargle is useful for ulcers of

C the mouth and throat: and for preserving the teeth and gums, Ass's milk is especially valuable. The milk of Sheep, Cow, and Goat cooked with small marine stones stops the ulcers of fluxes, and likewise the straining of the bowels, used as a clyster by itself with barley water and spelt extract: for in this way it wonderfully softens and eases the pains of the bowels. It is also instilled into the ulcers of the secret parts of women. Human milk is the sweetest and most nutritious. This drawn directly from the breast benefits gnawing pains of the stomach, and those with consumption. It is usefully drunk by those who have drunk sea-hare poison. Mixed with frankincense gum it is applied to eyes that have become bloodshot from blows, and it is usefully rubbed on gout with opium and wax. Truly every milk is harmful to those with ailments of the spleen, liver disease, vertigo, epilepsy, diseases of the nerves, fevers, and headaches: except if that already mentioned for purging were given. Some say that the milk from the first birth of a Bitch, rubbed on, causes hair to fall out, and drunk is effective against deadly poisons, and causes delivery of creatures that have died in their mothers' bodies.

D Of Cheese. Chapter 64.

Fresh Cheese eaten without salt as food is nourishing, is useful for the stomach, and is easily distributed through all the members of the body. It builds flesh and gently softens the body. There is a difference in quality among cheeses, according to the milk from which it is made. Cheese cooked by boiling, then pressed and roasted, restrains the fluxes of the body. Made into a liniment it is useful for inflammations and bruises of the eyes. Fresh salted cheese nourishes less, diminishes flesh, is contrary to the stomach, and disturbs the interior organs. Old cheese restrains the body. The whey that comes from Cheese nourishes dogs very well. That which is called Hippace is Horse cheese, and although it is unpleasant in smell, it nonetheless nourishes effectively, corresponding in its proportions to cow's milk cheese. There are some who said that Hippace was the rennet of the horse.

Wool soaked in the same manner in vinegar and rose oil is good for pains of the head, the stomach, and all other parts of the body. Wool is also burned for another purpose: because its ash causes an eschar on ulcers, consumes superfluous flesh, and consolidates it. This ash is then washed for medicines of the eyes in an earthen vessel by pouring water on it and rubbing it vigorously with the hands; then the residue is allowed to settle to the bottom of the vessel, and the first water is gently poured off, and fresh water is added, and the ash rubbed again with the hands, and this is done so many times until, tasting the ash on the tip of the tongue, it only slightly constricts and does not bite. To extract the greasy residue from the wool, which the Greeks call ESIPO, it is done thus. The raw soft wools are taken, not treated otherwise with the root of the herb called Lanaria, and washed with warm water, squeezing out the residue as thoroughly as possible; and then this wash-water, placed in a wide-mouthed vessel, is raised up with another vessel letting it fall from a height, or else it is beaten with a stick vigorously enough to produce a tall foam, and then sea water is sprinkled on it, and the foam being beaten down, the grease that floats on top is collected and set aside in another vessel. This is done again to produce new foam and to sprinkle it again with sea water, and the grease is collected by the same method, and this is repeated as many times as necessary until, the grease being all extracted, the water no longer foams. The Esipo is then worked with the hands, squeezing out any impurity found within it, and finally all the water being drained off, fresh water is added and the Esipo is well washed and mixed with the hands until, tasting it on the tongue, it feels slightly astringent and does not bite, and appears to the eye bright and white; and being thus prepared it is stored in earthen vessels: but all this must be done in the hottest sun. There are some who, draining off the grease of Esipo, rub it in cold water with their hands in the same manner that women wash wax, because it becomes whiter this way. There are also those who take the squeezed residue from the wool and cook it in a laundry basin over a slow fire with water, and then collecting the grease that floats on top they wash it, as said, in water, and then strain it into a vessel of warm water covered with a piece of linen, and set it in the sun until it thickens sufficiently and becomes white. But there are others who change the water every two days and renew it. That which is taken from wool not purged with the herb Lanaria is praised, since it is not rough to the touch, breathes of the smell of raw wool, and when rubbed in a small basin with fresh water becomes white and has no hardness in it, unlike that which is adulterated with fat and wax. Esipo has the virtue of warming, filling, and softening ulcers, and especially those of the fundament and of the natural parts of women, together with melilot and butter. Made into suppositories with wool, it provokes menstruation and causes the delivery of dead children in their mothers' bodies. Mixed with goose-fat it is useful for ailments of the ears and of the genital members. It benefits the corners of the eyes that are being corroded, mange, and calluses of the eyelids, and chapping of the armpits. Esipo is burned in a new earthen pot until all the grease is consumed and it becomes ash. The soot of Esipo is also collected in the manner shown elsewhere, which is usefully employed in medicines for the eyes.

On the Rennet of Certain Animals. Chapter 67.

The rennet of the hare, drunk in wine at the weight of three obols, is useful against the bites of venomous animals, against stomach fluxes and dysentery, and likewise against fluxes of women, against blood congealed in the stomach, and against that which is vomited from the chest. The rennet of the hare, placed within the womb of women together with butter, immediately after they have been purged of their menses, helps them to conceive. Drunk, it kills the creature in the mother's womb; and if drunk after childbirth, it renders women sterile. The rennet of the horse, which they call Hippace, is privately useful against stomach fluxes and dysentery. Of the same nature are the rennets of kids, lambs, roebucks, fallow deer, ibexes, chamois, stags, calves, and buffaloes, all of which are effective when drunk with wine against aconite poisoning, and with vinegar against milk that has curdled in the stomach. But the rennet of the roebuck in particular renders women sterile, if left within the womb for three days. That of the sea-calf has the same properties as castoreum, and is believed to be wonderfully beneficial against epilepsy and strangulation of the womb. One can tell whether it is truly from a sea-calf in the following manner: take the rennet of any other animal, especially of a lamb, soak it in water, and let it stand a while; then take that water and put it into the rennet of the sea-calf: for if it is genuine, it will immediately dissolve; but if it is counterfeit, it will remain in its former state. The rennet of sea-calves is taken before they are yet able to swim. In sum, every rennet dissolves things that have curdled, and causes liquids to curdle.

The rennets of animals are very commonly known, and according to Galen in book ten on the Faculties of Simple Medicines, every rennet is sharp, biting, digestive, and desiccative; and although Dioscorides and others praised the rennet of the hare for blood that is vomited from the mouth, Galen did not approve of it, as he wrote himself. Some said that the rennet of the hare stanches blood that is vomited from the chest. But truly I have never known anyone who used it, nor have I myself wished to use it, since it is a sharp and biting remedy for an ailment that calls for a constricting remedy.

On Fat. Chapter 68.

The fat of goose and hen, fresh and preserved without salt, is truly beneficial for ailments of the natural parts of women; salted fat is harmful for this, as is fat that has turned rancid with age. Take as much as you wish of the fresh fat of any of these, and having carefully removed all the membranes from around it, put it in a new earthenware vessel of double the capacity of the fat; cover it well, and then place it under the hottest sun, where as it melts it is strained into another pitched vessel, until it is all consumed, and then stored in a cool place for use. Some others, instead of placing it in the sun, set the vessel in boiling water, or over a very gentle coal fire. Fat is also treated in another way: having first cleaned it of its thin membranes, it is minced and set to melt in an earthenware vessel, with a little ground salt sprinkled over it, and after straining it through a linen cloth, it is stored. This is usefully employed in medicines prepared for fatigue. The fat of pig and of bear is treated in the following manner. Take from these animals the freshest and fattest, which is especially that of the kidneys; and thus stripped of its membranes, it is placed in a good quantity of cold rainwater, in which it is thoroughly worked with the hands; and then by pressing it, the water is renewed several times. This fat, thus washed many times, is then placed in an earthenware pot of equal capacity, with enough water inside to come above the fat and cover it; and it is placed over a slow coal fire, stirring it continuously with a stick; and when it is well melted, it is strained through a cloth into water, and left to set; and thus separated from the water it is placed in another well-washed earthenware pot, and again covered with fresh water, and the process is repeated to make

Melt it slowly. Once this is done, remove it from the fire, and let it settle until the sediment sinks to the bottom; then place it in a stone mortar that has first been well cleaned with a water-soaked sponge. Let it set there, and remove all the dregs that are found in it; then, without adding any more water, return it to melt again, and once melted, pour it back into the mortar. When it has been cleanly removed, store it in a well-covered earthenware vessel and keep it in a very cool place. The method, beyond this, for treating and preparing that of deer, goat, and sheep is as follows. Whichever of these one chooses, wash it and strip it of its membranes, as has already been described for that of pig, and place it in a stone mortar so that it softens somewhat; then, adding water little by little on top of it, rub it by hand until no trace of blood or any grease floating on top can be discerned, but the fat is entirely white and gleaming. Once this is done, place it in a pot and pour over it enough water to cover it, then bring it slowly to melt over a low fire; stir it, and when it is well melted, strain it into the water. When it has been removed and set, return it to the same pot, freshly cleaned, to melt again, following the same procedure described above. The third time, melt it without water and strain it into a stone mortar dampened with water; once removed and set, store it in the manner described for that of pig. The fat of oxen, taken especially from the kidneys, is treated by removing its membranes; wash it well with seawater, then place it in a mortar and pound it carefully, always pouring that same seawater over it; and when it has finally been well softened, place it in a pot and pour over it enough seawater to cover it by half a good foot, and cook this fat until it finally loses all its own natural odor. Once this is done, mix in for every Attic mina of fat four drams of Tyrrhenian wax, strain them together, scraping off all the dregs found therein, and store the preparation in an earthenware vessel. It is then necessary to expose it to the sun for several days until it turns white and loses every unpleasant odor. That of the bull is treated as follows. Take it likewise fresh from the kidneys, wash it with river water, and having stripped it of its cartilaginous membranes, place it in a new earthenware vessel with a little salt, melt it, then strain it into clear water; and as it begins to set, knead and break it up vigorously, changing and re-changing the water until it is very thoroughly washed. Return it then to the original vessel and cook it again with an equal measure of fragrant wine; when it has boiled twice, remove it from the fire and let it cool in its vessel throughout the night. If in the morning it still retains some bad odor, place it in another new pot with an equal amount of the same wine, doing everything as already described, until it loses all its corrupt odor. Fat is also melted without salt, for certain defects and ailments in which salt is harmful; but prepared this way it does not become very white. The fat of the panther and of the lion is treated in this same way. The fats of calf, bull, and deer, and also their marrow, are made fragrant in the following manner. First strip them of their membranes, wash them as described many times before, and boil them in fragrant and aromatic wine in which there is no seawater at all. Remove them once cooked from the fire and let them stand the whole night. The following morning, melt them again in an equal amount of the same wine and then strain carefully. Once this is done, add to nine heminae of this prepared fat seven drams of fragrant rush from Arabia. But if one wishes to make it much more fragrant, add forty drams of the flower of this rush, and of palm, cassia, and fragrant calamus, equal portions of each; of aspalathos and of xylobalsam, one dram each; of cinnamon, cardamom, and nard, one ounce each. Pound all these things carefully, and having placed everything in a covered vessel, pour the same wine over it and bring it to a boil over a charcoal fire three times; then remove it from the fire and let it rest the whole night. In the morning, pour out the wine and add fresh wine of the same kind, letting it boil three times and rest in the same manner. The following morning, remove the fat, pour off the wine, wash the vessel again, clean the fat from the sediment and dregs, and melt it again

On Blood, Chapter 71.

The blood of the goose, the duck, and the kid is usefully employed in antidotes.
That of the wild dove, the turtledove, the common dove, and the wood grouse are suitable as a liniment for fresh wounds and bruises of the eyes, for blood that collects within them, and for those who lose their sight when night comes on. The blood of the dove particularly stops flows of blood proceeding from the membranes of the brain. That of the woodcock, the goat, the hare, and the deer, eaten fried in a pan, stops dysentery and other flows of the body; and drunk with wine it helps against the poisons called "toliichi." Hare's blood applied warm as a liniment removes freckles and other blemishes of the face. Dog's blood is also usefully drunk against poison and against the bites of mad dogs. It is said that the blood of the land tortoise drunk helps epilepsy, and that of the sea tortoise drunk with wine, hare's rennet, and cumin helps against the bites of venomous creatures and against the poisons of toads that might be drunk. That of the bull dissolves and softens hard abscesses when applied with a poultice. That of mares that have been mounted by stallions is used in corrosive medicines. It is believed that the blood of the chameleon, and likewise that of green frogs, anointed on the eyelids, causes the hairs to fall away. And it is believed that menstrual blood applied as a liniment or rubbed over a woman makes her barren. Anointed on, this relieves the pains of gout and erysipelas (sacred fire).

G Galen, in the beginning of the tenth book, speaking of the blood of various animals, though he does not entirely deny that some usefulness may be drawn from them according to the virtues assigned them by Dioscorides and others who wrote on the matter, nevertheless he demonstrates that for the most part what is written about the operations and faculties of blood is falsehood. For, according to what he says, it is truly false to believe that the blood of the owl frees asthmatics, and that of the bat, anointed on the nipples of young virgins, prevents them from growing, and likewise that anointing prevents hair from growing — just as it is not true that the blood of a lamb helps epilepsy, and that of the green frogs called Bresàti prevents the hairs plucked from the eyelashes from growing back. These last words demonstrate that the text of Dioscorides in this chapter on blood is corrupt and badly written, for here one reads that the blood of these frogs anointed on the eyelashes causes the hairs to fall, meaning rather, as one sees in Galen, that it prevents them from growing back after they have been plucked. Another corruption can easily be seen in the same chapter, where Galen says of the blood of stallions what one reads in Dioscorides about the blood of mares that have been mounted by stallions. Beyond this, Galen says that although many use the blood of the turtledove and the dove for broken and trepanned heads — for which nothing surpasses well-made rose oil — and others praise the blood of roosters and hens for flows of blood from the brain membranes, that of the land crocodile to strengthen the sight, and that of stallions for corroding and causing a scab, yet not wishing to appear curious or mad, I have never wished to abandon the many remedies I have tried in the past for all these conditions, to trust more in the blood of these animals than in those others, knowing that those who try them in these cases, condemning those who wrote of them, will find themselves very greatly deceived. The blood of the bull drunk hot is listed by authors among poisons, because it chokes whoever drinks it, as Dioscorides says in chapter six and Aetius in chapter thirteen.

D On the Dung of Animals, Chapter 72.

The dung of oxen that graze together in herds, applied fresh, soothes the inflammations of wounds: for this use it is wrapped in leaves, warmed on hot ashes, and then plastered onto the ailment. Applied in the same way, it soothes the pains of sciatica. Made into a liniment with vinegar, it dissolves hardnesses, scrofula, and bread-like swellings. That of the male ox, used as a fumigation, particularly restores the womb that has prolapsed from its place. The smoke of burned dung drives away moths. The dung of goats, especially those that graze in the mountains, drunk with wine, helps overflow of bile; and drunk with aromatic substances, it provokes menstruation and childbirth. On the contrary, dried and ground with incense and applied with wool to the female parts, it stops menstruation. Mixed with vinegar, it likewise stops any other flow of blood. Anointed with pure vinegar and honey, it causes hair and fallen hairs to grow back. It heals gout mixed with grease and applied. Applied cooked in wine or vinegar, it helps against snake bite and ulcers.

On Wax. Chapter 75.

The finest wax is that which is moderately reddish, not too greasy, pure, and fragrant, with something of the smell of honey. Pontic wax and that of Crete are praised as the best. Second in quality is that which is whitish and by its nature greasy. White wax is made in the following way. Choose the purest and whitest wax, scrape it finely, and place it in a new earthenware vessel; pour over it enough sea water to cover it, scatter a little nitre over it, and set it to boil. When it has given two or three boils, remove it from the fire and let it cool. Then take out the cake of wax and scrape it; if any impurities appear, return it to boil again in sea water, and having already boiled (as has been shown), remove the vessel again from the fire, then taking the base of a new earthenware vessel well rounded, dip it lightly into the cold fresh water, pressing it gently into the wax so that it touches only the surface of the wax above, so that a thin layer sticks to it and quickly sets and congeals.
B Then raising the base up, remove the ring of wax that has condensed upon it, and filling it again with fresh water, repeat this many times until all the wax has been removed. Then thread these little discs of wax on a string, leaving enough space between one and the next so they do not touch, and suspend them during the day in the sun wetting them with water, and at night in the moonlight, until the wax becomes white. But if anyone wishes to make it much whiter, let him do all these things but boil it more times. There are some who, instead of sea water, boil it in very strong brine three or four times, as has been taught, drawing it out into rings with a round and shallow dish that has a handle on top, then placing the rings on thick grass in the open sun, until it becomes white. They recommend doing this in spring, because at that time the sun does not heat too harshly, and the dew prevents the wax from melting. All wax has the property of warming, softening, and moderately filling and closing wounds. It is given in drinks for dysentery; and ten pills of wax taken by mouth, as large as millet grains, prevent milk from curdling in the breasts.

L Wax (according to Galen in book eight of his work on the Properties of Simple Medicines) holds roughly equal quantities of hot and cold qualities, and of moist and dry, together with a certain amount of a thick essence, and some viscosity. It can therefore not only dry, but accidentally moisten the body, by blocking the perspiration that occurs through the pores. But wax is more properly a vehicle for combining with other medicines, both hot and cold, than something to be used alone by itself, since it is in truth of little digestive power; yet it is not so completely without effect taken internally as it is externally, since it retains a certain amount of the warm digestive virtue that it had from the honey.

On Propolis. Chapter 76.

D One should choose that propolis which is red in color, fragrant, similar to storax, workable in its dryness, and which can be drawn out lengthwise so as to resemble mastic. Propolis heats and draws powerfully, and therefore extracts splinters and anything else embedded in the body. Its smoke inhaled is beneficial for chronic coughs, and applied to scabby skin it heals it. Propolis is found near the entrances of beehives, where the bees go in and out, resembling wax both in appearance and in nature.

Q Although, as Dioscorides writes, and likewise M. Varro, propolis is found in hives near the holes or vents through which the bees enter and exit, Pliny nevertheless in book seven, chapter eleven, maintains that propolis is the first foundation to which bees attach their combs and the wax, beneath which he says there are two other foundations, one of which we call pisocero and the other metyn. Galen, making mention of this in book eight of his work on the Properties of Simple Medicines, said: propolis is not so alterative as it is powerfully attractive. In its essence it is subtle, and therefore heats at the end of the second degree, or at the beginning of the third. Now since propolis, wax, and honey, the three things treated by Dioscorides in the three preceding chapters, are all materials made with wonderful artistry by bees, it is not without value to know, as Pliny recounts in several places in books eleven and twenty-one, that bees are of two kinds, namely wild and domestic. The wild ones are rough, hairy, and very irritable, but most efficient in their work, making much honey and much wax. The domestic ones are of two varieties, of which those praised are the short ones, varied in color, and compact in themselves, like

On the contrary, those that are long like wasps are little esteemed. Bees hate foul odors and flee from them as if they were deadly things; but pleasant scents carry far and often greatly annoy those who enjoy going about heavily perfumed when bees are present. Bees die, as some say, when they sting, because in leaving their sting they leave behind a great part of their entrails. Sick bees show it by not working and sitting in the sun outside their hives, waiting for others to bring them food. Those that die inside the hives are promptly carried out by the others with wonderful orderliness. Bees have a King who governs them, and every swarm has its own; nor do they swarm out of the hives unless the King departs first. When he leaves, the whole crowd follows and settles wherever he settles first. When their King dies inside the hive they do not carry him out as they do the others, but all remain in a state of melancholy, do not go out, do not pasture, do not work; gathering all together with a certain mournful humming around him, they pile themselves one on top of another over him — for which reason he must be removed from beneath them, otherwise they all die of hunger. Bees delight in the sound of metals and in having planted near their quarters thyme, melissa, roses, violets, lilies, cytisus, beans, peas, coriander, poppies, sage, rosemary, and melilot. Keeping them near cornel trees kills many of them, because the flower of that tree causes them a flux that destroys them, though in men that same flower stops bodily fluxes. Likewise they do not like to be where there are olive trees, since their flowers greatly annoy them; whereas keeping them near other trees is beneficial, both for their flowers where they may pasture and likewise for the convenience of settling when they swarm out in spring. Bees truly have great order and great governance in their operations, as Aristomachus of Soli diligently observed over thirty-eight years, always tending to bees with wonderful care. Their tasks are divided among themselves, just as we see tasks divided among men in the building of castles and palaces: those that go out are solely appointed to bring back honey and wax. Of those that stay at home to work, some build the cells, some polish them, some supply the material, some prepare it, and some in great order unload those that come in from outside. When all the seed of the bees is lost, one can make them breed again from a two-year-old bullock, in the manner that Virgil teaches in detail in his Georgics.

On Wheat. Chapter 77.

The most excellent Wheat for preserving the health of healthy persons is the new grain, that which has grown and ripened sufficiently and is reddish in color. Next best after this is that of three months, called by some Sitanion. Eating raw wheat generates long and round worms in the body. Chewed and applied to dog bites it is beneficial. The bread made from the finest sifted flour of wheat nourishes much more than that made from unbolted flour, which the Greeks call Syncomisto. That made from three-month wheat flour is lighter and more easily digested. This same flour kneaded with the juice of henbane is usefully applied as a liniment against flatulence of the bowels and against fluxes descending into the nerves; and kneaded with honeyed vinegar it removes freckles. The bran boiled in very strong vinegar and applied hot cures scabies and at the outset mitigates all kinds of inflammations. Boiled in a decoction of rue it resolves swellings of the breasts that come on after childbirth; it helps with viper bites and bodily pains. Leavened bread made from wheat flour, being warm and drawing, is useful for defects of the soles of the feet and especially for calluses, because it reduces them. Mixed with salt it matures and breaks small pustules and boils. Wheat flour of three months kneaded with wine or with vinegar is usefully applied as a liniment to the bites or stings of all venomous animals. Cooked in the manner of a paste and licked, it helps with spitting of blood; and cooked with mint and with butter it helps the cough and the roughness of the throat. The finest wheat flour cooked in honeyed water or in oil with plain water, spread on as a plaster, resolves all inflammations; and raw bread does the same when cooked in honeyed water, since it is softening and somewhat cooling, and especially when mixed with herbs or juices that aid the same purpose. Dry, hard bread eaten alone and with other suitable things restrains the bowels. Fresh bread soaked in brine cures old skin eruptions. The paste used to glue the pages of books, made from the finest flour and taken warm as a drink in the measure of a spoonful, stops the spitting of blood.

Wheat, so called by us Tuscans, is called in Lombardy "formento," from which for our daily sustenance we make — I say good — bread, for wheat bread is the most praised, the most nutritious, and the most pleasing to the taste of any other bread. Wheat therefore, to make the best bread, must be well ripened, and it must be...

A grown in rich soil, free from every weed, difficult to break, full, heavy, bright, smooth, of color nearly golden, and of three months age, when flour is made from it: for as Galen says in the first book on the Properties of Foods, it sometimes happens that wheat which looks fine from the outside appears to be well-filled, yet deceiving the eye it is soft and light inside. For in milling it produces much bran, and thus makes bran-filled bread, which not only does not nourish but fills the stomach with many superfluities. The flour most praised is that which is made from good wheat, not ground too fine, so that it retains coarse bran, and that which has not been ground too recently nor too long ago: for flour ground too fine makes bran-filled bread, flour ground too recently contains a certain unnatural heat imparted to it in the mill by the millstone, and flour that has been ground a long time mostly smells of mold, or dust, or some other disagreeable odor. To make an excellent bread, one should seek, beyond having good flour, good water for kneading — water that is clear, from good springs, tasting of neither mud nor any bad odor — adding just enough leaven so the bread will not turn sour. Once the dough is made and shaped, not too soft nor too hard, it is first kneaded and then worked thoroughly: then loaves of moderate size are formed, and when they have risen sufficiently, they are baked in a hot oven well swept of ash, and proportioned in size to the quantity of bread: for just as in a large oven a small amount of bread either dries out too much or burns, so in a small oven a large amount clumps together and bakes poorly. And although we in Tuscany do not put salt in our bread as they do in other parts of Italy, nonetheless according to the opinion of physicians, salt greatly benefits it. Wheat sown in fields readily turns to darnel when the season is very rainy and very cold, of which more will be said in its own chapter. The oil pressed from wheat passed between two moderately heated iron plates is commended by some for fistulas, for roughness of the skin, and for chapping caused by cold. Wheat applied externally, as Galen said in the eighth book on Simple Medicines, warms in the first degree, though it is neither desiccating nor cooling; it has some tendency toward looseness and obstruction. Wheat eaten cooked (as Galen himself affirmed from personal experience in the first book on the Properties of Foods) is difficult to digest, heavy on the stomach, windy, and very prone to causing vapors in the head.

On Barley. Chapter 78.

C Good barley is that which is white and well cleaned. Barley nourishes less than wheat: yet ptisan, because of the slippery humor it produces in cooking, nourishes much more than barley porridge. Ptisan made from barley is suited to all acute humors, to roughness of the throat, and likewise to ulcers: in this it is similar to that made from wheat, which nourishes the body more and promotes urination. Barley ptisan cooked with fennel seed, given as a drink, promotes milk: and though it promotes urination, and is cleansing, it nonetheless generates windiness and is harmful to the stomach; it ripens abscesses. Barley flour cooked with honey-water and dried figs resolves all abscesses, and mixed with pitch, resin, and pigeon dung, ripens hard swellings. It relieves pains in the side when applied mixed with melilot and poppy husks. Applied usefully as a liniment for intestinal flatulence with linseed, fenugreek, and rue. Kneaded with wax, liquid pitch, children's urine, and oil, it ripens scrofulous swellings. Mixed with myrtle berries and wine, or with wild pears, or blackberries, or husks of unripe pomegranate, it checks flows of the body. Prepared with vinegar and quince honey, it relieves inflammations of the joints. Cooked in very strong vinegar and made into a plaster in the same way as this same flour with oil and water, and applied warm, it cures gravel. The liquid pressed from barley steeped in water and then cooked with pitch and oil is maturing. That extracted from barley first steeped in vinegar and then cooked with pitch is good for catarrhs descending to the joints. The porridge made from barley flour checks the body and soothes inflammations.

Barley is no less common in Italy than wheat, and as Theophrastus recounts in the fourth chapter of his eighth book, several varieties are found, as can be seen in their grains and their ears. For the grains are in some varieties round, small, and gathered close together, and in others long and larger. The difference in the ears is that some have only two rows of grain, others three, others four, and others up to five and six. Moreover some ears are long and sparse, others short and dense with grain: some are tall and far from the leaves, others low and surrounded by them: so greatly has nature delighted in varying barley. There is likewise a difference in the color of the grains, some being found white and some pink, and the pink ones are believed to produce more flour than the white. One variety is grown in France, which they call hulless barley because it comes out of the husk clean when threshed, as wheat does. Barley that receives too much moisture, whether from the soil or from rain, when sown in the fields, will turn.

On Zitho and Curmi. Chapter 79.

Zitho, which is drunk, is made from barley. When drunk it provokes urination, but is harmful to the kidneys and nerves, and especially to the membranes of the brain. It generates flatulence and bad humors in the body, and causes people to become leprous. The ivory that is soaked in Zitho becomes workable for making all kinds of things. Made from barley in the same way is a drink called Curmi, which is used in place of wine, but it causes headaches, generates bad humors, and is harmful to the nerves. These drinks are also made from grain in the regions of Brittany and Iberia facing the west.

As can be gathered from Dioscorides, Zitho is clearly a drink made from barley and grain, similar to what is called Cerevisia, as Pliny shows in the last chapter of book twenty-two, saying thus: From grains is made a drink which in Egypt is called Zitho, in Spain Celia and Cera, and in France Cerevisia. Not very different from this is Curmi: for it too is made from barley, being grain steeped in water, and is drunk in place of wine. So one can easily say that the Zitho and Curmi of the ancients were not far removed from the Cerevisia, or Beer, which is used in our own times in the northern regions throughout all of Germany, Bohemia, Poland, Flanders, France, and other regions of Europe. Nor do I think one can say there is any other difference between Zitho and Curmi — although both are drinks made from barley and grain — except that they are made by different methods, or by allowing the barley and grain to cook and ferment more in one than the other, as is done in Germany and Bohemia with their beers. For although they are made from barley and grain, they nevertheless produce in various ways sweet, bitter, rough, cloudy, and clear varieties. In Bavaria, a province of Germany, they steep barley and grain with a decoction of hop flowers to make their beer — hops which they cultivate in their fields on trellises and on trees, just as we cultivate our vines. For, as they report, these flowers give a wine-like flavor to the beer and make it more pleasing to the palate. Beer makes one drunk if too much is consumed, just like wine, and its ill effects last longer than those of wine.

On Zea, or Spelt. Chapter 80.

Zea is of two kinds. One is a simple single-grain variety, and the other, which is called Dicoccos, meaning double grain, because it has two small grains joined together in two husks. This nourishes more than barley, and is pleasant in food. Nevertheless its bread nourishes considerably less than bread made from wheat.

The Zea described by Dioscorides is not what throughout all of Italy is called Spelta — indeed among us it has practically disappeared. But that Zea is the same as Spelta may be conjectured from what Dioscorides writes about it, making it of two kinds, namely simple grain and double — for both of these are found in Tuscany. Pliny furthermore, in chapter eight of book seventeen, says that Zea grew most abundantly in Campania, and was specifically called Seme there, which shows — since Zea was so plentiful in Italy — that it could easily have persisted there down to our own times. This being true, Zea can be nothing other than Spelta, which we in Tuscany privately call biada, following the practice of the ancients who called it Seme: for just as seme is a name common to all seeds, so biada is common to all grains. In some parts of Lombardy Spelta is called Alga, which further supports the view that Zea is the

A Spelt: because the Halica among the ancients was nothing other than Zea pounded and ground in wooden mortars. Speaking of Zea, Galen in the sixth book on the properties of simples said that in its properties it was midway between wheat and barley.

On Crimno. Chapter 81.

Crimno is coarser in grind than flour, and is made as much from wheat as from zea. From Crimno is made a porridge which nourishes abundantly, though it is digested with some difficulty. That which is made from zea is more binding to the body, especially when made from zea that has first been roasted.

I Crimno is nothing other than a grain, or a zea coarsely ground, which the ancients used to make porridge, which for a long time served them in place of bread, as Pliny affirms in the eighth chapter of the eighteenth book.

On Olira. Chapter 82.

Olira is a species of zea, but nourishes somewhat less than it. From it is made bread and porridge likewise.

Olira, as may be seen from what Dioscorides writes about it, though it is not sown in Italy in our times, is a species of zea, or spelt. And speaking of their properties, Galen said the same of Olira as of spelt, placing both of them in temperament midway between wheat and barley. Marcello Virgilio believed Olira to be the common rye used widely to make bread in Italy, especially in places closest to the Alps, and likewise throughout Germany. This shows that he did not properly consider Pliny, his familiar author, not noticing that Pliny wrote quite differently about Olira in the eighth chapters and about Rye, which he calls Ferraggine, in the sixteenth chapter of the eighteenth book, saying that Olira makes the sweetest bread, and Rye bitter and ugly, and useful only to the starving. In this same error fell Otto Brunfels the German, because in his treatise on all the simples of Dioscorides, he too says, along with many other foolish things, that Olira and Rye are one and the same thing. But beyond this I cannot help but marvel at Hermolao, Manardo, and Ruellius, men all truly most learned, in saying unanimously as with one voice that Olira is called Siligine by Pliny, even though he treated of both separately, as of two very different things, in the eighth, ninth and tenth chapters of the eighteenth book, where any candid reader may clarify the matter. For by Siligine he understands a species of grain of the highest excellence, from which was formerly made the whitest and lightest bread, and by Olira another sort of grain that makes sweet bread, which he calls there, as he called it in the thirty-fifth chapter of the twenty-second book, Arinca, and not Siligine, as all these men said, without any further consideration, not remembering besides that Galen himself, knowing that Siligine was not Olira, in the first book on the Properties of Foods, speaking of bread, said thus: the purest bread is that which by the Romans and all those subject to their empire is called Siliginis, because Silignis, which in Latin is called Siligo, is not a Greek word, nor do the Greeks have any other that corresponds to it. This Galen would not have said if Siligine and Olira were one and the same thing, since Olira is a Greek word. Wherefore if Olira and Siligine had been the same thing, he would certainly have said that the Siligine of the Latins was called Olira by the Greeks. Nor would he have affirmed that Siligine had no proper word in the Greek language. Furthermore, there have been some who firmly believed that the Siligine of the Romans is the common rye of today, not realizing that Siligine, though it may have been of various kinds as one reads in Pliny in the aforementioned chapters, was nonetheless a species of grain from which was extracted a flower of flour that made the whitest and best bread to be found in those times. Which is the opposite of what we see in the common Rye that we have in Italy today.

On Athera. Chapter 83.

Athera is made from finely ground zea, and is a food to be sipped, like a thin gruel, very suitable for children. It is useful in poultices.

Dioscorides explains for himself what Athera is, and so there is no need to say more, except that according to various other authors it can also be made from wheat, Olira, and starch. The Germans call it mosa, and use it to feed not only nursing infants, as we use cooked bread, but also at their own tables, made from flour, milk, and butter.

On Trago. Chapter 84.

Trago in shape is similar to Halica. It nourishes considerably less than zea, because it is very astringent, and for this reason is not easily digested in the stomach. Its nature is solely to bind the body.
