The Trago, which some liken to Farro and others to Halica, we truly do not have in our own time in Italy. But it is not so great a wonder, since as Pliny recalls in the tenth chapter of the eighteenth book, it had been brought to us from the east, just as from day to day various other plants are brought to us; and being a foreign seed in Italy, over the length of years its seed has been lost among us, having returned to its ancient homeland from which it was first brought to us.

On Vena (Oats). Chapter 85.

The Vena has its stalk divided by several nodes, in which, and in its leaves, it resembles grain. At its tops it has some offshoots resembling small two-footed locusts, within which its seed is contained, which in poultices is no less useful than barley. A gruel is made from it, which is used to check the body. Its pressed juice given as a drink is usefully administered to those who cough.

Vena is a grain known to everyone, and although it was produced by nature chiefly for horses rather than for men, nonetheless among the Germans it is eaten hulled in food, as we in Tuscany use rice and farro; and likewise they make a gruel from it which they call "mosa," in the manner we described in the chapter on Athera. Vena (according to what Galen relates in book six of the Faculties of Simple Medicines) is similar in its virtues to barley, and therefore when applied in poultices it digests and mildly dries without any harshness. Its temperament is slightly cold, it has some astringent quality, so that it can check fluxes of the body. And writing later in book one on the Faculties of Foods, he said thus: This seed is most abundant in Asia, and especially in Mysia, which lies above Pergamon, where it is sown more as food for horses than for men, though sometimes the constraint of scarcity and hunger forces people to make bread from it; but outside of times of scarcity, Vena is eaten cooked with sweet wine, or with grape syrup, or with honeyed wine. Moreover, as Pliny said in chapter 25 of book 22, the flour of Vena removes blemishes when plastered on with vinegar, and its bread plastered with rose oil and water softens swellings, and with honeyed water softens hardnesses.

On Rice. Chapter 86.

Rice is counted among the species of grain. It grows in marshes and in humid places. It nourishes moderately and checks the body.
Rice is very well known on the tables of all Italy. And therefore it would be superfluous to say here anything more than what Dioscorides and Galen write of it.

On Halica. Chapter 87.

Halica is made from zea, that is, from the kind which, having two rows of grain, is called Dicoccon. This nourishes more than rice, is more binding to the body, and is more useful to the stomach. Cooked in vinegar and applied with it, it cures scabies, causes corrupted nails to fall off, and treats the early stages of lachrymal fistulas. Enemas made from its decoction are good for the pains of dysentery.

The ancients were accustomed to making Halica from Zea, pounding it (as Pliny wrote in chapter 11 of book 18) in certain wooden mortars until its grain was well separated from the husks and chaff; then when it was cleaned it was pounded again, and thus pounded it was sieved and the fine was separated from the middling, and the middling from the coarser, and in this way they made three grades of it, mixing into it finally a certain white clay, which was brought from Pozzuoli to make it more tender and white. Of this I cannot but marvel, that at that time earth was mixed into food, and also gypsum: for the Halica that was brought adulterated (as Pliny says) from Africa and other places, in place of white clay was composed with gypsum, which when eaten blocks the passages of the spirits and suffocates men. Unless one were to say that, however much some mixed clay and others mixed gypsum into it to make it whiter and more tender, one would remove it by washing it very well first, when one wished to use it in food. For we see even in our own time that red earth is given to ginger to preserve it from spoiling, and it is washed away when one wishes to pound it. This leads me to consider what Galen says in book one of the Faculties of Foods: One must be careful when preparing the gruels of Halica that it has been most diligently washed, etc. For in insisting that Halica be washed so very diligently, it is a sign that by this means it was stripped of the clay and gypsum. That it was not in fact eaten with that clay or gypsum, the same Galen demonstrated by saying: Halica is a species of very potent grain, endowed with a viscous humor, whether it is cooked in water with honeyed wine, or in sweet wine, or in tart wine, or with oil, or with salt. This, cooked very well and then strained and seasoned, benefits those who suffer from irritation of the bowels, whether from bilious humors or from any other cause. For Galen would not have praised it so, had it been eaten without first purging it of clay and gypsum. But since in our own time this practice is no longer in use, I will leave aside the various ways of making Halica from various grains, as recorded by the more ancient authors.

On Millet. Chapter 87.

The bread made from millet nourishes less than all other breads. Its porridge binds the body, but provokes urination. Placed hot in small bags, roasted millet applied to pains of the body and every other part of the person is beneficial.

Millet, as one reads in Galen, book 7, on the properties of simple medicines, is cold in the first degree and dry at the beginning of the third, or toward the end of the second. For this reason it nourishes less than all other grains, dries out, and binds the body. Applied in warm little bags it resolves those ailments that do not require treatment with mordant substances. It likewise dries when applied as a poultice, but its flour is so fine and dry that it is hardly mixed into a paste with liquids. Consistent with this is what Galen wrote later, in the first book on the properties of foods — that millet bread is dry and crumbly, like sand and ashes, because no fatness or viscosity is found in millet. Its flour is eaten by laborers and peasants cooked in milk. We still see this done in our own day in the Valle Anania by woodcutters who fell timber and make charcoal for iron furnaces, who have sworn to me many times that they find no other food on which they can sustain such labor as this flour of millet and milk.

On Panicle (Panic grass). Chapter 89.

Panic grass is counted among the grains. It is similar to millet, and bread made from it is in its properties similar to that of millet, though it nourishes somewhat less and binds the body less.

Galen said, in book 6 on the properties of simples, that panic grass is similar to millet and in its properties gives little nourishment and is drying. It stops fluxes of the body as millet does, and when applied in warm cloths it cools and dries. Ruellius said that panic grass is called in Italy Melega. For in Lombardy Melega is the plant called in many places Sorgo, and in Tuscany Saggina. I know of no place in Italy where it is called anything other than panico or panizzo.

On Sesame. Chapter 90.

Sesame is harmful to the stomach, and whenever it is eaten it causes bad breath from the residue left between the teeth. Applied as a poultice it resolves hardening of the nerves; it is good for bruises and inflammations of the ears, for burns from fire, and for colic pains, and for the bites of horned vipers. Rubbed on with rose oil it relieves headaches caused by the heat of the sun. The herb itself cooked in wine does the same, and is especially useful for inflammations and severe pains of the eyes. From the seed of sesame an oil is made, which is used in Egypt.

The sesame seed used to make oil is well known in apothecaries' shops, but few apothecaries actually know the plant that produces it — for it is hardly ever grown in Italy, since it exhausts the soil remarkably, but is imported from Greece and the Peloponnese. According to Theophrastus, the stalk of sesame is quite similar to that of millet, though somewhat thicker and taller; the leaves are reddish; the flower is green; and it produces its seed inside certain husks similar to those of poppies. Pliny, in book 18, says that sesame comes from the Indies, where it is grown abundantly for making oil, which the Indians and Egyptians use in their food as we use olive oil. Sesame (according to what Galen said, in book 8 on the properties of simples) is considerably oily and viscous, and therefore it is thick and mollifying — as is the oil pressed from it — and, as the same author also said in book 1 on the properties of foods, the seed of sesame, being fatty, quickly satiates those who eat it. Eaten, it is bad for the stomach, is digested with difficulty, and produces coarse nourishment in the body. It is therefore clear that it can neither strengthen nor reinforce the stomach, just as other fatty foods likewise do not strengthen it. Sesame generates thick humors and therefore passes only with difficulty downward through the stomach.

On Darnel (Lolium). Chapter 91.

Darnel grows among the grain crops. Its flour made into a poultice with salt and radishes arrests putrid and corrosive ulcers, and likewise gangrenes. The same flour mixed with sulphur, wine, and vinegar heals spreading malignant sores and scabies. Cooked in wine with pigeon dung and linseed it resolves scrofulous swellings and breaks up those abscesses that ripen only with difficulty. Cooked in honey-water it is applied usefully to the sciatic nerve. Applied as a fomentation with polenta, incense, myrrh, or saffron, it helps women to conceive.

SECOND BOOK 165

Darnel, which in Tuscany we call Gioglio, is truly well known to everyone. It grows in the fields of barley or wheat, when the soil is too humid, or when winter is rainy and cold, as Dioscorides describes above when speaking of barley and grain. Although some say it grows in Spring, nevertheless, as one reads in Theophrastus in the seventh chapter of the eighth book, it grows at the beginning of winter with narrow, hairy, and thick leaves. Leonardo Fuchsius the German, in his celebrated herbal, believed that the true Darnel is the Pseudomelanthio, which many call Gittone or Ghiottone — something truly not only entirely foreign to the common opinion of the good herbalists of our time, but also to the history described by the ancients. And to prove this he cites a text of Theophrastus, which he distorts to his own purpose, since neither in Greek nor in Latin can one find the third part of what Fuchsius alleges on his own authority. But that the true Darnel is indeed that which not only today's physicians know, but every villager who works and sows the land, is demonstrated by Dioscorides in the chapter on the Phoenix in the fourth book, where he says that the Phoenix produces a spike similar to Darnel. This clearly shows that Darnel produces a spike, and not a head or calyx, as the Pseudomelanthio, the poppy, and similar plants do. In Tuscany we remove Darnel from the crops with great diligence to avoid the harm it does to the head, causing drunkenness and sleep. Darnel, according to Galen in the sixth book on the virtues of simples, is hot in the beginning of the third degree, and dry at the end of the second.

On Starch. Chapter 92.

Starch is so called because it is made without a millstone. The finest is that made from three-month wheat in Candia and in Egypt. Starch is made in the following way. The clean three-month wheat is soaked five times a day, and if possible also at night; and as it begins to soften, the water is drained off gently, so that the part already released from the grain does not flow away with it. When it is well macerated and tender, more water is added over it and it is trodden well with the feet; and after fresh water is returned to it, it is trodden again; finally the bran that floats to the top is removed with a sieve, and what remains, well purged of bran, is first strained, then set to condense on new tiles under the hottest sun, for the moisture thus becomes acidic. Starch is good for fluxes that come to the eyes, and for hollow and pustular ulcers of the same. Drunk, it stops spitting of blood; it soothes the roughness of the throat; and it is also added to milk and to foods. Starch is similarly made from spelt, which is macerated for one or two days, then kneaded very well with the hands, as one does with dough when making bread; and once done as described, it is dried under the hottest sun. This, though not good for use in Medicine, is nonetheless useful in other things.
Starch, as it is commonly called in apothecaries' shops in our time, is well known to all. The choicest and best, as Pliny says in the seventh chapter of the eighteenth book, is that which is light, white, smooth, and fresh. Although Dioscorides praised what was made in Candia and Egypt, Pliny praised even more highly that which in his time was brought from Chios, whence he believes starch had its origin. Starch is made from grain, Galen said in the first book on the virtues of foods, and it has the virtue of polishing and smoothing the roughness of the limbs; and in its properties starch resembles washed bread, though it is less nourishing, nor can starch warm as unwashed bread does. Moreover, as one gathers from Pliny in the twenty-fifth chapter of the twenty-second book, starch checks the body and fluxes of blood, and is given in pains of the bladder, somewhat warm, in a quantity of half an ounce with an egg yolk and its paste.

On Fenugreek. Chapter 93.

The flour of Fenugreek softens and resolves. It is good for hernias both internal and external, made into a paste with honeyed water cooked; and mixed with vinegar and saltpeter and applied as a poultice it reduces the spleen. Sitting in the decoction of Fenugreek is beneficial for ailments of the womb and the natural places of women, caused either by obstructions or by tumors. The mucilages of Fenugreek cooked in water cleanse the hair, dandruff, and ulcers of the head that weep. They are applied with goose fat as suppositories to soften and open the natural passages of women. Green Fenugreek with vinegar is good for ulcers and weaknesses of the same parts. The decoction of Fenugreek similarly benefits the straining pains which physicians call tenesmi, and likewise the foul-smelling fluxes of dysentery. The oil of Fenugreek together with myrtle oil cleanses the eyelids and the scars of the eyes.

A Fenugreek seed is very commonly found in apothecaries' shops. Its plant produces slender stalks and leaves almost like those of clover.
E It bears its seeds in small horns, and therefore Theophrastus called it Buceras. Fenugreek, according to Galen in book VII of On the Faculties of Simple Medicines, is hot in the second degree and dry in the first, and therefore when applied as a plaster to hot swellings, it aggravates and inflames them more. On Linseed. Chapter 94.

Linseed is commonly known. The seed of Linseed has the same virtues as fenugreek, for it too resolves and softens inflammations both internal and external: cooked with honey, oil, and a little water, or made into a paste with cooked honey. Applied raw it removes smallpox and other blemishes of the face. It dissolves swellings that arise behind the ears, and likewise hardnesses, when made into a paste with nitre and lye made from ashes. Cooked in wine it cleanses corrosive ulcers and favus. Mixed in equal quantity with nasturtium and honey it causes rotten nails to fall off. Prepared with honey in the form of an electuary it purges the chest by inducing expectoration and soothes the cough. Cooked with honey and pepper and eaten copiously it arouses venereal appetite. Clysters are made from its decoction for corrosions of the intestines and the womb, and to draw out hardened excrement. It benefits no less women who sit in its decoction for inflammations of the natural parts: let the decoction of fenugreek also be prepared.

N Linseed and likewise its seed are commonly known, and therefore there is no need to recount further history, save to say that the oil pressed from its seed is wonderful against spasm. It is good for softening hardnesses of the nerves and joints, and it wonderfully benefits all infirmities of the lower body, and for softening the hardnesses of women's natural parts. Washed with rose-water or water of water-lily, it helps greatly with burns from fire and for removing the scabs left by cautery. Some use it given by mouth at a weight of three or four ounces for pleurisy, of which I myself have seen wonderful results, especially when given fresh at the beginning of the illness. The seed of Linseed (as Galen pleases to say in book VII of On the Faculties of Simple Medicines) is almost hot in the first degree, holding a middle place between dry and moist. But because COTTON is also a species of Linseed, according to Pliny in the first chapters of book XIX, no mention of it having been made by Dioscorides or Galen, it should be known that its fresh seed is good for the cough and for the chest, it warms and softens, and increases semen. Furthermore, cotton that has been burned powerfully stanches flows of blood.

On Chickpeas. Chapter 95.

Chickpeas that are cultivated are good for the body; they provoke urine but generate flatulence; they produce good color, promote childbirth and menstruation, and generate much milk. They are usefully applied as a plaster cooked with bitter vetch for inflammations of the testicles and for those types of warts that resemble leeks. Cooked with barley and honey they are good against scabies and ulcers of the scalp that weep, against ringworm and against malignant and cancerous ulcers. There is another variety called Ram's-head Chickpeas. Both varieties promote urine; their decoction with rosemary is given in overflow of bile and for dropsy, but they are harmful to ulcers of the bladder and kidneys. There are some who, to cure warts and hanging warts, on the new moon touch each one individually with as many grains of chickpea as there are warts and hanging warts, and then tie them in a piece of linen and throw them behind their shoulders, believing that by doing so the warts and hanging warts will fall off. The leaves of wild chickpeas are similar to those of cultivated ones, but they have a sharp smell, and although the seed differs from the cultivated kind, it is nonetheless useful for all the same purposes.

S Chickpeas are a very well-known legume in Italy, and they are found in white, black, and red varieties. Those called Ram's-head according to Galen in book I of On the Faculties of Foods are black; he says they have an astringent virtue in chickpeas, and considerably more powerful than that of broad beans, so much so that there is a certain variety that breaks and crushes the stones that form in the kidneys. These are black and small and grow particularly in Bithynia, and are called Arietini. Pliny called them Arietini because they resemble the heads of rams in shape. The red ones he called venereal, and therefore some believe they are better than the others for generating sperm and for arousing venereal appetites. Furthermore, he also said in chapter 25 of book XXII that when wild chickpeas are eaten copiously they loosen the bowels, but they generate flatulence and pains in the intestines.

On Beans. Chapter 96. A

Beans cause bloating and wind, are digested with difficulty, provoke frightening and terrible dreams, are good for coughs, and make the body fleshy. They are of moderate temperament between hot and cold. Beans boiled in water and vinegar and eaten with their shells check dysentery and fluxes of the stomach. Used as food they are useful against vomiting. They cause less bloating in the body when the first cooking water is discarded. Green beans are more harmful to the stomach and more wind-producing. Their flour, either alone or mixed with polenta, soothes inflammations that arise in wounds, restores scars to their natural color, benefits milk production in the breasts, extinguishes their inflammations, and suppresses milk. Mixed with fenugreek flour and honey it resolves swellings that form behind the ears, furuncles, and likewise bruises of the flesh. Mixed with egg white, roses, and incense it reduces dislocated eyes, the uvula, and swellings thereof. Macerated in wine it treats suffusions and blows to the eyes, and to stop their fluxes, chewed beans without their shells are usefully applied to the forehead. These same beans boiled in wine heal inflammation of the testicles, and placed on the pubic area of boys prevent hair from growing there for a long time; they cure vitiligo. The bean pods applied as a liniment to places where hair has been removed make it grow back finer. These same pods mixed with polenta, dried alum, and old oil, and made into a poultice, resolve scrofulous swellings. Wool is also dyed with the decoction of beans. Half a bean without its skin, tied to the wound, stops the blood from the bites of leeches.

Beans are very good for everyone, and according to Galen in the seventh book on the properties of simples, they are not far from a drying and cooling temperament. Their pulp has a somewhat astringent virtue, as do their pods to a degree.

On the Egyptian Bean. Chapter 97.

The Egyptian Bean, which some call Pontic, grows abundantly in C Egypt, though it is also found in the lakes of Asia and Cilicia. It produces large leaves like hats, a stalk a cubit long and a finger's breadth thick, a rose-colored flower twice as large as that of poppies, which when it withers leaves behind seed-pods resembling a wasp's nest, in whose cavities the beans lie, all of them visible above the lid somewhat like bubbles. The Egyptian Bean is called Cibotio, meaning little box, because to sow it one must first place it in a trough of wet earth and then throw it into the water. The Egyptian Bean has a root thicker than that of reeds, which is called Colocasia, and it is eaten both raw and cooked. The bean itself is also eaten green. When dry it turns black and is larger than common beans. It is astringent and good for the stomach; and so its flour usefully replaces polenta against dysentery and stomach fluxes, and in that case it is also given as a porridge; though for such conditions it is most beneficial to drink three cups of the decoction of the pods. The green part found in the middle of the bean, which is bitter to the taste, is good for earaches D if first ground, then cooked in rose oil and dripped inside.

The Egyptian Bean is called Colocasia because that name properly belongs to its root. This plant, as Dioscorides says, grows abundantly in Egypt and is found in the lakes of Asia and Cilicia; but it is also found in our own times in Italy, as I have myself seen it several times in certain gardens in Venice and Naples, where it survives even when not planted in water. Speaking of this plant, Theophrastus in the tenth chapter of his fourth book said: The Egyptian Bean grows in swamps and ponds; its tallest stalk, which resembles a tender cane without nodes, is four cubits tall, though no thicker than a finger. Within, it is divided throughout by cavities like those of lilies, and at the top it has a head like a wasps' nest, in whose cavities (each cavity holding one bean) the beans are placed, up to thirty per head, somewhat visible from outside. The flower is red, similar in color to roses, and equally larger than that of poppies. The broad leaves float on the water, and the root, which is very large and spiny, is considerably larger than that of the reed, and is cleft inside, as is the stalk as well. The people of those lands eat it both raw and cooked. The leaves of the Colocasia (according to Pliny in the fifteenth chapter of the twenty-first book) are such

A large, like those of the personata plant, which grows throughout Italy on the banks of rivers and ditches. The Egyptians make from its leaves various kinds of drinking vessels in order to glorify the gifts of their Nile, which they greatly appreciate. The beans of Egypt (as Galen said in the first book on the properties of foods) are, insofar as they are larger than our common ones, more and in greater degree moist than the latter, and they generate more superfluity in the body.

On Lentils. Chapter 98.

LENTILS used frequently in food impair the eyesight, are hard to digest, harm the stomach, and swell it together with the intestines. Eaten with their husks, they constipate the body. The good ones are those that cook well and, when soaked in water, leave no darkness in it. Lentils have an astringent property. For this reason they constipate the body, but if they are shelled and then cooked very well, their first decoction being thrown away, the body passes them easily. Lentils cause terrible and frightening dreams, and are
B harmful to the head, the nerves, and the lung. Their property — which they have for stopping fluxes of the body — is reinforced by mixing them with vinegar, endive, purslane, black beets, myrtle berries, pomegranate rind, dried roses, medlars, sorb-apples, pears, tamarinds, quinces, chicory, plantain, or whole galls (which, after being cooked, are thrown away), or with sumac, which must be cooked in vinegar diligently, otherwise it disturbs the body. It is useful to eat thirty grains of shelled lentils in cases of stomach upsets. Lentils cooked and applied as a poultice with polenta relieve the pains of gout; and with honey they consolidate hollow ulcers, break down the eschar, and cleanse ulcers. Cooked in vinegar they dissolve hardnesses and scrofulas. Mixed with melilot, quinces, and rose oil, they cure inflammations of the eyes and of the anus. They do the same in major inflammations and in hollow ulcers of the anus as well, when cooked with pomegranate rind and dried roses with honey added. They are good against gangrenes that eat the flesh, together with sea water. They are likewise beneficial for pustules and creeping
C ulcers, for erysipelas, and for swollen glands applied to the face in the manner described above. Cooked in sea water and applied as a poultice on the nipples, they prevent milk from gathering inside and remedy its intolerable abundance.

Lentils are a most excellent legume in Italy, and although Dioscorides has written about them here quite fully, it is nevertheless worth knowing (as Galen writes in the eighth book on the properties of Simples) that they hold in their temperament a middle place between cold and hot, and are desiccative in the second degree. Furthermore, it is worth noting that Dioscorides says that lentils shelled of their husks and with their first decoction thrown away are astringent. Galen does not agree with this, saying in the first book on the properties of Foods that cooked shelled lentils lose their astringent property and become more nutritious than others, and then he said: Lentils generate bad and malignant humors, and therefore those who use them too much become leprous and cancerous, because these coarse and desiccative foods are easily converted into melancholic humors. For this reason lentils should not be used in ordinary food, but only medicinally, in fluxes, and where it is necessary to thicken the blood, as is appropriate to do in fluxes of women's menstruation. In which case lentils eaten are an excellent and powerful remedy.

On Beans. Chapter 99.

D Beans cause bloating and generate flatulence in the body, are hard to digest, and when cooked and eaten while green they soften the body. In addition to these properties, beans are useful for stopping vomiting.
Beans are common throughout all of Italy, and are found in several sorts, namely white, red, yellow, and speckled with various colors. The white ones, which have a grain smaller than all the others, are sown in fields, like other legumes. But the red, yellow, and those of various colors are customarily sown in gardens and in other places where one wishes to create shade in summer, because besides producing their fruit, they cover and climb up, winding themselves around pergolas, loggias, huts, and windows, shading the sun's rays, as do vines, hops, bryony, honeysuckle, and other plant species that willingly wind and wrap themselves around trees and hedges. For this reason, I do not think anyone would stray far from the truth who said that this species of bean is the Smilax of gardens written about in this same book by Dioscorides: so much correspondence is manifestly visible there. And therefore I would say that Marcello Vergilio the Florentine is manifestly in error, being too eager to correct Hermolao, in saying that it is not possible for a legume to grow so tall.

...to grow and cover huts with its leaves and drape over pergolas: for it truly contradicts this opinion of his, not only based on the authority of Dioscorides, which is against him, but also on what one can see every day in the gardens throughout all of Italy. Furthermore, I do not believe one could be so greatly mistaken in thinking that the garden Smilax is nothing other than those Fagioli, which were described as Dolichi by Theophrastus in the third chapter of the eighth book of the History of Plants, and by Galen in the first book on the Properties of Foods, and likewise in the first book of Paul of Aegina: for, as we shall more amply explain (God willing) in the chapter on garden Smilax, the Dolichi are not that legume called Rouiglione in Lombardy, and Arabeia in the Trentino region, similar to peas, as Manardo of Ferrara would have it: for Galen wrote of Arabeia under the name of Ochrus, as is clearly seen in the passage mentioned above, and in this place Dioscorides wrote of white beans, not of Arabeia, as Manardo would have it; and in the chapter on Smilax he speaks of those of various colors.

On the Bitter Vetch. Chapter 100.

The Bitter Vetch (Eruo) is known to everyone. It is a small and slender plant, with narrow leaves, and it produces its seed in pods, from which a flour is made, called Eruina, used in medicine. The Bitter Vetch when eaten aggravates the head, disturbs the stomach, and causes blood to be passed in urine; when cooked it fattens oxen. The flour of the Bitter Vetch is made in the following way: the largest and whitest grains are selected, and after being put into water they are mixed, and left to swell and become moist; they are then fried until the husks break open; and after being thoroughly dried they are milled, and the flour, sifted through a fixed sieve, is stored away. This flour softens the body, promotes urination, and improves one's color, although when eaten or drunk in great quantities it causes a flux of blood through the body and through the bladder with pains in the bowels. Together with honey it purges ulcers; it extinguishes freckles, and cleanses infections of the skin of the face, and blemishes all over the body. It arrests ulcers that spread and creep, restrains hardnesses and gangrenes, and resolves hardnesses of the breasts; it breaks up carbuncles, and heals favus and ulcers that the Greeks call theriomata. The flour of the Bitter Vetch macerated in wine, and applied externally, cures bites from humans, dogs, and vipers; and with vinegar it mitigates the pains of urination, bodily pains, and the straining efforts called by the Greeks tenesmus. Fried in the quantity of a walnut, and eaten with honey, it suits consumptives who have no appetite for food. Its decoction benefits inflamed tonsils, and the itching of the whole body when used as a fomentation.

The Bitter Vetch is commonly called in apothecaries' shops Orobo, and so the Greeks also call it. But what is brought from Alexandria to Venice, which is almost similar to the Vetch, is in truth a different seed from the true Orobo, which grows and is sown abundantly in Tuscany. We call this mocho; its plant resembles that of the pea, but is shorter, and its leaves are quite similar to those of the chickling vetch. The flowers are likewise similar, but red. The pods, where the grains are, correspond similarly to those of the peas, but rounder and thinner. The color of the grains in some plants is pale, in some white, and in some red. But perhaps not knowing this, Brasavola thought that the Eruo was the Rouiglione, called by Galen, Theophrastus, and Paul, Ochrus, in which one feels no bitterness at all, nor does it, however much eaten in large quantities, cause blood to be passed in urine, as Dioscorides and Galen wrote of the true Orobo. The Orobo also grows by itself among the grain crops, but being recognized by few, it is considered a species of vetch. It should further be noted that although Dioscorides selects the whitest grains for making the flour, Galen in the first book on the Properties of Foods maintains that the white is far less useful medicinally than the red and the pale. The Orobo (according to what he further said in the eighth book on the Properties of Simple Medicines) is hot in the first degree and dry at the end of the second degree, and certainly the more bitter it is, the more cleansing, incisive, and opening in its operations. Taken by mouth with honey, it cleanses the chest and lungs of phlegm and other thick humors.

On Lupins. Chapter 101.

Domestic lupins are known to everyone. Licking the flour of lupins with honey, or drinking it, expels worms from the body. Lupins soaked in water and eaten, even when still bitter, do the same. For the same purpose, with the same benefit, their decoction is drunk with rue and pepper. This is why it also benefits those who suffer from complaints of the spleen. The decoction of lupins is usefully applied to gangrenes, and to the ulcers the Greeks call theriomata, to the itch when it is starting, to vitiligo, to the outbreaks of pimples, to ulcers of the head that run, and to blemishes of the face and skin. This same preparation, together with myrrh and honey, applied to the private parts...

A [for women used as pessaries], provokes menstruation and childbirth. The flour of Lupins softens the skin and reduces bruising. Made into a paste with water and polenta, it eases inflammations; with vinegar, it treats sciatica and boils. Lupins cooked in vinegar and applied as a poultice dissolve scrofulous swellings and break up carbuncles. Cooked in rainwater until they lose their bitterness, they cleanse the face; and cooked with the root of Black Chameleon, they cure the mange of four-footed animals, when washed with the warm decoction. The root of Lupins cooked in water and drunk provokes urine. Lupins soaked and sweetened in water, ground and drunk with vinegar, relieve stomach complaints and stimulate appetite. There are also wild varieties similar to the domestic ones, and although they are smaller, they are nonetheless useful for all the same purposes as the domestic ones.

Lupins are known to everyone. They are sown widely in Tuscany to enrich the fields, where wild ones grow in infinite numbers in May throughout the countryside, flowering in a reddish color. The domestic ones are sweetened in Italy and eaten almost as a pastime, just as many other fruits are eaten. Lupins (according to Galen in the first book of the Properties of Foods) when eaten sweetened are hard to digest: because their substance is hard and earthy. For this reason they generate gross and raw humors in the body.

Of Turnips. Chapter 102.

The root of the domestic Turnip, when cooked, nourishes, causes bloating, stimulates desire, and generates soft flesh. Baths made from their decoction are useful for gout and swollen glands, and the same root applied as a poultice serves the same purpose. Placing rose oil and wax inside a hollowed-out Turnip and setting it on hot embers until it melts produces a good ointment for ulcerated swellings. The tops or shoots of Turnips, boiled and eaten as food, provoke urine. The seed is used in antidotes and theriac medicines, especially in those called anodyne, which relieve pain. Drunk, it is beneficial against poisons and stimulates desire. Turnips preserved in brine, though less nourishing, when eaten nonetheless stimulate the appetite. The wild Turnip grows in fields up to about a cubit high. It is branched and smooth on the tops and leaves, which are about a finger's length long or sometimes more. It produces seeds in pods, which when opened reveal inside other smaller pods similar in shape to little heads, within which the seed is fine, black on the outside and white within. It is used in those medicines employed to improve the complexion of the face and of the whole body, and especially in those made of lupin flour, grain, bitter vetch, and darnel.

Turnips are very common in Italy, and especially in Lombardy, where they are mostly sown in fields immediately after the grain is harvested in June and July, and gathered ripe in October. There are three varieties of domestic turnip: the flat, the long, and the round, although Pliny in chapter 13 of book 18 says that the long ones are the wild variety. It is truly no small miracle of nature that from so tiny a seed there should grow in three or four months such a large root: for in Savoy (as they say) some are found that weigh hundreds of pounds. I myself have seen in the valley of Anania in the jurisdiction of Trento long ones of purple color weighing thirty pounds and more. In Lombardy, and especially near the Alps, where grain is not very abundant, Turnips are very useful both to men and to livestock, and it will therefore not be amiss to say that those especially which are sown in summer can be preserved from lice and caterpillars, which often devour them entirely, by mixing a good deal of soot with the seed, or by first soaking the seed for one night in the juice of Houseleek. This Columella affirms as a proven remedy. Of the wild variety, they grow abundantly in the fields throughout Tuscany on all the nights assigned to them by Dioscorides. The seed of the Turnip, according to what Galen said in book six of the Properties of Simple Medicines, increases sexual potency, since it generates windy spirits, and the root is hard to digest, causes the body to bloat, and generates semen. And in the second book of the Properties of Foods he said: Turnips well cooked do not lubricate nor bind the body, but they generate gross humors, and it is therefore no wonder that those who eat many of them accumulate gross humors in the veins when they do not digest them perfectly. Cooking them well greatly reduces the harm they do when poorly cooked to the stomach and body.

Of Navews. Chapter 103.

The root of Navews, cooked and eaten, bloats the body and nourishes little. Its seed drunk diminishes the strength of deadly poisons, and is therefore used in antidotes. The root of Navews is preserved salted.

On the Raphanus, which the Romans call Radish. Chapter 104.

The root, which the Greeks call Raphanus, is warming and generates flatulence; it is pleasant
to the taste but contrary to the stomach; it causes belching, promotes urine, and lubricates the body,
when eaten after a meal, because in this way it aids digestion. But when
eaten before a meal it suspends the food upon itself, and for this reason it is given to provoke vomiting before
eating. The Radish sharpens the senses. Eaten boiled it is usefully taken against chronic cough and against
the thick humors that collect in the chest. Its rind, drunk with honeyed vinegar, causes
vomiting more effectively. Applied as a poultice it is useful for those with dropsy B
and for those who suffer from disorders of the spleen. Combined with honey it removes bruises, stops corrosive
ulcers, and helps against the bites of vipers. It restores fallen hair; and combined with darnel flour it removes
freckles. Drunk or eaten it is effective against harmful fungi, and it promotes
menstruation. It also causes the expulsion of its own seed, promotes urine, and when drunk with vinegar it reduces
the spleen. Applied with vinegar in the form of a poultice over cancers, it scarifies them most effectively.
Cooked in honeyed vinegar it is usefully used as a gargle against throat ailments; and drunk
with wine it helps against the bite of the horned viper. The wild Raphanus, which the Romans
call Armoracia, produces leaves similar to the cultivated variety, but more similar to those of Lettuce. It has a
slender, tender, and somewhat sharp root. The leaves and root are cooked in food like other
herbs. The root has the virtue of warming and promoting urine, though it warms to
excess.

We in Tuscany commonly call the Raphanus Radice, although in other parts of Italy it is called Rauanello. As for the wild variety, the Romans still use its proper name: for in Rome the wild radishes are called C
Ramoracci, but they somewhat contradict the text of Dioscorides in being, as experience shows,
hard and not tender, as he says. The Radishes, according to Galen in book viii of the Properties of Simple Medicines, are warm in the
third degree and dry in the second, whereas the Ramoracci exceed both these degrees. And in the third book
of the Properties of Foods he said that after a meal radishes cannot be eaten without harm, even though some physicians
and other foolish men claim from experience that they are beneficial. This contradicts Dioscorides considerably. One can tell
whether radishes are more or less sharp, without tasting them, from their leaves: for the smoother they are,
the less sharp they are.

On the Skirret. Chapter 105.

The Skirret is known to all. Its boiled root is agreeable to the taste, useful to the
stomach, promotes urine, and stimulates appetite.

There have been some who truly believed that the Skirret is that variety of white Charote which in the D
S Trentino region is eaten in soups, as turnips are eaten. But what Pliny writes in chapter 5 of book 19 makes it clear that these people are mistaken,
for he says that the Skirret has a hard stalk inside the
root, resembling a nerve, which is removed before eating it, and that this root is somewhat bitter
in taste. This is not found in white Carrots, which have no nerve inside, and in tasting them
one perceives sweetness rather than bitterness. That the Skirret is likewise somewhat bitter is confirmed by Galen in book
viii of the Properties of Simple Medicines, where he says: the root of the Skirret cooked is agreeable to the stomach, and promotes urine,
warms in the second degree, is bitter, and mildly astringent. These characteristics show that there is no small difference between
the Skirret and the white Carrot. And it should be known that the Skirret does not grow or get sown in Italy, whereas in Germany
along the River Rhine it is sown very abundantly. A great quantity of it is brought to Mainz from Tincao, a place
under its jurisdiction. The Skirrets are about a good span long, of quite corresponding thickness, with a stalk in the middle, somewhat
bitter, and yellow in color, which is why in that country they are called yellow Rapes. The roots of the Skirret truly
resemble the domestic Parsnip in shape, color, leaves, and flower, although they are much more
pleasing to the taste. For this reason (as Pliny reports in the passage mentioned above) since Tiberius Caesar greatly favored the Skirret, they
were brought to him every year from Germany, from the fortress of Gelduba situated on the Rhine.

A On Lapathum, or Rumex. Chapter 105.

There are several species of Rumex, or Lapathum. Among them, the one called Sharp Lapathum grows in marshy places with stiff, pointed leaves. Another species also grows in gardens, quite different from that one. A third species is found as a small wild plant, resembling Plantain, soft and spreading along the ground. The fourth species is called by some Oxalida, from its sour flavor, and by others Anaxirida, or Wild Rumex. Its leaves resemble those of the third wild species, which has short leaves like Plantain. The stalk of this one is not too large; the seed is pointed, red in color, and sharp in taste, growing at the top of the stalk and its small branches. All species of Rumex, eaten cooked, soften the body. Applied raw, mixed with rose oil and saffron, they dissolve the swellings called melicerides. The seed of the wild, the sharp, and the Oxalida species is usefully drunk in water or wine against dysentery, stomach fluxes, stomach troubles,
B and scorpion stings. Indeed, if someone has previously drunk the seed and is afterward stung by a scorpion, he feels no harm. The roots of all Rumex species, raw or cooked in vinegar, applied as a plaster, cure scabies, impetigo, and rotting nails, but one must first rub the spot in the sun with nitre and vinegar. A decoction of Rumex, used to bathe in, cures itching of the whole body. Their decoction in wine, used as a mouth rinse, helps toothache, and similarly relieves earache when dripped inside. Rumex boiled in wine and applied as a plaster dissolves scrofula and abscesses that appear near the ears; cooked in vinegar, they reduce the spleen. Some people, to dissolve scrofula, carry the roots tied around their neck. The roots of Rumex, ground and applied to women's private parts, stop their excessive flows; drunk cooked in wine, they help with overflow of bile, break bladder stones, promote menstruation, and treat scorpion stings. What the Greeks call Hippolapathum is large, grows in marshes, and has the same virtues as all the other Rumex species mentioned above.

C In Tuscany Lapathum is commonly called Rombice, and although in our times it is not customary to plant Rombice in gardens, it grows there on its own with all the characteristics that belong to the domestic kind. Dioscorides calls Sharp Lapathum that which grows in marshy and watery places — not because it is sharp and sour in flavor, as the Oxalida is (which we commonly call Acetosa, i.e., sorrel), but because it has pointed leaves: for the Greek word oxy sometimes means sharp with respect to taste, and sometimes pointed with respect to shape, just as the word "acuto" in our language also means both things. Avicenna, not having noticed this, calls every Lapathum Acetosa, as does Seragione, thinking that Dioscorides meant the flavor when he described the shape of the leaves of the first species of Lapathum. Pliny, in chapter 21 of book 20, equated the domestic kind with that which grows in marshy places with stiff and pointed leaves, even though Dioscorides says the opposite. The Oxalida is nothing other than what we call Acetosa (sorrel), of which, although Dioscorides does not mention it, two species are found — the greater and the lesser. The greater is the one described here by him among the Lapathum species; but the lesser has arrow-shaped leaves, tender, smooth, reddish, full of moisture, and much more sour in taste than those of the greater species. The seed is similar in both, except that of the lesser is somewhat smaller. Moreover, the Hippolapathum — I have seen it grow not only in marshy places with large leaves and tall stalks, but also on mountains where the soil is thick and soft, resembling in every way that new plant now kept in gardens as Rhubarb. Galen wrote about Rumex in book 7 of his work on the Properties of Simples, saying: Lapathum has a moderately digestive virtue. In the Oxylapathum it is mixed: for while it has digestive power, it also has repercussive power. The seed is manifestly astringent, especially that of the Oxylapathum, so that it cures dysentery and other fluxes. Furthermore, the Oxylapathum that grows in marshes has the same virtues as those described above, but less powerful.

On Lassana. Chapter 108.
Lassana is a wild herb, more nourishing than Rumex, and more useful to the stomach. Its leaves and stalks are cooked in food.

Although Lassana is counted here by Dioscorides among herbs eaten as food, he nevertheless described none of its physical features, perhaps because in his time and country it was an herb known to everyone.
Which is not the case today in Italy. We will therefore say, together with Pliny in book 20, chapter 7, that Lassana is a

There is a species of wild Cabbage, a foot high in its stem. Its leaves are rough and similar to those of the Nagoni, but it produces a whiter flower. This plant grows in Tuscany, and in many places throughout Italy abundantly in uncultivated fields, although it is not used in our time either in food or in medicine. On Blite. Chapter 108.

Blite is eaten like other garden herbs. It has no use in medicine, since it only softens the body.

Blite is of two kinds, namely red and white, and both grow in gardens and in fields. The red produces a stem red like coral, though as it grows it becomes ever darker, as one likewise sees happening in the leaves, which are not unlike those of the amaranth, which we in Tuscany call the velvet flower. The white has somewhat broader leaves, but is otherwise in every way from color onward similar to the red. It produces its seed along the stem, and along the branches near the origin of the leaves, in small clusters, similar to that of wild panic-grass. Both kinds grow abundantly in the Trentino region, and are commonly called Biedoni. Some people use them in food, first boiled and then fried in a pan with butter, garlic, and verjuice. Although sometimes (as I have myself seen) such food provokes vomiting, abdominal pains, and also looseness of the bowels, stirring up the cholera. And so Pliny said in chapter twenty-two of book twenty: Blite is an insipid herb, which so disturbs the stomach that in some people it provokes cholera. Blite is (as Galen records in book six on simple medicines) cold and moist in the second degree. And so he also said in book two on the properties of foods: Blite is moist and watery, and therefore besides the oil and brine with which it is dressed in cooking, vinegar is conveniently added. For otherwise it harms the stomach.

On Mallow. Chapter 109.

There are two species of Mallow, one domestic and one wild. The domestic is more suitable for eating in food than the wild, though it is useless to the stomach. It softens the body, but its stems do so much more. Mallow is useful for the internal organs and for the bladder. Its raw leaves chewed with a little salt, and made into a plaster with honey, cure lacrimal fistulas, but afterward in sealing the scar they are used without salt. They are likewise useful applied in this way against the stings of bees and wasps; and so whoever anoints themselves with raw crushed mallow together with oil will not afterward feel the stings of such insects. Made into a plaster with human urine it treats dandruff and sores of the head that suppurate. The leaves of Mallow boiled and ground, and applied with oil, heal burns from fire and sacred fire (erysipelas). Sitting in its decoction softens the hardness of the private parts of women; and making enemas with it benefits the irritation of the bowels, the seat, and the womb. The decoction of Mallow made together with its roots, drunk, is beneficial against all deadly poisons, but it is necessary that those who drink it continually then vomit it up. It is likewise useful against the bites of spiders called phalanges, and it promotes milk. The seed drunk in wine together with that of wild Lotus eases the pains of the bladder.

Mallow is one of the most common and well-known herbs to be found among plants. It is found in several species. For what grows as a tree is nothing other than common Mallow drawn up by artificial cultivation, as Theophrastus records in chapter nine of the first book on the history of plants, saying thus: There are some plants which by cultivation become different and move away from their natural state, as is that Mallow which grows tall and transforms into a tree. This does not in truth happen over a long time, but in six or seven months, so that it can in this way grow to the height and thickness of a spear-shaft. For which reason its stems are conveniently used as walking sticks, though with more time they grow much larger. There is likewise a species of Mallow which, being now made common in all the gardens of Italy, produces its flowers red, and sometimes white, dense with leaves and large like roses, though poorly endowed by nature with fragrance; which, if they corresponded to the nose as their form and their purple color correspond to the eye, would truly rival the roses. Writing of Mallow in book two on the properties of foods, Galen said that it cools slightly, because it contains within itself a gentle warmth. As for the wild mallow and its species, since Dioscorides has made particular chapters on them in book three, there is no need to speak of them here, following the order that they be treated there afterward.

On Orache. Chapter 110.

Orache is a well-known garden herb. It comes in two kinds, namely wild and domestic. It is eaten boiled like other pot-herbs, and thus it softens the body. Applied both raw and cooked it resolves swellings. Its seed drunk with honeyed water cures those in whom the bile has overflowed.

A Atriplice [orache] is not sown in the gardens of Tuscany, though in Lombardy it is sown in great abundance in March and at the beginning of April. It is called in some places in those regions Trepese, in others Reppese, which is nothing other than its proper Latin name corrupted into the vernacular. It is used most often to make pies in the Lombard style, mixed with bundles of herbs, butter, and eggs. There is no herb that springs up or grows faster in gardens than this one; for within fifteen or twenty days of sowing, it grows large enough to be eaten in food. It produces leaves that are broad near the stalk and pointed at the tip, like an arrowhead, fleshy and full of moisture, more yellowish than green in color. The stalk, which is more often than not reddish, grows with many branches to a height of three or four cubits, along which the seed grows in certain flattened little pods similar to those of nasturtium, but considerably larger in form. Atriplice is used in food throughout the entire month of May. For as quickly as it springs up, so quickly does it age and lose the tenderness of its leaves. The opinion of those who believe that Atriplice and Spinach are one and the same plant is truly vain; for Spinach is a new herb, unknown and unwritten of, except by modern authors, though Manardo of Ferrara goes so far as to suspect that both Atriplice and Spinach are species of Chrisolachano. This does not satisfy me; for Chrisolachano in Greek means in Latin aureum olus, that is, golden herb — a quality which well suits Atriplice but does not suit Spinach, which in its leaves, stalk, flower, and seed is always green. Beyond this, wild Atriplice grows in forests and fields with all the same characteristics as the cultivated kind, except that its leaves are whiter. Atriplice (according to Galen in the sixth book on the properties of simples) is moist in the middle of the second degree and cold in the first, and when eaten, being very lubricating, it passes quickly through the body. Its seed is also an alterative, and is therefore useful against overflow of bile caused by obstruction of phlegm. Serapion reports that Rasis saw a man who, having drunk two drams of this seed, vomited and evacuated his bowels until he was reduced to extreme weakness. I know for certain this is no lie, for I have known a physician who used it frequently to cause vomiting and to purge the body.

On Brassica [Cabbage]. Chapter 111.

Domestic Brassica eaten when undercooked moves the bowels; on the contrary, when very well cooked — and even more so when cooked twice, or cooked in lye — it restrains them. In summer it is more sharp and harms the stomach. That which grows in Egypt, being bitter, is not eaten. Brassica used in food is beneficial for trembling of the limbs and for weakness of sight. The sprouts that grow back after it is cut, though more sharp, are nonetheless more useful to the stomach and more effective in promoting urine; but when pickled in salt they are enemies of the stomach and disturb the body. The juice of Brassica drunk raw with nitre and iris softens the body; and drunk with wine it is good against viper bites. A poultice made of it with fenugreek flour and vinegar is useful for the pains of gout and other joint pains, and for foul and old ulcers. Drawn up through the nose it purges the head by itself alone; and applied with darnel flour it promotes menstruation. The leaves, applied as a poultice on their own or ground with polenta, help all inflammations and abscesses; and they heal erysipelas, scabies, and shingles. With salt they break up carbuncles and prevent hair from falling out. Cooked and mixed with honey they are good for spreading ulcers and gangrene. Eaten raw with vinegar they benefit those who suffer in the spleen. Chewed, and the juice sucked from them, they restore a lost voice. The decoction drunk loosens the body and promotes menstruation. The flowers applied to the nipples after conception cause women to miscarry. The seed of Brassica, and especially that of the Egyptian kind, drunk drives out worms from the body. Used in theriacs it extinguishes freckles and refines the complexion. The green stalks burnt together with the roots and mixed with old lard, when applied, ease long-standing pains of the ribs. There is found a species of wild Brassica, which grows for the most part in marshes and ruined places, similar to the domestic kind, but whiter, more bristly, and more bitter. Its sprouts are not unpleasant to the taste when cooked in lye. The leaves applied as a poultice close wounds and resolve inflammations and abscesses. That which is called the sea kind is altogether different from the domestic: for it produces leaves somewhat longer than round Aristolochia, thin and hanging one by one from its red little branches, attached by a single small stalk, like ivy. It has white juice, though it is not very abundant, and is salty to the taste, somewhat bitter, and thick in substance. The whole plant is sharp and harmful to the stomach; it loosens the body more than all the other kinds when cooked in food. It is cooked, because it is so very sharp, together with fatty meat.

A It accommodates better for obstructions of the liver than mallow does, and especially when eaten with mustard and vinegar. It is marvelously beneficial for those who suffer from diseases of the spleen, so much so that one is inclined to regard it more as a medicine than a food in such cases. Pliny maintains, in chapter eight of book twenty, that the wild variety is also found, and that it is the one called Limonium, mentioned by Dioscorides in the fourth book and by Galen in the seventh book on the properties of simples. Galen does not accept this. For in the aforementioned passage on the properties of Foods, he says: I have never known any wild Beet, unless someone wished to say it was the Rombice or the Lapatio. The white Beet (as Pliny recalls in the passage mentioned above), cooked and eaten with raw garlic, is good against worms of the body. The purified juice (as I have tested many times) applied in clysters at a weight of one lira loosens the constipations of the body that cannot be relieved by other clysters, and clears obstructions of the viscera.

On Purslane. Chapter 113.

B Purslane is astringent. Applied with polenta it is good for headaches, inflammations of the eyes and other parts of the body, for the burning heat of the stomach, for St. Anthony's fire, and for pains of the bladder. Chewed, it relieves the numbness of the teeth, and eaten it eases the burning of the stomach and intestines, and likewise their fluxes. It is good for irritations of the kidneys, of the bladder and their related parts. It prevents bile from rising; for which it is equally beneficial, and its juice drunk is also good against fevers. Purslane very well cooked is effective against the long worms of the body, against spitting of blood, against dysentery, against hemorrhoids, and against fluxes of blood. It is good for the bites of the chalcidic lizard. It is usefully employed in eye medicines: and clysters are made from it for fluxes of the intestines and corrosions of the natural parts of women. Applied with common oil and rose oil it is good for headaches caused by heat. Together with wine it heals the pimples that arise on the head, and applied with polenta it is good for wounded limbs that are in danger of becoming corrupt and gangrenous.

In Tuscany Purslane is called Procacchia, and in other parts of Italy Porcellana. It is a plant well known to everyone,
L and although Dioscorides mentions only one kind, in our times one finds in gardens a domestic variety, which produces a round and elevated stem, with thick, shiny, and quite broad leaves. The wild
C kind spreads and creeps along the ground without rising up, with shorter and less thick leaves. Purslane, according to what Galen recalls in book six on the properties of simples, is in its temperament cold and watery, with little astringency. For this reason it restrains fluxes, and especially those that are choleric and hot: for being very cold it alters their quality, being cold in the third degree and moist in the second. Applied as a poultice (as Pliny states in chapter twenty-one of book twenty) it closes ruptures of the navel, and combined with Cimolia clay it is good for inflammations of the breasts and for gout. In sum it is good for all conditions involving heat.

On Asparagus. Chapter 114.

D Asparagus is commonly known. Its tops cooked in food soften the body and promote urination. The decoction of its roots drunk is good for retention of urine, for overflow of bile, for diseases of the kidneys, and for sciatica. The decoction made in wine is good for the bites of those spiders called phalanges, and held in the mouth on the side of the pain it is good for aching teeth. Its seeds drunk are beneficial for all of these conditions. It is said that if dogs drink its decoction they die. Some have said that if ram's horns are pounded and buried, Asparagus grows from them, though this seems to us hard to believe. Asparagus is a small plant, yet nonetheless branching, with numerous and long leaves similar to those of fennel. It has a long, round, and spongy root. Its tops pounded and drunk with white wine relieve pains of the kidneys. Cooked whether boiled or roasted, and eaten as food, they are medicinal for urinary distillations and retention of urine, and for dysentery. The roots cooked in wine or with vinegar are good for weakened limbs, and cooked boiled with figs and chickpeas and eaten as food they help against overflow of bile: they are medicinal for pains of the sciatica and of urination. Carrying the roots tied on the body, or drinking their decoction, renders both men and women sterile.

S Asparagus is very well known throughout all Italy, as one finds both the domestic cultivated kind in gardens and the wild kind that grows by itself in the countryside. According to what Galen recalls in book six on the properties of simples, they are cleansing, although they do not appear to be manifestly hot or manifestly cold. They are beneficial, as Pliny writes in chapter ten of book twenty, eaten mixed, and for pains of the chest and of the back-

Note: Furthermore, as Avicenna recounts in the last Fen of the fourth book, asparagus makes the whole body smell sweet, but makes the urine stink.

On Plantain. Chapter 115.

Plantain is of two kinds, that is to say greater and lesser. The lesser has narrower, smaller, more tender, smoother, and finer leaves; angular stems inclining toward the ground; pale flowers; and seed at the tops of the stems. The greater is larger and more beautiful, with wider leaves. Its stem is angular, reddish, about a cubit tall, entirely full from the middle to the top with small seed; its roots are tender, hairy, white, and as thick as a finger. Plantain grows in humid places, near lakes and near hedges. The best and most efficacious is the greater kind, whose leaves dry and bind, and are therefore usefully applied as a plaster upon all malignant and foul ulcers that spread and are of the nature of elephantiasis. They stanch flows of blood, arrest spreading ulcers, carbuncles, epinyctides, and eating ulcers. The leaves of Plantain heal old and uneven ulcers, and those called chironia. They heal cavernous fistulas; they help with dog bites, burns from fire, inflammations, bread-poultices, swellings that arise behind the ears, scrofula, and lacrimal fistulas — all applied as a plaster with salt. Plantain cooked with vinegar and salt, when eaten, is good for dysentery and stomach fluxes. The cooked plant is given in place of beet with lentils; and it is eaten against watery dropsy, provided however that those with dropsy eat dry things first without drinking, and take the plantain in the middle of a meal. It is given against epilepsy and tightness of the chest. Rinsing the mouth with the juice of its leaves cleanses ulcers in the mouth. This juice mixed with Cimolian earth and white lead applied to sacred fire (erysipelas) is good for fistulas, pains of the ears, and defects of the eyes applied inside. It is also put into eye-washes made for diseases of the eyes. Drunk, it helps bleeding gums and vomiting of blood; it is put into clysters for dysentery; given to drink for consumptives; applied with wool to women's genitals for strangulation of the womb and for their fluxes. Furthermore, the seed of Plantain drunk with wine restrains fluxes of the body and spitting of blood. The teeth that ache are usefully rinsed with a decoction of the root, which also helps when chewed. The leaves and roots are given to eat with raisin wine for ulcers of the kidneys and of the bladder. It is believed that drinking three whole roots of Plantain with three glasses of wine and three of water cures tertian fevers, and four doses cure quartan fevers. Some people carry the roots around their necks to drive away and dissolve scrofulous swellings.

Although from Dioscorides, Pliny, Apuleius, and all the other ancients only two species of Plantain have been written about — namely greater and lesser — nonetheless one cannot but say that what we in Italy call Lanciuola, because its leaves are long and pointed like the blades of lances, is nothing other than a certain species of Plantain. In Tuscany Plantain is commonly called Centinerbia, a word corrupted from Quinquenervia. The greater kind has a wide leaf with seven veins, the middle one has five, and the lesser has three. Galen, speaking of it in book six on the faculties of simples, said: Plantain has in itself a mixed temperament, for it possesses a somewhat watery and cold quality, along with some astringency. Accordingly it has of the terrestrial cold and dry, and thus cools and dries in the second degree. The medicines therefore (says Galen again) that both cool and bind together are all genuinely suitable for malignant ulcers that are hard to cure, for fluxes and dysenteries; they stanch flows of blood, cool burns, consolidate fistulas, both new and old cavernous ulcers. Among medicines of these kinds Plantain holds first place, which happens to it by virtue of the balance and proportion of its temperament, for in its dryness there is no sharpness, nor is its coldness so great as to cause numbness. The virtue of the seed and roots is not unlike that of the leaves, except that they dry more and cool less.

On Sium. Chapter 116.

Sium grows in and is found in water. It is a stout, upright plant, with wide leaves similar to those of wild olive but smaller, and fragrant. These leaves, eaten either raw or cooked, break up kidney stones and promote urination, stimulate urination, menstruation, and childbirth. Eaten in food they are good for dysentery. The herbalist Crateuas said that Sium was a shrubby plant with few leaves, round, larger than those of mint, dark, and resembling in shape those of Rocket,

A Whether Crow's-foot is the Coronopus of Dioscorides: nonetheless, for having been a friar, and for never being able to forget his friar's stubbornness, he has preferred to be condemned rather than abandon his support of falsehood. For he claims openly that the common Crow's-foot is the true Coronopus of Dioscorides, which, as will be stated in its proper chapter, is manifestly not the Coronopus: but rather the Batrachium, or Ranunculus, described by Dioscorides under various species, which are clearly visible in the common Crow's-foot. That, beyond this, the Coronopus of Dioscorides is the Sanguinella or the Capriola, as Leonicenus believed, I truly cannot credit: for although this herb produces at the top of its stalk five small spikes, which when they open take the form of a Crow's foot or that of some other bird: nonetheless (as Manardo says) it is not used at all in foods, as Dioscorides writes, nor does it produce cut leaves, nor is it sown in gardens, as Pliny stated in chapter xix of book xxii; and if we wish to follow him when he says in chapter xvi of book xxi, drawing from the eighth book of Theophrastus, that the stalk of the Coronopus, a thorny herb, creeps along the ground, it will be difficult to prove that it is the Sanguinella or the Capriola: for the stalk of this plant does not behave in that way, but rising up produces five small spikes, which persuades one to say that this Sanguinella is that species of thorny Couch-grass commemorated by Pliny in chapter xix of book xxiii, where he says: There are some who say that thorny Couch-grass is of three species, among which they call one Dactyl, which for the most part has five spines at the top of its stalk, which gathered together and put into the nose draw out blood. And concluding his account there, he did not say (as Ruellius believes) that this species of Couch-grass was the Coronopus.

B Beyond this, it is worth noting that Dioscorides made no mention that the Coronopus was a thorny herb, nor did he place it among the thorny ones in his ordering of it; but rather among those in common use for eating in foods, even though Theophrastus counted it among the thorny plants. This leads me easily to believe that the Coronopus of Dioscorides is quite different from what Theophrastus understood by it: and therefore Pliny in book xxi, following Theophrastus, made the Coronopus thorny, whereas in book xxii, following Dioscorides, he made no mention of thorns. Since the Coronopus of Dioscorides is not thorny, and it grows and is sown in Italy, I do not think those are wrong who wish the herb Stella to be the Coronopus: as no other plant resembles it more closely. It grows wild in poor soil in various places. A great deal of it is seen by Ligo at the River Lizzonzo in the county of Gorizia, where they call it Serpentina: for its root dried to powder and drunk in wine is an effective remedy for the bite of vipers, as I have tested many times.

On Sowthistle. Chapter 120.

C Sowthistle is of two species, one more wild and more thorny, and another that is eaten when more tender. It has an angular, hollow stalk, sometimes red, and its leaves are cut at intervals all around. Both species have the power to cool and moderately to bind, and therefore applied as a poultice to hot stomachs and upon inflammations they are beneficial. Their juice drunk soothes the gnawing pains of the stomach and produces much milk. Applied with wool it benefits inflammations of the seat and of the natural parts of women. The herb and the root applied as a poultice are equally effective against scorpion stings. Beyond these there is a third species, more tender, which grows into a tree with broad leaves that divide its branching stalk. This is as valuable as the others.

c The Sowthistle is commonly called in Tuscany Cicerbita and also Crespine, and all three species described by Dioscorides are seen in fields, gardens, and vineyards. We in Tuscany use the leaves and roots in winter salads, which, being still very tender and quite sweet, are pleasing to the palate. The Sowthistle, when mature, according to Galen in book viii on the properties of simples, is thorny; but when still tender and young it is eaten like other herbs. Its temperament is almost a mixture of terrestrial and aquatic essences,

D though each is only slightly cold. Beyond this it has a share of some astringent virtue. Applied externally or eaten it cools manifestly. But when dry it becomes terrestrial, and retains very little warmth.

On Endive. Chapter 121.

Endive is of two species, domestic and wild; the wild includes one species which from its bitterness is called picra and cicorea, and another with broader leaves that is sown and is more useful to the stomach. The domestic is likewise of two species, one of which produces broad leaves similar to lettuce, and the other narrow leaves, and it is somewhat bitter in taste. Both cool and bind, and are suited to the stomach. Cooked and eaten with vinegar they check the bowels. The wild is more agreeable to the stomach: for eaten it relieves its burning and weakness. All these species applied as a poultice alone or with barley meal are good for pains of the mouth of the stomach. They benefit gout and inflammations of the eyes. Applied as poultices...

SECOND. 181

They are also used together with roots, applied usefully to scorpion stings and to sacred fire (erysipelas), mixed with polenta. One anoints with their juice whatever needs to be cooled, adding also white lead and vinegar.

Most prized throughout all Italy are Endives and Chicories: for besides being used very frequently in apothecaries' shops for making syrups and other preparations, they are very commonly used by everyone in everyday life, particularly in salads. But although Dioscorides says that Chicory is, like Endive, of only two species, nonetheless the Chondrilla, which he describes as two species in the following chapter, is truly a species of Chicory, as is also of the same species what we in Tuscany call "Piscia al letto" (wet-the-bed), which others call Grugno di porco (pig's snout), others Dente di Leone (dandelion), others Dente di cane (dog's tooth), others Capo di monaco (monk's head), and others Ambubeia. But it seems to me truly foolish, and a great negligence of the Apothecaries throughout all Italy, that having their gardens full of most excellent and fine cultivated Endive, and the countryside full of Chicory — which is nothing other than wild Endive, as Dioscorides says — they take a certain species of wild, spiny, hard Lattugaccia (wild lettuce), full of milk, to make Endive water: a thing truly reprehensible. For even though wild lettuce has cooling properties, its abundant milky sap contains certain very warm parts that burn and ulcerate, and some so soporific (as Dioscorides says a little further below) that some mix it with poppy to make opium. Galen makes mention of Endive and Chicory in Book VIII of the Properties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Endive is a slightly bitter herb, but the wild one is much more so, which some call Amara (bitter) from its effect, and others call Chicory. It is cold and dry in the second degree; but certainly the cultivated one cools much more than the wild one does, and its great moisture quenches its dryness. Nevertheless, both the one and the other have an astringent quality.

On Chondrilla. Chapter 132.

Chondrilla, which some call Chicory and some Endive, produces stems, flowers, and leaves similar to wild chicory. Hence some said it was a species of Chicory; nonetheless it is altogether a more slender plant. In its branches is found a gum similar to mastic, as large as a bean, which, ground together with myrrh and applied on cloth in the quantity of an olive to women's natural parts, brings on the menses. The herb, pounded together with the root and made into lozenges with honey and nitre, cures vitiligo when the lozenges are dissolved in water. The gum preserves and restores the hairs of the eyelids. The fresh root does the same when its juice is introduced with the tip of a needle at the roots of the hairs. Drunk with wine it benefits those bitten by vipers. The juice of the cooked plant, drunk by itself or in wine, stops diarrhea. Another species of Chondrilla is found, which produces long leaves, cut all around the edges, and spread along the ground, whose stalk is full of milk. The root is round, slender, and pointed, reddish when broken, and full of the same liquid. The leaves and stalk have digestive properties. The juice preserves the hairs of the eyelids. It grows in rich, open, and cultivated places.

There is no doubt that Chondrilla, as Dioscorides says, is nothing other than a species of true Chicory, but with smaller leaves, stem, flowers, and seeds. One sees it throughout all Tuscany and in every other part of Italy, filling the field-borders and the banks alongside roads, no less in use for eating in salads (although it is somewhat more bitter) than Chicory itself. There is also another species, as Dioscorides says, not very different from this one, which from the abundant milk found in its roots, leaves, and stem we in Tuscany call Lattaiuola, and it too is used by country folk in salads. Galen makes mention of Chondrilla in Book VIII of the Properties of Simple Medicines, in the proper chapter on Endive and Chicory, saying nothing more than that it was a species of Endive.

On the Gourd. Chapter 133.

The Gourd, good to eat when grated raw, and applied as a poultice, softens tumors and abscesses. The peelings applied to the front part of the head are beneficial for children with inflammations of the membranes of the brain. These same peelings are applied as poultices for inflammations of the eyes and for gout. The juice pressed from the pounded peelings and distilled by itself, and with rose oil in the ears, benefits pains of the ears. It is likewise beneficial when rubbed on for the burning heat of very high fevers. The juice of the whole Gourd, first boiled and then pressed, with a little honey and nitre added, gently loosens the body. The wine placed inside a fresh hollowed-out Gourd, left outside overnight in the open air, and then drunk, soothes the body.
