For common and mechanical persons: being first most certain that those who pound it are very often cursed by it. And it is no wonder if those who gather it fresh from the tree stay far from its most burning fumes. Pliny also reports that Juba, King of Libya, found it on Mount Atlas beyond the Pillars of Hercules, and named it Euphorbium after his physician, the brother of Antonius Musa, physician to Caesar Augustus. Galen and Dioscorides did not write that Euphorbium had laxative properties, which was well noted by Aetius and Actuarius, who wrote in agreement as follows: Euphorbium purges phlegm downward, but even more so water. It is more acrid than anything else known, and most burning, and thus it is given to those who suffer from colic and a chilled body, but greatly disturbs others and causes great thirst. One mixes with it some aromatic seeds; give three obols with honeyed water, though it is best rolled into pills with cooked honey. Paul of Aegina likewise noted its laxative virtue: for in Book VII (though he did not mention it among simple medicines), in chapter four he numbered Euphorbium among the medicines that purge water and phlegm. Mesue likewise wrote of it among his simple laxatives, saying: Euphorbium is a gum that surpasses all others in heating and thinning. It is hot and dry in the fourth degree, aductive, rubefacient, penetrating, astringent, excoriating, and among those things that work with great effort and distress, and lead others into fainting and cold sweating. Its extreme heat harms the liver and stomach, and therefore it is customary to give it with things that counteract its sharpness. It purges thick, viscous phlegm from the deep parts of the body, and cleanses the coarseness of the joints from thick humors that are hard to eradicate: in which it truly has no equal. It cleanses the nerves and consumes the moisture trapped and absorbed within them. Anointed with oil of cherries it wonderfully helps cold ailments of the nerves, such as paralysis, contortion, spasm, tremor, and stupor. Applied externally it helps cold and windy pains of the liver and spleen; it strongly provokes sneezing. Anointed on the back of the head it helps the lethargic and forgetful. Euphorbium is among those things that purge the water of dropsies. Give from one to three carats, and thus Serapion, Rasis, and Avicenna said that three drams of Euphorbium kill whoever drinks it within three days, by corroding the stomach and intestines. According to Mesue it keeps well for four years. That which is less than one year old is not to be used because of its great acidity. It is stored in millet, beans, and lentils. Galen wrote only one line about it in Book VII of Simple Medicines, saying: Euphorbium is composed of subtle parts. It has caustic and burning virtue, similar to other resins.

On Galbanum. Chapter 91.

Galbanum is a liquor from a ferula plant that grows in Syria, which some call Metopio. The granular and pure kind is praised, similar to incense, fatty, not woody, retaining some of its seed and fragments of the ferula plant, of heavy odor, neither too moist nor too dry. It is adulterated with crude pitch, resin, and ammoniac. Galbanum has warm, combustive, and resolutive virtue. Applied or fumigated below it provokes menstruation and likewise childbirth; rubbed with vinegar and nitre it removes freckles. It is swallowed for old coughs, for breathing difficulties, for asthmatics, for hernias, and for spasms. Drunk with wine and myrrh it acts against poison; taken in the same way it causes delivery of dead fetuses. Plastered on it eases pains of the side and boils; it revives by its smell those who fall from epilepsy, those with uterine strangulation, and those who suffer from vertigo. Burned on coals its foul smell drives away all venomous animals, preventing them from biting those who anoint themselves with it. It kills serpents when mixed with oil and sphondylium placed around them; it eases toothache when placed inside or in the cavities. It is believed to help provoke retained urine. It is dissolved for use in drinks with bitter almonds, with water, or with rue, or with warm bread, or with honeyed water; otherwise with opium, burnt copper, or liquid bile. If you wish to purify Galbanum, put it in boiling water: for when it has melted, its impurities will float to the surface, which you can easily separate in this way. Hang the Galbanum tied in a fine, open-mesh cloth over a vessel of earthenware or copper, so that it does not touch the bottom, and then cover it well and place the vessel in boiling water: and so the pure part, made liquid, will strain out, and the woody part will remain enclosed in the cloth.

Although the true and perfect Galbanum is found in many warehouses and apothecaries in Venice, kept more as a sample than for sale: nonetheless what is most commonly used in apothecaries falls far short of the qualities that Dioscorides attributes to the pure kind, being not sophisticated but filled with sticks, fibers, and a thousand other mixtures. Therefore diligent apothecaries should endeavor always to obtain the pure kind, and if they cannot find it, they should at least purify it in the way that Dioscorides teaches: for in this way a great part of those co- [continues]

A those who adulterate and corrupt it. Galen wrote of Galbanum in book eight of his work on the faculties of simples, saying thus: Galbanum is the juice of a plant of the Ferula family. It has the virtue of digesting and softening. It is hot in the beginning of the third degree, or else at the end of the second, and dry at the beginning of that same degree.

On Ammoniac. Chapter 92.

Ammoniac is a juice of a ferula that grows in Libya near Cyrene; the plant together with its root they call Agasyllis. The best kind is praised for its good color, fine granules like incense, dense, pure, with a smell similar to castoreum, bitter in taste, not dirty, and free from admixtures of wood or stones. What is made in that way they call thrausma, meaning crumbled matter; and phirama they call that which contains earth and stones. It grows in Libya near the oracle of Jupiter Ammon, the juice dripping from a ferula tree. Ammoniac softens, draws, and warms; it dissolves tumors and hardnesses. Drunk, it loosens the body and promotes labor. Drunk with vinegar to the weight of a drachm, it dissolves the hardness of the spleen; it heals pains of the joints and sciatica; it helps those with tight chest, asthmatics, those who have epilepsy, and those with empyema, if they lick it with honey or drink it with ptisan juice. It causes blood to be passed in urine; it removes cataracts from the eyes and softens the roughness of the eyelids. Ground with vinegar and applied, it softens hardnesses of the liver and spleen. Plastered on with honey or pitch, it dissolves the concretions that form in the joints. It is useful rubbed on together with niter, vinegar, and privet oil, in place of those medicines called acopi, for tiredness and sciatica.

B This juice is commonly called Ammoniac in the apothecaries' shops, but it seems to me that little of what is granular like incense is to be found there; for all that I have seen used in medicine in the apothecaries' shops is lumped together like resin, and not without admixtures of stones and small sticks. Thus one may easily say that what is commonly sold is the inferior kind called Phirama by Dioscorides. Dioscorides is likewise cited by Pliny in chapter 23 of book 12, saying thus: Africa, which lies below Ethiopia, distills in its sands the Ammoniac juice, so named from the oracle of Jupiter Ammon, near which grow the trees beloved of the Metopian bees, from which it drips like resin or gum. There are two kinds: one more excellent called Thrausma, similar to incense; and the other greasy and resinous, which they call Phirama. The ancients used it, as is seen from Paul of Aegina, in perfumes and aromatic preparations for their sacrifices; and it is therefore to be supposed that for such purposes they always used the better kind, that is the first, granular and similar to incense. This is made manifest by reading what is written about medicines containing Ammoniac in Paul of Aegina and Aetius, who always call it Ammoniac elected, meaning choice Ammoniac. Galen wrote of Ammoniac in book six of his work on the faculties of simples, saying thus: Ammoniac is the juice of a certain ferula, which has an intense faculty of softening, so that it dissolves the concretions that form in the joints, heals the hardnesses of the spleen, and dissolves scrofulas.

On Sarcocolla. Chapter 93.

Sarcocolla is a juice from a Persian tree, similar to manna of incense, reddish in color and bitter in taste. It consolidates wounds, prevents fluxes from descending to the eyes, and is used in plasters. It is adulterated with gum.

D This juice has been called Sarcocolla by the Greeks, which means nothing other than flesh-glue, because it wonderfully consolidates wounds and likewise ulcers. A good supply reaches us, as well as much that is counterfeit (as we have said above regarding several other juices and tree gums), mixed with Arabian gum and other gums. Diligent apothecaries can guard well against this by tasting it, since that which is not bitter is adulterated and corrupted. Pliny, in chapter 11 of book 12, praised the white kind as the best, saying: From the Sarcocolla (as the tree is called) a gum is made useful to painters and physicians, similar to manna of incense, and for this reason the white is better than the red. Beyond this I find no ancient author, nor any modern Greek, who recognized Sarcocolla as laxative, as the Arabs write, and knowing this, Mesue, writing of it among his laxative simples, said: Sarcocolla purges raw phlegm and likewise gross humors, especially those in the joints and hips. It cleanses the brain, nerves, and lungs; it helps with coughs and asthma. It is among those things beneficial to the elderly and to those of phlegmatic constitution, though its use causes baldness. It is an excellent medicine for impediments of the eyes, kept for five days in a small glazed vessel with ass's milk, adding fresh milk each day. Pledgets soaked in honeyed water and then rolled in powdered Sarcocolla, placed in ears that are running, will heal the ulcers therein. It is an excellent medicine for fresh wounds and old ulcers, for it cleanses them, fills them with flesh, and closes them, this being its proper operation. It acts as a laxative slowly, and disturbs those who have an excess of choler in the stomach; and

Galen wrote of it briefly in Book 7 of his work on the properties of simples, saying the following: Sarcocolla is a liquor from a tree of Persia, and has a virtue composed of a viscous substance, with a little bitterness, and therefore it dries without biting, and can excellently close wounds.

On Glaucium. Chapter 94.

Glaucium is a juice of a herb that grows in Hierapolis in Syria: its leaves are almost similar to the horned poppy, but thicker, spread along the ground, of bad smell, and bitter to the taste. This plant is entirely full of yellow juice. The inhabitants warm its leaves by placing them in earthenware vessels in half-warm ovens until they wither, then they pound them and press out the juice. Its use, being cold in nature, is primarily for ailments of the eyes.

Glaucium is called in Arabic by the Apothecaries, and by the greater part of physicians, Memithe, because Serapion and Avicenna thus named it, and as far as can be judged from the descriptions given of it by Dioscorides, and similarly by Serapion, what is commonly in use corresponds truly quite well to the real thing: because besides having been many times tried as a wholesome remedy for the eyes, it is reddish on the outside, yellow within, and bitter in taste, and of an unpleasant smell. But it should be noted that in Serapion, besides the chapter on the true Glaucium of the Greeks, one reads in the chapter on Curcuma that the lesser celandine is called Memithe. This can easily be understood as an error of the translator: because Dioscorides, whose authority Serapion cites in that passage, makes no mention of Glaucium, concerning which Galen, writing in Book 6 of his work on the properties of simples, said: Glaucium constricts unpleasantly; but it refreshes so usefully that often it alone cures erysipelas that is not too severe. It is composed of earthy and watery substance, one cold and the other also cold, but not excessively so. And therefore it may be compared to spring water.

On Xylocolla, that is, Hide Glue. Chapter 95.

The most excellent glue, which some call Wood Glue and others Bull Glue, is that which is made from bull hides in Rhodes, white and transparent: for the black kind is less good. Dissolved in vinegar it cures mange and ringworm; dissolved in hot water and applied to burns from fire, it prevents blistering. Softened with honey and vinegar it is good for wounds.

On Fish Glue. Chapter 96.

Fish glue is the belly of a fish of the whale family. The best praised is that which is brought from Pontus, somewhat rough, but not too coarse, and that which quickly dissolves. It is useful in plasters, in medicines for the head, for scabies, and in those preparations made to smooth the wrinkles of the skin of the face.

Both Hide Glue and Fish Glue are well known to everyone, and therefore need no further discussion. Galen left no account of either of them in his books on the properties of simples, but he does mention that paste made from flour and brine, used for binding books, is good for bringing abscesses to a head in every part of the body. Fish glue was mentioned by Paul of Aegina, but he said nothing more about it than Dioscorides had said.

On Mistletoe. Chapter 97.

The best Mistletoe is that which is fresh, new, green inside like a leek, and reddish outside, and that is neither rough nor spongy. It is made from certain berries that grow on oak trees from a certain plant, which has leaves similar to box. The berries are ground, then washed, and afterwards cooked in water. There are those who know how to make it into a chewing substance. It also grows on apple trees, pear trees, and many other trees. It is also found in the roots of certain shrubs. Mistletoe softens, resolves, and draws out: it ripens the swellings that come up behind the ears, tubercles, and all other swellings, with resin and wax. It heals spinittide when applied in a small plaster. Applied together with incense it softens old ulcers and malignant swellings. On Alyssum. Chapter 99. A

Alyssum is a small plant, rather rough, with rounded leaves, near which grows the fruit, resembling double shield-shapes, containing within it a somewhat broad seed. It grows in the mountains and in rough places. Its decoction, drunk, stops hiccups that are not accompanied by fever. The same effect is achieved by holding the herb in the hand or smelling it. Ground with honey, it removes blemishes from the skin of the face, and likewise freckles. It is believed that when pounded and added to food it helps against rabies in dogs, and that hung about the house it is wholesome. It is also believed to be a good remedy for both humans and animals against bewitchment. Tied in red cloth around the neck of livestock, it drives away their ailments.

Alyssum, as far as one may read in Pliny, book 24, chapter 11, is nothing other than the plant we commonly call Lesser Madder, since it resembles it in all ways except that its stems are somewhat finer and its leaves slightly smaller on the outside, of which Pliny gives clear indication when he says: Erythrodanum, which we call madder, with which wool is dyed and hides are cured, provokes urine. Drunk with honey-water it cures excess of bile, and applied as a plaster with vinegar it cures ringworm. The root and seed promote menstruation, check the body's fluxes, and dissolve swellings. This plant differs from what we call Alyssum in nothing other than having somewhat smaller leaves and branches. This name was adopted to prevent those bitten by rabid dogs from going mad. Some indication of this might be inferred from the fact that Dioscorides placed it after Alfine, to which he compared it in appearance, if its form and features corresponded: for the Alyssum described by Dioscorides has rounded leaves and fruit resembling double shields, within which is a somewhat broad seed. This in no way can be seen in our lesser madder. Beyond this, the matter becomes more confused upon reading Aetius. Some say that Alyssum is the herb called Sideritis heraclea, which grows everywhere along roadsides: for this resembles not madder, but rather what we commonly call Roberta, as we shall explain more fully in its own chapter in the next book. Thus, seeing so many varied opinions and accounts of Alyssum, it seems to me difficult to affirm which plant might truly be shown as Alyssum in Italy. Ruellius holds that what Dioscorides wrote about is the herb called wild hemp, but how closely it resembles it I leave to others, in the judgment of those who practice the study of simples. Galen discussed Alyssum in book 6 of On the Properties of Simples, saying as follows: This plant has been called Alyssum because it wonderfully benefits those bitten by rabid dogs, having healed many who had already become rabid. This it does by its own property, which operation, as has been said many times, is known by no rational explanation but only by experience. Experimentally it is found that Alyssum has a moderately drying and digestive virtue, with some astringency; by which it quenches and drives away ringworm. B C

On Asclepias. Chapter 100.

Asclepias produces long branches bearing leaves that resemble those of ivy but are more elongated; its roots are fine, plentiful, and fragrant; its flower has a heavy scent; its seed resembles that of the securidaca; it grows in the mountains. The roots drunk with wine relieve bodily pains and are likewise effective against snakebite. The leaves are applied as a poultice against malignant ulcers of the female organs and likewise of the breasts.

It seems to me that those are in error who identify, as the Asclepias described by Dioscorides and likewise by Pliny as growing in the mountains, a plant with rounded, sparse, rough leaves, not very finely cut around the edges, attached by a long thin stem to a lengthy, if slender, vine, which creeps along all the public roads with small reddish flowers and very fine roots, and which some call Ground Ivy. For beyond the fact that Dioscorides said it creeps far along the ground on all paths, he said it had leaves longer than ivy and not more rounded, as this plant which they call Ground Ivy has. Therefore one may safely say that these two plants are very different from each other. This plant is used by some practitioners for what they proclaim to be a wonderful thing in preparations made for healing wounds and internal ruptures. But the true Asclepias, which according to some Greek authors and good scholars (if so much trust is to be given to the learned Marcello Fiorentino) produces a rose-like flower, I have not yet been able to find, though I have many times searched for it in the very fertile mountains of the Anania valley. Fuchs (as one may see in his great herbal) believes that Asclepias is the plant that produces laurel-like but more pointed leaves, which some call Vincetoxicum, but in truth such a plant does not seem to me to correspond to it at all. Galen wrote of this in book 6 of On the Properties of Simples only one line, saying: Dioscorides wrote about this herb in the third book, but we have not yet made any trial of it ourselves. D

But it is sown and cultivated in every garden. It is extremely bitter in flavor, and so I would say it is composed of earthy parts refined by a warm faculty. It has a very great reputation throughout Italy, and especially against plague, and against all deadly poisons, whether those taken by eating or drinking, or those introduced by the bite or sting of any venomous animal. Its decoction is drunk for quartan fever and for every other fever that begins with chills; at which time one also gives the powder of the herb with wine, or its distilled water. It works in the same way against epilepsy in small children. The decoction made in wine with half a dram of its powder wonderfully eases pain in the side. It cures all pains of the body, vigorously promotes sweating, kills worms, and benefits the womb. It is used in our time to make that wine of Indian wood which is given for the French pox, because of its remarkable property of healing all old and malignant ulcers and of curing internal ailments.

On Policnemone. Chapter 102.

Policnemone is a climbing plant. It produces leaves similar to those of oregano, and a stem like that of pennyroyal, divided by many nodes without any umbel, in place of which it has small corymbs at the top, of good odor and sharp taste. Applied fresh as a plaster, and likewise dried with water, it usefully closes wounds, not losing its effectiveness until the fifth day. Drunk with wine it is good for urinary distillations and for ruptures.

N    In our time we cannot be truly certain about Policnemone, although many plants are found that somewhat resemble it. We shall therefore leave it aside along with other plants that remain unknown to us.

On Clinopodium. Chapter 104.

Clinopodium is a plant that produces leaves similar to those of wild thyme, climbing, two spans tall. It grows in rocky places; its flowers resemble those of horehound, arranged at regular intervals, shaped in their form like the feet of a bedstead. The herb and its decoction are drunk for spasms, ruptures, urinary distillations, and serpent bites; it provokes menstruation and likewise promotes childbirth; but drunk over many days together it drives out those kinds of warts called acrocordons. Its decoction drunk restrains the body when made with water where there is fever, but otherwise with wine.

I    Clinopodium is rendered in our vernacular only as "bedstraw foot," a name given to it from the wheel-like shape of its flowers, which surround the entire stem at regular intervals. It grows abundantly on the mountains of the Valle Anania, resembling in its leaves not only wild thyme but very much mountain calamint. Galen wrote about this in his seventh book on the faculties of simples, saying thus: Clinopodium has the virtue of warming, but not however of burning. It is composed of subtle parts; and therefore it is to be judged as warm and likewise dry in the third degree.

On Leontopetalo. Chapter 104.

Leontopetalo has a stem a span tall, and sometimes taller, along which there are several wing-like hollows; at the top of these are small pods similar to those of chickpeas, with two or three small seeds in them; its flowers resemble in their red color those of the anemone; its leaves are like those of cabbage but are cut, like those of poppies; its roots are black but similar in shape to turnips and often scrofulous in many places. It grows in fields and among grain. The root drunk with wine is good against the bites of venomous serpents; nothing else is found that sooner ends the pain. It is also placed in clysters for sciatica.

I    Leontopetalo, and its black and knotty root, resembling a turnip, I myself have seen transplanted in many and various domestic gardens in Italy, as well as growing wild in many places of Tuscany. Pliny made mention of it in the eleventh chapter of the twenty-seventh book, saying thus: Leontopetalo, which some call Rapeione, has the leaves of cabbage, a stem half a foot tall, with many wing-like hollows. It has its seed at the top in certain pods, like those of chickpeas. Its root is like a turnip, large and black; it grows in fields. We use (said Galen) the root of Leontopetalo greatly. It has the faculty of digesting, and it warms and dries in the third degree.

On Teucrium. Chapter 105.

Teucrium is an herb that resembles a small rod, similar to germander. It produces slender leaves, not very unlike those of chickpeas. It grows abundantly

A te in Cilicia near Gentiade, or Cissade. Drunk fresh with water and vinegar, or indeed the decoction of the dried plant, it powerfully resolves the spleen: for defects of the spleen it is applied as a plaster with dried figs and vinegar; and for serpent bites with vinegar alone, without other figs.
Throughout the entire valley of Anania there grows a plant so similar to Trifagine that it often deceives the eye of one who does not know it well enough: and I have therefore considered many times whether it might be the true Teucrium described by Dioscorides; and although he says that Teucrium grows near Gentiade and Cissade, this does not prevent it from also growing in Italy. Pliny wrote of another species of Teucrium in book 25, chapter 5, with stalks like hyssop and leaves like a bean, which has led many to think he meant the plant called by some Favagrassa and by others Fava inversa, which some mistakenly take to be the Telephium written of at the end of the second book by Dioscorides. Of Teucrium, Galen wrote in book 8 of the faculties of simples, saying: Teucrium has an incisive virtue; it is composed of fine parts, and therefore heals the spleen. It is dry in the third degree and warm in the second.

On Trifagine, or Camedrio. Chapter 106.

B The Greeks call it Hamedris, and the Latins Trissagine. Some call it Teucrio, on account of its resemblance to it. It grows in rough and rocky places; it is a plant a span long; its leaves are small and bitter, in shape and carving similar to those of oak trees; it has a small flower, almost purple. It is gathered when it is full of seed. Boiled green in water it benefits those suffering from spasms, from cough, from hardened spleen, from retention of urine, and in the early stages of dropsy; it promotes menstruation and aids in childbirth. Drunk with vinegar it resolves the spleen; and drunk with wine it is most powerful against the bites of venomous serpents, as is its use as a plaster. It is ground and made into lozenges, which are then useful for all the aforesaid purposes. It cleanses old ulcers together with honey; and rubbed on with oil it removes cloudiness from the eyes. Its nature is warming.

I The Camedrio is a plant well known to all, called by Tuscans very appropriately Querciuola (little oak), since Camedris means nothing more than little oak. In Lombardy it is called for the most part Calamandrina, and by many the fever herb: for its decoction drunk for several mornings often frees one from tertian fever. This herb is in great repute in Tuscany, since (as those who experiment with it declare) eaten raw like a salad in the morning on an empty stomach, it is a most reliable remedy for protecting oneself from the plague. Theophrastus wrote of it in book 9, chapter 10, saying: The leaves of Trifagine are good for ruptures and likewise for wounds. The seed purges choler, and the leaves ground in oil remove cloudiness from the eyes. This herb has oak-like leaves, is fragrant and pleasant, and with difficulty grows to the height of a palm. Galen wrote of it in book 8 of the faculties of simples, speaking in this way. In Camedrio the bitter quality prevails, though it has somewhat of the sharp as well; and therefore it fittingly resolves and liquefies the hardness of the spleen. It promotes menstruation and urine, cuts through thick humors, and cleanses obstructions of the viscera. It may therefore be placed among those things that warm and dry in the third order, though it is more warm than dry.

On Leuca. Chapter 107.

D The mountain Leuca produces broader leaves, a more pungent, more bitter seed, and one less agreeable to the taste than the domestic kind; nonetheless it is far more powerful than the domestic. Both, drunk with wine and applied as a plaster, are beneficial against the bites of venomous animals, especially sea creatures.
Although Hermolaus and Ruellius have taken much trouble to identify the Leuca as a certain plant very similar to marcorella, which grows in vineyards, nonetheless, since no account can be found that describes it more clearly than Dioscorides does, it does not seem right to me to affirm in any way that the Leuca resembles marcorella. Furthermore, Marcello Vergilio the Florentine holds that a portion of Dioscorides is missing from the beginning of this chapter. This seems to be shown by the fact that, when speaking of the mountain kind, he would have first spoken of the domestic, as he says he found in an ancient Latin translation of Dioscorides, in which this chapter reads as follows: The Leuca is of two kinds, one domestic and the other mountain. Etc. Which I think may well be true.

On Lichnide. Chapter 108.

The Lichnide coronaria produces a flower similar to white violets, but purple, from which garlands are made. Its seed drunk in wine is beneficial against the stings of scorpions.

On the Wild Lychnis. Chapter 109. A

The wild Lychnis is in every way similar to the domestic one. The seed, drunk at a weight of two drachms, purges choler from the body; it is beneficial for those stung by scorpions. They say that scorpions touched by this herb become stupefied and sluggish.

It is quite a difficult thing to judge which plant in Italy today is the domestic Lychnis and which the wild, since neither Dioscorides nor any other writer of simples has described their leaves; nonetheless one sees grown today in gardens, and especially in the Trentino region, a plant used for garlands, which produces a purple flower very similar in form to violets, which the Arabs call Cheiri, and likewise similar to the flower of wild hemp. Its leaves are small, rather long, downy, and whitish; its stalks woolly, more than a span tall: at the top of the stem one sees the purple flower, but of a most disagreeable odor. For this reason anyone might easily be persuaded that this is indeed the Lychnis Coronaria. This is further confirmed by finding the wild variety also very truly similar to the domestic. Pliny, in the fourth chapter of the twenty-first book, mentions Lychnis among the roses as a particular species, which grows in marshy and watery places, with only five leaves. The seed of Lychnis (as Galen says in the seventh book of the Faculties of Simple Medicines) is hot and dry at the end of the second degree, or at the beginning of the third.

On the Lily. Chapter 110.

The royal Lily is a flower for garlands, called by some Lirio; and therefore some call the ointment made from it Lirino, and others Susino; it is suitable for softening the nerves and especially for hardnesses of the womb. The leaves applied as a poultice are good for snakebites; boiled, they help burns; pickled in vinegar they are good for wounds. The juice is cooked together with honey, or with vinegar in a copper vessel, and makes a suitable medicine for old ulcers and fresh wounds. The root, roasted and then ground with rose oil, heals burns from fire; it softens hardnesses in the natural parts of women; it promotes menstruation and cicatrizes ulcers. Ground with honey it heals cut nerves and displaced limbs; it cleanses vitiligo, scurf, and dandruff; it purges running ulcers of the head; it beautifies the face and stretches the skin. It is ground with vinegar, henbane leaves, and wheat flour to relieve inflammation of the testicles. The seed drunk counteracts snakebites. The leaves and seed are applied as a plaster with wine for St. Anthony's fire. They say that purple lilies are also found. The most valuable for making ointments grow in Syria and Pisidia in Pamphylia.

Lilies are among the most well-known flowers in Italy, and it would therefore be superfluous to recount at length their whole history, were it not to satisfy in part those who always desire new things, so that their gardens may display and flower with them. This leads me to reveal (if one can trust the ancient observers of nature) that white lilies can be made to grow with a purple color; Pliny teaches how to do this in the fifth chapter of the twenty-first book, saying as follows: Lilies are gathered in the month of July when they have finished flowering and are beginning to dry, and are hung in the smoke beneath chimneys. They are then stripped of their nodes, and in the month of March they are placed in the lees of red wine, so that they may take on the color; they are then planted in small pits and covered with the same lees, and so they come up ruby-colored. Green and fresh lilies can be preserved all year (as Anatolius testifies) by picking their long buds before they flower, and sealing them in a jar of earth tightly stoppered so that no air enters; when taken out at whatever time of year and placed in warm water in the sun, they immediately open and flower. A true species of Lily is the plant commonly called Martagon. This produces a yellow root similar to that of the white Lily, and a similar stalk, on which grow leaves very similar to those of the common Soapwort, arranged in a wheel-like circle at regular intervals. The flowers, which grow attached to small stalks at the top of the stem, are similar to the Lily, but much smaller, turned backward, of a violet color, spotted with red, fragrant, and pleasing to the eye. This species of Lily called Martagon, Fuchs in his great Herbal claims to be the female Asphodel. How well this corresponds, let those judge who have some knowledge of the history of plants, for they will quickly recognize the error. Galen wrote of it in the seventh book of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The flower of the Lily is composed of a mixed temperament, and therefore it has part of a subtle essence and part of a terrestrial one, from which arises the bitterness that one finds in it by taste, and part of a temperate watery nature. Hence the oil made from this flower digests and softens without irritating, and is therefore most suitable for hardnesses of the womb. Moreover the roots and leaves, ground alone by themselves, dry, cleanse, and digest moderately; and therefore they help burns from fire; for which purpose the root is best used first roasted, then ground and incorporated with rose oil, applied until the wound heals. This is truly

A This is a convenient medicine for all other ulcers of the body, to make them heal and harden the skin. It also softens the womb and promotes menstruation. Some cook the leaves and apply them as a poultice to heal and re-cover with skin not only burns from fire, but all other wounds. Others preserve the leaves in vinegar to apply them in due time on wounds. B On Ballote. Chapter 110.

The Ballote, which some call Black Horehound, produces square, black, slightly hairy, and numerous stems that grow from a single root. It has leaves larger than horehound, rough, spaced somewhat apart, nearly round, of unpleasant odor, and similar to Apiastrum; and for this reason some have called it Apiastrum. All its white flowers surround the stem all around at distinct intervals, like a wheel. Its virtue is powerful against dog bites, when the leaves are applied as a poultice together with salt. The leaves are withered on warm ashes to reduce swellings of the posterior, and together with honey they purge foul ulcers.

N Black Horehound grows, which some call Fetid Horehound because of its unpleasant odor, along field banks and public roads, so similar to Melissa, which Dioscorides calls Apiastrum, that if its fetid odor did not betray it to the nose, it would often deceive the eye into gathering it instead. In Italy it is known everywhere, and is called by some Marrobiastro, and by others Bastard Horehound. Paul of Aegina wrote about it (even though Galen passed over it in silence) in his seventh book, saying thus: The Ballote, which some call Black Horehound, is sharp and cleansing. Applied as a poultice with salt it heals the bites of rabid dogs.

On Melissa, or Apiastrum. Chapter 112.

Melissa, or Melittena, has taken the name Apiastrum because it delights the bees with its herb. Its stems and leaves are similar to those of Ballote, of which we spoke a little above, but they are larger, more slender, and less hairy; they have the scent of a citron apple. The leaves drunk with wine, or applied as a poultice, help against the bites of those spiders called phalanges, and likewise against scorpion stings and dog bites; a decoction is also good for bathing in: it is equally good for women who do not purge, by sitting in a bath of it; rinsing the mouth with it helps toothache; and enemas are made from it for dysentery. The leaves drunk with saltpeter help against the suffocating effects of evil mushrooms, and against intestinal pains; given as an electuary to asthmatics. Applied as a poultice with salt on scrofulous swellings it resolves them. It cleans ulcers, and applied on joints it relieves their pain.

C In Tuscany Apiastrum is commonly called Cedronella, and likewise Melissa, as it is also called in Lombardy. It is a very common plant, of good odor, and held in great value by the physicians of the Arabic school (even though the Greeks passed it over in silence) in conditions of the heart, and thus Serapion said: the property of Melissa is to gladden the spirit. It helps cold and moist stomachs, aids digestion, opens obstructions of the brain, and benefits those weaknesses of the heart that impede sleep. It removes palpitations, false anxieties, imaginings, and fantasies caused by melancholic humors and burnt phlegm. This was confirmed by Avicenna in his book on the powers of the heart, when he said: Melissa is warm and cool in the second degree. It has a wonderful property of gladdening and comforting the heart; aided by its aromatic quality, its astringency, and its subtle aperitive nature, which are found in it, with which qualities it also benefits all other uses. It has a mildly laxative virtue, yet enough to dissolve from the spirits and from the blood in the heart the melancholic vapors, which it cannot do in other members, nor in the whole body. Galen wrote about it in the seventh book on the faculties of simples, saying: Melissa in its faculties is similar to Horehound, though less powerful, and therefore no one uses it, since it would be superfluous to use Melissa, having

...present the Horehound, of which throughout the world a great abundance is found. But truly if by chance one could not obtain Horehound, one may certainly use [a substitute], provided its quality approaches as nearly as possible to that which is of value in horehound, by which doctrine it appears that the good properties assigned to it by the Arabs were hidden from Galen and the other Greeks, for which reason it is very frequently used in such cases by those Physicians who consider themselves skilled practitioners.

On Horehound. Chapter 113.

Horehound is a branching plant rising from a whitish, somewhat hairy root. It produces square stems: leaves about an inch across, rounded, hairy, rough, wrinkled, and bitter. It produces its seed up along the stem at several intervals: and the flower likewise is wheel-shaped and rough. It grows near buildings, among ruins, and in lime-rubble. Its dried leaves together with the seed, boiled in water, or the juice of the fresh plant mixed with honey, are given for tightness of the chest, for coughs, and for consumptives. Combined with dried iris it draws thick phlegm from the chest: it is given to women in labor who do not purge, to stimulate their menstruation and the afterbirth, and likewise to those who cannot deliver, and to those who have drunk poisons, or been bitten by serpents: it is harmful to the bladder and kidneys. Its leaves are used as a poultice on foul ulcers to cleanse them: they arrest pterygium of the fingers, and ulcers that corrode the flesh: they ease pains in the side. For all these purposes the juice squeezed from the fresh plant and then dried in the sun is also useful. Rubbed on with honey and wine it clarifies the sight, and placed in the nose it helps greatly with excess bile. It is distilled on its own, or with oil, for pains in the ears.

Horehound is a very well-known and common plant in Italy: concerning which Theophrastus in the second chapter of his History of Plants assigns two species, saying thus: horehound is of two kinds, one of which has greener leaves, more finely cut around the edges, and which is used by those who make fragrant ointments, and the other which has rounder, less finely cut leaves, rougher and more coarse. This shows that he understood by the second species what in the preceding chapter Dioscorides called Baltosse. Galen wrote of Horehound in book eight of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Horehound, being bitter as it is, when used one finds it to have an action appropriate to such a flavor: for it frees the liver and spleen from obstructions, cleanses the chest and lungs, and stimulates menstruation; applied as a poultice it cleanses and promotes digestion. Place it therefore, everyone, warm at the end of the second degree, and dry in the middle, or in the last degree of the third. Use its juice combined with honey for conditions that dim the sight; drawn up through the nose it purges excess bile; and it is placed in the ears for chronic pains in them, and to open the passages which, being blocked, impede hearing.

On Stachys. Chapter 114.

Stachys is a plant resembling Horehound, but taller. It produces many leaves, hairy, sparse, stiff, whitish, of good odor, and many stalks growing from a single root, whiter than those of Horehound. It grows on mountains and in rough places. Its virtue is warm and sharp, and therefore a decoction of the leaves drunk stimulates menstruation and the afterbirth.

Stachys grows very abundantly in various parts of Italy, and fully corresponds to the description given by Dioscorides: for it grows with many square stalks, all proceeding from a single root, hairy, whiter and somewhat longer than those of horehound, upon which are the leaves, hairy, sparse, stiff, whitish, somewhat elongated, and of good odor. It produces flowers that are reddish-white, and the seeds at regular intervals along the stems among the leaves, just as horehound does: by these marks I would not know how to identify it as anything other than true Stachys, especially since it is found to have upon tasting a sharpness and bitterness, as Galen says. Pliny wrote in the fifteenth chapter of the twenty-fourth book that Stachys produces leaves similar to the leek, misled by the similarity of the Greek words: for prason means the leek and prasion means horehound. Galen mentions it in book eight of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Stachys, a plant similar to horehound, is sharp and bitter to the taste, and is among those things that heat in the third degree, and therefore reasonably it stimulates menstruation, causes miscarriage, and draws away the afterbirth.

On Phillitis. Chapter 115.

Phillitis produces leaves like sorrel, but longer and greener, which are six or seven in number, straight, smooth on top, but on the underside bearing certain marks like hanging little worms. It grows in shady places and in the dark spots of gardens, in...

A bitter taste: it produces no stalk, no flower, no seed. The leaves drunk in wine are contrary to the bites of serpents; in this they also help four-footed animals when given to them to drink. Drunk, they help fluxes of the body and dysentery.

C Whoever carefully examines the notes given by Dioscorides regarding Phillitis cannot but confess that it is the plant commonly called Hart's Tongue, and perversely called Scolopendria — perversely, I say, because the true Scolopendria, as will be said in its proper place in this same book, is the one the Greeks call Asplenos and the Arabs Cetrach. We are therefore compelled to believe that Phillitis is indeed Hart's Tongue, seeing that it manifestly grows for the most part in shady, dark, and humid places; that its leaves are larger, longer, and greener than those of sorrel, straight and entirely smooth on the upper surface; and that on their underside, which faces toward the ground, one sees certain raised lines of reddish color, similar to small worms, as Dioscorides writes. What further confirms this belief is the manifest bitterness one tastes upon trying it, and its producing no stalk, flower, or fruit at any time. And even if one finds of this plant quite a few that in a single clump have more than fifty or sixty fronds, contrary to what Dioscorides writes of six or seven per plant, this does not argue against us: for as experience has shown us many times, when one pulls up the entire clump from the ground, one can clearly see that the many fronds proceed separately from multiple and distinct roots, which agrees perfectly with Dioscorides. And therefore it seems to me that Manardo of Ferrara, Leoniceno, and Ruellio — men truly consummate in the good letters of medicine — were not a little mistaken, and after them more recently Fuchs in his great herbal, in believing so readily that the common Hart's Tongue is not the Phillitis, but rather that plant which Dioscorides names a little further on as Hemionitis. For although Hemionitis produces no stalk, flower, or seed, it nevertheless produces leaves similar to those of Dragonwort, which Dioscorides compared to those of ivy — though large — crescent-shaped and curved. Moreover it has many fine roots, which is not so easily found in Phillitis. Dioscorides did not describe the leaves of Hemionitis as smooth on top and marked beneath, as the common Hart's Tongue is, nor did he say that it grew anywhere but among rocks. This clearly demonstrates the error into which these men have fallen. It may well have been caused by their having paid more attention to the uses spoken of by common people — that is, that Hart's Tongue is a medicine for the spleen — than to its actual appearance and form. And though Hemionitis might easily serve that purpose, it is shown nonetheless that Phillitis in no way treats the spleen; but as Galen says in book eight on the faculties of simples, being bitter it checks, not without reason, the humoral fluxes of the body, and likewise dysentery.

C On Phalangio. Chapter 116.

Some call the Phalangio "Phalangite." It produces two, or three, or more branches, spread in different directions; the flower is white, similar to the lily, very finely cut. It has a black seed, wide, similar to a small lentil, but much finer. It produces a small root, slender and green in color while being pulled from the earth, and once pulled it shrinks and draws back into itself; it grows on hills. Its leaves, seed, and likewise its flowers drunk in wine help those pierced by scorpions, and likewise by those spiders called phalangi, and they relieve pains of the bowels.

S Pliny wrote in chapter 12 of book 27 everything about Phalangio that is here found in Dioscorides; however for all that, it is not known in our times in Italy. Galen wrote of it in book 8 on the faculties of simples, saying thus: the Phalangite is so called because it helps those bitten by phalangi. It is composed of fine and drying parts, and therefore benefits those who suffer pains in the bowels.

D On Trefoil. Chapter 117.

Trefoil, which the Greeks call Triphillon, others Oxiphillon, others Menianthes, and others Asphaltio, and some Cnicium, is a plant that grows to about the height of a cubit, with slender, dark stems similar to rushes, from which hang small petioles, from each of which grow three leaves similar to the lotus herb. When freshly grown these have the odor of rue, but once fully grown, the odor of bitumen. Trefoil produces a purple flower, and a somewhat wide, hairy seed, a span long, with a small horn projecting from it; its root is slender, long, and hard. The seed and leaves drunk in water benefit those with pleurisy, retention of urine, the falling sickness, and the early stages of dropsy, and women who suffer from diseases of the womb; they promote menstruation; give three drams of the seed and four of the leaves. The leaves ground up and drunk with honeyed vinegar are contrary to the bites of serpents. Some say that a decoction of the whole plant, roots, and leaves applied as a fomentation removes the pains of those who are

A ni. The true Polio can be seen in Venice in the most pleasant garden of the most excellent physician M. Mapheo de Maphei, where I myself have several times seen it growing green. Pliny wrote about it in chapter 7 of book 21, taking the first part of its history from chapter 9 of book 21 of Theophrastus, saying thus: The Polio is a plant held in great glory among the Greeks, for both Hesiod and Musaeus have praised it as useful for all things, and especially for acquiring fame, dignity, and honor. Beyond this it is marvelous: for its leaves are white in the morning, purple at midday, and blue-green at sunset. There are two varieties: the field variety, which is larger, and the wild variety, which is smaller. Some call it Teuthrio. One can recognize here the confusion of the Tripolium described by Dioscorides in book four with the Polio: for the Tripolium is that plant which changes color three times a day, and not the Polio; and according to Dioscorides it changes color in its flower and not in its leaves, as Pliny writes, thus corrupting the history on two counts. Galen wrote of Polio in book 8 of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Polio is bitter to the taste and somewhat sharp, and therefore clears all obstructions, provokes menstruation, and promotes urination. The green plant heals large wounds, especially the looser and larger variety: the dried plant heals ulcers. This is done even more effectively by the smaller variety, which we also use in antidotes: for this is more bitter and sharper than the larger, so that it may be placed in the third order of desiccants, and at the end of the second order of warming things.

B On Scordium. Chapter 119.

Scordium grows in marshy mountains, with leaves like germander but larger, not so deeply cut around the edges, breathing somewhat of a garlic odor, bitter and astringent to the taste: its stalks are square, and its flower is reddish. The herb has the virtue of warming, and provokes urination. It is drunk fresh and boiled, and likewise dried with wine against the venomous bites of serpents, and similarly with honeyed water, two drams of it are drunk against gnawing pains of the stomach, against dysentery, and urinary retention: it draws from the chest thick and putrid matter. The powder of the dried plant incorporated in the manner of an electuary with nasturtium, honey, and resin is good for old coughs, ruptures, and spasms: incorporated with wax it calms the chest organs that have been inflamed for a long time. It is conveniently applied as a plaster on gout with strong vinegar or with water. Applied it provokes menstruation: it heals wounds, cleanses old ulcers, and mixed with honey consolidates them. The dried plant removes all excrescences of the flesh. Its juice is drunk for all these defects. The best Scordium, and the most potent of all others, is that of Pontus, and likewise that of Crete.

For a long time now the true Scordium has begun to be found and recognized in Italy: for before this everyone used wild garlic for Scordium, following the errors of the Arabs, and especially of Avicenna. In this they deceived themselves through the similarity of the words, not realizing that Scorodon, which means garlic, and Scordion were not the same thing. Avicenna gave occasion for error to physicians of past times by placing Scordion in one description of theriac and wild garlic in another: for finding wild garlic plainly written, physicians concluded that the Scordium placed in the other theriac was nothing other than wild garlic, seeing that Avicenna seemed to be saying the same thing about himself. The true Scordium, very similar to germander, which grows in mountains and also in plains in marshy and swampy places with an odor very similar to garlic, is now made known to everyone, and there is no need to say more of its history. Galen praises in his book on antidotes the Scordium from Crete as the best, saying thus: The finest Scordium comes from Crete, although quite good may be found in other regions as well. This plant, according to some very worthy writers, preserves dead bodies from putrefaction. Evidence of this was provided by some dead bodies on battlefields, which having lain on Scordium for several days were found to be much less corrupted than the others, and especially those parts that had touched the Scordium. And so everyone has since been persuaded that Scordium powerfully fights against the venoms of those animals that can putrefy and kill bodies. Galen also wrote further of it in book 8 of the Faculties of Simples, saying: Scordium is composed of diverse faculties and various tastes: for it has bitterness, astringency, and sharpness much like garlic, from which (in my judgment) it takes its name. Scordium cleanses, heals all ulcers, and likewise promotes menstruation and urination. Drunk, it heals ruptures, spasms, and pains of the ribs caused by cold or by obstructions. Applied green as a plaster it heals wounds however large they may be, and dried it cleanses and consolidates putrid and stubborn ulcers.

On Tussilago. Chapter 120.

Tussilago has leaves larger than ivy. It produces six or seven from a single root, white toward the ground and green on top, with more down around the edges. Its stalk grows to the height of a hand. It produces in spring a pale flower, of which it strips itself in a short time, and likewise of its stalk: and therefore some thought it was always without them: its root is thin and of no value. It grows in pla

...in pleasant and grassy places, and along the banks of streams. Their leaves, ground and mixed with honey, are applied as a plaster for St. Anthony's fire and all inflammations. The smoke of the dried plant, inhaled through a funnel held open at the mouth, cures those afflicted with dry coughs and asthma; it breaks up abscesses of the chest. The same effect is produced by fumigation with the root. Boiled in honey-water and then drunk, it brings about the delivery of dead children.

In Tuscany, Coltsfoot is commonly called Farfara, or Farfarella, and in other parts of Italy, Horsefoot. It is a very well-known and common plant. Pliny believed that it produced neither stalks nor flowers, not having observed it properly in spring, and not having noticed that Dioscorides had noted clearly in this regard, saying that many people think Farfara is always without flower and stalk, because they do not know that in spring it produces them and loses them again almost at the same time. Pliny therefore wrote of it in the sixth chapter of the twenty-sixth book, saying: It soothes the cough called Bechio, which they call Coltsfoot. It is found in two varieties; one, where it grows, those who practice the profession of finding water believe it grows above underground water. It produces six or seven leaves larger than ivy, whitish toward the ground and pale on top, without stalk, without flower, without seed. The other is similar to mullein, which some call Wild Sage. Of this last variety, Dioscorides made no mention, nor could I tell today where it is found in Italy. In the roots of the Farfara, when they are well ripe, at the beginning of winter a certain downy wool is found, which, cleaned very well from the scales and husks, and then cooked like thread in lye, with a little saltpeter, and dried well in the sun, becomes the most wonderful tinder for lighting fire with a flint-and-steel that is in use in our time in Italy. The Germans use it and carry great quantities of it to their fairs to sell. Indeed it catches at the first strike without fail. Galen wrote of Coltsfoot in the sixth book on the faculties of simples, saying: Coltsfoot has been so named because it was believed that the smoke of the plant, dried and burned on coals, or from the root, received through the mouth, is beneficial for coughing, asthma, and other ailments of breathing. It is mildly sharp, and it has therefore been thought that without any harm or discomfort it can break up all the internal abscesses of the chest. Its fresh leaves, applied as a plaster, are helpful for all inflammatory swellings of the body, because of the watery substance found more or less in green and tender plants; for the dried leaves of Coltsfoot are considerably sharper than what is required for treating phlegmons.

On Artemisia. Chapter 121.

Artemisia grows for the most part in coastal marshlands, branching and open like wormwood, but with larger and fuller leaves. It is of two kinds: one more beautiful and fuller, with wider leaves and thicker stalks; the other is more slender, with small, minute white flowers of disagreeable smell. It flowers in summer. Among those in the Mediterranean region who call Artemisia single-stemmed, there is a slender herb producing only a single, slender stalk full of reddish flowers, which breathes a more pleasant scent. Both varieties are warming and drying. Boiled and used usefully in baths in which women sit, they provoke menstruation, childbirth, and the afterbirth, and help with obstructions and inflammations of the womb; they break up kidney stones and promote retention of urine. Applied as a plaster to the lower abdomen, they provoke menstruation. The juice, placed with myrrh in the female parts, draws out everything that sitting baths draw out. The flower-head of Artemisia is drunk in a dose of three drams for all the purposes mentioned above.

On Artemisia with fine leaves. Chapter 122.

The Artemisia with fine leaves grows near water channels, along riverbanks, and in cultivated places. Its leaves and likewise its flowers, when rubbed, breathe out an odor of marjoram. Ground and mixed with almond oil and applied to the stomach, it relieves pain there. Its juice, mixed with rose oil, is good for nerve pains.

There are three species of Artemisia described by Dioscorides. The first two differ only in that one is larger and the other smaller, both producing small white flowers of heavy scent; the third is a slender herb with a single stalk full of small reddish flowers, which some call Artemisia as well. This is confirmed by Pliny in the seventh chapter of the twenty-fifth book, saying: Artemisia grows open like wormwood, but with larger and fuller leaves. There are two kinds: one that produces wider leaves, and the other more tender, producing narrower and finer leaves. There are some who, underground, call Artemisia likewise a plant that produces a single stalk with small and minute leaves and very abundant flowers of pleasant scent, at the time when grapes ripen, which some call Botrys, and others Ambrosia. And so it seems to me that the first two species are well known in our time in Italy, and especially in Tuscany, where one can plainly see the greater and the lesser Artemisia, between which in neither scent nor flavor does one...

Although Ruellius writes that Ambrosia grows among the grain crops in France, similar in every noted characteristic to the one here depicted by Dioscorides, and that reapers make garlands from it at harvest time; nevertheless, although I have searched for it in many parts of Italy in the fields when the grain is ripe, I have not yet been able to find it. Of Botri. Chapter 124.

Botri is a dense, branching herb, entirely red, and spread out into many branches. Its seed grows all around its stems; its leaves are similar to those of chicory. It breathes entirely of a sweet odor, and for this reason it is placed among garments. It is found on the banks of rushing rivers and in valleys. Drunk, it cures asthmatics. The people of Cappadocia call this plant Ambrosia, and others call it Artemisia.

The true Botri grows abundantly throughout the Trentino region on the gravel beds of the Fersena and the Lauigio rivers, and likewise on many hillocks of the Ananis valley, red, with leaves like chicory, full of branches, loaded throughout with its seeds which are very sticky to the touch and gummy, breathing a sweet and sharp odor. Pliny said the same in chapter eight of book twenty-seven. Of this plant I find no mention made by Galen, although Paul of Aegina described it among other simples in his seventh book, saying thus: Botri, which some call Ambrosia and others Artemisia, is a plant of powerful fragrance. Drunk in wine it helps asthmatics.

Of Geranium. Chapter 125.

Geranium has leaves similar to the anemone but more deeply cut; the root is nearly round and sweet. Drunk at the weight of a dram in wine, it resolves the wind of the womb. There is another species with small, hairy stems, a foot and a half tall; whose leaves resemble those of mallow. At the tops of the stems are small crane-bill seed heads with their beaks pointing upward, or resembling dog's teeth. It has no known use in medicine.

On the difference between the Latin and Greek names for Geranium. And so Pliny said in chapter six of book sixteen: Some call Geranium Mirrbite, and others Mirrhida. It resembles hemlock, but its leaves are smaller and its stem shorter, with a pleasant odor and similar flavor, and thus our writers describe it. But the Greeks describe it as having leaves smaller than mallow, with thin, hairy, branching stems full of leaves, among which at the tops of the stems are beak-like heads resembling those of cranes. They also describe another species with leaves like anemone but more deeply cut, with a round, sweet root. This shows that there are three species of Geranium (which means nothing other than Gruaria, from the crane-bill seed heads), that is, one of the Latins, and two others of the Greeks, all of which are known in our time and seen in the countryside and along hedges in public roads. The one that Pliny describes as the Gruaria of the Latins cannot in truth be denied to be what we commonly call Rostrum gruis, and others Rostrum ciconie, and others Acus muscata, because it has (as Pliny says) a very sweet odor; for this plant has leaves cut like hemlock but smaller, and a short, round stem, and afterwards produces seeds resembling crane bills, from which all these species take the name Geranium, that is Gruaria or Gruina. Beyond this, the one Dioscorides describes here as having small, hairy stems, a foot and a half tall, whose leaves resemble those of mallow, and which produces small crane-bill heads at the top, seems to me undeniably to be what we commonly call Colombino (dove's foot), as there is no feature to contradict Dioscorides's description, except that the leaves are much smaller than those of mallow, as Pliny rightly noted even if Dioscorides alone was silent on this. The other of the Greeks, written about in the first place by Dioscorides, I have seen many times in the Ananis valley and in many other places, with tender leaves, deeply cut like the anemone, with nearly flesh-colored flowers, and afterwards crane-bill heads. Its root is white, nearly round, and of a sweet flavor. And so it seems to me that Ruellius errs here: for he maintains that Acus muscata, which he calls Acus pastoris, is this plant described in the first place by Dioscorides; but Acus muscata has no round root at all, nor does it have leaves similar to and more deeply cut than those of the anemone; rather it resembles in its leaves, stems, and odor the plant that Pliny describes as the Gruaria of the Latins. Furthermore, Ruellius criticizes Hermolao and those who presume that Acus pastoris is what we call Ruberta. In this matter, although one cannot altogether deny that the Ruberta may be a second species of Geranium, Pliny noted that the Latins recognized it by its deeply cut leaves, nearly similar in shape, a very sharp odor, a reddish flower, and heads...

A [This plant grows] likewise with cranesbill-like features, as do other species of Gruaria. Ruellius holds that this Ruberta is the Mirrhis of Dioscorides, described later in book four. I find it impossible to agree with this in any way: for beyond the question of Dioscorides' ordering — which, if that were so, should place the chapter on Mirrhis here under Geranium, since Ruberta is a species of Gruaria — I do not see that Dioscorides says in book four that Mirrhis is entirely red, nor that it has crane's heads, nor a very sharp odor, as is plainly seen in Ruberta; but rather that it resembles hemlock in its leaves and stalk, and that its root is soft and round, and not unpleasant to eat. None of which is found in Ruberta, as we shall discuss more fully in book four under its own chapter. Furthermore, Hermolao wishes that the Geranium of the Latins is the Mirrhis of Dioscorides, deceiving himself as well because Pliny said that some call it Mirrhis and Mirrhida, without noticing that Pliny made a true particular mention of Mirrhis in chapter six of book twenty-four. Nor should it be surprising that Pliny called his Geranium Mirrhida and Mirrhis, since it is found in all the ancient Greek copies of Dioscorides that it was likewise so named by Dioscorides. Brasavola also errs regarding Geranium, saying that it is in no way credible that those who say the common Columbine is the Geranium are right, because it produces leaves with more incisions than the anemone — not realizing that the common Columbine is not believed to be the first species, but the second, which Brasavola did not find in his Dioscorides, perhaps not having finished reading the entire chapter. Another kind of Geranium, which produces round and incised leaves like those of Columbine but as large as those of mallow, which some wish to be the true Momordica, I have several times seen planted in various gardens; it likewise produces crane's heads, and is praised above all other species for the drinks made from it for wounds both external and intestinal, consolidating them (as they say) marvelously. This, in my judgment, corresponds better to the second species of Dioscorides than the Columbine does, since its leaves are more like those of mallow. I do not therefore think that one would be wrong who said that Dioscorides meant this plant, although one cannot deny that the Columbine is the lesser species of this large Geranium called Momordica. The root of that plant, which has anemone-like leaves, as Pliny writes in the place cited, is good for restoring the weak and for those with consumption. Its juice benefits ear pain. The seed is given to those with spasms, drunk at a weight of four drams with pepper and myrrh. That which is called Columbine was in Dioscorides' time not in any use in medicine, although in our time some use it in drinks for wounds and fistulas as very good. But I doubt that they are mistaken in thinking that the common Columbine is that which Serapion identifies as the true Amomum of Dioscorides, which the translator interprets as Columbine: because the property of healing internal ulcerations belongs to Amomum, not to the common Columbine. No mention of Geranium is found in Galen, although Paul in his seventh book, drawing from Dioscorides, writes the same thing.

C On Gnaphalium. Chapter 136.

The leaves of Gnaphalium are used — they are tender and small — in place of stuffing material. The leaves drunk in dry wine are usefully taken for dysentery.
The history of Gnaphalium is so brief that it seems to me impossible to come to any certain knowledge of it.
T Because I find no one else who describes it more fully. Pliny passes over it with equal brevity in chapter eleven of book twenty-seven; although Fuchs does depict it in his herbal.

On Typha. Chapter 137.

D Typha produces leaves similar to those of cyperus; the stalk is white, smooth, and flexible, embraced at its top by a tightly packed flower, which dissolves into down, and is called by some Panicola. The flower of this herb, mixed with lard, is medicinal for burns from fire. It grows in marshes and in still waters.

Typha is a very well-known plant in Italy: for there are few waters in marshes, lakes, and ponds that do not produce endless numbers of Typha plants. In Tuscany the Typha — that is, its stalk together with its club — is called Mazza sorda (deaf mace), because it has been found by experience that its down makes people deaf when it enters their ears. From this down, from its flower, which (as Dioscorides says) tightly embraces the smooth stem of its stalk, some of the lower sort make mattresses for beds; and from its leaves, flasks are covered throughout all Italy, and chairs — or as we would say, seats for women — are woven from them, and these we call in Tuscany in common parlance stiance. Regarding this plant I find no mention in Galen or in Paul of Aegina, although it is named by Theophrastus in chapter thirteen of the first book, among those marsh plants that have no node in their stalk, such as rushes and the gladiolus.

Circaea, which some also call Dircaea, produces leaves similar to those of the common garden nightshade. It has many branches, small black flowers, abundant, and the seed —

Oenanthe has leaves similar to parsnip, a white flower, and a thick stem a handspan tall: its seed resembles that of orache; it produces a large root that spreads out into many rounded heads, and it grows among rocks. The stem, the seed, and the leaves drunk in honey-wine stimulate the afterbirth. The root drunk in wine is good for the dripping of urine.
