         On Fleabane (Conniza).             Chapter 130.

Fleabane is of two kinds. The lesser is more fragrant, but the greater is a taller plant with broader leaves and a stronger smell. The leaves of both are similar to those of the olive, hairy and thick. The stem of the greater grows to the height of two cubits, and that of the lesser reaches a foot: the flower is fragile, yellow, and somewhat bitter, and it breaks up into flying tufts; its roots are useless. The whole plant, whether spread on the ground or used as a fumigant, drives away serpents; it drives away gnats and kills fleas. The leaves are conveniently applied as a plaster to snake-bites, to stings of bees, and to wounds. The flowers and leaves drunk with wine stimulate the menses and childbirth, and are likewise good for dripping of urine, overflow of bile, and pains of the bowels; drunk with vinegar they help against epilepsy. The decoction added to baths for sitting in treats defects of the womb. The juice applied causes abortion. It is effectively rubbed on with oil against chills and trembling. The lesser variety rubbed on lightly relieves headaches. There is a third kind which produces a thicker and more tender stem, with somewhat larger leaves than the lesser, not as thick as the greater, but with a much heavier and less pleasant smell, and not as potent. It grows in humid places.
   A Fleabane, both the greater and the lesser, grows abundantly in Tuscany, with leaves, stems, and flowers entirely in agreement with what Dioscorides writes. It also grows in other parts of Italy, and especially in Friuli in the territory of Gorizia. It is commonly called Pulicaria, because it kills fleas, as Dioscorides says; Theodorus Gaza, the interpreter of Theophrastus, likewise calls it Pulicaria. Theophrastus, in chapter 2 of book 6 of his history of plants, wrote as follows: Of the Pulicaria there is a male and a female, between which there is a difference as in other species, and they are distinguished from one another thus: the female is more compact and has thinner leaves, and in the whole plant is smaller. The male is larger, has a thicker stem and broader, fatter leaves, with a considerably more splendid flower. Both bear fruit, though they germinate and flower late, for they do not produce their flower until after the rising of Arcturus. The male has a stronger smell and the female a sharper one: and

278 BOOK

A it is therefore more useful against the bite of beasts. The third species, as one reads at the end of the chapter on Dioscorides, is intermediate between the male and the female. It grows most abundantly in the valley of Anania along the public roads, and in other places where certain small springs of water arise and seep from the banks of fields and meadows. Galen wrote of Coniza in book seven of his work on the faculties of simples, speaking in this manner: the greater and lesser Coniza are similar in faculty and in temperament; they appear bitter and sharp to the taste. They heat excessively when their small branches are applied as a poultice (for it is a bushy plant) to any member of the body, or when one anoints oneself with the oil in which it has been cooked; and thus one sees that such oil cures periodic and circular tremors, and likewise the cold. Their flowers also have similar virtue; and therefore there are some who pound them together with the leaves and give them to drink in wine to strongly provoke menstruation and childbirth. There is a third species, which grows in humid and marshy places, of stronger odor and of lesser virtue than the others. But the first ones mentioned above heat and dry in the third degree.

Of the Hemerocallis, that is the Wild Lily. Chapter 131.

B The wild lily has leaves and a stem similar to the common lily, green like those of the leek. It produces three or four flowers on each scape, divided like the lily, of a very pale color when they begin to open; its root is large and bulbous. This root, pounded and drunk, and placed with wool in pessaries, provokes in women the water gathered in the womb, and the menstrual blood. The pounded leaves soothe the inflammations of the breasts after childbirth, and likewise those of the eyes. The leaves and roots applied upon burns from fire are also most useful.

The Hemerocallis, that is the wild lily, grows on every mountain and throughout every field of Italy among the grain crops, on the hills, in the woods, and in other places, and is properly called the wild lily. Its roots are similar to those of the domestic lily, but somewhat yellowish like those of the Martagon. The flowers, as Dioscorides says, are very pale when opening, although they then acquire a vivid color, like gold. And therefore it seems to me that those who take for the Hemerocallis what we call Lilium conuallium (lily of the valley) are clearly in error; for this plant produces leaves almost similar to plantain, though somewhat finer and not so clearly ribbed. Its stems are slender and flexible, no thicker than those of the plantain, bearing near the top one slightly distant from the other very white and most fragrant flowers, smaller than violets, and nearly in the form of Balaustia, whose roots are loose, long, and hair-like, without any bulb. Dioscorides described the Hemerocallis with leaves and stems similar to the lily, with pale flowers and a bulbous root. The Germans use Lilium conuallium to strengthen the heart, the brain, and all the spiritual members; and therefore they give it for palpitations, dizziness, the falling sickness, and in apoplexy. Beyond this, against the bites and stings of venomous animals, to speed delivery, and for inflammations of the eyes. For these ailments they are accustomed to make wine with its flowers at the time of the grape harvest, and others infuse them in old wine for forty days in the sun, and then distill it, and use it for such ailments as one of the most precious things to be found in medicine. Leonardo Fuchsius believes that the Lilium conuallium is the Ephemeron described by Dioscorides in book four, but he is clearly mistaken, as we shall say in that place later. Galen wrote of the root of the Hemerocallis in book six of his work on the faculties of simples, as follows: the root of the Hemerocallis is not only similar to that of the lily in its appearance, but is also not inferior to it in its virtues. It is useful for burns from fire, for it has a light, digestive, and somewhat astringent virtue.

Of the Leucoium, that is the White Violet. Chapter 132.

D The white violet is known to everyone; yet there is nonetheless a difference among its flowers: for in some they are white, in some yellow, in some blue, and in some purple. That which is most useful in medicine is the one with yellow flowers. A decoction of these dried flowers, when one sits over it, cures inflammations of the womb, and provokes menstruation. Combined with wax they heal fistulas of the anus, and with honey, ulcers of the mouth. The seed drunk with wine at the weight of two drams, or applied beneath the natural parts with honey, provokes menstruation, the afterbirth, and delivery. The roots applied as a poultice with vinegar reduce the spleen and benefit gout.

Q Although Leucoium may mean only the white violet, it is nonetheless also used for the yellow, the blue, and the purple. Apothecaries and physicians of the Arabian sect commonly call this Keiri. These flowers are common in Italy in gardens, in loggias, and on windowsills, on walls, and on rooftops; for in all these places, now in pots and now in boxes, women who are very curious about them cultivate them for garlands, on account of the goodness of their fragrance and the beauty of their varied colors. The blue ones truly do not appear in Italy in our times; and therefore one must believe

THIRD [BOOK]. 279

I will believe, together with the learned Marcello Fiorentino, that these blue varieties are additions multiplied and inserted into the Greek text. For there are copies of Dioscorides written in very ancient Lombard script in which no mention of the blue varieties is found. In Persia, the flowers of the white ones are used — because of their scent — to make the ointment called Jasmine, as was sufficiently discussed in the first book, against those who believe they can make the same ointment from the flowers of our common Jasmine. Concerning these, Galen makes mention in book seven of the Faculties of Simples. The plant (he said) of all Violets has an astringent virtue, and is composed of fine parts. In this the flowers surpass every other part, and among these, the dried ones are more effective than the fresh, insofar as they smooth away thick scars on the eyes. Their decoction stimulates menstruation, expels the afterbirth, and promotes delivery; and it is therefore a medicine comparable to any other relaxant. When these flowers are mixed with plenty of water, or with something else that moderates their strength, they become a good remedy for inflammations. Similarly, their decoction, when not too pure, applied internally heals inflammations of the womb, especially those that have become hardened over a long time. The flowers mixed with wax heal stubborn ulcers that are difficult to close. Some use them with honey on ulcers of the mouth. The seed, being of the same nature, is very suitable applied internally or taken as a drink to stimulate menstruation and delivery. The roots likewise have the same virtue, but are somewhat coarser and more earthy in substance. These, ground up together with vinegar, heal an indurated spleen.

Del Crateogono. Chapter 133.

The Crateogono produces leaves similar to those of Melampiro, and has rather knotty stems from a single root; its seed resembles millet; it grows in shady places and among brushwood, and is quite sharp throughout the whole plant. Some say that if women drink its seed three times a day, at the weight of three obols in two cups of water on an empty stomach, continuing for forty days after their purges and before lying with a man — and if likewise the man does the same for the same length of time before intercourse — they will afterwards conceive a male child.

Although some wish to say that Crateogono is a second species of Persicaria, which does not correspond well to me, nor does it seem credible, I have not yet been able to identify it in Italy.

Del Folio herba. Chapter 134.

The Folio, which is called Eleofolio, grows in rocky places. It is of two kinds: the female, which they call Theligono, has mossy leaves, greener than those of the olive tree, a short and slender stem, a white flower, and a seed similar to that of the poppy but somewhat larger. The male, called Arrhenogono, is in every respect similar to the other, except in the seed, which it produces in clusters, resembling the flower of the olive when it has already shed its petals and begins to show its fruit. They say that when its seed is drunk by women it generates males, and the male seed generates females. All of this was written by the herbalist Crateua, and I have therefore been content to relate only the history.

The Folio has not been identified in Italy in our times, although Ruellius believes it to be the greater Persicaria. In this he shows himself to be mistaken, since Persicaria grows in watery and humid places, and not in rocky places, where Dioscorides says the Folio grows — and Dioscorides, as far as can be understood, had no other information about it than what he found written in Crateua's herbal. It is therefore no wonder that both the male and female remain hidden from us. Galen, as if it were something unknown, left no mention of it in his books on simples, nor did Paul of Aegina.

Del Testicolo di cane. Chapter 135.

The Testicolo, which the Greeks call Canino, produces leaves around the lowest part of its stem, spread on the ground, similar to those of the olive but longer, narrower, and smoother. Its stem grows to the height of a span, above which is a purple flower; its root is bulbous, rather long, double, and tapering like an olive. The lower one is full and fleshy, the upper one is flabby, languid, and hollow. This root is eaten like bulbs, boiled or roasted. They say that the larger one, eaten by men, causes the conception of males, and the smaller one, eaten by women, generates females. Beyond this, they say that the women of Thessaly give the fleshier root in goat's milk as a drink to stimulate venereal desires, and the flabby one for the contrary effect. It grows in rocky and sandy places.

A → On Another Testicle-Plant. Chapter 46.

This other testicle-plant, which the physician Andrea calls Serapias because its root is used for many purposes, has leaves similar to those of the leek, somewhat long, but wider and thicker, which come out bending from the hollows of the wings. It produces stems a hand's-span tall, flowers that are almost purple, and a root resembling testicles. Applied as a plaster, it resolves swellings, cleanses ulcers, and prevents them from spreading; it heals fistulas and reduces inflammations. The dried roots check corrosive ulcers and heal decay and sores of the mouth that are difficult to consolidate. Drunk with wine, they bind the body. Everything said of the Dog's Testicle is likewise said of this plant.

On Satyrium. Chapter 47.

B Some call Satyrium a Trefoil, because it produces three leaves spread out on the ground, similar to those of dock or lily, but smaller and reddish. It produces a stem a cubit tall and bare; the flower is white in the shape of a lily; the root is bulbous, large as an apple, golden on the outside and white within like an egg, sweet in taste and not disagreeable in the mouth. Drunk in red wine, it is good for that spasm they call opisthotonos. It should be used by those who are eager for intercourse, for they affirm that it makes them more ready for amorous exercise.

On Satyrium Erythronium. Chapter 48.

C There is another Satyrium, which they call Erythronium, or Erythraicum, red, which produces a seed like that of flax but larger, hard, smooth and lustrous, which is said to stimulate amorous appetite no less than the skink. The bark of its root is red and thin, but within it is white, of sweet flavor and not displeasing to the mouth. It grows in mountains and in open sunny places. Holding its root in the hand provokes (as they say) to intercourse, but much more so when drunk in wine.

C. In our time most physicians and apothecaries commonly err by substituting for Satyrium the twin Dog's Testicles, since the species of Satyrium described by Dioscorides differ greatly in appearance from the Dog's Testicles, even though in virtue they are not very different. This is shown by Dioscorides' statement that the Dog's Testicles produce two roots resembling two testicles, of which the lower is always full, fleshy and heavy, and the upper is shrunken and half empty, whereas the Satyriums produce a single root, round as an apple, red on the outside and white within like an egg. Although I have searched for these species in many places, I have not yet been able to see them; but I have seen the Testicles — in the mountains of the valley of Anania and in many other places — up to five species, not counting that species which produces two roots resembling human hands, which they commonly call Palma Christi, and which Avicenna calls Digiti citrini, of which there are likewise two species, the larger of which has leaves like lettuce, open, smooth and spotted with black in several places, a round smooth stem, and a flower very variegated with purple, white and red, of quite a good smell. Its roots would be the same as those of the Dog's Testicles, were it not (as said) for the finger-like divisions resembling human hands. The smaller has leaves like saffron and produces its flower at the top of the stem, which is a hand's-span tall, of a dark violet color, smooth as velvet, pyramidal in form, almost like that of Amaranth, which we call the velvet flower. When fresh it breathes from this flower a most sweet and pleasing odor, almost like musk and amber; and according to some experimenters, the powder of the dried plant is a ready remedy for dysentery, and likewise the water prepared from it. The roots resemble those of the larger species but are smaller and much more modest. According to Avicenna, these are hot and dry in the second degree. They resolve gross superfluities of the body, cleanse the face when applied externally, benefit the mad and all nervous members; and according to some experimenters, taking one grain of the seed of the larger plant for nine consecutive mornings, ground with wine, cures epilepsy; likewise the decoction of the root used to flavor wine. It is also useful against quartan fever, to which Niccolò Fiorentino bears witness, as appears from the story he tells of having cured a quartan patient named Bisioto by giving him these roots three times. Fuchs includes this species among the Satyriums, as one may see in his great herbal. Moreover, from what the illustration of his Trifoglio Satyrium shows, it is clear that he did not fully grasp Dioscorides, since he depicts it with two roots as the true Dog's Testicles have, which the true Satyriums do not — having only one, large and round as an apple — and it produces flowers like those of the lily. This likewise demonstrates that together with Mesue the Venerable Fathers err, who have recently commented on his Antidotary, since they hold that Satyriums have and produce two roots as the dog's testicles do, not perceiving how greatly they too are mistaken for not having carefully considered Dioscorides. But returning to the primary account of Satyriums and Dog's Testicles, we return to say

A On the Hedisaro. Chapter 140.

The Hedisaro, which the Latins call Securidaca, and the apothecaries Pelecino, is a bushy plant whose leaves resemble those of chickpeas. It produces certain pods bent like little horns, inside which is a red seed shaped like a small hatchet of the kind that has two heads, from which the plant takes its name Securidaca. It is bitter in taste, and drunk it is beneficial to the stomach. It is used in antidotes. Placed in the manner of a suppository with honey in women's intimate parts before intercourse, it makes them sterile. It grows in fields among wheat and barley.

Although the Securidaca can be seen growing throughout all of Italy among wheat and barley, an especially great abundance of it is found among Aphaca. And so Theophrastus said, in chapter eight of book eight, that this plant is the proper pest of aphaca, because it grows from it just as darnel grows from wheat and barley. Pliny erred in this matter, deceived by the similarity of Greek words, in chapter seventeen of book twenty-eight, saying that Securidaca, wrapping itself around them, kills off the lentils, thinking that aphaces, which means (as we said above in its own chapter in book two) a type of vetch, signified lentils — which the Greeks call not aphaces but phacos — because, according to Theophrastus, the enemy of lentils is the one called aparina, as was stated in its own chapter a little above. Galen made mention of Hedisaro in book six on the faculties of simple medicines, saying thus: The seed of Hedisaro is red in color, with a head on each side resembling a small hatchet. In taste it is somewhat sharp and bitter, and therefore when drunk it is beneficial to the stomach, and it opens obstructions of the internal organs — which the young shoots of the whole plant also do.

On the Onosma. Chapter 141.

B The Onosma has rather long leaves similar to those of anchusa, which are four fingers long and one wide, tender and spread along the ground. It produces neither stalk, nor flower, nor seed. It has a long root, thin, weak, and reddish; it grows in rough places. Its leaves drunk with wine induce labor. It is said that if a pregnant woman walks over it, she will miscarry.

L As for Onosma, there is no one in our time who can point it out to us in Italy, and so we shall pass it over along with the others among the simples that remain unknown to us.

C On the Nimphea (Water Lily). Chapter 142.

The Nimphea grows in marshes and ponds, with leaves that resemble those of the Egyptian bean, though smaller and longer, some of which float on the water while others are submerged below; many grow from a single root. The flower is white, resembling a lily, but in the center it is saffron-colored, and after it finishes flowering a round head forms like an apple or a poppy head; its seed is black, broad, firm, and viscous to the taste. It produces a smooth, black, slender stalk similar to that of the Egyptian bean. Its root is black, rough, knotted, and shaped like a mace; it is harvested in autumn. This root, dried and drunk with wine, helps with stomach fluxes and dysentery, and reduces the spleen. Applied as a poultice it helps with stomach pains and bladder troubles. Applied with water it cures skin blemishes. Applied with pitch it helps with a skin condition called pelagione. It is drunk to prevent nocturnal emissions. Drunk continuously for several days it diminishes the generative faculty, and its seed does the same. It is believed the plant got the name Nimphea from its love of watery places. It is found in abundance in Elis at the river Anigro, and in Boeotia at Aliarto.

D On another Nimphea. Chapter 143.

There is another Nimphea similar to the one described above, but it has a white, somewhat rough root, and its flower is yellow and splendid, resembling a rose. Its seed is usefully drunk, as is its root in dark wine, for women's fluxes. It grows in Thessaly along the river Peneus.

C The Nimphea is commonly called Nenuphar, of which both types are found in infinite abundance wherever there are lakes, ponds, and marshes, and so it is a very well-known and common plant. Galen, making mention of it in book eight on the faculties of simple medicines, said thus: The root and seed of the Nimphea have the virtue of drying without biting, and therefore they check fluxes of the body and likewise the flow of semen that occurs in dreams or for other reasons; they are beneficial in dysentery. The kind that produces the white root is more potent, and therefore it can check menstrual fluxes; but both are drunk with dark, dry wine. They also have somewhat of a cleansing quality, with which they cure vitiligo and hair loss,

THIRD BOOK. 283

applying them to alphi [skin blemishes] macerated first in water, and to alopecia with liquid pitch. For which purpose the one with the black root is most effective, just as in all other matters the one with the white root is most potent.

Of Androsace. Chapter 144.

Androsace grows in the marshlands of Syria, and it is a slender, bitter herb that spreads several small tendrils without any leaves, at the tips of which are its seeds, contained within. Drunk in wine at the weight of two drachms, it wonderfully promotes urination in dropsical patients. The seed drunk has the same effect, as does a decoction of the herb. The herb applied as a poultice is usefully employed against gout.
Androsace is not brought to us in our times from Syria to Italy, and therefore it too may be left among the plants that remain unknown to us.

Of Aspleno. Chapter 145.

Aspleno is called by some Scolopendrio, by others Splenio, and by others Hemionio. It produces several fronds from a root resembling that venomous creature called the Scolopendra. It grows on walls and rocks, in shaded places, without a stem, without flowers, and without seeds: its fronds are cut around the edges, yellow and rough on the underside, and green on top. The fronds cooked in vinegar and drunk for forty continuous days diminish the spleen; but they must also be applied as a poultice with wine over the spleen: they are useful for urinary dripping, for overflow of bile, and for hiccups: they break stones in the bladder. It is believed that, tied onto women alone, and with mule's spleen, they cause sterility; and to achieve this effect, people are instructed to gather them at night when the moon does not shine.

What the apothecaries of our time call — however barbarically — the true Scolopenaria is the Cetrach, and it has not been long since physicians came to recognize that this is the true Aspleno and the true Scolopenaria: for in its place, everyone used to use the common plant called Lingua ceruina, named Phillitis by Dioscorides, as we discussed at some length a little earlier above. Although this is now well known to all physicians in Italy, there are still many old apothecaries who, out of a certain stubbornness and from long habit, will not be persuaded that the Phillite is not the true Scolopenaria, or that it is not beneficial for the spleen. In this they are clearly mistaken, as the descriptions and characteristics that Dioscorides gives for Aspleno plainly demonstrate: from which it is perfectly clear that Aspleno is none other than Cetrach, which some call "golden herb" because its underside is a fine yellow. Some imagine that Cetrach is not the Aspleno, because Dioscorides says that Aspleno produces fronds similar to polipodio, which those of the common Cetrach do not appear to match; but if these people had seen that species of polipodio with many narrow, greenish fronds that grows in the mountains one crosses when traveling from Gorizia to Ljubljana in Carniola, they would have no further reason to doubt: for it produces fronds similarly cut, like those of the common Cetrach, so much so that the first time I saw it, I thought it was Cetrach itself. The finest grows in Crete, where Vitruvius writes that it was found near the river Potero, which flowing past passes between two cities, namely Gnosone and Cortina; because so much Scolopenaria grows on that side, the sheep grazing on it daily have no spleen in their bodies: Vitruvius said this did not happen to those on the side of Gnosone. Galen wrote of Aspleno in book six of his work on the faculties of simples, saying briefly: Although Aspleno is composed of fine parts, it is not therefore warm. For this reason it breaks stones and diminishes the spleen.

Of Hemionite. Chapter 146.

Hemionite, which some call Splenio, produces fronds similar to those of dragonwort, crescent-shaped and curved. It has many fine roots, produces no stem, no flower, and no seed. It grows in rocky places and is bitter to the taste. Drunk in vinegar it diminishes the spleen.

Ruellio, Manardo, and Leoniceno were indeed wrong (as we said above in the chapter on Phillite) in believing that Hemionite is the herb that common people call Lingua ceruina, falsely naming it Scolopenaria; and since in the aforementioned passage anyone who wishes can clarify these errors, let whoever desires to see the truth read the chapter on Phillite: for there the matter will be fully resolved. This plant has not been shown to us in our time in Italy; and since it has never been demonstrated, these authors imagined it to be the Phillite. Pliny mentions it in book 25, chapter 5, saying: Teucrius in the same era discovered the herb called Teucria, named Hemionio by some, which spreads slender shoots with curved fronds: it grows in harsh places, with an austere flavor, and never produces flowers or fruit. It is a remedy for the spleen, which was discovered by certain persons who, having placed this plant over the internal organs of certain animals, found that it had attached itself to the spleen and had already dissolved it.

On Parthenium. Chapter 149. A

Some call Parthenium "amaracus." Its leaves are similar to coriander and slender. Its flowers are white around the outside and yellow in the middle. It is a plant of unpleasant smell and bitter taste. Drunk dry in honey-vinegar, or in wine with salt, it purges the bile and phlegm as epithymum does, and is beneficial against impediments of breathing, and likewise for the melancholic. The herb without its flowers is given to drink to those who suffer from kidney stones and tightness of the chest. It is useful for women who sit in its decoction for hardness and inflammations of the womb. It is applied as a poultice together with its flowers for erysipelas and inflammations.

N Parthenium grows throughout Italy in gardens, with leaves similar to coriander, flowers yellow inside and white outside, bitter and of unpleasant smell. It is commonly called in Tuscany by some Matricaria, and by others Amarella, in which it retains in part its ancient name of Amaracus. Brasavola, Fuchs, and likewise the venerable Fathers who have commented on the antidotary of Mesue are plainly mistaken here in imagining, as we said above, that Amarella was that second species of a wormwood of disagreeable smell, not recognizing that it was Parthenium. Beyond this, those who believe Parthenium to be the wild cotula are greatly mistaken, B because this plant produces the leaves of fennel and not of coriander, and does not have in itself that great bitterness which the Matricaria, true Parthenium of Dioscorides, has. Some also called Parthenium the Helsine, that is, what we commonly call parietaria, which grows on the walls of buildings, and vitriola for making glass vessels bright, as one sees Galen affirm in book six of the faculties of simples in the chapter on Helsine, and Pliny in chapter seventeen of book twenty-two. Some also place among the species of Parthenium the Athanasia, or Tansy, commonly called Daneda, although (as was said above) Ruellius, Fuchs, and the venerable Fathers who have commented on the antidotary of Mesue were mistaken in imagining it to be the third species of artemisia. This plant is used in our times for flatulence of the stomach and intestines, to kill worms, and to promote urine and the passage of kidney stones.

On Buphthalmos, that is, Ox-eye. Chapter 150.

Buphthalmos, which some call Cachla, produces tender and slender stems. Its leaves are similar to fennel. Its flowers are yellow, larger than those of chamomile, resembling eyes, from which it takes its name. It grows in the countryside and around cities. Its flowers mixed with wax dissolve tumors and hardnesses. It is said that C drunk immediately after bathing for a period of time it restores the natural color to those who suffer from overflow of bile.

D I find that the opinions of modern writers differ concerning which plant today might be shown to be Buphthalmos. Some believe it to be a certain plant about a cubit tall, which grows in meadows and along the margins of fields, with slightly cut leaves and a flower yellow inside and white around the outside, much larger than chamomile. Others say that Buphthalmos is that plant similar to common chamomile, commonly called non-fetid cotula, as Fuchs agrees with these latter. But it seems to me that neither of these opinions is to be believed, because although the leaves of cotula resemble those described by Dioscorides for Buphthalmos, nonetheless its flowers yellow in the middle and entirely white around the outside greatly contradict the text of Dioscorides. The same applies to the first plant we mentioned: because if he had used, as he did for chamomile and parthenium, his usual diligence in describing, noting also that their flowers are yellow inside and white around the outside, it is safe to believe that if Buphthalmos had been like one of these two, he would have compared it to one of them or described it similarly, and not made it entirely yellow throughout. Galen wrote about Buphthalmos in book six of the faculties of simples, saying thus: Buphthalmos has been so named from the appearance of its flowers, because they seem similar to the eyes of oxen; but in color they resemble those D of chamomile, though they are truly much larger and more pointed, and therefore more digestive, so that they also cure hardnesses when mixed with cerato. By this teaching one should understand that where Galen here compares the color of the flowers of Buphthalmos to those of chamomile, he means the variety that produces flowers entirely yellow.

On Peony. Chapter 151.

Peony, which some call Glicisside, grows with a stem two spans tall, from which many branches proceed. In it one finds the male and the female. The male has leaves like walnut, and the female has them cut like Smyrnium. Both produce at the tops of their stems certain pods similar to almonds, in which when they open one finds many red granules, similar to the seeds of pomegranates, and in the middle five or six of a color tending toward purple. The root of the male is as thick as a finger, a span long, white in color and astringent to the taste. The seed-

THIRD BOOK. 289

hollow and long stems, and round seeds, which eaten in abundance extinguish the generative power. The juice pressed from the green plant, distilled into the ears, conveniently relieves the pain in them.

On Wild Hemp. Chapter 160.

Wild hemp has stems similar to althea, but smaller, darker, and rougher, about an elbow in height; its leaves are similar to the domestic variety, but darker and more harsh; the flower is reddish, like that of the lychnis. The seed resembles that of althea, and likewise the root, which when cooked and applied as a poultice relieves inflammations, resolves swellings, and disperses the hardnesses that form in the joints. Its bark is useful for making rope.

Domestic hemp is so well known in our time in Italy that it would be superfluous to narrate any further history of it. The wild variety, although found in woods and in the countryside in many parts of Italy, is rarely shown correctly today. The seed of the domestic plant works in hens contrary to what Dioscorides writes about it in men: for in men it extinguishes and ruins the generative power, yet in hens it increases the production of eggs — because those hens that eat hemp seed in winter lay eggs in great abundance, even though others lay very few during the hard cold of winter. Galen writes about hemp in book seven of his work on the properties of simples, saying: the seed of hemp resolves flatulence, and dries to such a degree that if too much is eaten it dries up and extinguishes the generative power. There are those who press the juice from the green plant and distill it into the ears, for pains caused, in my judgment, by obstruction. And nearly at the end of the first book on the properties of foods, he says: the seed of hemp, when eaten, is hard to digest, is harmful to the stomach and to the head, and generates bad humors. Some people use it toasted and ground at the end of a meal to drink better. It heats strongly; and therefore its hot and medicinal vapor rises upward and harms the head. All of this about hemp was said by Galen. In light of whose teaching, let those consider how much harm they do to children who are epileptic when they give them a decoction of hemp seed.

On Anagiri (Anagyris). Chapter 161.

Anagyris is a plant that grows into a tree, of an unpleasant odor; its leaves and likewise its branches are similar to vitex; the flower is like that of the cabbage; it produces its seeds in certain long pods, varied in shape, resembling kidneys, rounded, firm, which harden when the grape ripens. The tender leaves, ground and applied as a poultice, disperse abscesses. Drunk at the weight of one drachm with boiled must, they benefit asthmatics; they promote menstruation, labor, and afterbirth. They are given in wine for pains of the head; they are hung around the necks of women who labor with difficulty in childbirth, but are removed immediately after delivery. The juice of the root resolves and ripens. The seed eaten powerfully provokes vomiting.

Anagyris adorns the woods with no little spectacle in May and likewise in June: because the golden color of its flowers, which hang like plumes among the branches, easily draws from afar the eyes of every passerby to gaze at it; and therefore one need not doubt that, were its unpleasant odor taken away, it would have had a place among the foremost flowers in the garlands of the ancients. Anagyris grows throughout all the woodlands of the jurisdiction of Trento as a tree of quite adequate height, whose wood — which is black inside near the pith and yellow outside, like the Guaiac wood brought to us from the Indies — is used by workers to make stakes for vineyards, and they say no better ones can be found, so great is the toughness of fiber within it. They commonly call this plant "l'ghelo," and it is seen in infinite abundance on all the mountains of the valleys of Anania and del Sole. Its characteristics do not deviate one iota from the description Dioscorides gives of it. Vomiting (as he said) is sometimes caused by its seed: because I have seen simple shepherds who, having eaten it, vomited even to the point of blood. Galen wrote about this in book six of the properties of simples, saying: Anagyris is a shrubby tree of unpleasant odor; it has a ripening and warming virtue; but the green leaves, on account of the great moisture they contain, are less sharp in action; and therefore they disperse abscesses, which the dried ones do not, since those are cutting and drying in nature. The bark of the root has similar and equal virtues. The seed is composed of finer parts and provokes vomiting.

On Cepea. Chapter 162.

Cepea resembles purslane, but has darker leaves and a slender root. The leaves drunk in wine benefit disorders of urination and scabbing of the bladder. They are even more effectively beneficial when drunk with a decoction of those asparagus called miacanthi.

Cepea, according to Pliny, grows on sandy shores; but although some wish it to be a garden herb cultivated in kitchen gardens, there is no one in our time who can show it in Italy. Galen in his books on simples made no mention of this

290 BOOK

A any mention of it: but Paolo Egineta wrote about it well, saying thus: The Cepea resembles purslane; its leaves, when drunk, are usefully employed against inflammation of the bladder. The root, taken as a drink with a decoction of wild asparagus, is good for urinary dripping caused by obstruction of the passages, through which it passes.

On Alisma. Chapter 163.

Alisma, which some call Damasonio, has leaves similar to plantain, though narrower and turned toward the ground, a simple and slender stalk taller than a cubit, with some small heads similar to a thyrsus. It produces delicate flowers that tend toward a pale white; the roots are similar to black hellebore — slender, fragrant, sharp, and somewhat thick. It grows in marshy places. The root, taken in a dose of one or two drachms, helps those who have drunk sea-hare, those bitten by venomous toads, those who have drunk opium, those with bodily pains, and those with dysentery, either alone or mixed with an equal weight of daucus seed. It helps those suffering from spasms, and those with defects of the womb. The herb staunches the body, provokes menstruation, and applied as a poultice it soothes abscesses.

Although Ruellius asserts, as does Fuchs in his great herbal, that he recognizes Alisma, and that some call it Shepherd's Pipe and others Aquatic Plantain, nevertheless it is clearly apparent that the characteristics of the aquatic plantain — which some also call Wood Beard — do not correspond to those given by Dioscorides for Alisma: because this plant produces leaves narrower than plantain, lying flat on the ground, with a simple and slender stalk, while the aquatic plantain has leaves much larger than common plantain, all pointing upward like lance-heads toward the sky, and produces not one stalk but many, proceeding from a single root. Therefore one can hardly claim that Wood Beard and Alisma are the same plant. Pliny, in chapter 10 of book 25, made mention of two species, saying thus: Alisma, which some call Damasonio and others Liro, would have plantain-like leaves if they were not narrower, more incised, and inclined toward the ground; otherwise they are similarly veined. It produces one single slender stalk, a cubit in height, whose tip is like a thyrsus. The roots are dense, slender, like those of black hellebore, sharp, aromatic, and thick. It grows in marshy places. There is another species that grows in woods, greener and with larger leaves. This plant was known to Galen, who spoke of it in book 6 of Simple Medicines. Dioscorides treated Alisma in the third book, and said that the root, taken as a drink, cures dysentery and staunches the body; but we have not put it to the test in such cases. However, that its decoction breaks kidney stones in those who drink it, we have well proved by experience, and it is therefore known to have in it something astringent.

On Onobrychis. Chapter 164.

Onobrychis has leaves similar to lentils, but somewhat longer, a stalk a span in length, a purple flower, and a small root. It grows in humid and uncultivated places. The herb, pounded and applied as a poultice, resolves small abscesses. It is drunk with wine for urinary dripping. Rubbed on with oil it provokes sweating.

It grows, according to Pliny in chapter 16 of book 24, near riverbanks and fountains, with leaves longer than those of the lentil, a red flower, and small, slender roots; but I have found no one who can point it out to me in Italy. Galen wrote of it in book 8 of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Onobrychis has the virtue of rarefying and digesting; and therefore its fresh leaves, applied in the form of a poultice, ripen small abscesses. But taken dried as a drink they are useful against urinary dripping, and rubbed on with oil they provoke sweating.

On Hypericum. Chapter 165.

Some call Hypericum Androsemum, others Coris, and others Chamaepitys, because its seed has the smell of pine resin. Its leaves are similar to rue. It is a small branching plant, a span in height, and reddish. The flower is yellow, similar to white violets; when rubbed with the fingers it exudes a juice resembling blood, and for this reason it has been called Androsemum. It has small hairy seed pods, somewhat elongated and round in shape, the size of barleycorns, inside which is a black seed of resinous fragrance. It grows in cultivated and rough places; it stimulates urination; applied below, it draws out menstruation. Drunk in wine it cures tertian fever, and likewise quartan fever. The seed drunk for forty consecutive days cures sciatica. The leaves applied as a poultice together with the seed are good for burns from fire.

On Aseirus.

On Ascyron. Chapter 166. A

Ascyron, or Ascyroid, or Androsemum, is likewise a species of St. John's Wort, but different in its size: for it is more open, and its branches are larger, more woody, and more reddish; its leaves are thin and its flowers yellow. Its seed produces a resinous substance similar to that of St. John's Wort: for when rubbed between the fingers it immediately stains the hands red; and for this reason some called it Androsemum. The seed is beneficial when drunk in a sextarius of honeyed water for sciatica: because it strongly purges choleric humors; but one must continue drinking it until fully recovered. The seed may also be usefully applied as a plaster on burns from fire.

On Androsemum. Chapter 167.

Androsemum differs from St. John's Wort and from Ascyron: for it grows with hard, woody, and slender stalks, reddish in color, and with leaves three or B four times larger than those of rue, which when crushed yield a juice resembling wine. At the tops of its stalks there are many wing-like hollows, from which emerge several feathery little branches, around which are small yellow flowers. Its pointed seed is enclosed in small vessels similar to those of the black poppy; when the heads are crushed they give off a resinous smell. The seed drunk at the weight of two drachms purges choleric humors from the body; it cures sciatica, but after the purging one must drink a little water. The herb applied as a plaster heals burns from fire and staunches bleeding.

On Coris. Chapter 168.

Coris, which some call Hypericum, is a plant that produces leaves C similar to those of heather, red, somewhat thick, and smaller, not taller than a hand's span, of a pleasant and sharp scent. The seed drunk provokes menstruation and urination. Taken with wine it helps against the bites of spiders called phalanges, against sciatica, and against the spasm called opisthotonos. Rubbed with pepper it is useful during the rigors that precede fevers, and for opisthotonos when used with oil.

Hypericum, Ascyron, and Androsemum are truly (as Dioscorides writes) all plants of the same species, although there is some difference among them in their stalks and leaves — some being more red, some more green, L some with larger and some with smaller leaves, and likewise in their stalks. In our own times all these species are very well known, and they may be seen flowering in June, separately one from another, not at all diverging from the account that Dioscorides gives us of them. But that species which they call Coris does not so closely resemble Hypericum as do Ascyron and Androsemum: for it grows no taller than a hand's span at most, with small, somewhat thick, reddish leaves, of a good and most pleasing scent. It has been shown to me several times, and as far as I have been able to examine it, I am most certain that it is the true Coris, and that it is not lacking in any part of Italy. Hypericum is commonly called Perforata, because (as its transparency shows) all its leaves are perforated by very tiny points. This Dioscorides perhaps did not note, nor did Pliny, who was so very diligent a writer. But it seems to me rather that Pliny erred when he says, in chapter 8 of book 26, that the seed of Hypericum is black, enclosed in certain pods, and that it ripens with barley. Of which error Dioscorides gives clear evidence by saying D that the pods are similar to barley grains, not that the seed of Hypericum ripens when barley ripens: for barley ripens (as experience shows) at the end of May, and the seed of Hypericum at the end of July. And so I conclude that Pliny badly misunderstood this account, which he drew from Dioscorides or from another Greek author. Beyond this, Brassavola errs doubly regarding Hypericum, saying that the true Hypericum (according to the teaching of Dioscorides) has a white flower and not a yellow one, and that therefore our Hypericum cannot be the one described by Dioscorides; and that it is rather Wild Rue. As for the first error — that Dioscorides gave Hypericum a white flower — I do not know how he can excuse himself: for in the Greek I find ἄνθος ἔχον μήκωον, meaning the flower of Hypericum is yellow, not white, as Marcello Fiorentino interprets it, and upon whose interpretation Brassavola has apparently relied, thus falling into the same error with him. That Hypericum should be the Wild Rue described somewhat above in this same book by Dioscorides is truly an altogether mistaken opinion, as any candid reader can verify in its own chapter; and from this has followed the error of the Reverend Fathers who recently commented on the Antidotary of Mesue, who — believing Brassavola more than they should have in this matter — were likewise deceived into thinking that Wild Rue and Hypericum are one and the same thing, as they left written in the commentary on the fetid pills and likewise in that on the ointment of Bdellium. Which would not have happened to them if they had

292 BOOK

A The true wild Rue, of which enough has been said in its own chapter above. Galen wrote about St. John's Wort in book eight on the properties of simples, saying thus: St. John's Wort warms and dries; it is composed of such fine parts that it stimulates menstruation and urine. For this one need not take only the seed, but the whole fruit, which when applied green as a plaster not only binds wounds and ulcers but also heals burns from fire. Used dry as a powder it heals ulcers that are very moist and putrid. Some give it as a drink for sciatica. Beyond this, speaking of Androsemum and Ascyron in book six on the properties of simples, he said: Androsemum is a branching plant of two species, one of which is called Asaron, and Ascyroid, which is a species of St. John's Wort, and another which some call Dionysium. Its seed has a purgative virtue, and the property of its leaves is somewhat drying and cleansing, so that one can believe it may cure burns from fire. But their decoction made in wine is a valuable medicine for large wounds. Regarding Coris, I found no mention of it in the books of Galen's simples, although Paul of Aegina recites everything that Dioscorides writes about it, from whom he took his account. Some Greek manuscripts of Dioscorides are found, however, which have somewhat more at the end of the chapter; but since many are of the opinion that it was added later, I have not taken the trouble to translate it.

On Ajuga, or Chamepitys. Chapter 169.

B Ajuga is a herb that creeps along the ground, similar to houseleek: its leaves resemble those of lesser stonecrop, but hairy, more slender, and clustered more densely around the stems, with the smell of pine. The flower is delicate, golden, or sometimes white; and the roots resemble those of chicory. The leaves drunk in wine for seven days cure congestion of the bile, and drunk in honey-water for forty days are good for sciatica. They are given to those with liver ailments, retention of urine, kidney defects, and intestinal pains. In Heraclea of Pontus they use its decoction as an antidote against aconite. Polenta soaked in its decoction and applied as a plaster is useful for all the above-mentioned conditions. Ground into powder and mixed with figs and taken in pill form it softens the body; and with honey, copper scales, and resin it loosens it. Applied below with honey it purges the womb. It resolves hardness of the breasts, binds wounds, and applied with honey it checks ulcers that are spreading.

On another Chamepitys. Chapter 170.

C There is another species of Chamepitys, which produces stems a cubit tall, twisted in the manner of an anchor, and slender; its foliage resembles the other, the flower is white, the seed black, with the smell of pine. There is also a third species, which is the male, whose leaves are small, white, and hairy; it produces a white and rough stem, a red flower, and the seed close to the hollows of its wings. This one also breathes out the smell of pine. Both of these have the same properties as the first, though not as effective.

Ajuga, or Chamepitys, is commonly called Iva, and of the three species written about by Dioscorides, I have up to now been able to see only the first and the last. The German who taught Brasavola erred in saying that in their language it is called Vergissmeinnit: for this plant, as far as the use of the Germans has shown me, differs from Iva as much as crows from doves. There is another species of Iva, with leaves much smaller than the first, and of sharper smell, and more pleasing to the nose, and therefore called by some Iva muscata. It grows in lean, sandy places, and spreads its small branches along the ground in the manner of foliage, in very beautiful tufts. It produces a flower very similar to that of meadow clover but smaller, less frequent, and of a color tending toward yellow-white. Some who do not know the true Polio use this in its place, since it closely resembles it. It is helpful in all kinds of cold ailments, and especially of the nerves and joints. Galen made mention of Iva in book seven on the properties of simples, saying thus: Chamepitys has a more bitter than sharp taste, and one sees by its effect that it cleanses and purges the inner parts more than it heats them; therefore it is a good remedy for congestion of bile, and for those whose liver easily becomes blocked. Beyond this it promotes menstruation when drunk or applied below with honey, and causes urination. Some also give it cooked in honey-water for sciatica. This herb heals large wounds when fresh and putrid ulcers; it resolves hardness of the breasts. It is dry in the third degree and warm in the second.

End of the Third Book.

THE FOURTH BOOK OF MEDICAL MATERIAL
OF PEDACIUS DIOSCORIDES OF ANAZARBUS TRANSLATED
into the common Italian tongue by Pietro Andrea
Matthioli, Physician of Siena.

We have until now, dearest Ario, treated in three books of perfumes, oils, ointments, trees, animals, grains, garden herbs, roots, juices, herbs, and seeds. But in this, which will be the Fourth, we shall treat of roots and the other herbs that remain.

On Betony.     Chapter One.

The Cestrum, which the Latins call Betonica, is called Psychotropon, because it grows in cold places. It is an herb that produces a thin, square stalk, about one cubit high and sometimes taller; its leaves resemble those of the oak, long, soft, notched all around, and fragrant, among which those closest to the root are the largest. It produces its seed at the top of the stalks in the form of a spike, similar to that of thyme. The leaves are gathered and dried for many uses. Its roots are slender, like those of hellebore, and when drunk in honeyed water cause phlegm to be vomited up. The leaves are given to drink at the weight of one dram in plain water, or water made with honey, for those suffering from spasms, ruptures, defects and suffocations of the womb, and at the weight of three drams in a sextarius of wine for the bites of venomous animals. The herb applied as a poultice on the bite does the same; it helps against poisons when one dram is drunk in wine. Eaten beforehand, it prevents deadly poisons that are swallowed from causing harm. It provokes urine and loosens the body. Drunk with water it heals epilepsy, and similarly helps the frenzied. It is given at the weight of one dram in honeyed vinegar for liver ailments and disorders of the spleen. Eaten after dinner with skimmed honey in the quantity of a fava bean, it aids digestion. It is given in the same manner for sour belching, and when the juice is swallowed, followed by diluted wine, it benefits weak stomachs. Given in a cup of diluted wine at the weight of three obols, it helps with spitting of blood. Drunk in water it helps sciatica and pains of the bladder and kidneys; with honeyed water at the weight of two drams it helps those with dropsy accompanied by fever, and where this is not present, with honeyed wine: it heals the overflow of bile. Taken with wine at the weight of one dram it provokes the menses; and with ten glasses of honeyed water at the weight of four drams it purges the body; it benefits consumptives when taken with honey, and helps with spitting of pus. Its leaves are kept dried and ground in an earthen vessel.

Betony is truly a universally known herb, full of infinite virtues. Hence arose that proverb, as they say: "You have more virtue than Betony." Antonio Musa, physician of Caesar Augustus, wrote a treatise on it in this manner, saying: The herb Betony grows in meadows, and on clean hillsides, and in shady places near thickets. It guards the souls and bodies of men, and protects night journeys from dangers and malefices; it keeps safe and defends holy places and cemeteries from visions that induce fears and frights. It is truly, beyond this, holy in all things. It is found in cold places with slender roots, a thin and square stalk, more than a cubit high. It produces leaves similar to those of the oak, of good fragrance. Its seed is at the top of the stalk in the form of a spike, as does thyme. The entire plant is endowed with infinite virtues: for when first pounded and applied as a poultice on wounds of the head, it closes them with marvelous speed. This it does even more effectively if it is replaced fresh every third day. It is said to be of such great power that it can even draw out broken bones. A decoction of the roots ground together with a third part helps earaches when distilled into them. Drunk at the weight of one dram in four glasses of warm water, it draws downward that blood which makes the eyes cloudy and dim. Eaten, Betony sharpens the vision. Ground fresh with a little salt and placed in the nose, it powerfully stanches blood flowing from it. A decoction made with it in old wine or vinegar, used to wash the mouth, removes toothache. Drunk at the weight of one dram in warm water, it helps with tightness of the chest, and

...on the road, where he had left behind the Britannica, I say that Galen wrote of it in book six on the faculties of simples, saying thus: The leaves of the Britannica are astringent and heal wounds. They resemble wild lapathum, though they are darker and more hairy. The juice pressed from the leaves is astringent, and some cook it down and preserve it as a most valued stomach remedy, and it seems also to heal putrid ulcers. Beyond this, it should be known that certain Greek manuscripts of Dioscorides, after this chapter on the Britannica, contain another chapter on Betony, which manifestly appears to have been taken from the treatise on Betony composed by Antonius Musa, physician to Caesar Augustus. Therefore the most learned men of our time conclude that this second chapter was inserted into Dioscorides by someone more curious than necessary, and passed off as genuine. Clear evidence of this is that the manner of writing does not at all accord with the style and usual treatment of Dioscorides, and furthermore, it would not have been necessary to write twice about the same subject in two chapters so close together. This is why such a chapter is not found written in our commentary, although other interpreters include it in theirs.

On Loosestrife. Chapter Four.

Loosestrife, which some call Lythron, produces stems of about a cubit in length, sometimes longer, but slender and branching; from its nodes grow slender leaves similar to those of the willow, astringent in taste; its flower is red, or golden in color. It grows in marshes and other watery places. The juice pressed from the leaves, whether drunk or administered in clysters, arrests through its astringent virtue the spitting of blood and dysentery. Applied below, it is good for menstrual fluxes; the herb used to plug the nose effectively stops bleeding, and likewise it is placed on wounds. Burned on coals it produces a very sharp smoke, and therefore drives away serpents and kills flies.

Loosestrife takes its name from King Lysimachus, who was the first to discover it, as Pliny relates in book twenty-five, chapter six, saying: King Lysimachus discovered Loosestrife, from whom it took its name, and it was thereafter greatly celebrated by Erasistratus. It has leaves like those of the willow, but greener, and the flower is red, or truly golden in color. Its branches are dense, upright, and of an unpleasant smell; it grows in marshy places. This plant has such virtue that placed on the yoke of oxen, or other four-footed animals that will not work together in harmony, it immediately calms them. Ruellius believes that Loosestrife is the herb with which, after the woad bath, woolen cloths are dyed green, called by us Tuscans Cerretta, or Braglia. In this he is manifestly mistaken, for Cerretta produces stems and leaves like those of flax, not like those of the willow, the flower is yellow, the seed is in pods as in broom; it grows in meadows, and one senses no astringency whatsoever in chewing it. There are others who identify Loosestrife with another plant that grows with a four-angled stem, willow-like leaves, and a spiked red flower; but one senses no astringent taste in chewing it either. Therefore I will say that Loosestrife as known to the ancients does not appear to us in Italy in our own times. Galen made mention of it in book seven on the faculties of simples, saying: In Loosestrife the astringent faculty prevails, by which it heals ulcers and arrests nosebleed when applied inside the nose. It can do the same for all other fluxes of blood from whatever part of the body, and especially its juice. Drunk, it cures dysentery, menstrual flux, and the spitting of blood.

On the Male Knotgrass, or Bloodwort. Chapter Four.

The male Knotgrass is an herb that produces slender, tender, pliant stems, all full of close-set nodes, creeping along the ground in the manner of couch grass. It produces leaves like those of rue, but longer and more tender, and beneath each one the seed is found, which is why it is called male. Its flowers are sometimes white and sometimes red. Its juice drunk has a cold and astringent virtue; it arrests the spitting of blood and bodily fluxes; it is good for choleric complaints and urinary distillations, for it clearly promotes urination; drunk with wine it heals the bites of serpents. In fevers that are not continuous it is drunk one hour before the onset. Applied below it arrests women's fluxes; distilled into ears that discharge and ears that ache; boiled in wine with honey added it excellently heals ulcers of the male members. The leaves applied as a poultice are useful for stomach inflammations, spitting of blood, corrosive ulcers, erysipelas, inflammations, swellings, and fresh wounds.

On the Female Knotgrass, or Bloodwort. Chapter Five.

The female Knotgrass or Bloodwort is a small plant that produces a single stem, resembling tender little reeds, with many nodes gathered in upon themselves, like those...
BB ii

A of the reeds, around which in a rounded shape grow leaves similar to those of the pine. Its root is useless: it grows in watery places. It has the virtue of binding and cooling, and is as good for all things as the preceding, though somewhat less potent.

The male Polygonum is commonly called Corregiola, or Centinodia, which can be found universally in every place, in the fields and along public roads; but truly the female is not so frequent or abundant everywhere. The male, which travels along the ground with its creeping branches, is called Proserpinaca by Apuleius. Galen mentions it in book eight of his work on the faculties of simples, saying thus: The Polygonum has somewhat of an astringent quality, and truly there is in it such a cold and watery nature that it is easily placed among those medicines that are cold in the second degree, or at the beginning of the third; and therefore it is so beneficial when applied as a poultice to those whose stomach is too hot, as also for erysipelas and hot swellings, and therefore being of such a nature it rightly checks fluxes and dries them up, and from this it follows also that it is useful not only for corrosive and malignant ulcers, but equally for all others. Beyond these it heals cuts and benefits all ulcers of the ears, in which it dries up the pus and absorbs it. It stops the flux of menstruation, dysentery, spitting of blood, and flux from whatever part of the body. Dioscorides reports that Polygonum provokes urine in those from whom it distills drop by drop from the outlet; nevertheless it does not do this so powerfully as to be good for use where there is great need. The male in all these matters is much more potent than the female.

On Polygonatum. Chapter 6.

Polygonatum is a plant more than a cubit tall, which grows in the mountains, whose leaves resemble those of the laurel, but are broader and smoother, of a flavor somewhat similar to quinces or pomegranates, with a certain astringency. The flowers, which it produces white, come out from each base of the leaves, and are considerably more numerous than the leaves, counting them from the root to the top. It has a white root, tender, long, full of knots, hairy, dense, a finger thick, and of a strong odor, which when applied as a poultice benefits wounds and removes those blemishes of the face which the Greeks call spili.

Polygonatum is commonly called in Tuscany Frassinella, and in other places in Italy, following the Greek, it is called Ginocchietti, whose roots women willingly use to make water for their lye washes. Beyond this there are some others who call it the Seal of Saint Mary, and some the Seal of Solomon, of which I could not in any way give the reason. Others believe, as did Manardo of Ferrara, that Frassinella is the Secacul of the Arabs, in which they are manifestly mistaken; because one does not see that Serapion, the translator of Dioscorides, referred any word in writing of Secacul to what Dioscorides wrote of Polygonatum; nor in that chapter does he ever cite it, as was always his custom to do with every other simple he took from him. Moreover this shows that Manardo was mistaken, as Serapion describes the Secacul as having leaves similar to peas, and not to laurel, and the virtues of the Secacul do not agree with those of Polygonatum; for the latter is praised by the Greeks for wounds and for removing certain blemishes of the face, while the former is praised by the Arabs for increasing sperm and venereal potency. Of Polygonatum Galen wrote in book eight of the faculties of simples, saying thus: Polygonatum has mixed virtues, with a certain astringency, and likewise something sharp, and a certain disagreeable bitterness truly difficult to describe. And therefore it is not much in use, except that there are some who apply the root as a poultice to wounds, and others who with it remove moles from the face.

On Clematis. Chapter 7.

D The Clematis creeps along the ground: it grows in rich soil. It produces small tendrils, of the thickness of rushes. It has short leaves, in shape and color similar to those of the laurel, though much smaller. Its leaves, and likewise its stems drunk in wine, stop dysentery and other fluxes of the body. Applied below in pessaries with milk and rose oil, or privet ointment, they ease the pains of the womb. Chewed, they relieve toothache. They are usefully applied as poultices to the bites of venomous serpents. It is said that drunk in vinegar it is likewise beneficial against the bites of asps. It grows in rich and uncultivated places.

On Another Clematis. Chapter 8.

There is another Clematis, which produces its small tendrils reddish, flexible, and woody, whose leaves are most sharp and ulcerative to the taste: this one twines itself around

A gno. Its root is short, and it grows most commonly near water on the banks of ditches and in rich soils, and not in the rough mountains, as Dioscorides says the Polemonium grows, which Galen mentioned in book eight of the properties of simples, speaking thus: Polemonium is composed of subtle parts, and has a drying virtue, and therefore some give its root in wine to drink against sciatica, dysentery, and hardening of the spleen.

Of the Rocky Symphytum, or Alo. Chapter x.

The Symphytum called rocky grows among rocks, its branches are slender, similar to oregano: it has little heads like thyme. It is an entirely woody and fragrant plant, with a sweet taste; when chewed it easily stimulates saliva; it produces a long root, purplish, about the thickness of a finger. A decoction made in honeyed water, when drunk, cleanses defects of the lungs. It is given with water for spitting of blood, and for pains in the kidneys; it is drunk cooked in wine for dysentery and for red menstrual fluxes. It is given in honeyed vinegar to those who are bruised and to those with spasms: chewed it quenches thirst, and helps with roughness of the windpipe: it consolidates fresh wounds, and intestinal ruptures when applied as a plaster thereupon. When cooked,

B meat cut with Symphytum warms again and rejoins together.

Of Another Symphytum. Chapter xi.

The Symphytum, which some call pecton, produces a stem two cubits tall, and sometimes taller, angular, thick, light, and hollow within, like that of the sowthistle, around which are leaves not too far apart, hairy, narrow, long, similar to those of bugloss: the stem along its length is entirely feathered, and from the wings emerge some small leaves, among which are yellow flowers like those of rue. The seed is similar to that of mullein, and over the leaves, and likewise over the entire stem there is a rough down, which when handled causes itching. Its roots are black on the outside and white within, and of a viscous substance, from which comes its use. These ground up are usefully drunk for spitting of blood: they are beneficial for those with ruptures, and consolidate fresh wounds when applied as a plaster. Put to cook with cut meat they bind it back together: they are usefully applied as a plaster with

C leaves of groundsel in inflammations, and especially of the seat.

I The Symphytum which Dioscorides placed in the first position here, I have truly not yet been able to see in Italy, although Ruellius writes that it is found most abundantly in France, with all those characteristics attributed to it. It would seem that it might also be found in Italy, if the true rocky Symphytum was that which Manardo of Ferrara requested of Giovanni Paolo da Castiglioni, having written to him that he had found it, in the fifth Epistle of book six: but I remain somewhat in doubt that this was so, because it seems to me that by now it ought to have been made publicly known throughout all Italy. But as for the one which Dioscorides placed in the second position, there is no doubt whatsoever, given its many corresponding characteristics, that it is our greater Consolida, which some also call Alo, which grows most abundantly in meadows, and I truly cannot understand those who hold that the rocky Symphytum is that very common plant which apothecaries call Consolida minor: for it corresponds to it not at all in resemblance, nor can one declare it to be that plant whose leaves have much blue in them, called the middle consolida, and by some Lauretina, and by some Sienese Morándola, of which plants, although

D neither the Greeks nor likewise the Arabs make any mention, it is believed nonetheless that they can be very useful for internal and external ruptures, and likewise for consolidating ulcers and wounds. Some experimenters say that half a measure drunk causes extravasated and clotted blood to exit through the stomach, or through another part of the body, and they praise it as a most powerful remedy for all corrosive ulcers of the mouth, of the testicles, of the male member, and of the natural parts of women. The Germans count among their consolidas the one they call Sanicula, similar in leaf to cinquefoil, whose white roots are so artfully made by nature in a chain of knots, that they cause no small wonder to whoever carefully observes such great workmanship. They use it in drinks for internal wounds, and especially ruptures, and intestinal tears. They show moreover several species of these Sanicula, of which one produces leaves the size of those of plantain, but thick, almost like those of Sabaria, with a little border around them made with great artistry by nature, of a color tending toward yellow-white. This grows most abundantly at Gorizia on the mountain of Saint Valentine, and according to what has been tested many times, it is wonderful for intestinal ruptures, and for drinks for rupture wounds and those of every other part. They also have the Royal Consolida, which in their language they call the knight's spur, whose stems are one cubit tall, full of small branches, and very slender leaves. The flowers are truly purple, the size of violets, from the base of which projects outward a little horn in the manner of a spur. They praise these flowers for redness of the eyes, for which use they grind them

A all day it moved between the Cyperus and the Phleo. But since I find no mention of the Scabiosa among the ancients, I say that the moderns use it to drive away the itch, not only by drinking its decoction, but also by placing its juice in ointments. It is used for all defects of the chest, the diaphragm, and the spiritual members, and to cause the abscesses that form there to break. It is applied as a plaster on anthrax and pestilential carbuncles, since it is believed for certain that it kills these within three hours. But returning to the Stebe, I find that Galen mentioned it in book seven of the Faculties of Simples, saying as follows: The leaves and fruits of the Stebe are in great use, for having a constrictive virtue without any mordancy. It clearly purges in the beginning of the third order; and therefore its decoction is put into clysters that are given for dysentery, and likewise into ears that are running. The Stebe heals large wounds. This it does even more evidently with black wine and the south wind. It effectively dries up unnatural moisture. The leaves plastered on green check the flow of blood and dissolve that which has been extravasated into the eyes by blows.

On Clematis. Chapter XIV.

B Clematis produces a square stem, similar to that of the fava bean; it has leaves of plantain, and at the tops of the stems little follicles rolled in upon themselves, as one sees in the tendrils of the iris and of the polypi. The best is that of the mountains. The juice is pressed from the whole plant together with the root, which, being cold and constrictive, is usefully given for spitting of blood, for stomach fluxes, and likewise to stop the red menstrual flow of women; it also stops the blood that comes from the nose. The leaves, or the follicles, ground and plastered on fresh wounds, heal and cicatrize them.

V I truly see great correspondence with the notes that Dioscorides gives for Clematis in that common and very widespread plant which throughout Italy is called Saponaria: for it produces its quadrangular stem, similar to that of the fava bean, the leaves equal to plantain, and the follicles from which the flowers grow at the tops of the stems, similar to those of the iris; whose characteristics do not at all disagree with the description of Clematis. This plant (according to what Pliny reports in chapter seven of book twenty-five) was discovered by King Climenos, from whom it afterwards took its name, in whose place he attributed to Clematis everything that Dioscorides attributed to Periclimenos. Of this I find no mention either in Galen
C or in Paul of Aegina.

On Periclimenos, i.e., Matrisilva. Chapter XV.

The Periclimenos grows simply with whitish leaves, distinct at intervals, which clothe it, in the shape of ivy. Among the leaves there emerge certain buds in which the seed is similar to that of ivy; it produces a white flower, equal to that of the fava bean, somewhat round, which nearly spreads out over the leaves; its seed is hard and difficult to gather; the root is round and large. It grows in fields and in hedges, and wraps itself around all those plants that are near to it. The seed, gathered when fully ripe, and then dried in the shade, is drunk at the weight of a dram with wine for forty consecutive days to reduce the spleen and remove the pain; it resolves weariness and provokes urine, but after the sixth day it becomes bloody; it helps with asthma and hiccup; it accelerates childbirth. The leaves have the same virtues; which, they say, when drunk for thirty-seven days make one sterile, and when rubbed on with oil are good for cold and for the tremors of
D periodic fevers.

C People commonly call the Periclimenos by some Matrisilva, by others Vencibosco, and by others Caprifolio; and we are compelled to believe that our common Matrisilva is the Periclimenos, not only because we find all the most learned students of Simples of our time of this same opinion, but also because we ourselves recognize, from the descriptions that Dioscorides gives of it, that this is the case. For the Matrisilva produces its simple stem, along which, two by two, at certain intervals, the ivy-like and whitish leaves are seen, the flower similar to those of the fava bean, and the seed of ivy, hard, and from a round and large root; it winds marvelously around trees and shrubs, through the hedges, so much so that it often grips them so tightly as to leave a very visible impression on them, from which effect it has been called by some Vencibosco. But those are truly mistaken who, among whom I find Ruellius and Jacopo Manlio, who shed the greatest light upon the apothecaries, believe that the Caprifolio and the Matrisilva, or Periclimenos, are one and the same thing. The cause of this error was Matteo Silvatico, author of the Pandects; for he called his Caprifolio Matrisilva, which, as one reads further on in the text, is the Pixiacantha of Dioscorides, and not the Periclimenos, of which he made particular mention under the title of Matrisilva. Not perceiving this, those others have since believed that the Caprifolio is our
