The common name is Matriselva, or Periclimeno. Matriselva is commonly used in chief ointments, as something very remarkable, of which I have found no mention among the ancients up to now. Giovanni da Vigo, a most famous surgeon, praised it for leg ulcers, having (as he writes) found it recommended by Galen for this purpose in book eight of the Faculties of Simple Medicines; but truly in my copy of Galen I have not found any such thing: for there he treats the subject in this manner, saying: The leaves of Periclimeno are useful, and likewise the fruit, which are of such warm and heating nature that if one drinks too much of them over many days they cause one to urinate blood, though at first they merely provoke urination. Rubbed on externally with oil they warm: they benefit those with disorders of the spleen who breathe with difficulty. The proper dose is one dram drunk in wine. The seed is desiccating: and therefore some say that it makes sterile those who use it. To achieve this effect, according to the opinion of others, a course of thirty-six continuous days is required, as Dioscorides wrote.

On the Water Chestnut (Tribulus). Chapter XVI.

The Tribulus is of two kinds, one terrestrial and one aquatic. The terrestrial produces leaves similar to those of purslane, but more slender: its little tendrils run along the ground, and in them, according to the origin of the leaves, are rigid and hard spines, of bitter taste. It grows near rivers and among the ruins of houses. The aquatic grows in rivers, upon whose waters it spreads its foliage, and beneath the water its spines: its leaves are broad, attached by long stalks: the stem is much thicker at the top than at the bottom: it has certain filaments arranged like an ear of grain: the fruit is hard, like that of the other. Both kinds are astringent and cooling, and therefore are usefully applied as poultices upon all inflammations. Together with honey they heal ulcers of the mouth, rottenness, the gums, and the throat. The juice of both is pressed out for medicines of the eyes. The green seed of both, drunk to the weight of one dram, is useful against kidney stones. The terrestrial, taken by mouth at a weight of one dram, and likewise applied as a poultice, is particularly effective against viper bites: one dram taken with wine counteracts deadly poisons. A decoction of both sprinkled on the ground kills fleas. In Thrace, those who live near the river Strymon fatten their horses with the green herb of the tribuli, and grind the sweet fruit into flour, making bread from it for their own use.

Although Dioscorides wrote of only one species of terrestrial Tribulus, Theophrastus nonetheless holds that there are two species, saying so in chapter five of book six of his History of Plants as follows. The Tribulus has the peculiarity of producing its spiny fruit, of which two varieties are found: of these, one has leaves similar to chickpeas, and the other produces them spiny; both are terrestrial and rich in shoots. The one with spiny leaves grows later, and is usually found near the hedgerows of farms. The fruit of the first resembles sesame; but that of the later-ripening kind is round, black, and enclosed in pods. Of these species, in our times there is no one in Italy who can show us any of them. The one that Dioscorides wrote grows with leaves like purslane, I have collected many times, and saw it most recently in Venice near the church of San Nicolò. Ruellius believes that the spiny Tribulus of Theophrastus is the plant we commonly call Cacatreppola, because it grows along the banks of rivers: but since we cannot know what shape the leaves of that plant were for Theophrastus, and since we see that the Cacatreppola does not produce shoots, nor any pod containing seed, it does not seem to me to correspond at all. Our Sienese apothecaries season its roots, mistaking them for those of sedge, as we said above. But returning to the Tribulus, I say that the aquatic kind is found in many rivers and lakes of Italy, and especially in those of Mantua and Ferrara, and grows not only in fresh waters but also in salt, like those sold in the squares of Venice, grown in the surrounding lagoons. These are often made by those going on pilgrimage into rosary beads to wear around the neck, to give greater appearance of piety. Some eat the fruit, which resembles chestnuts, cooked under hot ashes. Galen mentioned both in book eight of the Faculties of Simples, saying: The Tribulus is composed of a slightly cold moist essence and a not moderately cold dry one. In the terrestrial kind a cold earthiness prevails, which is astringent, and in the aquatic a watery one. Therefore by both qualities they prevent the formation of inflammations and the onset of fluxes. The fruit of the terrestrial, being composed of fine parts, breaks kidney stones when drunk.

On Saxifrage. Chapter XVII.

Saxifrage is a plant with many small branches, which grows among rocks and in rough places, similar to epithyme. Its decoction made with wine is usefully drunk for fevers, for urinary discharges, and for hiccups: it breaks the stones of the bladder and promotes urination.

A Although it is the common opinion of all learned herbalists of our time that this chapter does not correspond to the Sassafrage of Dioscorides, since the Latin word does not match the Greek; nonetheless, since it appears in the majority of the Greek manuscripts of Dioscorides, I have not wished to leave it out, especially since this plant is clearly found by us in Italy, and is used with no little success in breaking up kidney stones and promoting urination. It grows in many places in Tuscany among very hard rocks, with hair-like leaves, and a great abundance of it is found in our Maremma on the most arid crags of Mount Argentario, resembling epithyme.

On Limonio. Chapter 18.

Limonio has leaves like beet, but longer and finer, about ten in number, sometimes more: its stem is straight and slender, equal to that of the lily, and full of red seed; its taste is astringent. Ground up and drunk in wine at the measure of one acetabulum, it stops fluxes of the stomach, dysentery, and likewise the menstrual flow in women. It grows in meadows and marshy places.

B Pliny names it, in book 20, chapter 8, "wild beet" (Bietola saluatica), although (as was said above in the proper chapter on beet) Galen, in his second book on the properties of foods, argues against this, saying he never knew any wild beet, unless someone means by that word the sorrel. One can therefore conclude that Limonio is a plant in its own right, which I have seen many times in the marshes of the Val d'Ania, as far as my judgment can determine. Galen wrote about it in book 7 on the properties of simples, saying thus: the seed of Lemonio is given, like something astringent, for fluxes of the stomach and dysentery, and likewise for spitting of blood and menstrual flux; and for this purpose it suffices to give each time the measure of one acetabulum.

On Lagopo. Chapter 19.

Lagopo drunk in wine restrains the body; but where there is fever, it is given with water. Bound upon the groin, it prevents inflammations there. It grows in the furrows of gardens and among grain crops.

C So briefly did Dioscorides write about Lagopo, without giving any description of its appearance, that it seems truly impossible to determine what plant it is among so many simples that remain unidentified. And Matteo Silvatico, the compiler of the Pandette, was truly dreaming when he believed that Lagopo was the plant we call Gariophilata (avens/clove-root): for that plant does not grow in the furrows of gardens, but in mountains and along hedgerows. I find no mention of this plant among the ancients, although one may believe, from the aromatic fragrance of Garofani (cloves), which emanates from its roots, that it is a plant of no little value. Modern practitioners use it in drinks for festering and penetrating wounds, and also infuse its juice with verdigris into malignant fistulas. It comforts and refreshes the spirits and the brain, and is useful drunk for stomach fluxes, dysentery, menstrual flow, and for spitting of blood. It helps ruptures taken by mouth and likewise as a poultice. In its temperament it is warm and dry, as is clearly indicated by the taste of its roots, which are aromatic, styptic, and astringent in quality, by which qualities it can thin, dissolve, bind, and strengthen. But returning to our first point, I note that Galen wrote just one line about Lagopo in book 7 on the properties of simples, saying thus: Lagopo has the faculty of drying, so that it can very well arrest fluxes of the body.

D On Medio. Chapter 20.

Medio grows in shady, rocky places; it has leaves similar to iris, a stem three cubits tall, large round purple flowers, and its seed resembles safflower; its root is a palm's length long and thick as a staff, with a harsh taste. Ground into powder and made into an electuary with honey, and taken by mouth for several days, it stops the red flux of women. The seed drunk with wine promotes menstruation.

N Medio grows, according to the opinion of some, only in Media. If this were so, it would not surprise me that it is no longer found in Italy in our time. Some compare it not to iris but to Seride, that is to chicory — among them Ruellius and Marcello Fiorentino — but truly in my Dioscorides it reads ἴξει φύλλα ὅμοια ἶρις, that is, it has leaves similar to iris. Galen wrote of it in book 7 on the properties of simples, saying thus: the root of Medio has a quality contrary to that of the seed; for the root is austere and stops not only other fluxes but particularly those of women. In everything the seed does the opposite: for it promotes menstruation, being composed of fine parts and having an incisive virtue.

On Epimedium. Chapter 21.

Epimedium produces its stem not very large, with leaves similar to ivy, of which there are sometimes ten and sometimes twelve; it produces neither seed nor flower. Its roots are slender, black, of an unpleasant odor, and bland to the taste. It grows in watery places. Its leaves, ground with oil and applied as a poultice, prevent the breasts from growing. The root prevents conception. The leaves, drunk pounded to the weight of five drams in wine for five consecutive days immediately after the purging of the menses, render women sterile.

N There is no one in Italy in our times who can demonstrate the Epimedium, and therefore one must suppose that it is a plant which grows in other distant countries, or else that, if it does grow in Italy, it has not yet come to our knowledge. Pliny in book 27 borrows its history word for word from Dioscorides, as Galen likewise did in book 6 of his work on the properties of simples.

On the Xiphium, or Gladiolus. Chapter 22.

The Latins call the Xiphium Gladiolus, and this plant has been so named from the shape of a sword, which its leaves resemble: it would be similar to the iris, were its leaves not shorter and narrower, pointed like a blade, and veined. It produces a stem of one cubit, along which the purple flowers are arranged, spaced from one another, and evenly distributed. Its seed is round; it generates two roots, one above the other, similar to small bulbs, of which the lower one is smaller and the upper one larger. It grows for the most part in fields. The upper root, applied as a poultice with incense and wine, draws out splinters, thorns, and arrows from the body; mixed with darnel flour and honey-water it softens hard swellings, and therefore it is used in such poultices; and applied it provokes the menses. They say that the upper root, drunk with wine, arouses venereal appetites, and that the other makes women sterile. It is said moreover that the upper root, given to drink with water, cures intestinal ruptures in children.

C The Gladiolus, which the Greeks call Xiphium, grows abundantly throughout all of Tuscany in the fields among the grain, and its flowers are commonly called Monacuccie. The leaves are much shorter and narrower than those of the iris, veined and pointed; the stem is one cubit tall, along which the purple flowers are seen arranged at equal intervals from one another, and in their appearance and shape they very much resemble those of the iris, although they are much smaller. These generate black seed when they ripen, as Dioscorides says. The roots are double, similar to the testicles of a dog, one lower than the other. The account written by Pliny differs from that given by Dioscorides: for Dioscorides says the Gladiolus grows in fields, while Pliny affirmed it is found in watery and marshy places. This leads me easily to believe that by his Gladiolus Pliny meant what is commonly taken for Acorus. Galen wrote of the Xiphium in book 8 of his work on simples, saying: The root of the Xiphium, and especially the upper part, has attractive, digestive, and desiccative virtue.

On Sparganium. Chapter 23.

Sparganium has leaves similar to those of the gladiolus, but narrower and more inclined toward the ground; it produces at the top of its stem certain small balls, inside which its seed is contained. The root and seed are drunk for the bites of serpents.

C Ruellius believed that Sparganium is the common plant growing in watery places, called by everyone Stinking Spatula. This in no way corresponds with the account given by Dioscorides, because the Stinking Spatula has leaves much wider and longer than the Gladiolus, and they do not twist toward the ground, nor do I find that the Stinking Spatula produces any small balls at the tops of its stems inside which the seed might be found. Matteo Silvatico describes the Stinking Spatula on the authority of Paul of Aegina. I think he was rather dreaming when he compiled his glorious Pandects with such diligence. Some make a juice from the Stinking Spatula and use it for mange and flying ringworm. But returning to the Sparganium, I say that I have truly seen it many times in the territory of Rome at Tolfa, where rock alum is manufactured at the foot of Mount Roncone, where it grows with leaves narrower than those of the Gladiolus and produces at the top of the stem certain small green balls, almost similar to those of the serpentaria, inside which the seed is enclosed. Galen wrote very briefly about Sparganium in book 8 of his work on simples, saying: Sparganium also is desiccative.

A On the Xiride. Chapter 24.

The Xiride has leaves similar to the iris, but wider and more pointed at the tip; from their middle rises a quite thick stalk, about an elbow's height, from which hang some triangular seed-pods in which its flower is purple and reddish in the middle. Its seeds are in follicles similar to bean seeds, round, red, and sharp. Its root is long, knotted, and red in color, and is useful for wounds of the head and for fractures of bones. Applied as a poultice with a third part of flower of copper and a fifth part of greater centaury and honey, it draws out all splinters and arrows lodged in the flesh without pain. Applied as a poultice with vinegar it heals tumors and all inflammations. Taken ground up, drunk with must at a weight of three oboli in wine, it is most effective for promoting urination, and taken in vinegar it reduces the spleen.

The Xiride grows in many and diverse places in Italy, and especially in Tuscany, with all those particular qualities that Dioscorides describes. Galen writes of it in book seven on the faculties of simples, saying thus: The Xiride is composed of subtle parts; it has an attracting, digestive, and drying virtue, and this is found not only in the root but much more in the seed, which can powerfully promote urination and heal hardness of the spleen.

On the Anchusa. Chapter 25.

The Anchusa, which some call calica and onoclea, has leaves similar to those of the lettuce that produces its leaves pointed, but they are hairy, rough, dark, plentiful, spread all about close to the root on the ground, and spiny. Its root is a finger's width thick, and when touched in summertime it stains the hands a blood-red color. It grows in rich soils. Its root has an astringent virtue. Cooked with oil and wax it is good for burns from fire and for old ulcers. Applied as a poultice with polenta it heals St. Anthony's fire, and with vinegar it heals skin spots and scabies. Applied below it promotes childbirth. Its decoction is usefully given for overflow of bile, for disorders of the kidneys and spleen, and wherever there is fever it is given with honeyed water. The leaves drunk with wine restrain the body. Perfumers use its root to thicken their ointments.

On the Second Anchusa. Chapter 26.

Another Anchusa, called by some alcibiade and by others onochile, differs from the first in having only smaller leaves, but of the same roughness. Its branches are slender, and on them is a flower of purple color inclining toward reddish. Its roots are long and reddish, from which at harvest time distills a blood-like liquid. It grows in lean, sandy places. Its leaves and those of vipers: and therefore it is said that if anyone chews its leaves and then spits them in the face of a venomous animal, it kills it immediately.

D On the Third Anchusa. Chapter 27.

The Anchusa of the third kind is similar to the preceding one. Its seed is reddish and smaller; when chewed and spat into the mouths of serpents it kills them. Drinking the weight of one acetabulum of its root with hyssop and nasturtium expels broad worms.

These are the species of Anchusa that Dioscorides writes of in this passage, although in Pliny, in chapters twenty and twenty-one of book twenty-two, there is found yet a fourth species, which he calls false Anchusa, very similar to the first species, although it is more hairy, more woolly, less fleshy, and has thinner and more limp leaves. This fourth species I have truly never seen myself, but I have seen the other three in many and diverse places in Italy, and have extracted the reddish juice from their roots in summertime. They all produce flowers almost all along the stalk, which are purple in their clear parts, not very different in their form from those of the common Bugloss, though somewhat more reddish and more open. A Having applied the herb from which he had squeezed its juice onto the bite, he was thus freed from the venom, from which event the plant came to be called Echio Alcibiade, because Alcibius was the first to demonstrate how effective Echio was against serpent bites. Nunenius, a very ancient writer, reports finding two species of Echio, one of which, he says, is called Ocimoide because it has leaves similar to basil, and the other, which produces spiny leaves, is called simply Echio. Dioscorides supports this view by placing immediately after the chapter on Echio the chapter on Ocimoide. Pliny likewise alludes to this opinion in chapter 19 of book 25, saying: Echio is of two species, one that grows with leaves similar to Pennyroyal, and another that produces a certain spiny down, on which there are small heads resembling those of vipers. Yet for all that, he did not know that the Alcibiade was the same as the Echio, because in chapter 5 of book 27, he stated that he did not know what the Alcibiade was, having found no account of it from any writer. This shows that he had not carefully read Nicander and Dioscorides. Beyond this, it is no small wonder to consider how most sagacious nature produced Echio with viper-like heads, thus signaling to men — of whom she is the most loving protector — that this plant is a powerful remedy against the bites of such venomous and deadly animals. I myself have seen this plant many times and collected its viper-like seed in Tuscany and in the territory of Trento. It is a plant very similar to the lesser Anchusa, and many call it wild Bugloss. It produces flowers that are reddish-purple from the middle of the stem
B up to the top, among small leaves, and the seed is black, small, and similar to viper heads. Of Echio I find no mention made by Galen in the books he wrote on the properties of simples, although Paul of Aegina did write of it, following Dioscorides.

Of Ocimoide, that is Wild Basil. Chapter 30.

Ocimoide, which some call Philiterio, produces leaves similar to basil, and hairy stems a span in height, on which grow pods similar to those of henbane, filled with a black seed resembling that of nigella. Drunk in wine it has virtue against the bites of vipers and all other venomous serpents; it is given in cases of sciatica together with myrrh, honey, wine, and pepper. Its root is thin and of no value.

C Wild Basil grows abundantly throughout all of Italy, and especially among the grain crops, with leaves similar to those of the domestic kind, square hairy stems more than a palm's height, at whose tops white flowers grow — which Dioscorides failed to mention — and after these there appear certain small seed-vessels similar to those of henbane, toothed around the opening, inside which is found a black seed, much like that of nigella. Our Tuscan children gather these seed-vessels when they are dry, because when they have shed their seed, if you blow into them with your lips they whistle very shrilly. Galen mentions Ocimoide at the end of book 7 of his work on the properties of simples, saying: The root of Ocimoide, which some call Philiterio, is entirely useless, although the seed is composed of fine particles and is drying without any biting quality.

Of Erino, that is Water Basil. Chapter 31.

N Erino grows near springs and streams, with leaves smaller than those of basil and cut at the tip. It produces five or six stems a span in height, with white flowers, and a small, unripe-tasting black seed. The leaves and stems are full of a milky juice. The seed, taken at the weight of two drams and mixed with four drams of honey, checks, when rubbed on, the fluxes that descend to the eyes. Its juice distilled into the ears with sulfur and nitre relieves their pain.

Although many Greek manuscripts of Dioscorides do not state that Erino produces any milky juice,
Q some are nevertheless found in which this is clearly stated, and for good reasons it seems to me more credible: because I myself have many times gathered this plant along streams, and in doing so stained my hands with its milk; and furthermore one sees that Pliny, in chapter 7 of book 22, writes that Erino is a milky plant, saying: The herb which the Greeks call Erino deserves to be commemorated here for its fine qualities. It grows to the height of a palm and produces five stems similar to basil, with white flowers and small black seeds, which when ground with honey are good for dimness of vision. It is very full of milk, and sweet. The herb is truly most useful for pains in the ears, with a little nitre, and the leaves are effective against poisons — of which Dioscorides made no mention, although Nicander commemorated it for that purpose in his Theriaca. Galen calls this plant Echino, not Erino. This is no wonder, because in some ancient copies of Dioscorides it is likewise written as Echino, of which in book 6 of the Properties of Simples Galen said: The seed of the herb Echino is repercussive and drying. It is used as a powder for the eyes, and likewise for the ears.

FOURTH BOOK. 307

On Couch Grass. Chapter 32. A

Couch grass creeps along the ground with knotted stems, from which spread many sweet roots, which are likewise knotted. It produces hard leaves, like those of a small reed, broad and pointed at the tip, on which cattle and other livestock feed. The root, ground up and applied as a poultice, heals wounds. Its decoction, drunk, helps with pains of the bowels, with retained urine, and breaks kidney stones.

On Reed Couch Grass. Chapter 33.

Reed couch grass is much larger than the preceding kind, which (as they say) kills livestock that eat it, especially that which grows in Babylon along the roadsides.

On Parnassus Grass. Chapter 34. B

The grass that grows on Mount Parnassus is much more branched than the others. It produces leaves similar to ivy; its flower is white and fragrant; its seed is small but useful. It produces five or six roots, as thick as a finger, white, tender, and sweet, whose juice, when cooked with an equal part of honey and wine and half as much myrrh, with a third part of pepper and incense added, becomes an excellent medicine for the eyes; but it must then be stored in a copper vessel. The decoction of the roots is good for the same purposes as the herb itself. The seed powerfully promotes urination, stops vomiting, and checks fluxes of the body. The grass that grows in Cilicia, which the inhabitants call Cinna, inflames cattle that eat it when it is green.

There are many and various species of couch grass: for besides these three mentioned by Dioscorides, Pliny records three other prickly species in Chapter 19 of Book 24, saying the following. Couch grass is among the most common of plants, creeping along the ground with stems full of joints, from which, as well as from the tips, it spreads new roots. Its leaves in all other respects are slender and pointed, and only on Mount Parnassus are they found to resemble ivy leaves and to be dense, among which is the white and fragrant flower. No other herb is more pleasing to livestock than this one, whether green or dried in hay. It is pounded after first being soaked in water. They say that the juice is obtained from the Parnassus variety, because it is very rich in moisture. It is truly sweet to the taste, whereas in every other place in the world its decoction is used to consolidate wounds. The herb pounded and applied as a poultice also works, as it preserves against inflammations. Some add wine and honey to its decoction, and others put in three parts of pepper, incense, and myrrh, and then cook all these things together in a copper vessel for toothache and eye ailments. The root cooked in wine treats pains of the bowels, helps with retained urine and ulcers of the bladder, and breaks stones. The seed powerfully promotes urination and stops vomiting and fluxes of the body. That variety which has seven internodes in its stems is most effective for headaches when tied around the head. Some use three prickly species because at the top of their stems they have five pointed fingers, which are inserted into the nose to stop nosebleeds; this species they call Dactyl. Another produces leaves similar to houseleek and is used mixed with grease for growths of flesh on the fingers and for pterygium. The third, which is quite small, grows on rooftops and in the walls of buildings; it is ulcerative, and therefore applied firmly it stops the malignancy of corrosive ulcers; placed around the head it stops nosebleeds. All of this Pliny wrote about couch grasses. Therefore one can easily discern that the varieties of Babylon and Mount Parnassus do not grow among us, although the most common and most widespread of the first species is very abundant, as is likewise that which produces at the top of its stems the five fingers used in the nose to provoke bleeding, which we in Tuscany call Sanguinella, and others call Capriola, as we said above. No credence should be given to the opinion of Ruellio and Leoniceno, that this is the Coronopus written about by Dioscorides, of which Pliny wrote at length in Chapter 3 of Book 22. Galen wrote about couch grasses in Book 6 of his work on the faculties of simples, saying the following. The roots of couch grass are eaten where they are found to be tender, in which there is a certain sweetness like that of water, which has in it something of the sharp and the bitter. This herb is truly watery to the taste, from which one may easily judge that its root is cold and dry, and therefore it can consolidate fresh bleeding wounds. But the herb applied as a poultice does not cool too much, because it is moderately moist and dry. Moreover, the sharpness and pungency found in the root is truly slight, although its decoction when drunk is sometimes known to break kidney stones. The seed of the common kind is of little value, but that of the Parnassus variety promotes urination and stops stomach and body fluxes. It is desiccative, somewhat bitter in taste, and composed of subtle parts.

On Sideritis. Chapter 35.

Sideritis, which some call Heraclea, produces leaves longer than those of horehound, very similar in shape to those of oak, or of sage, though smaller than either, and rougher. It produces square stems, which most often exceed the height of a palm, not unpleasant to the taste, with something of an astringent flavor; along them, at regular intervals (as is seen in horehound), there are certain small whorls in which the seed is black. It grows in stony places. The leaves have the virtue of consolidating wounds without allowing inflammation to arise.

On another Sideritis. Chapter 36.

Another Sideritis, which grows with slender branches two cubits tall, whose many leaves are similar to those of fern, cut all around their edges, and attached by a long petiole. From the upper cavity of its wings there emerge certain long, slender branchlets, at the tops of which is a round, rough button, inside which is the seed, similar to that of beets, though rounder and harder. Its virtue, as well as that of the leaves, is to close fresh wounds.

On the third Sideritis. Chapter 37.

They say there is another Sideritis, which Cratevas likewise calls Heraclea, that grows on walls, in ruins, and in vineyards, whose numerous leaves proceed from the root and resemble those of coriander. The stems are a hand's span tall, dry, tender, and of a color that whitens toward red. The flower is red, small, sticky, and bitter. This plant has the virtue of consolidating every fresh bleeding wound.

C T The species of Sideritis without Achillea, of which we shall speak in the following chapter, I find commemorated by Dioscorides; of these, the second species I have not yet been able to trace in Italy, but the other two I have seen and collected several times in the valley of Anaunia in the jurisdiction of Trento. Let no one be surprised that Dioscorides should have described its leaves so variously, making them at one time similar to those of horehound, at another to those of oak, and at another to those of sage; for the shape and length of the leaves is like those of sage, the surface hairy and whitish like horehound, and the cutting around the edges like oak, to which all the other notes given to it are then added. I do not think, therefore, that the plant illustrated in the great herbal of Leonhart Fuchs resembles at all the Sideritis of the first species, since it is clearly to be seen there that, besides having neither leaves nor stems that correspond to it, it produces flowers spiked at the tops of the stems, and not along the stem as horehound does. Ruellius moreover says that some call it Herba Giudaica; but if he means the one described by Avicenna in the second book, he cannot in any way be excused from error, since Avicenna understands by the Herba Giudaica nothing other than the ervum. Herba Giudaica and likewise Herba Pagana are called by some the plant which is commonly called Goldenrod, whose stem is red, two cubits tall, sometimes taller, smooth and polished, upon which it produces leaves like those of olive, very finely toothed all around, and smooth on their surface. It produces flowers spiked at the top of the stem, of golden color, which at maturity

D turn into the lightest down and fly away in the air. German surgeons use it in drinks for internal wounds and fistulas, and likewise in ointments, for rubbed on it is most wonderful for consolidating wounds. Arnaldo da Villanova praised it as a marvelous thing for making one urinate and for breaking kidney stones; but I have found this written by none other than himself. But returning to the Sideritis, I say that that of the first species cannot by any means be the goldenrod. Galen wrote of the siderites in book eight of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Sideritis truly has a kind of cleansing faculty, though it is for the most part moist and moderately cold. It has a little of the astringent, and therefore heals wounds and prevents inflammation.

On Achillea. Chapter 38.

Achillea, which some call Achillea siderite, produces stems a hand's span long, sometimes longer, almost similar in form to the stems, surrounded by small leaves cut very finely crosswise, like those of coriander, of a reddish color, flexible, of a very medicinal and not unpleasant scent. It produces at the top a round umbel of white, purple, and golden flowers. It grows in rich soils, and

FOURTH BOOK. 309

When the plant's foliage is ground and applied as a poultice, it heals fresh wounds and protects them from inflammation; it stops flows of blood, and likewise menstrual flows when applied below with wool, and so women who suffer from uterine flux sit in its decoction. It is also drunk for dysentery.

All those who believe that Achillea is the common yarrow (millefolio) are plainly mistaken: for this plant, as we shall discuss more fully in the course of this book at the chapter on Strattore, does not produce leaves cut like coriander, but rather like small bird feathers, very closely packed; and even if yarrow does produce an umbel that is white, flesh-colored, or yellow at different times, one cannot therefore conclude that yarrow and Achillea are the same thing. For Dioscorides does not say (as Ruellius does) that Achillea produces flowers now white, now purple, now yellow; but rather that its umbel is varied in all these colors, as is indeed true of the genuine Achillea, of which I have myself collected plants many times in various and diverse places, in all of which one finds every distinguishing feature that Dioscorides assigns to Achillea. The belief that Achillea is our yarrow has been encouraged by Pliny, who in chapter 25 of book 25 said that the Latins called Achillea millefolium; but as far as one can see, he is not describing Achillea but rather the plant Dioscorides calls Myriophyllon, and so he adds a little further on: but some say that the true Achillea produces a bluish stem, a foot tall, without branches, and round leaves that clothe it elegantly. This shows that Pliny was uncertain which plant was the true Achillea, and so one cannot place much confidence in his account. Serapion calls Achillea "Dragon's blood" because the juice pressed from it is reddish (which one does not see in the common yarrow), in place of which a counterfeit and adulterated substance sold as dragon's blood has taken over in all the apothecary shops, made from resin, goat's blood, dried service-berries, and a thousand other mixed ingredients. Galen wrote about Achillea together with Sideritis in book 8 of his work on the faculties of simple medicines, saying as follows: there are also some who call Achillea "Sideritis," because its virtues are not far from those of that plant, although it is more astringent, and is therefore very useful for stopping blood, dysentery, and the fluxes of women.

On the Bramble. Chapter 39.

The bramble, known to everyone, has the virtue of drying and binding: it blackens the hair. A decoction of the branches drunk constrains the body and likewise the fluxes of women; it helps with the bites of the prestero serpent; it strengthens the gums. The leaves, when chewed, help ulcers of the mouth, and restrain the corrosive ones, and benefit those of the head that run, and eyes that water. The leaves are applied as a poultice on abscesses of the seat, and likewise on hemorrhoids; when ground they are used beneficially for pains of the heart and weaknesses of the stomach. The branches and leaves are pounded and the juice pressed out; this juice, thickened in the sun, is a considerably more powerful medicine for all the aforementioned conditions. The juice of its well-ripened berries is very suitable for medicines of the mouth; when eaten half-ripe, they constrain the body. The flowers drunk in wine do the same.

On the Ida Bramble. Chapter 40.

This is specially called the Ida Bramble because it grows only on Mount Ida in Crete. It is more tender than the first kind described, and armed with smaller thorns, though it is also found without them; it is effective for everything for which the above-mentioned bramble is useful. Beyond that, applied as a poultice with honey it helps inflammations of the eyes; it quenches erysipelas (sacred fire). It is given to drink in water for ailments of the stomach.

Brambles are very common plants, and of several kinds, as Theophrastus writes well in chapter 18 of book 3. For some grow tall and thicken, others twine around hedges and trees, others creep along the ground and root themselves like couch grass, and others grow in various and diverse ways. In the mountains throughout the territory of Trento one finds some that bear pink berries without seeds, called by the local people "Ampomele," similar to strawberries, and truly very pleasing to the taste in summer. Bears are fond of them, and so hunters gather there when they ripen. The Ida bramble we do not have in Italy, unless perhaps it has recently been transplanted there from Crete. Galen made mention of brambles in book 6 of his work on simple medicines, saying thus: The leaves, buds, flower, fruit, and root of brambles all share to a considerable degree in astringency; but they differ in this respect, namely that the tender, newly sprouted leaves contain quite a lot of watery quality and little astringency, and I say the same likewise of the buds, and so when chewed they heal ulcers of the mouth and can also consolidate wounds. Their temperament is composed partly of a cold, earthy quality and partly of a tepid, watery one. But the fruit when ripe has no small amount of warm, tempered juice, because it is sweet; and so, both for this reason and for a slight astringency,

A which is found in it, is quite agreeable to the taste when eating it. That which is ripe has in itself quite a bit of earthiness, since it is tart and drying. The flower has the same strength as the unripe fruit, and therefore both are useful in dysentery, in bodily flux, and in spitting of blood. The root, besides being constrictive, contains no small amount of subtle substance, by virtue of which it can break up kidney stones.

On Helsine. Chapter 41.

The Helsine, surnamed Cissampelos, has leaves similar to ivy, but smaller. Its stems are slender, with which it embraces whatever it touches. It grows in hedges, in vineyards, and among grain. The juice pressed from the leaves purges the body.

N There is truly no reason whatsoever to doubt that the Helsine named Cissampelos, that is, ivy-vine, is not a species of Bindweed or Convolvulus; but what exactly it is cannot be easily determined. Yet Dioscorides saying that it has leaves similar to ivy, but much smaller, with slender stems by which it clasps whatever it touches, and that it grows in hedges, vineyards, and among grain, seems to indicate that it is the plant which in the fields winds around grain, flax, and legumes, and in vineyards around stakes and vines, which we call Vilucchio, and in the Trentino region Minutola, although Leonardo Fuchs the German believes the Helsine to be that plant which winds around hedges and small trees, and which produces in summer those white little bells. Pliny calls this Convolvulus in chapter 15 of book 21, saying that nature learned to make lilies when it made the flowers of Convolvulus. Some call this flower (as Servius the Grammarian did, being mistaken) privet, but the error was demonstrated above in its proper chapter in the first book. Galen wrote briefly about Helsine in book 6 of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying: The Helsine called Cissampelos has the virtue of aiding digestion.

On Elatine. Chapter 42.

Elatine has leaves similar to Helsine, but smaller, hairy, and more rounded. Its small stems are slender, about a hand-span long, numbering five or six, full of leaves from the root upward, astringent to the taste. It grows among grain and in cultivated fields. It is useful for fluxes and for inflammations of the eyes, when the leaves are crushed and applied as a poultice with polenta. Drinking the decoction is beneficial in dysentery.

C Although Ruellius affirms that Elatine is found in France, and that the peasants call it wild turnip, eating it daily in salads; nonetheless in Italy I have not yet been able to find what it might be, knowing however for certain that our wild turnip cannot in any way be Elatine. Galen wrote very briefly about it in book 6 of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying: Elatine is slightly drying and slightly cooling.

On Eupatorium. Chapter 43.

Eupatorium is a tall plant, and produces a single stem, woody, blackish, straight, slender, hairy, about a cubit long, sometimes longer, along which the leaves are arranged at intervals, similar to those of cinquefoil, or more precisely of hemp, divided into five or more parts, blackish, and toothed around the edges. The seed grows from the middle of the stem upward, hairy, hanging toward the ground, and when dry, it clings to clothing. The leaves, when crushed and applied with lard, heal ulcers that are slow to consolidate. The seed, or the herb drunk with wine, benefits ailments of the liver, dysentery, and serpent bites. Some mistakenly call Eupatorium by the name Argemone, since this, as we have shown, is entirely different from Eupatorium.

D Some, indeed almost the greater part of pharmacists, offer for Eupatorium a certain plant that grows on the banks of streams and on the edges of ditches, up to three cubits tall, whose leaves, though larger, resemble those of hemp; they are whitish, hairy, and bitter to the taste. The stem is reddish, round, solid, and hairy, and where the branches emerge there are many hollow cavities. The flowers grow in an open umbrella shape at the tops of the stems, of a flesh color, and somewhat like those of our (though false) Italian oregano; when ripe they shed their down and float off into the air. The root, from which quite a few smaller ones branch off, is useless and of no value. And although they know that the true Eupatorium of the Greeks is that plant which we call Agrimony, as some also called it in the time of Dioscorides, nonetheless, unwilling to depart from their old habits, they are not easily persuaded to change for the purposes of preparations drawn from the Greeks. Yet I say this not to disparage their Eupatorium, which is the same one described by Avicenna, but only so that each plant may be given its proper place. I know well enough that, as far as the matter goes

A In his volume on illustrious men he names him from Como, not from Verona. German surgeons use this fourth variety frequently in drinks for internal wounds, fractures, and fistulas, and in every other case where consolidation is needed. But one should know that this Sanniccolo is not the plant that produces only five leaves and the white root so artfully inlaid by nature, of which we spoke above in the chapter on Comfrey; it is far from that. Galen wrote about Cinquefoil in book eight of his work on the faculties of simples, saying: The root of Cinquefoil desiccates greatly, and is not at all sharp; and therefore it is much in use, as are all those other things which, being composed of fine parts, desiccate without biting. This root is therefore desiccating in the third degree, and possesses no warmth that can be clearly perceived.

On the Phenice. Chapter XLV.

T he Phenice has leaves like barley, but shorter and narrower; the spike resembles darnel; the stalks are six fingers tall and grow up around the root, bearing six or eight spikes. It grows in fields and on newly made rooftops. Drunk in astringent wine, it restrains the fluxes of the body, the menses, and the urine. Some say it is also good for restraining
B fluxes of blood, when carried on the person wrapped in red wool.

The Phenice is called in Tuscany wild darnel, and grows commonly in the valleys along roadsides and on the
C banks of fields, differing not at all from Dioscorides' description. Pliny, in book twenty-five, chapter twenty-two, said that the Latins called the Phenice mouse-barley, perhaps because mice eat that which grows on rooftops. It grows abundantly in Gorizia in the cemetery of San Francesco in front of the great door of the church, and I have likewise seen plenty of it near Venice on the Lido.

On the Root Idea. Chapter XLVI.

T he Root Idea produces leaves similar to butcher's broom, and near them are certain small things like little tendrils from which the flower emerges. The root is powerfully astringent and suited to every case where staunching is needed; and so it is usefully drunk for fluxes of the body and the menses. It also restrains all fluxes of blood.

This plant is not brought to Italy in our time, nor could I find anyone who writes where it grows, although its name suggests
C Q it is a plant particular to Mount Ida in Crete, as was mentioned a little above regarding the Idaean bramble. Galen demonstrates its virtues in book six of his work on the faculties of simples, saying: The Root Idea is powerfully bitter to the taste, and experience shows it clearly to act as the taste suggests: for whether drunk or applied as a poultice externally, it restrains dysentery, fluxes of blood, of the body, of the menses, and of every other part of the person.

On the Rhodian Root. Chapter XLVII.

T he Rhodian Root grows in Macedonia, similar to costus but lighter and more uneven. When pounded, it gives off the scent of roses. Applied ground up on the forehead with rose oil, it helps with headache.

A The Rhodian Root is known to few in Italy, although it could easily grow there, and on the Apennine mountains and those of
L Sant'Angelo. The one I have planted in my garden in Gorizia was sent to me from Graz in Styria by the most excellent physician Messer Pietro Saliceto; and so that it may become better known, I will describe it here, since Dioscorides passed over its characteristics. I say, then, that the Rhodian Root produces several round stems, somewhat hollow, a palm to a cubit in height, from which grow fairly long, pointed, fleshy leaves, like those of purslane, with small teeth around the margins; it produces at the top of the stems a green umbel, somewhat like that of lithimimalosma, which after flowering turns reddish. The root is uneven, thick like that of costus, smooth and shiny on the outside, and white inside when fresh; but when dry it is light, reddish inside, and scaly outside. This root, chewed or pounded, gives off a most natural scent of roses, from which it has acquired the name Rhodian. Moreover, it is among the most long-lived of all roots: for once dug up and stored, if it is not kept in very dry places, and then replanted after many months, it immediately sprouts again. It grows on very high mountains, rocky and precipitous, where there is barely enough soil around for it to take hold. It is usefully applied as a poultice moistened with rosewater or lavender water, according to the nature of the pain, on the forehead and temples for headache. It strengthens the brain with its pleasant scent, so that it can be used for every kind of headache whatever the cause. For, as Galen attests, it is composed of temperate qualities, as its flavor, which imitates roses, confirms. Galen wrote of this Root in book eight of his work on the faculties of simples, saying: The Rhodian Root, that is, the one that grows in Macedonia, is composed of fine parts. It is digestive and warm at the end of the second degree, or at most at the beginning of the third.

On Horsetail. Chapter 48. A

Horsetail grows in watery places and along ditches. Its stems are hollow, knotted, full in themselves, reddish, and rough, around which grow leaves similar to rushes, dense and slender. It grows tall, surpassing the neighboring small trees, from which its dark tresses then hang, like a horse's tail: its root is woody and hard. The herb is astringent, and therefore its juice stanches nosebleeds. It is drunk with wine for dysentery and to stimulate urination. The leaves, ground and made into a poultice, consolidate fresh wounds. Some say that the leaves drunk with water consolidate wounds of the bowels and of the bladder, and likewise intestinal ruptures.

On Another Horsetail. Chapter 49.

The other Horsetail has a straight, uniform stem, a cubit tall or somewhat more, hollow, whose tresses, which it bears at distinct intervals, are shorter, whiter, and more tender than the one described above. This, ground with vinegar, closes wounds, and has the same virtues as the first.

Horsetail is most commonly called Cauda equina, and both these species are very well known in Italy: for one is called by most people Asperella, which women use to polish ponds, and the other is still called Horsetail. This produces, almost at its first sprouting, a certain thick and tender shoot, similar to an acorn, which our people of Siena call Paltrufali, used by them as food in Lent, first boiled in water and then floured and fried in a pan in place of fish. But eaten in this way they sometimes so constipate the body that those affected easily fall into what is called (as they say) the disease of the strawberry tree. Galen wrote of Horsetail in book six of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Horsetail has, together with bitterness, an astringent virtue, and therefore it dries powerfully without any sharpness. It closes large wounds, even if the nerves have been cut through, and heals intestinal ruptures. The herb drunk in wine, or indeed in water, is a most powerful remedy against vomiting and spitting of blood, against women's fluxes, especially the red ones, against dysentery, and other bodily fluxes. Some have written that at times the juice drunk has closed wounds of the delicate bowels, and likewise of the bladder. It benefits the flux of blood from the nose, and bodily ailments caused by fluxes, being drunk with dry wine and with water in which a fever has dissolved.

On Grain (Kermes). Chapter 50.

The Grain, which dyers use, is a small, branching plant, to which certain small grains similar to lentils are attached, and these are gathered and stored. The best comes from Galatia and Armenia, and next in quality is that which is brought from Asia and Cilicia. The least good of all is the Spanish. The Grain has the virtue of staunching: it is usefully applied, ground with vinegar, on wounds and on cut nerves. It grows in Cilicia on oak trees, resembling small snails, and the women of that country collect it with their mouths, and call it Grain.

Although the Grain with which in our time in Italy a very great quantity of woolen cloth is dyed, as well as silk, is very well known to everyone, I do not know that anywhere in Italy one finds the small tree that produces it. That which is kept in apothecaries' shops is round of grain and hollow within, and therefore does not at all resemble lentils, as Dioscorides asserts. For which reason one must believe that the Grain is of more than one species, and that this is indeed the one which Pliny said grew in Attica and in Africa, whose pith quickly turns into a small worm. The Grain is used among women to prevent miscarriages in pregnant women, for which purpose they give it with good success in powder, with an equal quantity of male Frankincense, in a fresh egg to drink. Galen wrote of it in book seven of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The Grain of the Dyers is in its faculties astringent and bitter, and both these qualities dry without any sharpness, and therefore it is very suitable for large wounds, especially of the nerves. For this purpose some grind it with pure vinegar, and others with honey-vinegar.

On Tragium. Chapter 51.

Tragium grows only in Crete, with leaves, fruit, and branches similar to the lentisk, though all are smaller and shorter. From it distills a liquid like milk, similar to gum. The seed, the leaves, and the liquid, applied externally...

A They draw out from the flesh thorns, arrows, and every other pointed thing. Drunk, they promote retained urine and menstruation, and break up bladder stones: one takes a drachm's weight per dose. It is said that wild goats wounded by arrows heal themselves with this plant, for when they graze on it, the arrows fall out of their backs.

Of Another Tragium. Chapter 52.

Another Tragium, which some call Tragoceros: whose leaves are similar to those of scolopendria. The root is white and slender, resembling horse-radish, and eaten raw as well as cooked it benefits dysentery. In autumn the leaves give off the smell of a he-goat, from which the plant has acquired the name of Tragium.

The Tragium which Dioscorides writes grows in Crete, similar in every part to the mastic tree, Pliny in chapter 21 of book 14 said was similar to the terebinth, and in the last chapter of book 27 made it in every part similar to the juniper. This shows that he himself had not seen it, but had written about it based on the opinions of various writers from whom he gathered what he wrote. This plant is not brought to us in our time, and therefore I cannot offer any further knowledge of it. The second species is to be judged more readily an herb than a shrub, since the root is eaten both raw and cooked, and it resembles horse-radish. But I cannot find anyone who can show me any plant that produces leaves similar to scolopendria, which the Greeks call Asplenon and Ceterach, or one that, as the Arabians say, smells of a he-goat; nor can I affirm that this Tragium is the common plant called by some Pimpinella, and by others Saxifraga hircina, even though one does detect a very sharp and true goat-smell on it; for the leaves do not correspond to those of scolopendria, nor is it known to anyone to be used for dysentery, though it is good for promoting urine and opening obstructions. Galen wrote of Tragium in book 8 of his work on simples, saying thus: the leaves, the stem, and the gum of Tragium have the virtue of digesting and drawing. They are composed of subtle parts, and are therefore heating in the beginning of the third degree. The gum draws out thorns, splinters, and every other pointed thing embedded in the body; it breaks up stones and provokes menstruation when one drinks the weight of a drachm of it; but it grows only in Crete, similar to the mastic tree. The other, much smaller than this one, is seen in many places, with leaves similar to scolopendria, and it is not a little astringent, and so it is useful in fluxes. It grows on mountains and in steep places.

C Of Trago. Chapter 53.

The Trago is an herb which some call Scorpion, or alternatively Tragano. It grows abundantly in the coastal marshes, reaching the height of a palm's breadth, sometimes more, branchy, low, somewhat long, and without leaves; it produces around its branches many small berries, like grains of wheat, pointed at the tip, reddish, and very astringent to the taste, of which, drinking ten in wine, they benefit stomach fluxes and those of women. Some pound them and make lozenges, and preserve them and use them when needed.

The Trago (Pliny said in the last chapter of book 27) is an herb which some call Scorpion, half a foot tall, dense, and without leaves. It produces small clusters full of grains pointed at the tip, similar to wheat, and grows in the coastal marshes. And therefore it could readily be that species of small rushes which grows dense and bushy at the foot of Mount Argentario in our marshes of Siena, with some clusters of small red and somewhat elongated grains. Of this I find that Galen made no mention at all, perhaps because he had not taken it into consideration.

D Of the Rush. Chapter 54.

The Rush is of two species, one called smooth, and the other sharp, being well pointed at the tip, and of this there are likewise two sub-species, one sterile, and the other which produces black, round seeds, and this one is thicker than a cane and more fleshy. There is also a third species called Holoschoenus, more fleshy and more rough than the aforesaid, which produces its seed similarly to the others. The seed of both, roasted and drunk with diluted wine, restrains the body and the red fluxes of women; it promotes urine and causes headache. The tender leaves closest to the root are beneficially applied as a poultice to the bites of those spiders called phalanges. The seed of the Ethiopian variety is sleep-inducing, and therefore one must take care in administering it, so that it does not cause one to sleep beyond what is fitting.

The Rushes

FOURTH BOOK. 315

Rushes are well known to everyone, and all the species that Dioscorides describes in this place can be found in Italy near water. Galen wrote about them in book eight of his work on the properties of simples, saying: Among the rushes there is one species called Oxischenos, and another called Oligoschenos, whose fruit induces sleep. Of the one called Oxischeno there are two varieties: one sterile, which is of no value in medicine, and another whose seed is likewise useful for inducing sleep, though not as effectively as that of the Oligoscheno, which also causes mental derangement. Both, when roasted and then drunk with wine, check the flow of the body and likewise of the menstrual blood. From this it is clearly understood that their temperament is of an earthy substance, slightly cold, and of a watery substance slightly warm, so that they can dry up the lower humors and carry cool vapors to the head, from which sleep is caused.

On Lichen. Chapter 55.

Lichen, most familiar among rocks, is called Brion by some. It attaches itself to stones moistened by water, as moss does. Applied as a poultice it checks flows of blood; it extinguishes inflammations and heals skin eruptions. Applied with honey, it is good for overflow of bile and prevents flows that descend to the tongue and mouth.

Lichen (according to the most learned herbalists) is what the apothecaries call Epatica, and the Greeks called it Lichen because it cures the skin patches they call esslichene. Its fronds are thick and somewhat elongated, attached to stones where some trickle of water seeps out; below these there emerge certain small stalks, bearing tiny star-shaped heads, especially in the month of June. Pliny in book four, chapter twenty-six, recorded two species, saying: The Lichena herb grows in rocky places with a single frond, broad near the root, and produces a single small, slender stem from which several long fronds hang. There is also another species which attaches itself to stones as moss does. Applied to wounds, and likewise to abscesses, it checks the flow of blood; and made into an electuary with honey it heals overflow of bile — but those who follow this treatment must wash with salt water, anoint themselves with almond oil, and abstain from greens. Galen recorded it in book seven of the properties of simples, saying: Lichen, which grows on rocks, is truly like a moss, but may rightly be counted among plants. It has been called thus because it cures lichen. It has a cleansing virtue, but little cooling one, and both varieties have a drying quality. The cleansing and drying it derives from the rocks, and the cooling from the water; for it grows on moist stones that have an unpleasant smell. Being thus composed of such qualities, it helps those phlegmy conditions they call aphlegmaton. But whether it helps flows of blood, as Dioscorides writes, I cannot affirm.

On Paronychia. Chapter 56.

Paronychia is a small plant that grows on stones, similar to peplo but shorter, and with larger fronds. Pounded and applied it is the remedy for whitlows and hardnesses of the fingers.

Paronychia grows everywhere, with fronds near the roots that are rounded and larger than those of peplo; at the tip they are smaller and closely resemble those of peplo. The stem is not as long nor as thick, nor does it contain the milky sap found in peplo. An immense abundance of it can be seen in the great forest along the road from Ljubljana to Gorizia, on rocks and dry tree trunks. Galen wrote about it in book eight of the properties of simples, saying: Paronychia is so called from the effect it produces in medicine, for it heals (as Dioscorides says) whitlows of the fingers, and likewise favus. Its virtue is composed of subtle parts. It dries without any biting quality, for that is what is needed in those things that heal whitlows.

On Chrisocome. Chapter 57.

Chrisocome grows to the height of a span; its corymb-shaped head resembles that of hyssop; it has a hairy, slender root, similar to that of black hellebore, with a taste not unpleasant to the palate, quite like cyperus — that is, austere with a certain sweetness. It grows in shady and rocky places. Its root is warm and astringent, beneficial for inflammations of the liver and lungs. It is taken boiled in honey-water to stimulate purgation in women.

As for Chrisocome, I have found no one up to this time who could identify it for me in Italy; and therefore we shall set it aside in that garden of nature which reserves for itself unknown simples, so as not to deprive itself of anything, and leave us as its masters.

316 BOOK

On Chrysogonum. Chapter 58.

Chrysogonum is a low plant whose leaves are similar to those of the oak, and whose flower resembles that of the coronary mullein. It produces a root similar to a turnip, which is very red inside and black outside. When ground and applied as a plaster with vinegar, it heals the bite of the wolf spider.

If Chrysogonum is not brought from elsewhere into the gardens of Italy, it will remain unknown to us, like all the other plants that nature hides in its secret garden.

On Helichrysum. Chapter 59.

Helichrysum, which some call Chrysanthemum and others Amaranth, with which the statues of the Gods are crowned, has a stem that is upright, white, turning green, and firm: along it grow narrow leaves similar to southernwood, spaced at intervals throughout. It produces a round head of golden color, drawn into an umbel like clusters of dry hanging corymbs; the root is slender. It grows in rough places, on riverbanks, and in riverbeds. Its head, drunk with wine, is beneficial against snake bites, sciatica, urinary distillations, and ruptures; it provokes menstruation. Drunk with honeyed wine, it resolves blood clotted in the bladder and likewise in the bowels; drunk likewise on an empty stomach in diluted white wine at the weight of three obols, it prevents catarrh descending from the head. It is placed among clothing to preserve it from moths.

Helichrysum grows abundantly in Tuscany in poor meadows, in uncultivated lands, on hillsides, and likewise in the sandy gravel of riverbeds. It grows to the height of a cubit, with southernwood-like leaves arranged at intervals along the very straight and firm stem, at the top of which is a golden-colored umbel, similar in appearance to common yarrow and to that eupatorium described by Mesue. The color of their dried flowers lasts quite a long time; and so in winter when fresh flowers are lacking, the dried ones of Helichrysum are used, like those of amaranth, which we call velvet flower. Pliny wrote about it in chapter 25 of book 21, saying thus: Helichrysum, which some call Chrysanthemum, has white stems and pale leaves similar to those of southernwood, whose umbel is full of hanging corymbs that never rot. When struck by the rays of the sun it shines as if made of gold; hence it is customary to crown the gods with it. This was observed with great diligence by Ptolemy, King of Egypt; it grows among scrub. Of Helichrysum, though it is so glorious, it is not found that Galen made any mention of it in his books on simples, though after him Paul of Aegina did not omit it.

On Chrysanthemum. Chapter 60.

Chrysanthemum, which some call Caltha and others Buphthalmum, is a tender and bushy plant that produces smooth stems and finely cut leaves; its flowers are exceedingly brilliant, of a color inclining to yellow, and in shape similar to the roundness of an eye, from which it has taken the name Buphthalmum; it grows around the walls of fortresses. Its stems are eaten like other garden herbs. The flowers, ground and mixed with wax (as they say), resolve those abscesses called adipine; they are good for an overflow of bile, quickly removing the discoloration if they are drunk after prolonged bathing when one exits the bath.

Although there are some who believe that Buphthalmum and Chrysanthemum are one and the same plant, because of the correspondence seen between them, nonetheless, considering certain particular features of each, it seems easy enough to believe that they are different plants. This is shown first by Dioscorides, who devoted two separate chapters to them, one earlier in the third book and another here in the fourth; for he would not have done this had he not seen some difference between them, which is apparent from his saying that Buphthalmum has leaves similar to fennel, which are hair-like, while those of Chrysanthemum are finely cut. Furthermore he said that the stems of Chrysanthemum are eaten in food like other garden vegetables, which he did not say of Buphthalmum; and he compared the flowers of Buphthalmum to those of chamomile, but did not compare those of Chrysanthemum to them, since he wrote that the latter is a tender and bushy plant, which he did not say of Buphthalmum. Furthermore, speaking of their virtues and properties, he said that the flowers of Buphthalmum ground with wax resolve tumors and abscesses, speaking generally and affirmatively; but then he said that the flowers of Chrysanthemum, mixed with wax (as they say), resolve those abscesses called adipine, and by the Greeks steatoma, speaking specifically and with some uncertainty.
Which

What makes me believe that some of the ancient Greeks imagined that Buphthalmon and Chrysanthemum were the same thing, is that they transferred to Buphthalmon everything that Dioscorides wrote in his third book, as one finds was also done with wild rue, St. John's wort, and likewise with asarum and baccara. For which reason I would say that the chapter on Chrysanthemum in Dioscorides should be read thus: THE CHRYSANTHEMUM is a tender and leafy herb, which produces smooth stems and finely cut leaves, whose flowers are of a color that shades toward yellow, exceedingly brilliant. Its stems are eaten like other garden greens. The flowers, ground with wax, are said to dissolve those swellings called steatomas, that is, fatty tumors. In this way, then, the Chrysanthemum is restored to its true history, which, upon careful consideration, differs greatly from that of Buphthalmon. I myself have seen the Chrysanthemum growing most abundantly in the territory of Montenero, a castle of our most magnificent city of Siena, entirely matching the reformed description noted here by us; our peasants eat it cooked, as one eats beets, spinach, and cabbage. However, I have never yet been able to see the true Buphthalmon anywhere in Italy. Leonardo Fuchs the German is deceived in his otherwise glorious herbal, believing that the Chrysanthemum is that species of Ranunculus which grows in meadows with parsley-like leaves and yellow flowers: for the true Chrysanthemum is quite different from this, and I find no mention of it in Galen's books that treat of plants.

Of Ageratum. Chapter 61.

Ageratum is a bushy plant, one span tall, simple, low-growing, very similar to oregano. It produces an umbel, in which the flowers resemble small golden buttons, smaller than those of helichrysum; and it bears the name Ageratum for no other reason than that it preserves the color of its flower for a long time. Its decoction is quite warming. The herb applied as a fumigation stimulates urine and softens hardness of the womb.

Ageratum grows commonly throughout Tuscany, with leaves and stems like oregano, although its umbel is full of tiny golden flowers. Galen wrote briefly of it in book seven on the faculties of simples, saying thus: Ageratum has the virtue of digesting and gently resolving inflammations.

Of Verbenaca. Chapter 62.

Verbenaca, or Peristereon, grows in watery places. It seems to have taken its name from being frequented willingly by doves, wherever it grows. It is a plant one span tall, sometimes taller, whose leaves, which come from the stem, are cut and whitish. This herb is often found with a single stem and a single root. It is believed that its leaves, combined with fresh pig fat or rose oil and applied as a poultice, relieve pains of the womb. Applied with vinegar, it extinguishes St. Anthony's fire and stops putrid and corrosive ulcers. It heals wounds and, with honey, cicatrizes old ulcers.

Of Sacred Herb. Chapter 63.

The sacred herb called Peristereon produces little branches about one cubit tall, sometimes somewhat taller, square-stemmed, on which the leaves are arranged at intervals similar to those of oak leaves, but smaller and narrower, though cut in the same manner, of a somewhat bluish color. The root is long and slender. The flowers are purple and fine. The leaves drunk with wine together with the root, and likewise applied as poultices, are good against snakebite; and drunk at the weight of one dram in a hemina of old wine with three obols of incense, for forty continuous days on an empty stomach, they help against overflow of bile; applied as poultices they soothe old swellings and inflammations, and cleanse foul ulcers. The decoction of the whole plant, used as a gargle, breaks up the crusts of the throat, and stops corrosive ulcers of the mouth. It is said that if its infusion is sprinkled in the places where banquets are held, the guests become merry. The third node of its stem, counting from the ground upward, with the leaves near it, is given for tertian fever, and the fourth node for quartan fever. It is called sacred herb because it is used greatly in the purification of places, and for being worn suspended about the person.

In Tuscany the Verbenaca is called Verminacola, and in other parts of Italy Berbena; of this plant, as is clearly seen from the above-written chapters, there are two species, between which there is no other difference than that one produces its stems upright with sparse leaves, and the other spreading toward the ground and more leafy; nor is there any further difference in leaves or flowers, as Fuchs imagined, who in his great herbal said that the upright Verbenaca bore flow-

This I do not find stated by Dioscorides, nor by Pliny, who wrote about it in chapter nine of book twenty-five, saying thus: Verbena has two species, one leafy, which they call female, and another with fewer leaves, which they call male. The branches of both are numerous, an elbow's height tall, slender and square. The leaves smaller than those of the oak, narrower and more deeply cut. The flower grayish-blue, that is, tending toward sky-blue. The root long and slender. They grow everywhere, in plains and in marshy places. Some do not distinguish between them, but make both into a single species, since they have the same virtues one as the other. This doctrine shows that Fuchs was dreaming when he said that the upright one produced a yellow flower. But before him, Otto Brunfels the German erred even more grossly, who in his herbal depicted as female Verbena the plant that some commonly call Cardoncello and others Speliciosa, not agreeing that this is the Erigeron, or the Senecio described in the course of this book by Dioscorides. Galen, knowing that there was no difference between the one and the other, wrote briefly under a single species, saying thus: Peristereon has been so named from frequenting the places where it grows, the Peristere, that is doves, whose drying virtue is so powerful that it can readily consolidate wounds.

On Astragalus.          Chapter 64.

B The Astragalus is a plant of low height from the ground, whose leaves and small branches are similar to those of chickpeas. It produces a small purple flower, and the root is round and large, like that of the radish, with other small rootlets around it, firm, hard, dark, and tangled upon themselves like horns, astringent to the taste. It grows in shaded, wooded places where snow lies for a long time. It is found in abundance in Memphis of Arcadia. The root drunk in wine checks the bowels and stimulates urine. When dried and powdered it is applied to old ulcers; it stops bleeding, but is so hard that it is difficult to pound.

Astragalus grows abundantly in the mountains of the valley of Anania, with leaves similar to those of chickpeas, with a purple flower,
N and a root similar to the radish, from which proceed more small rootlets tangled upon themselves. It therefore seems to me that, agreeing with the writings of Dioscorides, one may readily say that this is the true Astragalus. It also grows in the region of Gorizia, where its roots are used to promote urination. Pliny wrote about it differently from Dioscorides in chapter eight of book twenty-six, saying thus: Astragalus has long leaves, deeply cut and twisted near the root. It produces three or four stems, all full of leaves, the flower of hyacinth, the roots hairy and tangled upon themselves, red and very hard. It grows in sunny, rocky and snowy places, such as Mount Pheneus in Arcadia. Galen wrote about it in book six of
C his work on simples, saying thus: Astragalus is a small plant whose roots are astringent, and therefore it is counted among those things that powerfully dry; for it consolidates old ulcers and checks the fluxes of the body when its roots are boiled and drunk in wine. It grows abundantly on Mount Pheneus in Arcadia.

On Hyacinth.          Chapter 65.

The Hyacinth has bulbous leaves and a stem one span tall, smooth and slimmer than the little finger, green in color, whose head bends toward the ground, full of purple flowers. It produces a bulb-like root, which it is believed, when applied to the pubic area of boys, prevents hair from growing. Drunk it checks the bowels and stimulates urine, and it helps against the bite of those spiders called phalangia. The seed, being more astringent, checks stomach fluxes, and when drunk in wine clears overflowing bile.

The Hyacinth grows universally in the fields throughout the countryside among the crops, with leaves and roots like an onion, the stem a span tall, slender, smooth and green in color. It flowers at the end of March and at the beginning of April, when the violets bloom. It produces its head from the middle of the stem upward, all full of brilliant purple flowers, which as they ripen bend toward the ground, and last for some time before the flowers drop. In Tuscany, not knowing any other name, they are called wild or dog onions, and children gather them when the flowers first push up from the ground, for their beauty. But it should be known that this is not the Hyacinth that the poets write was born from the blood of Ajax, where even the letters of his name may be found written upon it; for that plant (according to their fables) produces a red flower similar to the lily. Galen made mention of the Hyacinth in book eight of his work on simples, saying thus: The root of the Hyacinth is bulb-like, dry in the first degree and cold at the end of the second or beginning of the third. It is therefore believed, when applied as a plaster to boys, to prevent the growth of hair around the virile parts. Its fruit is mildly astringent and binding, and therefore it is given to drink in wine against overflowing of bile. It dries in the third degree, and is found to be almost midway between hot and cold.

The wild poppy, which is called Rhea, grows in the fields in spring, with a flower that is entirely fleeting, from which it takes its name among the Greeks. Its leaves are similar to those of rocket, or to oregano, or to chicory, or to thyme, but longer, cut and rough. The stem is like a rush, straight, tall as one
