On the Horned Poppy. Chapter 68.

The Horned Poppy has white, hairy leaves similar to those of mullein, toothed around the edges like those of the wild poppy, from which its stalk is not so different. It produces a pale flower, and a small fruit, twisted like a horn, similar to the small horns of Greek hay, from which it takes its name; inside it are seeds similar to those of small poppies, and black. Its root lies near the surface of the dark, coarse soil. It grows in rough places and in coastal marshlands. A decoction of the root drunk in water, boiled down to half, is beneficial for sciatica, for disorders of the liver, and for those who pass thick, rough urine like cobwebs. The seed drunk at the weight of one acetabolo in honeyed water gently purges the body. The leaves, and likewise the flowers, applied as a poultice with oil, remove scabs. Placed with oil in the eyes of livestock, they clarify cloudiness and corneal opacities. Some people, deceiving themselves, thought that glaucium was made from this poppy, on account of the similarity of the leaves.

On the Foam Poppy. Chapter 69.

The Foam Poppy, which some call Heracleo, produces a stalk a span tall, with very small leaves similar to the woolly herb, and next to them its white fruit: the whole plant is white and entirely like foam; it has its root at the top. The seed is gathered in summer when fully ripe and when it falls off when dry. This, taken with honeyed water at the weight of one acetabolo, causes vomiting, and this purgation is privately beneficial for those who suffer from epilepsy.

N The Horned Poppy grows abundantly in our marshlands of Siena, in the territory of Grosseto, of Orbetello, and of Porto Ercole, and likewise in many places on Mount Argentario; but elsewhere in Italy I have not seen it, except sown in gardens for public display, as is done with other rare and not very common simples. Theophrastus wrote of it in chapter 13 of book 9, saying thus: Among wild poppies there are many species, of which the one called Cornicular produces leaves similar to those of black mullein, but somewhat less dark: the stalk is a cubit tall, the root short and not deep in the ground, and its seeds are inside certain twisted little horns. It is gathered at harvest time, purges the body; its leaves remove cloudiness from the eyes of sheep. It grows near the sea in sandy places. Some thought that Glaucium, which the Arabs call Memithe, was made from the juice of the Horned Poppy; but as Dioscorides very well points out, they are plainly mistaken. As for what they call Foam Poppy, I have truly not yet been able to find anyone to show it to me in Italy, and so I will set it aside along with other plants that remain unknown to us. Galen wrote of the Horned Poppy in book 7 of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The Horned Poppy is so called because it produces its seed slightly twisted, similar to that of fenugreek, so that it resembles a cow's horn. Some call it Paralio, because it grows abundantly near the sea. It has cutting and astringent properties; and therefore a decoction of its root boiled down to half is good for disorders of the liver. The leaves and flowers are good for foul and stubborn ulcers, but they should not be used until the wounds have first been cleansed. The leaves are so abrasive that they dissolve some of the fleshy matter; and so through the force of this property they not only draw out the discharge of an ulcer, but also remove the scab.

On Hipecoon. Chapter 70.

D Hipecoon, which others call Hipopheo, grows among grain crops and in fields, with leaves similar to rue and with slender branches. It has the same properties as the juice of the poppy.

C Whoever diligently searches the fields among grain crops and legumes will easily find Hipecoon. Piero Spezzalancia, an apothecary and my very dear companion, used to show this to me as wild rue, telling me that this is what other apothecaries had shown him. It grows to a height of a span, or a little more, with leaves quite similar to rue, a tender and smooth stem, and small yellow flowers. Galen wrote briefly of it in book 8 of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Hipecoon has a cooling virtue of the third degree, so that it is not far removed from the poppy.

On the herb Apollinaris, or Henbane. Chapter 71.

Henbane is a plant that produces thick stems and broad, somewhat long, cut, dark, and hairy leaves. The flowers come out in orderly fashion along the side of the stem, similar to those of the pomegranate, enclosed by certain little cups and full of seed, like the poppy. It comes in three varieties: one that produces black seed and flowers that are almost purple, the

Both cause sleep and delirium, and therefore their common use is discouraged. The third, being more pleasant, has been accepted by physicians for medicinal use. This one is tender, downy, and fatty; its flower is white, as is likewise its seed. It grows in the maremma marshlands and in the ruins of buildings; in their absence one may use that which produces the reddish seed, since the black, being the worst, is rejected. The juice is extracted from the tender seed, from the leaves, and from the stalks by pounding and pressing them, and then drying the juice in the sun; it keeps for a full year, since it spoils easily. It is also extracted from the dry seed pounded separately with warm water and then pressed. This liquid is better than the juice squeezed from the fresh plant, and more effective at relieving pain. The fresh herb is pounded, combined with meal that is three months old, made into lozenges, and stored. The first liquid, and likewise that drawn from the dry seed, are commonly mixed with those
B preparations which, by inducing sleep, relieve pain; they are useful for acute catarrhs, for pains of the ears, and for afflictions of women's private parts. Mixed with meal or polenta, they calm inflammations of the eyes, feet, and every other part of the body. The seed does all these things and is also useful for coughs, catarrhs, fluxes of the eyes, and their pains. It is drunk in the weight of one obol with poppy seed and honeyed water for menstrual flux and other fluxes of blood; it benefits gout. Pounded with wine it is applied as a poultice to swellings of the testicles and of the breasts that swell after childbirth, and it is mixed with other poultices made to draw out pain. The leaves are usefully applied with all medicines that mitigate pain, both on their own and also together with polenta. Applied fresh with wine they mitigate every kind of pain. Three or four leaves drunk with wine cure those fevers called ephialtes. The leaves cooked like other garden herbs, and eaten in the measure of one acetabulum, make a person half mad. The same effect occurs when they are applied in clysters for ulcers of the gut called the colon. A decoction of the roots made in vine-

Of all the species of Hyoscyamus, which the apothecaries commonly call iusquiamo, I have not up to now been able to find in Italy any other than that which produces the yellow flower, placed here in second rank by Dioscorides; for the white and likewise the black, I cannot find anyone who can point them out to me, though I have taken no little trouble to track down one or the other species. Scribonius Largus wrote of this, saying: "The Alterce, which the Greeks call Hyoscyamus, when drunk weighs down the head and makes the veins swell, causes delirium and quarrelsomeness in whoever eats it" — from which it is also called Alterce. This I have many times seen in some children who had eaten the seed in the mountains of the Ananta valley, where it is commonly called Disturbio, because it greatly disturbs the brain. Hens and other birds that eat it die within a short time. Wild boars eat it and are all stupefied, as Aelian writes, but they immediately run by natural instinct to water and eat crabs there, and so free themselves. Galen mentioned it in book seven of On the Properties of Simple Medicines, saying: "Hyoscyamus that produces the black seed causes madness and likewise sleep. That which has the reddish seed has almost the same nature; therefore both are to be avoided as useless, poisonous, and deadly. But that which produces the white flower and white seed is most suitable for medicine and cools in the third degree."

D On Psyllium. Chapter 72.

Psyllium has leaves similar to those of coronopus, but hairy. It is an herb wholly branching, similar to hay; its stalks are a hand's breadth tall; its head of foliage begins in the middle of the stalk, and at the top it has two or three coiled heads of seed, inside which is the seed, black, hard, and resembling fleas, from which it takes its name. It grows in fields and uncultivated places. It has the virtue of cooling, softening, and thickening. Applied as a poultice it benefits pains of the joints, abscesses that arise behind the ears, those that follow them, swellings, and dislocations of the bones. It is placed on the head for headache with rose oil, water, or vinegar. Applied as a poultice with vinegar it heals intestinal ruptures in children and swellings of the navel. A measure of one acetabulum is steeped in a sextarius of water, and as the water thickens it is used as a liniment; for it refreshes powerfully, and placed in hot water it cools — it is a most efficacious medicine against St. Anthony's fire. It is said that carried green in houses it prevents fleas from breeding. Pounded with fat-

FOURTH BOOK. 323

[Psyllium] cleanses foul and malignant ulcers. Its juice taken together with honey is good against worms of the ear and for discharges from them. A

Psyllium is a very well-known plant in Italy, and grows for the most part in the coastal marshlands, as may be seen in Tuscany in our territory of Siena, toward Giuncarico and Castiglioni della Pescaia, though it is also found in the countryside in other places. It is used in apothecaries to keep the seed for the use of its mucilages, which are suited to cooling, checking hot fluxes, quenching thirst, and lubricating the body. Mesue wrote of it among his simple purgatives, saying as follows. Psyllium is one of those things that alters the constitution and loosens the body by lubrication; of it one finds some that is whitish, some reddish, and some purplish. The best is that which is perfectly ripe, heavy, and which when placed in water sinks to the bottom. It is composed of two substances which can be separated, namely the pith separated from the rind: for one resides in its pithy substance, and the other is spread over its outer cortex. The pithy part is hot and dry in the fourth degree, powerfully sharp, incisive, rubefacient, ulcerative, and of a venomous nature. That which is contained in the rind is one of those things that greatly cool, and according to Rhazes is cold and moist in the third degree. When psyllium is beaten with fresh spring water until it becomes mucilaginous, and this water is then drunk with oil or violet syrup, it purges the body downward; but fried and beaten with rose oil it is a medicine for flux of the body and for dysentery. One must be warned, however, never to give psyllium by mouth to be drunk in any way: B for grinding it over the substance of the pithy part is ulcerative and excoriating. Beaten with fresh water (as we said) it resolves cholera; and therefore it serves against fevers that inflame violently, against great thirst, against inflammations of the vital spirits, and against roughness of the chest. Beaten with vinegar it is good applied over hot swellings, namely erysipelas, miliary rash, and other inflammations applied on top; and especially it is good for pains of the body caused by a hot cause; but fried and beaten (as we said) it is good for dysentery and for cholerical and medicinal flux, and most especially that caused by Scammony and other sharp medicines. All this about Psyllium was said by Mesue, from whose words one may easily consider that Psyllium is a poison by being hot and dry in the fourth degree. Against this is what Dioscorides wrote in the sixth book, saying thus: Psyllium drunk cools the whole body, inducing a certain torpor, weakness, and sadness, in such a way that it dissolves the whole body. For which one has recourse to all those remedies that are customarily given to someone who has taken coriander. Galen made brief mention of Psyllium at the end of the seventh book of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Psyllium has its seed, which is most useful. It is cold in the second degree; but in moistening and drying it is likewise moderate.

On the Garden Nightshade. Chapter 73. C

The garden nightshade is a plant not too large, used in foods, with many hollow branches, whose leaves are dark and larger than those of basil and broader: it produces a green and round fruit, which after ripening becomes black or yellow; eaten in foods it does no harm. It has the virtue of cooling; and therefore its leaves plastered with bean flour are good for sacred fire [erysipelas] and for serpentine ulcers. Ground and applied alone they heal lacrimal fistulas and pains of the head; they benefit the ardors of the stomach, and ground with salt and made into a poultice they dissolve swellings that come after the ears. The juice mixed with rose oil, white lead, and silver foam is good for sacred fire and for corrosive ulcers, and incorporated with bread for lacrimal fistulas; made into a liniment with rose oil on the heads of children it is useful for inflammations of the membranes of the brain. It is substituted for eggs and likewise for water in those eye-washes made against acute fluxes of the eyes; distilled into the ears it removes pain; applied below with wool it stanches the flow of menstruation. The juice mixed with the yellow dung of hens that live in the courtyard, and plastered on a cloth, is a D ready remedy for lacrimal fistulas.

On the Nightshade called Halicacabo. Chapter 74.

Another species of Nightshade, which some call Halicacabo and others Physalida, which produces leaves broader than the other, whose stalks, once they have grown sufficiently, bend toward the ground. This plant produces its fruit round, red, and smooth, resembling grape berries, enclosed in certain red husks, which some are accustomed to place in garlands. It has in medicine the same use and the same virtues as the garden nightshade, except that it is not eaten in foods. The fruit drunk is good for overflow of bile and provokes urine. The juice is pressed from both of these nightshades together, and is kept dried in the shade for the uses mentioned above.

324 BOOK

A On the Sleep-Inducing Nightshade. Chapter 75.

The sleep-inducing nightshade, which some also call Halicacabo, grows with many branches, dense and twiggy, difficult to break, and full of thick leaves similar to those of quince trees. Its flower is large and reddish, and its fruit is enclosed in husks the color of saffron. Its root is long, covered with a reddish bark. It grows among rocks, not far from the sea. The bark of the root, drunk in wine at the weight of one drachm, has a more pleasant sleep-inducing virtue than opium. Its seed powerfully provokes urination. Twelve of its flower clusters, taken internally, are beneficial in dropsy, but if more are taken they cause delirium — the remedy for which is to drink copious amounts of honeyed water. The juice is mixed into pastilles and medicines that relieve pain by inducing sleep. Boiled in wine and then held in the mouth, it eases toothache. The juice of the root mixed with honey, applied externally, is beneficial for weakness of the eyesight.

B On the Raving Nightshade. Chapter 76.

The raving nightshade, also called Manikon by some, Persio by others, and Thrion by still others, has leaves like those of rocket, but somewhat larger and close to those of acanthus, which is called pederota. It sends up from the root ten or twelve stalks, a pace high, at the top of which is a head resembling an olive, hairy, like the berries of the plane tree but larger and broader. Its flower is dark, from the falling of which grows a round, dark cluster containing ten or twelve berries resembling ivy corymbs, and as tender as grapes. Its root is white, thick, hollow, and a cubit long. It grows in the mountains, in windy places, and among plane trees. The root, drunk in wine at the weight of one drachm, presents to the mind images of things truly pleasant; but if the dose is doubled, it causes a person to remain in a state of ecstasy for three days, and if four drachms are given it kills. The remedy is to drink a great deal of honeyed water and then to vomit.

C There are truly four species of nightshades commemorated and described by Dioscorides and Galen, of which only the first two are found in Italy — namely the Garden nightshade, which was formerly sown in gardens with other edible herbs and now grows by itself in fields and along roadsides; and the one called Halicacabo by some and Alchakhingi by the Arabs. For the Sleep-inducing and the Raving nightshade, which agree with the description of Dioscorides, are not found among physicians in Italy in our time. What is commonly called by some the Greater nightshade and by others Herba bella donna, which grows abundantly in many places in Italy, is not (as Fuchs imagined) the Sleep-inducing nightshade of Dioscorides; because, although it is true that its fruit kills by putting to sleep forever those who eat it in quantity, as has often happened to small children who ate it instead of grapes, nonetheless its failure to produce siliques containing a seed with a yellowish-red color shows that there is no small difference in form between them, even if their virtues might perhaps be equal. It is therefore to be believed that this is another species of nightshade, not recognized by ancient writers on account of the similarity of its leaves. There is yet another species, of which I found the greatest abundance in the territory of Trent, whose stalk is twiggy, sometimes four or five arm-lengths long, white, difficult to break, and knotty in many places where the small branches emerge. It winds itself willingly around plants and hedges, as honeysuckle does, which is called Periclimeno. It produces nightshade leaves, but somewhat smaller, firmer, smoother, more solid, and more pointed. Its flower is purple, from which are produced berries gathered in elongated clusters, red, tart in taste, and the size of chickpeas. Their juice, being cooling and drying, is of great service, as I have many times experienced, in malignant and stubborn ulcers, and likewise in inflammations of wounds. Another species of Halicacabo has, in our time, overgrown arbors, fences, and garden hedges, as well as windows and house loggias. It produces long, notched leaves, a white flower, and pods similar to those of Halicacabo, inside which is a white, round seed upon one side of which can be discerned a true heart-shape in black. This was perhaps noted by nature, not without cause, to indicate that it may have considerable virtue in disorders of the heart, just as it was shown in the case of Echium, which has virtue against the bite of vipers, its seed resembling their heads in every way, as was said above in its own chapter. Similar to the nightshade seems to me also that plant now common in all gardens, which they call Stramonia, which produces certain green, round fruits, somewhat concave in the middle and spiny, with leaves that resemble those of nightshade, with a smell equal to that of opium. Its flowers, which are like bells, breathe a sweet scent of lilies, and it is the common belief of nearly everyone that the virtue of this plant is not far removed from that of the nightshades, of which Galen, writing in Book VIII of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, said the following: The garden nightshade, which is eaten in food, is known to everyone, and is used in all

In all those cases where there is need to constrict and to cool, it is rated in the second degree for both these qualities. Among those that are not eaten, one is called Halicacabo, which produces a red fruit, similar in size and shape to a grape, which people use in garlands. Another is bushy and dense, and sleep-inducing; and the third, which makes men go out of their minds, they call Manico. The Halicacabo, then, in the properties of its leaves is similar to the garden nightshade; but the fruit is suitable for promoting urination. For this reason, many compound virtues are attributed to it, beneficial to the liver, the kidneys, and the bladder. The bark of the root of the one called the sleep-inducing variety, when drunk in wine at the weight of one drachm, causes sleep, and in every other respect is similar to opium, except that it is somewhat weaker, being ranked only in the third degree of things that cool, while opium is in the fourth; nonetheless, its seed has the virtue of provoking urination: but if more than twelve berries are taken, it causes delirium. The last one, called Manico, is truly altogether useless for medicines taken by mouth, since four drachms kill whoever drinks them, and less than that sends a person out of their mind. It is true that one drachm does no harm; but in truth no benefit from it is observed. When a poultice of it is applied externally, it cures difficult ulcers that need to close up, and those that corrode. Most praised of all is the bark of its root: for it dries in the end of the second degree and at the beginning of the third, and cools at the beginning of the second.

On Doricnium. Chapter 77.

Doricnium, which Cratevas calls Halicacabo, or truly Calea, is a plant similar to a young olive tree: it grows among rocks not far from the sea, with branches smaller than a cubit, and leaves the color of those of olive trees, but smaller, firmer, and very rough. It produces white flowers, and at the tops, pods similar to chickpeas, dense and round, inside which are five or six seeds, as large as the smallest seeds of the bitter vetch, smooth, firm, and of various colors. The root grows to the thickness of a finger and the length of a cubit. It seems to be also sleep-inducing: if drunk in excess it causes death. The seed (according to some) is used in love matters.

On Mandrake. Chapter 78.

Some call Mandrake Antimalo, and others Circea: because it seems that the root is useful in matters of love. It comes in two kinds: one black, which is considered the female, called thridacia, which produces leaves narrower and smaller than lettuce, of an unpleasant smell, spread along the ground. This one produces fruits similar to serviceberries, pale and fragrant, in which the seeds are similar to those of pears. Its roots are large, sometimes two, sometimes three, intertwined with each other, black on the outside and white inside, covered with thick bark; and this species of Mandrake produces no stem. The second species, which is white, is the male, called by some norion: it produces large, wide, white, smooth leaves like those of beet, and its fruits are twice as large as those of the other variety, of a color tending toward saffron, with a certain pleasant heaviness of scent; eating some of these fruits, shepherds sometimes fall asleep. Its root is similar to the other, but larger and whiter, and also lacking a stem. The juice is extracted from the bark of fresh roots, first ground up and then pressed in a press; this juice, once dried in the sun, is stored in an earthen vessel. The juice is also pressed from the fruits, but it is not as potent. The roots are peeled and the bark is strung on thread to be used when needed: some cook the roots in wine until a third of it has reduced, then clarify it and store it, giving a cupful at a time during long vigils to induce sleep, and also to those who need to be cauterized or have a limb cut off, so that they may not feel the pain. The juice drunk at the weight of two obols in honeyed wine purges by vomiting, as hellebore does for black bile and phlegm; but truly if too much is taken, it is altogether deadly. It is used in medicines for the eyes, and likewise in those made to relieve pain, and in mollifying suppositories. Applied below on its own at the weight of half an obol, it draws out the menses, and likewise brings on delivery: placed

A placed as a suppository induces sleep. It is said that by boiling the root with ivory for six continuous hours, one can soften it so thoroughly that it may be molded into any shape desired. The fresh leaves are applied as a poultice with polenta for inflammations of the eyes and for ulcerous swellings; they dissolve all hardnesses, swellings, and scrofulous and other small tumors; they reduce the edges of scars without ulcerating them, if rubbed on gently for five or six days. The roots are preserved in brine for all these uses. The root, ground and made into a plaster with vinegar, heals erysipelas; with honey or oil it treats snake bites; applied with water it resolves scrofulous swellings and small tumors, and with polenta it eases joint pains. Wine is made from the bark of the root without boiling, in the following way: three measures of the bark are placed in a cask of sweet wine, and three cups of it are given to those who, as stated above, need to have a limb amputated or cauterized without feeling pain, for sleeping deeply they feel no pain at all. The fragrant fruits induce sleep, as does eating them. This effect is also produced by the juice pressed from them; but those who use them too freely, both eating and smelling them, become mute. The seed of the fruits, drunk, purges the womb, and applied below with live sulfur it stops women's menstrual flows. The root is deeply scored and the liquid that drips from it is collected in a concave vessel, although the juice is more effective than this; but not in every location, as experience has shown, does this liquid weep from the roots. They say there is another Mandrake called Morion, which grows in shady places near caves, whose leaves are similar to those of the white variety, though smaller, a span long, white, and situated around the root, which is tender and white, slightly more than a span long and as thick as a man's large finger. They say that drunk at the weight of a dram, or eaten with polenta in flatbreads or other foods, it causes madness. Whoever eats it falls asleep as soon as the eating is done, losing all sensation for three or four hours. Physicians use it when they need to amputate or cauterize. They say the antidote is to drink the root with nightshade, which they call furious.

N Mandrakes grow on their own in many places in the mountains of Italy, and especially in Puglia on Mount Gargano, which they call the Mountain of Saint Angelo, from where certain herb-sellers bring us the bark of the roots and the fruits every year. I have seen them many times growing in gardens and in pots in Naples, in Rome, in Venice, and in other parts of Italy, both varieties planted together; but not at the time when they bore fruit. It is truly a fable to believe that Mandrakes have roots of human form, as the ignorant common people believe, and that they cannot be dug from the earth without danger, by tying a dog to them; for those which certain charlatans and quacks carry around, falsely convincing simple barren women that eating them will make them bear children, are roots of reeds carved into that shape, artfully made, and then replanted with grains of barley around those places where they wish these little roots to sprout the hairs, beard, and other body hair. Of this I can give good testimony: for when I was once treating one of these wandering charlatans in Rome for the French disease with wood wine, he showed me, alongside many other tricks of theirs by which they deceive poor people, the method he used to make these Mandrakes, of which he had quite a few already made, assuring me that sometimes he sold them for more than 25 or 30 ducats apiece. I therefore wished to warn the world of this manifest fraud, and to make plain to everyone how such falsity has flourished, and still flourishes in our times, in the hands of such villains,
D who, to lend the matter more credibility, allege that Pythagoras called the Mandrake Anthropomorphos, meaning human form. Regarding which it must be known that Pythagoras did not give it this name without reason: for Mandrakes are most often found to have a forked root resembling human legs, and when dug up bearing their fruit, which resembles a small apple attached by a short stalk among the leaves at the top of the root, it does truly resemble the form of a man without arms. Few people have been able to explain this clearly, and indeed I mostly find modern writers blaming both Pythagoras and Columella, not understanding the matter, for having written fabulously that the root of the Mandrake has human form. Beyond this, as for that third species called Morion, which grows in shady places, I find no one in our time in Italy who has demonstrated it. Brassavola and the German Leonard Fuchs, treating of it, reproach Hermolao Barbaro quite harshly (though without any good reason), saying that it was believed that those fruits which are called in Lombardy Melanzane and in Tuscany Petronciani were the fruits of this third species of Mandrake. Reading this in Hermolao, I have not been able to find it anywhere: for he only writes of it in this way, saying: Of the Morion species of Mandrake I have nothing to add to what Dioscorides writes. But because the fruits of the Mandrake are called earth and dog apples, they bring to mind those which are called Melanzane,

A These are better called (as I think) Insane Apples, about which I am not surprised that the ancient writers did not write, since many things were unknown in their time, just as many things that existed then are no longer known in ours. The Insane Apples are therefore fruits of a common plant, which grows everywhere, as melons and squashes do, cultivated in the same way, and they are commonly eaten fried in oil, with salt and pepper, like mushrooms. All this was said by Hermolaus, from which one can well understand that those who accuse him have little reason to do so. In Italy these fruits are eaten to arouse lust, which they easily do, being windy and hard to digest: and therefore using them too much in food generates, as Avicenna says, melancholic humors, obstructions, cancers, leprosy, headache, sadness, obstructions of the liver and spleen, and they cause a bad color throughout the body and long fevers. In our times another variety is brought into Italy, sliced like rose apples and cut into wedges, green in color when unripe and golden when mature, and these are eaten in the same way. Galen wrote of the Mandrake in book seven on the faculties of simples, saying: In the Mandrake the cooling virtue predominates, so that it is placed among those things that are cold in the third degree. Nevertheless, in its fruits there is some warmth and likewise some moisture: and therefore they have the power to cause sleep. The bark of the root, being most potent, not only cools but also dries. But the inner part is of no value.

B On Aconite. Chapter 79.

Aconite, which some call Pardalianche, others Cammoro, others Theliphono, others Mioctono, and others Theriophono, produces three or four leaves similar to those of cyclamen or cucumber, but smaller and slightly hairy: the stem is a hand's span tall, and the root resembles the tail of a scorpion, but shining, like alabaster. If you touch scorpions with this root (as is said) they become stupefied: but if you then touch them with hellebore root they immediately revive. It is used in eye medicines made to relieve pain: it kills panthers, pigs, wolves, and all wild beasts when mixed with meat and fed to them.

C On Another Aconite. Chapter 80.

There is another Aconite, which some call Cinoctono and some Licoctono. There are three varieties of this, of which hunters use one, and the other two have been adopted for medical use, of which the third, called Pontic, grows abundantly in Italy in the Justinian mountains. It differs from the first: for it produces leaves similar to those of the plane tree, but more deeply cut, longer, and much darker: its stem resembles that of a fern, smooth like a stylus, a cubit tall or sometimes taller. It produces seeds in some elongated pods: the roots are dark, similar to the tendrils of sea squill, which hunters use to catch wolves by mixing them with raw meat: for when eaten they kill them.

F Dioscorides treated the Aconites in two separate chapters, calling the first species Pardalianche because it is a deadly poison to leopards, and the second Cinoctono and Licoctono because it kills dogs and wolves, and he divided this last chapter's subject into three varieties, describing only the history of the third. For this reason Hermolaus and likewise the Florentine Secretary thought that in this last chapter there was a gap in the text: for it seems that when Dioscorides says that one is used by hunters and the other by physicians, the description of how each is used by physicians and hunters is missing, and D likewise the account of the leaves, stem, roots, flower, and seed is lacking. That this is clarified in the third species, called Pontic, lends credibility to this view. This third species grows on almost every mountain in Italy, with leaves more deeply cut than the plane tree, a fern-like stem, yellow flowers similar in shape to those of the buttercup but much larger, and is commonly called Luparia, though in the Trentino region it is called fox-herb: because its roots, when crushed, kill foxes that eat them with meat. The plant of the first species, which kills leopards and panthers, I have gathered many times in the Trentino, where it grows abundantly, and it is this species that some people in the territory of Rome and in the kingdom of Naples use for nothing other than killing wolves, and they often sell its roots on the Ponte Sant'Angelo to whoever wants them: for these roots kill wolves immediately. These, however (as far as I have been able to judge), are not the Luparia: because those roots are dark, while the ones sold by these people are somewhat yellowish-white. The German Leonardo Fuchs believes, as one can see in his great Herbal, that the Aconite of the first species is the plant commonly called Herb Paris. In this I think he is plainly mistaken: for Herb Paris produces a single stem, round, two spans tall, from the middle of which, a span above the root, emerge four leaves equally

The decoction of oregano, horehound, rue, or alternatively of wormwood made in wine of wormwood, or of houseleek, or of southernwood, or of ground-pine. Also beneficial is a dram of balsam liquor drunk with honey, or likewise with milk, with castor added, pepper, and rue in equal measure. Lye given with broth of cock, or of fat beef, is likewise beneficial, as is wine. It is said that particularly helpful for this is that species of ground-pine which is smallest and least.

Of Hemlock. Chapter 81.

Hemlock produces a knotty stalk, like fennel, large, and branching at the top: its leaves similar to those of ferula, but narrower, of an unpleasant smell: the branches bear at their tips umbels, whose flowers are whitish: the seed is like that of anise, but whiter: the root is hollow and not very deep.
Hemlock is a deadly poison, and kills by its great coldness: the remedy for which is pure wine drunk. Its juice is pressed out by pounding the tops before the seed and foliage dry, and it is thickened in the sun: for it is used dry in many things in medicine. It is usefully applied in collyria made to relieve pains: applied as a plaster it arrests the sacred fire and ulcers that spread by creeping. The herb pounded together with the foliage and applied as a plaster around the testicles removes the imaginations that during sleep provoke lustfulness in others: but it harms the male member by dissolving the heat within it. Applied to the breasts of women in childbirth it dries up the milk, and applied to the breasts of virgins, prevents them from growing: applied as a plaster around the testicles of boys it dries them up, to prevent their nourishment. The most potent is that of Crete, the Megarese, the Attic, and that which grows in Chios and in Cilicia.

Hemlock is very well known in Italy: for it grows most often near fortified places, with a stalk and leaves similar to ferula, but of an unpleasant smell. The most potent and most poisonous (according to Pliny) is that which grows in Parthia, Laconia, Candia, Megara, Asia, and Athens in Greece, and therefore in Italy it does not appear to be so poisonous. The donkeys that eat it in Tuscany fall into such a stupor that, becoming insensible, they appear dead. Whence it has happened several times that peasants who skinned them to take their hide have found them waking up half-skinned, to the great terror of those doing the skinning. That hemlock is a poison was written about by Dioscorides in book six, among other poisons, saying thus: Hemlock drunk immediately causes dizziness, and so darkens the sight that it prevents one from discerning anything. It brings on hiccups, disturbs the intellect, freezes the extremities of the limbs, and finally produces convulsions and so tightens the breath that it immediately suffocates. The cure at the outset is therefore vomiting, and then purging the bowels, so as to draw out whatever portion may have passed into the intestines. Once this is done it is necessary to drink a good deal of wine, several times over. In addition it is useful to drink the milk of a she-ass or cow, or alternatively wormwood with pepper and wine, or castor with mint and rue also with wine, or amomum, cardamom, or styrax to the weight of one ounce, or pepper with nettle seed and wine, or bay leaves. Likewise useful is laserwort with oil and cooked wine: indeed cooked wine alone drunk copiously is very helpful. Galen wrote briefly on this, saying: Hemlock is known to all as being most cold.

Of the Smilax. Chapter 82.

The Smilax, which the Latins call Tasso (Yew), is a tree that grows to the size of the fir, to which its leaves likewise bear resemblance. It grows in Italy and in the part of France called Narbonne, which borders Spain. The birds that feed on the berries of that which grows in Italy turn black, and men who eat them suffer from diarrhea. In Narbonne it is so poisonous that if some people sleep beneath it or sit in its shade, they fall ill, and sometimes die: and therefore we have wished to say this about the Yew, so that we may guard ourselves against it.

The Yew grows abundantly in the valley of Anania on the mountains among the Firs, with leaves and form very similar to them; but it does not however grow to their height, and is commonly called Nasso. It produces a red fruit similar to that of the Holly, sweet to the taste and somewhat vinous, which when eaten on occasion by shepherds and others who cut timber in the woods, causes them immediately to develop fever and thereafter diarrhea: for it greatly inflames the spirits. Theophrastus wrote of it in the tenth chapter of the third book, saying thus: The Yew is of a single species, tall and large, resembling the fir, though not quite so large, but with more pronounced grain in its wood. That which grows in Arcadia is dark or reddish in color; but that of Ida is yellow and resembles cedar; and it is therefore said that sellers often deceive buyers, frequently selling Yew in place of Cedar. It has no pith at all, and its bark resembles that of the cedar both in roughness and in color. It produces short, thin roots, growing not very deep in the earth. In Ida it is rare, but abundant in Arcadia and Macedonia, where it produces fruit in abundance, round, slightly larger than a bean, red in color, and tender to the touch. Its leaves, eaten by non-ruminating animals, cause their death; but they do not harm in any way animals that ruminate; there are some men who eat it without any harm. It is sweet and pleasant to the taste. Plutarch writes that the shadow of the Yew kills whoever sleeps beneath it. Pliny writes in the tenth chapter of the sixteenth book that driving a copper nail into the trunk of the Yew tree removes all its harmful power. The smoke of its leaves kills mice. Dioscorides also wrote of it among the poisonous plants in the sixth book, saying thus: The Yew, called Smilax, when eaten causes great cold throughout the body, tightness of breath, and kills quickly. All the remedies that work against hemlock are also effective against it.

B On Apocynum. Chapter 82.

Apocynum, or dog's cabbage, is a plant that produces small tendrils, of an unpleasant odor, pliant and flexible like vine shoots and difficult to break, whose leaves resemble those of ivy, but more tender and more pointed at the tip, of an unpleasant smell, and somewhat sticky, and full of a yellow liquid. It produces certain pods similar to those of broad beans, of a follicle type, a finger's length, inside which there is a small, black, hard seed. The leaves, mixed with fat and dough and made into bread, kill dogs, wolves, foxes, and panthers when given to them to eat, for they immediately dissolve their vitals.

Apocynum, or Dog's Cabbage, is not found in Italy in our time, and therefore we shall leave it aside along with other simples that are unknown here, not failing however to mention that, having it in memory, Galen wrote of it in the sixth book on the faculties of simples, saying thus: Apocynum kills dogs in the same way as hemlock does wolves,

C and it also poisons humans. It is an herb of the most oppressive odor: for which reason it must be greatly heating in nature, though not correspondingly dry, and therefore when applied as a poultice it is very maturing.

On the Nerium. Chapter 84.

Some call the Nerium Rhododaphne, and others Rhododendron: it is a very common plant, whose leaves are longer than those of the almond tree, and rougher. Its flower resembles the rose, and its fruit resembles the almond, and when it opens it shows the form of a horn filled with a certain wool similar to the tufts of thorns. It produces a long, pointed, woody root, salty to the taste. It grows in pleasant places, in marshlands, and along the banks of rivers. Its flowers and leaves are a deadly poison to mules, dogs, donkeys, and many other quadruped animals; but for humans they are most beneficial against the bites of serpents, when drunk with wine, and all the more so when rue is added. Furthermore, smaller quadrupeds such as sheep and goats die when they drink water in which the leaves of the Nerium have been soaked.

The Nerium, or Rhododendron, is commonly called Oleander in Italy, of which I have myself very often seen quite an abundance growing among the myrtles and laurels on the banks of Lake Benaco, commonly called today Lake Garda, and also in great quantity on Monte Argentario in our Maremma of Siena. It is truly a pleasing and delightful plant to the sight, especially when it is well laden with its roses, by which the poor Apuleius was nearly deceived when, having been turned into a donkey, he sought to eat roses in order to return to his former human form: for having seen them from a distance and imagining them to be true roses, he ran toward them with such eagerness to devour them that he barely stopped himself from eating them without a second thought; but since it was still in his memory that these were an immediate and deadly poison to donkeys, finding himself to be a donkey, battered by fortune, he finally left them alone and turned back with his ears down. Galen wrote of it in the eighth book on the faculties of simples, saying thus: The Nerium, or Rhododaphne, a tree known to everyone, has shown an externally digestive virtue; but when taken by mouth it is harmful and poisonous, not only to humans but also to animals. This greatly contradicts the opinion of Dio-

On Colchicum. Chapter 86.

The Colchicum, which some call Ephemeron and others the wild Bulb, produces at the end of autumn its whitish flower, similar to saffron, and after the flower the leaves similar to those of the bulb, but thicker. Its stalk is a palm's height, on which the red seed is produced; the outer bark of the root is blackish, but when peeled it is white, tender, sweet, and full of moisture. This bulbous root has a cleft in the middle, from which its flower rises. It grows most abundantly in Messenia and in Colchis. Eaten, the root kills by strangulation, as mushrooms do, and we have described it for no other reason than to warn people not to eat it without thinking, mistaking it for a bulb: for its agreeable taste remarkably entices the ignorant to eat it. The same remedies that are given for mushroom poisoning are useful here: cow's milk drunk is helpful for this, and if one has that, there is no need for other remedies.

On Ephemeron. Chapter 87.

The Ephemeron, which some call wild Iris, produces leaves like those of a lily, but more slender. The stalk is similar, the flower white and bitter, the seed tender; it has a single root, as thick as a finger, long, astringent, and fragrant. It grows in woods and shaded places. The root is useful for toothache when the mouth is rinsed with its decoction. The leaves cooked in wine dissolve tumors and abscesses that have not yet fully matured.

C There are the two species of Ephemeron placed together here by Dioscorides, namely the Colchicum Ephemeron and the Ephemeron called Wild Lily. The first is said to be so poisonous that when eaten it kills within a single day, and therefore Dioscorides said he wrote about it for no other reason than to warn people of its deadly nature: for many could easily be deceived, enticed by the sweetness of its taste. This teaching and warning has been little heeded by the Arabs and our other predecessors: and yet, though it was clearer than the sun, it has not prevented the continued falling into this error: for the Colchicum Ephemeron, a poisonous and deadly plant, is nothing other, when one examines all its characteristics, than the Hermodactyl used in apothecaries' shops, whose harmfulness to our bodies anyone can judge who understands what not only Dioscorides and Galen, but also Paul of Aegina, Nicander, and Pliny wrote about it as a kind of deadly poison; which, even if in our times it does not manifestly kill those who use it in medicines, this can easily be because it is not as poisonous in Italy as it is in Colchis, or because not enough of it is taken to be sufficient to kill a man: but there is no doubt that it can cause very great harm to our bodies. The true cause of this error was Serapion, who in a single chapter treated confusedly both the Ephemerons and the Hermodactyl under the heading of Hermodactyl, not noticing that to the Greek authors, from whom he drew everything, the Ephemerons and the Hermodactyl are quite different things. Of this Paul of Aegina gives clear evidence: for in his seventh book he treated both the Ephemerons and the Hermodactyl in separate chapters, saying thus: the root of the Hermodactyl alone, and likewise its decoction, has the virtue of purging, and is given privately for pains in the joints when the humors are in flux: but it greatly harms the stomach. And a little further on, about the Ephemerons, he said: the Ephemeron — not the one that is a poison, but the one called Wild Lily — is composed of mixed, repercussive, and wind-resolving qualities. This clearly demonstrates that the Hermodactyl is quite different from the Ephemerons, and that Serapion grossly erred here by lumping together in one bundle both the Ephemerons and the Hermodactyl, which the other Arabs and our predecessors then imitated, handing down to each other this continuous error. Therefore it must be considered that in no way can it be conceded that the Hermodactyls commonly used in apothecaries' shops should continue to be used, since not only do the above reasons show they are not the true ones, but it is clearly known that they are a deadly and detestable poison. Moreover, that last Ephemeron called Wild Iris grows abundantly in the meadows and woods of the high mountains of the valley of Ananis, and the inhabitants call it Crazy Lily: in which all the true characteristics that Dioscorides attributes to it can be seen, and therefore Leonardo Fuchs the German greatly erred in his great herbal, wishing to make people believe that the Ephemeron of the second species

This is that plant which is commonly called Lily of the Valley, which produces that small white flower, almost in the shape of a pomegranate blossom, remarkably fragrant; for its leaves at first do not resemble those of the lily, nor do its stems, which are as slender as threads. The root, moreover, is hairlike, divided into many parts, and not as thick as a finger, as is that of the true Ephemeron. Beyond this, I do not find that the flower of the Ephemeron is fragrant, as is that of the Lily of the Valley, which is truly so fragrant and pleasing to the nose that there are few men who in the month of May do not carry it in their hand or keep it in their rooms — which is strong evidence that the Lily of the Valley, whose history we described above in the chapter on Hemerocalle in the fourth book, is quite different from this kind of Ephemeron. It also seems to me worth considering that the Hermodactyl, about which Paul and Actuarius wrote as being distinct from Colchicum and from Ephemeron, though not described by anyone, should perhaps resemble Colchicum in some way — which has always been used in apothecaries in its place — and that from this arose the error of taking Colchicum for Hermodactyl. I have often thought that the plant which grows abundantly in spring in nearly all meadows, thick with leaves broader than those of leeks, which without producing any flower yields a seed first white, then reddish as it matures, about the size of a cabbage seed, in certain small green shells like nuts that emerge from between the leaves without any stem, one next to another, is truly the Hermodactyl that Paul and Actuarius meant. For the root of this plant is covered by a thin membrane which in color is truly similar to that which surrounds the root of Colchicum, and the root itself also closely resembles it, except that it is somewhat more rounded, thicker, and lacks that cleft in the middle from which the flower emerges as in Colchicum; but in whiteness, in substance, and in appearance it much resembles it. It is true, however, that in taste this plant is very bitter, while Colchicum is sweet and pleasant to the palate. This, it seems, was not understood by those venerable Fathers who have recently commented on the Antidotary of Mesue; for, as one reads in the commentary on the pills of Hermodactyl, they make no distinction between the true Hermodactyls and the Colchicum written of in the fourth book of Dioscorides — which, as can be seen from the arguments given above, matters greatly for the lives of men. Galen wrote of the Ephemerons in the sixth book on the Faculties of Simple Medicines, as follows: "The Ephemeron — I do not mean the deadly and poisonous one — but that other which they also call wild Iris, produces leaves and a stem similar to the lily, with a somewhat long root, not round like that of Colchicum, a finger's breadth thick, and of a good and sweet odor. It is therefore clearly evident that its temperament is mixed, and that it has a repercussive and resolutive faculty for vapors. Taken in the quantity of a cup, it cures chronic coughs. It is used as a gargle and as a poultice for inflammations of the throat. Distilled into the ears with rose oil, it removes pain."

What is commonly called in the vernacular the Helsine written of here by Dioscorides is called Parietaria, because it grows on the walls of buildings, and Vetriola because it is used for scouring glass and other glass vessels. Since it is a very well-known plant, there is no need to treat it at length. Galen mentioned it in the sixth book on the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying as follows: "The Helsine has an astringent and constrictive virtue with a certain cold moisture, and therefore heals all phlegmons in their beginning and likewise in their growth, even up to their peak, and especially hot ones — which it also does at the onset of boils and other tumors when applied as a poultice. The juice distilled into the ears is beneficial for apostematic pains in them. Some use it as a gargle for abscesses of the throat, and there are some physicians who give it to those who are continually troubled by chronic cough. Its detergent virtue is clearly seen in glass vessels."

On Alsine. Chapter 89.

Alsine, which some call Antillo and others Myosota, because its leaves resemble the ears of mice, grows in shady woods and dark places, from which it has been called Alsine. It would be the same as Helsine, were it not somewhat smaller and without longer, smooth leaves. When crushed it gives off the smell of cucumber. It has the virtue of stanching and cooling. Applied as a poultice with polenta, it treats inflammations of the eyes. Its juice distilled into the ears removes pain, and it is useful for all the same purposes as Helsine.

                        On the Duckweed of the Marshes.              Chapter 90.

   Duckweed of the marshes is found in standing waters. It is a moss similar to lentils, whose virtue is to cool. Therefore it is conveniently applied as a poultice by itself, or with polenta, upon swellings, upon sacred fire [erysipelas], and upon gout. It also heals intestinal ruptures in children.
      Marsh Duckweed is commonly called Lenticularia. It is a thing well known to everyone. It grows for the most part in the ditches of water surrounding cities and towns. Galen wrote of this in book eight of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying: The Lenticula of the marshes is almost in the second degree of cold and moist.

                        On the Greater Houseleek.                     Chapter 91.

   The Greater Houseleek has been so named because its leaves are always green. It produces stalks a cubit high, sometimes more, as thick as a large finger, fleshy, green, and notched, like those of the sea spurge. The leaves are fleshy, thick, as long as a large finger, pointed at the top like tongues, the lower ones spreading along the ground, and the upper ones arranged together in the manner of an eye. It grows on mountains and in pots; it is also planted on rooftops. Its virtue is to cool and to constrict. The leaves are medicinal for sacred fire, for malignant and stubborn ulcers, and for creeping sores; they help with inflammations of the eyes, ruptures, and gout, applied both on their own and together with polenta. The juice used in infusion with polenta, or with rose oil, is usefully applied for headaches; drunk, it is good against the bite of spiders called phalangi, against dysentery, and other fluxes of the body; drunk in wine it expels long worms from the body. Applied below with wool it stops the flow of women. Anointed on, it helps defects of the eyes caused by blood.

                        On the Lesser Houseleek.                      Chapter 93.

   The Lesser Houseleek grows on rocks, on walls, in ruins, on the crowns of walls, and in tombs, where the sun does not strike. It produces many branches coming from a single root, slender, all covered with small, round, fleshy, pointed leaves. From the middle rises its stalk a span in height, at the top of which it forms an umbel, with small, pale-colored flowers. Its leaves have the same virtues as the one described above.

D                       On Another Houseleek.                         Chapter 94.

   The third Houseleek, which some call Wild Spider, others Telephion, and the Latins Illecebre, produces leaves that are fleshier and hairy, similar to those of purslane. It grows among rocks. Its virtue is warm, sharp, and ulcerating. Applied as a poultice with grease it resolves scrofulous swellings.

   These then are the species of Houseleeks mentioned here by Dioscorides, of which the greater and likewise the lesser are well known to everyone. The greater is called by the name Houseleek everywhere; but the lesser is called in some places Vermicularia, in others Herba grassa, and in others Granellosa, of which there are two kinds: one of which produces yellow flowers and smaller and more compact leaves, which I truly believe to be the male, and the other, which produces longer and sparser leaves, and white flowers, which can reasonably be believed to be the female. The one of the third species, of a contrary nature to these two, is found in some copies of Dioscorides described with more detail; but we have here followed the order of the Aldine correction, where many superfluities have been cut away. This one then, which produces leaves similar to wild purslane, I have not yet found anyone who can point it out to me in Italy; but the other two are found in great abundance everywhere. Galen made mention only of the first two species, saying thus: One and the other Houseleek, the greater...

Yet truly its cooling virtue is not negligible, since it is ranked among those things that cool in the third degree. On the Venus's Navel. Chapter 94.

The Venus's Navel has roundish leaves similar to a small cup, and so concave that they are not easily distinguished from one another; from the middle of each rises a short stem in which the seed is contained. Its root is round, like an olive. The juice, distilled or rubbed on with wine, reveals the genital parts that are covered with flesh, and it likewise benefits sacred fire, inflammations, scrofulous swellings, and bubo sores; it extinguishes the burning heat of the stomach. The leaves eaten together with the root break stones and promote urine; given with honey they benefit dropsical patients. Some use the herb for amorous purposes.

On another Venus's Navel. Chapter 95.

Another species of Venus's Navel, which some call Cymbalion, has leaves that are fat and broader, thick after the manner of small tongues, and near the roots they resemble the rim of an eye, as one sees in the greater houseleek. They are astringent in taste; they produce a thin little stalk on which the flowers are found, and the seed is similar to that of St. John's Wort; the root is larger. It is useful for all the same things as houseleek.

The first species of Venus's Navel grows most abundantly throughout all Tuscany on old walls, and the people commonly call its leaves "cupertouole," because they resemble the earthen covers made to cover pots; and it grows not only on walls but also on stones, wherever one wishes. The second species I recently saw in a small garden of simples belonging to Messer Giuliano da Marostica, an excellent physician, in Cividale d'Austria in Friuli. In Lombardy people use for Venus's Navel a certain herb called Cymbalaria, hanging like a mane from walls, with thin stems and ivy-like leaves, somewhat pointed at their tips in many places; they think that, since it is popularly called Cymbalaria, it must be the true Venus's Navel, because Dioscorides said that some call the second species Cymbalion. Galen mentions it in book seven of the Faculties of Simples, saying as follows: Venus's Navel is composed of mixed faculties, that is, of a mildly cold and humid quality, and of a certain not overtly astringent one, together with a slightly bitter one. And so it cools, repels, cleanses, and resolves. Thus it treats phlegmonous erysipelas and phlegmatic erysipelas; applied as a plaster with moisture it wonderfully relieves the burning of the stomach. It is believed that the leaves eaten can break stones and promote urine.

On the Nettle. Chapter 96.

The Nettle is of two species, one of which produces leaves that are wilder, rougher, broader, and darker, with seed like that of flax but smaller; the other is not so rough and has smaller seed. The leaves of both, plastered on with salt, benefit dog bites; they heal gangrenes, cancerous sores, foul and stubborn ulcers that are difficult to consolidate, and likewise dislocated limbs, buboes, small tumors, burst swellings, and those called parotids; applied with wax they benefit those suffering from a diseased spleen; placed ground together with juice in the nose, they stop the flow of blood; pounded together with myrrh and applied below, they bring on the menses; touching the relaxed womb with them fresh returns it to its place. The seed drunk with raisin wine stirs up lust; it opens the mouth of the womb; licked with honey it benefits defects of the chest, pain in the sides, and inflammations of the lungs; it purges the chest and is mixed with corrosive medicines. The leaves cooked with mussels soften the body, promote urine, and resolve flatulence; cooked with barley-water they benefit defects of the chest; drunk with a little myrrh they bring on the menses. The juice gargled resolves inflammations of the uvula.

The Nettle is so well known a plant that it is recognized by everyone even in the dark of night, and so there is no need to say what it looks like; though it is not without value to know how many species it has. Even though Dioscorides records only two species, nonetheless three are found in Italy — the two mentioned above, and a third with small leaves and short —

A The stalks are considerably more stinging than either of the others, and are called by some Wild Nettle. Galen writes of it in book six of the Properties of Simple Medicines, saying this: The leaves and seeds of the Nettle, which are the parts in use, are highly digestive, such that they heal swellings, and especially those that arise behind the ears. They contain a certain windy quality, by means of which they gently move one to lust; a fact attested by the drawing out of gross and thick humors, and likewise the itching that it causes in the limbs it touches. This windy quality arises in it as it digests, and thus the Nettle is not actually windy in itself, but potentially so. It loosens the belly to some degree, not however through a solutive action, but rather because it is astringent and irritating. It heals cancerous ulcers, and all those that need to be dried without any mordant quality: for since it is subtle and dry in temperament in its parts, it is not so hot as to be able to bite.

Of Galeopsis. Chapter 97.

B Galeopsis is a plant whose stalk and leaves are in every way similar to the nettle, but its leaves are smoother, and when bruised they emit a disagreeable odor: the flower it produces is purple and slender. It grows beside hedges, in the yards of houses, and everywhere along roads. The leaves, the stalk, the seed, and likewise the juice dissolve hardnesses and cancers, and heal scrofula, lumps, and swellings that arise behind the ears. For these purposes they are applied warm with vinegar, twice a day, and fomentations are made with its decoction. They are also applied with salt with benefit upon putrid, gangrenous, and corrosive ulcers.

N Galeopsis grows everywhere, in yards, along roads, in public squares, and near houses, and is called in Italy Stinking Nettle, because it smells strongly when handled. It produces leaves and a stalk similar to the nettle, but they do not sting, and the flower is purple and slender. It is indeed a most well-known plant; and therefore it seems to me that Leonardo Fuchsius the German errs greatly in his celebrated herbal, in wishing the Galeopsis to be that plant which is commonly called Scrofolaria, Ferraria, Castrangola, and Millemorbia, on the grounds that it produces a flower similar to a helmet or casque. Of this error a clear demonstration is the fact that it produces leaves not very similar to those of the nettle, and not disagreeable to the smell. Furthermore, one of the most notable features of the plant is its very knotty root, which Dioscorides would surely not have omitted to mention, had he understood by Galeopsis the common Scrofolaria, which for the most part grows beside ditches and along the banks of small streams, and not in yards beside hedges and along roads. There is therefore no reason at all to believe that Galeopsis and Scrofolaria are one and the same thing. There is another species altogether similar to the above-mentioned, which on each of its leaves has a white spot like milk, long and pointed, which we in Tuscany call Milk Nettle. This has led me on more than one occasion to believe that this is the true Galeopsis, thinking that the name Galeopsis would more naturally derive from Gala, which means milk, than from Gales, which means helmet — a name that is more Latin than Greek. For Dioscorides does not use the practice of forming names partly from Greek and partly from Latin, as Fuchsius imagines, nor is this practice used among other Greek writers. Moreover, I am led to believe that this Milk Nettle is the true Galeopsis because I observe that Dioscorides placed immediately after it the Chapter of Gallio, a herb so called because it causes milk to curdle just as rennet does. For Dioscorides, as has been said, followed an orderly method of placing and connecting together herbs and other plants according to their similarities, whether of form, or virtue, or name, so as to create a certain chain of all things: and therefore it appears that he placed the Gallio after the Galeopsis because in both the name derives from milk, and because there was no other resemblance between them that would justify placing one after the other; and all the more so because I do not find that either Dioscorides or Pliny wrote that the flower of Galeopsis resembles a helmet, from which it would take its name, although some modern writers have imagined so, having seen its flowers to be fairly helmet-like.

D Regarding Galeopsis, I do not find that Galen wrote anything about it in his books on Simple Medicines, although it was later included by Paul of Aegina among his own.

Of Gallio. Chapter 98.

Gallio has been so called because it is used in place of rennet to curdle milk. It produces a straight stalk, with leaves similar to those of cleavers, and at the top a flower that is yellow, thick, slender, abundant, and fragrant. The flower is applied to burns from fire, and staunches fluxes of blood. Gallio is put into plasters made with rose oil, and left in the sun until they turn white, and these are used for fatigue. The root provokes desire. It grows in marshy places.

N Gallio grows in great abundance all along the roads, quite similar to the lesser madder, which they call aparine; but its virtue of curdling milk is not known to everyone: for otherwise it would also be used in place of that other herb which we call presura, which is used throughout Tuscany to make fresh cheese.

About this Galen wrote in book six on the properties of simples, saying thus: Cleavers (Galium) has taken that name because it causes milk to curdle when placed inside it. It is similar to Aparine, and has a drying virtue, somewhat sharp. Its flower is good for flows of blood, and for burns from fire. It has a pleasant smell, and its color is yellow.

On Senecio, or Groundsel. Chapter 99.

Senecio, or Groundsel, produces a stem about a cubit tall, reddish, with continuous leaves cut like those of rocket, but much smaller: it produces yellow flowers, which shed their petals quickly and fly away as fluff: it is called Erigero for no other reason than that in spring its flowers turn white like hair, as hair does with age. Its root is of no value; it grows mostly in waste places and around fortifications. The leaves, and likewise the flowers, have a cooling virtue: and so, applying the leaves with a little wine, or by themselves, they heal inflammations of the testicles and of the seat, and beyond this, mixed with frankincense resin, they commonly treat not only all wounds, but those of the nerves in particular. The fluff of the flowers applied by itself with vinegar does the same: but drunk fresh, it causes choking. Cooked entire with the stem, and drunk with raisin wine, it heals choleric pains of the stomach.

Senecio, or Groundsel, is commonly called Cardoncello or Spellicciosa, and it is a plant well known to everyone, whose stems, as Dioscorides writes, are reddish, the leaves long and cut like those of rocket, though smaller: it produces yellow flowers, which then turning white and downy, fly away into the air. It grows everywhere, even on old walls. Not recognizing this, the German Otto Brunfels placed it in his herbal as a species of Verbena. Galen wrote of it in book six on the properties of simples, saying briefly: Groundsel has a mixed virtue, and likewise cooling, with some digestive quality.

On Thalictrum. Chapter 100.

Thalictrum has leaves like coriander, but somewhat thicker: the stem like rue, on which are leaves which, crushed and applied as a poultice, heal old ulcers. It grows mostly in open fields.

Ruellius says that Thalictrum is a herb which herb-gatherers call Argentina, because its coriander-like leaves shine greatly, and that it is found everywhere, but more often in fields and waste places. I neither deny nor affirm this, having not yet found anyone who can show me the true Thalictrum; of which Galen, writing in book six on the properties of simples, said: Thalictrum has leaves of coriander, and its stem grows thick like rue. It has a drying virtue without biting, and so it heals old ulcers with great effect.

On Sea Moss. Chapter 101.

Sea Moss grows on rocks and in the shells of fish near the sea, thin, hair-like, without any stem. It has a powerful virtue to restrain and resolve abscesses, and likewise gouty conditions, where it is necessary to staunch them.

The common opinion of every herbalist of our time is that what Dioscorides records as sea moss is what is commonly called Corallina, which vendors at market stalls often sell for children's worms: in which use, as I have many times seen by experience, it is extremely effective, from which opinion I cannot truly depart, knowing that those who go fishing for corals, from which it takes its name, find it attached to rocks, shells, and also around corals, in the same way that moss attaches to the bark and branches of trees: but they praise as best that which is found attached to corals, under the guise of which they sell countless bags of the other kind. This property it has of killing worms was not known to the ancients, since no one is found to have described it. Galen wrote of it in book six on the properties of simples, saying: Sea moss is composed of earthy and watery substance, both cold. Wherefore it is astringent to the taste, and applied as a poultice to hot conditions, it cools and heals them.

On Sea Wrack. Chapter 102.

Sea Wrack (Phuco) is of several kinds: one broad, another rather long and reddish, and the third, which grows in Crete, is white, very florid, and incorruptible. All have a cooling virtue, not only for gout, but also for inflam-

A greater uses. This it does effectively when plastered on fresh: but one must use it fresh, before it dries. Nicander prescribed the red variety for serpent bites. Some believe this was that Phucus which women use to color their faces, not knowing that what they use is a root of the same name.

On marine Phucus Pliny in chapter 24 of book 13 writes thus: In the sea there grow shrubs and trees,
S which in our sea are smaller than in the Red Sea: for that sea and the eastern Ocean are full of forests. In no other language does the plant that the Greeks call Phicos have a proper name: for Alga is more of a word for herbs; but this is a shrub. Since this plant is unknown to me, I can say nothing other than that if it is not an Alga, it may at least be a species thereof. Theodorus in his interpretation of Theophrastus calls the marine Phucus nothing other than Alga. Though Blinius in this passage said that name was not appropriate, in other places (as Marcello Fiorentino also said) he called it Alga. But I would not for this reason affirm that it is this Alga which is placed in Venice between glass vessels to prevent them from breaking; but I would say that the Phucus is also called Alga, for lack of another Latin name. Galen mentions it in the eighth book of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The Phucus, so moist when drawn from the sea, dries and cools in the second degree, and has some astringency.

On Potamogeton. Chapter 103.

Potamogeton produces leaves similar to beet, but hairy and somewhat raised above the water. It cools and stops bleeding: it is useful for itching and for old and corrosive ulcers. It has been given the name Potamogeton because it grows in marshes and other watery places.

Potamogeton is said to float with its beet-like leaves in lakes and marshes in many places. I have seen it many times myself, especially in certain lakes in the valley of Anania, and collected it with my own hands. Potamogeton (said Galen in book 8 of the Faculties of Simples) constricts and cools like Polygonum; but its substance is coarser than that of Polygonum.

On Stratiotes. Chapter 104.

Stratiotes, which is born in water, floats upon it and lives without roots, from which it takes its name. It is an herb similar to houseleek, except that it has larger leaves. These leaves, when drunk as a beverage, cool and stop bleeding from the kidneys: they prevent inflammation in wounds that threaten to suppurate. They are applied as a plaster with vinegar for erysipelas, and likewise for tumors.

It is no wonder that the aquatic Stratiotes does not grow in Italy. For (as Pliny reports in chapter 18 of book 24) it grows only in Egypt during the flooding of the Nile, resembling houseleek but with larger leaves.

On Stratiotes Milfoil. Chapter 105.

The milfoil Stratiotes is a small plant, a hand-span tall or sometimes taller, whose leaves resemble the feathers of small birds, being short and cut at their origin. The leaves resemble wild cumin, especially in their roughness and shortness, but are even shorter: the umbel however is denser and fuller. It produces at the top of the stem fine flower-stalks, from which the umbel is formed as with dill, with small white flowers: it grows in rough fields and along roadsides. It is in great use for old and fresh ulcers, for the flux of blood, and for fistulas.

Milfoil Stratiotes still retains in Italy today the name of Milfoil: for the common Milfoil is seen growing in uncultivated fields, in meadows and along roads, with stems taller than a hand-span, along which are leaves almost like the feathers of small birds, very similar to those of wild cumin, with an umbel of very white flowers, which sometimes blush with an incarnate tinge, and it produces from a single root four, five or more stems. This shows that the Milfoil in common use is this Stratiotes, and not the Myriophyllum described a little earlier by Dioscorides, as Brasavola believed: for Myriophyllum has a single tender stem growing in marshes, with abundant spreading leaves similar to those of fennel. This concludes that the common and everyday Milfoil is the terrestrial Stratiotes described here by Dioscorides. Galen made mention of both Stratiotes in book 8 of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The aquatic Stratiotes is truly cold and moist: but the terrestrial has some astringency. For this reason it can heal wounds and be useful for ulcers. There are some who use it for fluxes of blood and for fistulas.
