C Coloquintida is a very common plant, and as Mesue says in his treatise on simple purgatives, though it is highly valued for various reasons, it is nonetheless an enemy of the stomach, liver, and heart. It disturbs the whole body, purges with great pain and discomfort, opens the mouths of the veins, causes a flux of blood, and abrades all the passages through which it passes. Therefore it should not be given unless combined with cordial, stomachic, and hepatic medicines, and with glutinous and emollient medicines. Coloquintida purges phlegm and viscous humors, drawing them from the depths of the limbs; its action extends to the nerves and to the joints: it cleanses the brain, nerves, muscles, chest, and lungs. And therefore it is given for vertigo, epilepsy, apoplexy, migraine, and longstanding headaches. It prevents the descent of water to the eyes, and is wonderful for asthma and chronic cough. Its action is truly valuable for all cold pains of the joints, and especially for sciatica and gout, not only when given in purgations, but also in enemas, where it is the ultimate medicine for colic pains caused by flatulence and cold humors. It is very effective in dropsy. Oil boiled over coals in the fruit of the Coloquintida, hollowed out from the pith, makes the hair black, prevents it from turning white, and stops it from falling out. Distilled into the ears, it removes the pain and the ringing that is often felt there. Galen wrote about Coloquintida in book seven of On the Properties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Coloquintida is truly most bitter to the taste, but the operations of the bitterness it possesses it cannot clearly demonstrate when drunk, on account of its powerful purgative virtue, because it passes out of the body before those humors that it purges. The juice of the green plant is good for sciatica.

In writing about Dioscorides, as to what Empetron is made of in its parts, one would truly need a new Oedipus to guess it, even though there are some who, without any other guessing, venture to say that Empetro is sea fennel, which some call the herb of Saint Peter, of which we spoke fully in the second book in the chapter on Crithamus, where anyone can easily clarify this dispute for themselves — if they consider that Empetro and the herb of Saint Peter are one and the same thing. Galen made mention of Empetro in the sixth book on the faculties of simples, speaking thus: Empetro seems suitable only for purgation, for it purges cholera and phlegm. It is salty to the taste, and thus it may also be used in all those cases for which we have already shown that salty things are beneficial.

On the Wild Vine. Chapter 182.

The wild vine produces long shoots, like those of the grape vine, rough and woody, with bark entirely full of cracks; its leaves are similar to those of the garden nightshade, but longer and wider; it produces a mossy, delicate flower, and a fruit resembling a small grape, which when ripe turns red; the shape of its berries is round. The root, boiled in water and drunk in two cups of wine diluted with sea water, purges the moisture of the body, and for this reason it is given to those with dropsy. Its grapes remove blemishes and spots from the skin of the face and every other place. Its shoots are seasoned with salt when they are tender, and are kept to be eaten as food.

The wild vine is very well known to our Tuscan women, for there are many of them who rub their faces with its grapes to appear more colorful, since being sharp and acrid, it reddens wherever it touches, quickly and easily. One can truly observe in this plant all the characteristics that Dioscorides attributes to it. Its grapes redden upon the trees where it winds itself, throughout the whole winter, so that from a distance the trees appear to have the most beautiful strands of coral. It keeps, attached by the women from one year to the next without spoiling, and even if it dries out somewhat, it loses neither its moisture nor its color. Galen wrote of it in the sixth book on the faculties of simples, saying: The clusters of the wild vine truly have an astringent virtue, such that they can cure spots, moles, and other marks on the skin. The tips of the ends of the shoots are somewhat astringent, and for this reason they are customarily preserved in brine.

On the White Vine, that is, Bryony. Chapter 184.

The white vine, which some call Bryony, resembles the domestic vine in its shoots, leaves, and tendrils, but all these parts are more hairy; it clasps with its tendrils all the plants growing nearby; it produces a clustered, red fruit, with which hides are weighed. Its young shoots, eaten as food when tender in their first sprouting, loosen the body and stimulate urine. The leaves, fruit, and root have an acrid virtue, and for this reason they are usefully applied with vinegar and salt to ulcers called chironian, and to those that turn into gangrenes, which are corrosive, and to stubborn and foul sores of the legs. The root with bitter vetch, chalk of Chios, and fenugreek cleanses the body and tightens the skin; it removes spots from the face, those from smallpox, freckles, and dark scars. The same root cooked in oil, until it becomes liquid, removes bruises and hangnails from the fingers. Plastered on with wine, it resolves inflammations and breaks abscesses; it is conveniently used in corrosive medicines; ground and applied, it draws out broken bones. It is given throughout a whole year, every day, in a weight of one dram, to those who suffer from epilepsy; it is given in the same way to those who are stunned and to those suffering vertigo. Drunk at the weight of two drams, it is beneficial against viper bites; it kills the unborn child in the womb; it sometimes disturbs the intellect. Applied below to the private parts of women, it provokes the afterbirth and likewise labor; drunk, it stimulates urine. An electuary is made with honey for those who breathe with difficulty and are in danger of choking from cough, for those afflicted with spasms, ruptures, and pains in the ribs. Drunk with vinegar at the weight of three obols for thirty days, it consumes the spleen, and for the same purpose it is plastered on the outside with figs. A decoction is made for women to sit in, for their ailments, for it purges the womb, but causes miscarriage. The juice is pressed from the root in spring, which when drunk with honey-water loosens phlegm. The seed is rubbed on effectively for mange and scabies. The juice drunk with cooked grain produces an abundance of milk.

Some modern writers report that if sterile women first enter a bath made with womb-herbs, and then anoint the mouth of the womb with this oil, and afterwards sleep with their husband, they easily become pregnant. Beyond this, it is said to be most beneficial for ulcers of the womb, for some have tested it there with miraculous success, where many other remedies had no effect. It is excellent for intestinal cracks, applied warm frequently to the area. The powder of the herb, given in the amount of a spoonful (as some faithful experimenters attest under oath) with plantain water, consolidates interior wounds, even if the wound passed from one side to the other. Others say the same powder is good for colic pains and for those of the bowels, working with wonderful speed. Beyond this, so that no one confuse this plant's name, it should be known (as was said above in Book IV, in the chapter on Geranium) that there are some who also call Momordica that species of Geranium which produces the wider leaves.

On the Fern. Chapter 185.

The Fern produces its fronds from a single stalk without stem, without flower, and without seed, of the length of a cubit, cut like a spread wing, of a somewhat unpleasant odor. It has a root between the soil, black and somewhat long, from which many shoots emerge, somewhat astringent to the taste. It grows in mountains and rocky places. The root, drunk at the weight of four drams with honeyed water, drives large worms out of the body. This it does more powerfully when given with four obols of scammony or black hellebore: but those who take it in this way must first eat garlic. It reduces the size of the spleen. The root, drunk and applied as a plaster with grease, helps wounds made by reed arrows. This is proven by the fact that all Fern perishes when surrounded by planted reeds, and conversely, reeds die when encircled by Fern.

On the Female Fern. Chapter 186.

The Female Fern has fronds like the fern, but not like that one proceeding from a single stalk; rather from many, taller, and more branched. It has many long roots, twisted, somewhat reddish-black, as though some of them are red. These, eaten in an electuary made with honey, drive large worms from the body; and drunk with wine at the weight of three drams, they drive out roundworms. Eaten by women they make them sterile, and cause pregnant women who walk over it to miscarry. They are usefully applied, ground in flour, to moist ulcers that heal with difficulty. They are good for diseases of the necks of animals put to the yoke. The fresh fronds are eaten cooked, when they sprout, together with other vegetables, to soften the body.

Both the male and female ferns are in our time very well known in Italy. Of them Theophrastus wrote in Book IX, Chapter 20, saying: The female fern, combined with honey, is useful against large internal worms, and given with barley flour in sweet wine against the long ones. Pregnant women miscarry if they drink it, and others (as they say) become sterile. The female fern differs from the male in various ways: for the female has fronds that proceed from a single stalk, and a long, black, thick root. It is believed that nature made it more for causing sterility than for anything else. Pliny also wrote of it in Chapter 9 of Book 27, saying: There are two kinds of fern; they produce neither seed nor flower. That believed to be the male produces more fronds from a single root, more than two cubits long, and not of an unpleasant odor. The other has but one stalk, is not branched or thick, but shorter and more tender. It has denser fronds and is hollow near the roots. Pigs are fattened on the roots of both, which are in each species long, twisted and black, and especially so when dry. They grow everywhere, but much more in cold places. They purge the body first of bile, and then of water. And in Chapter 6 of Book 18, the fern (he said) dies in two years if it is not allowed to put forth fronds. This is done most effectively when its shoots are broken with a stick, for the juice that then distills from them kills the roots. It is not to be given to women in any way: for it makes them sterile, and if they are pregnant, causes them to miscarry. Galen mentioned the fern in Book VIII on the Properties of Simples, saying: The fern has a root that is truly most useful, for it kills large worms in the body. It is therefore no wonder that in the same way it kills the child in the mother's womb, and expels the dead fetus. It is bitter to the taste and somewhat astringent. This causes it, when applied to ulcers, to dry them out effectively without any biting. The plant called female has the same virtues.

A On the Filicola, or Polypody. Chapter 187.

The Filicola grows on mossy stones and on the old trunks of trees, especially on those of oak trees, standing about a hand's breadth tall, similar to a fern but somewhat hairy, though not so finely cut. It produces a hairy root, full of certain curly fibers similar to those seen on the octopus, as thick as the little finger of the hand, greenish inside, somewhat sweet and bitter to the taste. It has the virtue of purging: it is cooked to loosen the body, with hens, or with fish, or with beets, or with mallow. The flour of the dried plant, drunk with honey-water, relieves bile and phlegm. Applied as a poultice it is effective for dislocated joints and for splinters that grow between the fingers.

A The Filicola is so called by the Latins; modern physicians and likewise apothecaries, following the Greek, call it Polypodium. It is a plant today very well known to all and very abundant in Italy. There are two species of it, of which the first is this one, which Dioscorides discusses here and which is in daily use in the apothecaries' shops. The second does not grow in every location, but mostly in the forests of the mountains. This second produces fronds very similar to those of the aspleno, but longer, greener, and more finely cut, and a root similar to the other in form, flavor, and color. An infinite quantity of it grows in certain mountains one passes through going from Gorizia to Carniola, where I have seen and gathered it many times. Mesue praised the one that grows on tree trunks, and especially on oaks, affirming that the one growing on stones has a certain superfluous indigestible moisture which easily causes flatulence, stomach upset, and nausea. He then said this generally of all Polypody, without excepting one more than the other, saying thus: Polypody is among those things that powerfully attenuate and dry out the body, and causes stomach upset and nausea. This did not please Manardo of Ferrara at all, who refused in any way to accept the opinion of Mesue, saying that because Polypody is very gentle in purging, it cannot consequently too much attenuate the body, and that he has always found by experience that Polypody purges without any discomfort: and therefore one should believe Averrhoës more in this matter, who said that Polypody is a safe medicine and better than the Epithimo, which is Mesue. Polypody dissolves (according to Actuarius) black bile and phlegm, when six scruples of its well-cleaned root are given with honey-water: and it loosens the body moderately without any discomfort when its root is cooked in chicken broth or in barley water. Galen wrote about Polypody in the eighth book on the properties of simples, saying thus: Polypody is simultaneously sweet and astringent, so that it dries powerfully without any sharpness. This seems to me to demonstrate that Mesue was quite right in saying that Polypody attenuates and dries powerfully, having derived this opinion from Galen: and therefore it appears contrary to reason that he was corrected by Manardo, who truly deserves greater censure.

On the Dryopteris. Chapter 188.

The Dryopteris grows among the moss of old oak trees, similar to the fern, but with much less finely cut fronds, whose roots are tangled in upon themselves, hairy, bitter to the taste, with a certain sweetness. This herb, ground up and applied, causes the hair to fall out: it is applied first until it causes sweating, then the sweat is dried off, and then fresh herb is applied again.

Dryopteris means nothing other than Oak Fern: because it grows (as Dioscorides states here) on old oak trees among the moss, with fronds similar to the fern but smaller and less cut. It is a very well-known plant in Italy: and therefore there is no need to recount here any long history of it, especially since it is found common in all forests where oak trees grow. Galen wrote of it in the sixth book on the properties of simples, saying thus: Dryopteris presents to the taste a mixed quality, that is sweet, pungent, and bitter, and acrid in the root. It has a cutting virtue: and therefore it causes hair to fall out.

On the Cnicus. Chapter 189.

The Cnicus produces rather long fronds, toothed around the edges, rough and spiny: its stalk is a foot and a half tall, at whose summit is a large head like a large olive: it produces a saffron-colored flower, a white seed, and sometimes red, long and square. The flower is used in food. The liquid pressed from the pounded seed, drunk with chicken broth or honey-water, purges the body but is harmful to the stomach. Lozenges are made to loosen the body, mixing its liquid with almonds, saltpeter, anise, and cooked honey. These are then divided into four parts of the size of a walnut each, of which it suffices to eat two before supper, or at most three. The method of making them is as follows. Take one sextary of its white seed, three cyathi of peeled toasted almonds, one sextary of anise, one drachm of saltpeter foam, and thirty dried figs. The liquid of the seed thickens milk and makes it more laxative.

On the Greater Heliotrope. Chapter 192.

The great Heliotrope produces a flower similar to the tail of a scorpion, whence it is called Scorpiuro; and because it turns its leaves together with the sun, it is called Heliotrope. It has leaves like basil, but more hairy, whiter, and larger; it produces three, four, and often five stalks from its roots, with many hollows along their sides, at whose tips are white or reddish flowers, which bend in the manner of a scorpion's tail. Its root is slender and useless; it grows in rough places. A decoction of a handful of the herb made in water, when drunk, purges the body of choler and phlegm. It is equally effective drunk with wine and applied as a poultice to scorpion stings. It is bound to the body to prevent conception. They say that if four seeds are given to drink in wine one hour before the onset of fever, they free one from quartan fever, and three seeds from tertian fever. The seed applied as a poultice dries up flat warts and hanging ones, thymi, and likewise epinittides. The leaves are usefully applied to heat inflammations of children's heads, to gout, and to dislocations of joints; they promote menstruation, and applied crushed beneath, they bring on labor.

On the Lesser Heliotrope. Chapter 193.

The lesser Heliotrope grows in marshes and near lakes, with leaves similar to those of the aforementioned, but more rounded; it also produces a round seed, like those hanging warts they call acrochordons. The herb drunk together with its seed, nitre, hyssop, nasturtium, and water, drives out from the body worms both wide and round; applied as a poultice with salt it removes those warts called acrochordons.

The greater Heliotrope grows most abundantly in Tuscany, and our Apothecaries call it Verrucaria, and the common people call it the herb of leeks, because rubbing leeks with it removes them effectively. And so those are wrong who think that the Calendula, which we call the orange flower, is the greater Heliotrope, for it does not correspond to it in any feature. Some, seeing that its seed is somewhat twisted, similar to the tails of scorpions, have believed the Calendula to be the Heliotrope, not noticing that Dioscorides said that the flowers, and not the seed, of the Heliotrope resembled scorpion tails. Ruellius says that in France it is called herba Cancri because its flower resembles the tails of crayfish. With this I do not agree, since the tails of crayfish are formed differently from those of scorpions; but I am more inclined to believe it is called herba Cancri for the wonderful effect it has on cancers and on all cancerous ulcers, in which the Surgeons of Tuscany use it with marvelous success. I have seen the lesser one many times near lakes and in marshes in the district of Trento, entirely similar to the one described by Dioscorides, and I have shown it to various Physicians and Apothecaries. Of this plant I do not find that Galen made any mention in the books on simples; although Paul of Aegina recites what he took from Dioscorides.

On Scorpioid. Chapter 194.

The Scorpioid is a small herb that produces few leaves, whose seed resembles the tails of scorpions. Applied as a poultice on scorpion stings, it is truly an immediate remedy.

If the other features corresponded to the account that Dioscorides gives of the Scorpioid as the seed corresponds, one might truly say it was the Calendula; but since the Calendula produces many leaves, both long and large, and the Scorpioid few and short, one can only say that those are wrong who believe the Calendula to be the Scorpioid, which up to this time I have not yet been able to trace. Galen wrote briefly of it in book seven on the properties of simples, saying thus: The Scorpioid consolidates in the third degree and dries in the second.

In the four books written above, most beloved Ario, we have treated of perfumes, ointments, oils, trees, and likewise of their resins and fruits, and beyond that of animals, honey, milk, fats, grains, garden herbs, and every sort of roots, plants, juices, and seeds. But now in this fifth volume, the conclusion of the whole work, we will speak of wines and of metallic substances: and therefore we shall begin our discussion with the vine.

On the Wine-bearing Vine. Chapter One.

The leaves of the Vine, and likewise the crushed tendrils, applied as a poultice relieve pains of the head; and with polenta they soothe inflammations and burning of the stomach: the leaves alone serve the same purpose, being cold and astringent in nature. Their juice, when drunk, aids dysentery, spitting of blood, weak stomachs, and the corrupted appetite of pregnant women. The tendrils steeped in water and drunk do the same. The sap of the vine, which is found thickened like gum in the trunk, when drunk with wine drives out kidney stones; applied externally it cures ringworm, mange, and scabies, though one must first rub the area with nitre; and when applied as an ointment it frequently causes hair to fall out. The humor that flows from the cuttings when they are burned green does even more, and with it one can also eradicate those kinds of warts called ants, by anointing them. The ash of the cuttings and of the vine-shoots, made into a poultice with vinegar, heals fissures of the rectum and thymi; it benefits paralyzed limbs and bites of vipers; a poultice for inflammations of the spleen is made with it together with rose oil, rue, and vinegar.

On the Wild Vine. Chapter Two.

The wild vine is of two kinds, one of which does not ripen its grape but produces it only up to flowering, and this is called Enanthe; the other ripens with small berries, turning black and astringent. The leaves, stalks, and tendrils have the same virtue as those of the cultivated vine.

On the Grape. Chapter Three.

Fresh grapes disturb the body and inflate the stomach. The less harmful kind is that which, after being harvested, has been dried somewhat, because in this state the excess humor has already been removed; it is therefore useful to the stomach and to the sick, and stimulates the appetite. That which is preserved in grape-marc or in jars is very pleasing and agreeable to the mouth and likewise to the stomach; it is binding to the body, but harmful to the bladder and the head; it is good for spitting of blood. The same applies to grapes preserved in must. Grapes preserved in cooked must or in raisin wine are more harmful to the stomach. Those that are first dried in the sun and then kept in rainwater have less of a wine quality and are beneficial in long, burning fevers that cause extreme thirst. Preserved grape-marc applied as a poultice together with salt is useful for inflammations of the breasts and for those caused in women by an excess of milk. A decoction made from it is beneficial in dysentery, in stomach fluxes, and also in those of women; and it is used to make sitz baths. The seeds of the grapes have astringent properties and are useful to the stomach. The powder of roasted seeds is sprinkled on the body for dysentery and likewise for fluxes and weaknesses of the stomach.

On Raisins. Chapter 4.

White raisins are more astringent than black ones. Their flesh, when eaten, is beneficial for coughs, the throat, the kidneys, and the bladder. They are eaten in dysentery on their own, or cooked in a pan with honey, flour of millet, barley, and eggs. They are useful on their own, and chewed with pepper to purge phlegm from the head. Prepared as a poultice together with flour of spelt or cumin, they relieve inflammation of the testicles. Ground without the seeds and applied as a poultice with rue, they heal chilblains, the condition called epinyctis, and corrosive ulcers of the joints, as well as gangrene. Applied to gout with the juice of opopanax, they bring suitable relief. Placed on loose nails, they cause them to fall off in a short time.

On Enanthe. Chapter 5.

They call Enanthe the fruit of the wild vine when it flowers. It is preserved for use in unlined earthenware. It is gathered and dried in the shade, having first been wrapped in a cloth. The best comes from Syria, Cilicia, and Phoenicia. It has astringent virtue, and thus drunk is useful for the stomach and for promoting urine. It stops fluxes of the body and spitting of blood. Applied dry as a poultice it works against acidity and revulsion of the stomach. It is used both dry and fresh, with vinegar and rose oil on the forehead for headaches. It is applied as a poultice to prevent inflammation of fresh wounds and fistulas of the tear ducts that are just beginning. It also heals, ground with honey, myrrh, saffron, and rose oil, ulcers of the mouth and corrosive conditions of the genital parts. It is placed in pessaries to stop menstrual blood. Applied with wine and fine flour, it benefits watering of the eyes and the burning sensation of the stomach. The ash of the plant burned between two earthenware tiles over live coals is used in medicines for the eyes. With honey it heals whitlows and proud flesh growing around the nails, as well as eroded and bleeding gums.

On Omphacium, that is, Verjuice. Chapter 6.

Omphacium is the juice of unripe Thasian grapes, or else Aminean grapes. It is pressed in summer before the rising of the Dog Star, and the juice is placed in a copper vessel, covered with a linen cloth, in the sun, until it thickens, mixing back in what dries out around the sides of the vessel with what remains in the middle. At night it is brought under cover and not left at all in the open air, because the dew that falls at night prevents it from thickening. The best is the red, the brittle, that which is strongly astringent and bites the tongue. There are some who thicken it by cooking it over fire. Mixed with honey or raisin wine, it is beneficial for roughness of the throat, the uvula, and the tonsils, for ulcers of the mouth, and for moisture of the gums and for ears running with discharge. With vinegar it works similarly for fistulas, old ulcers, and corrosive ones. It is put into enemas used for dysentery and for fluxes of women's natural parts. It is a suitable medicine for the brightness and roughness of the eyes and their corrosions. It is drunk for fresh spitting of blood, even if proceeding from some ruptured vessel, though used in small quantity and very well diluted with water, since too much of it burns.

On the Nature of Wine. Chapter 7.

Old wine is harmful to the nerves and to all the other senses, yet it is more pleasant to the taste. Therefore let those who have some weakness in the internal parts beware of it. In health, however, one may drink a little at a time without harm, provided it is diluted with water. New wine causes bloating, is digested with difficulty, produces terrible dreams, and provokes urination. Wine of middle age causes neither the one nor the other harm, and is therefore commonly used for the living of both the healthy and the sick. White wine of light body is beneficial to the stomach and distributes itself easily through the limbs. Red wine is thick and more difficult to digest; it nourishes the flesh and causes drunkenness. Vermilion wine, of a color between white and red, similarly has its qualities midway between the two. White wine is praised above all others, in both health and sickness. Among those of Greece, the most excellent are the Chian, the Lesbian, and the Phigelite from Ephesus. Wines that are thick in substance and dark in color are very difficult to digest, generate flatulence, and increase body weight. Those that are thin and astringent are good for the stomach, but do not thicken the body. Old white wines, thin in nature, stimulate urination more powerfully, but drunk in large quantities they harm the nerves. Those of middle age, that is, seven years old, are truly the healthiest to drink. One must consider the quantity required for drinking, according to age, time of year, custom, and the quality of the wine. It is strongly advised never to drink to quench thirst. It is truly most healthful to moisten food with a little wine. All forms of drunkenness are harmful, but habitual drunkenness most of all: for the nerves, continually besieged, must eventually yield; and drinking too much always gives rise to acute illness. Nevertheless, it is useful to drink somewhat more than usual for a few days, after
B having drunk only water for a time: for it draws humors to the surface, opens the passages through which it then imperceptibly purges the superfluities of the senses; but afterward one must drink water, since that is the remedy for this deliberate drunkenness. What they call Omphacite is made especially in Lesbos from unripe grapes harvested just before maturity, and dried in the sun for three or four days until they become somewhat dry, after which the wine pressed from them is put into casks and left in the sun. This wine has an astringent virtue; it helps with vomiting from relaxed stomachs, pains in the sides, the corrupted appetite of pregnant women, and indigestion; and it is believed to be very useful drunk during plague. These wines cannot be drunk until many years have passed. What the Greeks call deuteria, meaning secondary wine, and the Latins call lora, is made as follows: take three measures of water and pour them over the grape-skins from which thirty measures of wine have already been pressed; mix everything together well and press it; the wine thus obtained is cooked down to a third, and then two sestarii of salt are added per congius of the aforesaid wine;
C after winter it is transferred to other vessels. It is drunk in the same year it is made, since it quickly loses its goodness. It is given to the sick when it is not safe to give them other wine, when we are obliged to satisfy their desires, and likewise to convalescents. There is also what they call impotent wine, similar in strength to the foregoing. To make it, take equal parts of must and water, and boil them gently over the fire until all the water has evaporated; when cool, it is put into a pitched cask. Some take equal parts of seawater, rainwater, honey, and must, put them all together in vessels exposed to the sun for forty days, and use it for all these purposes in the same year. That which is made from the grapes of the wild vine, being very black in color, is truly useful by virtue of its astringent property, for fluxes of the body and likewise of the stomach, and in all other cases where there is need to bind and stanch.

On Melitite Wine. Chapter 8.

D Melitite wine is given in prolonged fevers that weaken the stomach, because it gently moves the body, stimulates urination, settles the stomach, helps with pains in the joints, ailments of the kidneys, weakness of the head, and for women who drink particularly large amounts of water; it is fragrant and nourishes the body. It differs from mulsum, which is made of old austere wine mixed with a little honey; for Melitite is made by putting one congius of honey and one cyathus of salt into five congii of austere must. This wine must be made in large vessels so that there is room for it to boil freely; scatter the salt over it little by little as it boils, and when it has finished boiling, transfer it to other vessels.

On Mulsum Wine. Chapter 9.

The best of all mulsum wines is held to be that made from old wine and good honey, because wine made in this way generates less flatulence and more quickly becomes good to use. Old wine nourishes the body. Wine of middle age softens the body and stimulates urination. Drunk after a meal it is harmful, and before a meal it satisfies; but a little afterward it stim-

FIFTH BOOK. 385

stimulates the appetite. Must is made from two measures of wine and one of honey. There are some others who, so that it may be drunk sooner, cook the wine together with honey and then bottle it. There are others who, to spend less, add one measure of honey to six measures of must while it is boiling during the grape harvest, and once it has finished boiling, they store it in barrels, and thus it remains sweet.

On Honey-Water Chapter 10.

Honey-water has the same properties as honey-wine. It is used as a drink, cooked, when we want to move the body or induce vomiting, as we do when we give it with oil to those who have taken poison; likewise we give it cooked to those who are naturally weak and of feeble pulse; it is given to those who have a cough, and to those suffering from ailments of the lungs, and to those who waste away from excessive sweating. That which is kept prepared and stored, called Hydromele, is as potent at room temperature as the wine called adinamo or acquarelo; and therefore it helps with inflammations of certain limbs more than acquarelo does. The aged variety is given to those who are inflamed and constipated, as it is suited to conditions of the stomach, to nausea from food, and to those who sweat excessively. It is made by combining two measures of old rainwater with one measure of honey, and then leaving it in the sun. Some make it with spring water and boil it down until it reduces by a third, and then store it. Some call honey-water the reserved water with which the wise wash themselves. It is drunk in greater quantities. Some cook it, but it is harmful to the sick because it retains too much waxy matter.

On Water. Chapter 11.

It is truly a difficult thing to determine universally the properties of water, given the particular natures of different places, the conditions of the air, and many other factors. Nevertheless, the best is that which is sweet, pure, and does not partake of any other quality, and that which does not remain long in the chest, descends easily without pain, does not generate flatulence, and does not putrefy in the body.

On Sea Water. Chapter 12.

Sea water is hot and sharp. It is harmful to the stomach, disturbs the body, and purges phlegm. Applied warm in baths, it draws and resolves; it helps with ailments of the nerves and with swellings, before they become ulcerated; it is used in poultices made from barley flour; it is also usefully applied in resolving poultices; tepid baths of it are used to stop purging. Applied warm, it is good for bodily pains, for mange, itching, skin eruptions, for chapped skin, and for breasts that are overly engorged with milk after childbirth; used as a fomentation it removes bruises. It is truly beneficial for venomous stings, especially those of scorpions, of the spiders called phalangi, and of asps, which cause trembling and numbness in the limbs. This is also achieved by entering a warm bath of it. It is beneficial in baths for those who, through long illness, are swollen throughout the body, and likewise for the nerves; inhaling its vapor when it boils is beneficial for those with dropsy, for headaches, and for deafness of the ears. The pure kind, which has no trace of fresh water, when stored, loses its harmful quality over time. Some first cook it and then store it in preserves. It is given alone to purge the body, or with diluted vinegar, or with wine, or with honey; but after its operation one should give chicken broth or fish broth to quench the sharpness of its mordacity.

On Thalassomele. Chapter 13.

What is called Thalassomele purges powerfully. It is made from equal parts of sea water, rainwater, and honey, and then all these things are strained through a colander and placed in the sun in a pitch-lined vessel during the dog days. There are others who make it with two parts of cooked sea water and one of honey, and...

386 LIBRO

A they are put back into their vessel: and this for purging is truly more pleasant than water, and lighter.

On Vinegar, Chapter 14.

Vinegar cools and is astringent: it benefits the stomach, stimulates appetite, and stops flows of blood from whatever part of the body, when drunk, and when one sits in it. Cooked into foods it helps with fluxes of the body, and placed on bleeding wounds it stops the blood: applied with unwashed wool or a sponge it heals inflammations: it returns the intestine that protrudes from the seat to its place, and likewise restores a prolapsed womb in women: it stops flows from the gums and the blood that comes out of them. It is good for ulcers that eat away at the flesh, for erysipelas, for corrosive ulcers, for scabies, for ringworm, for growths of flesh around the nails, and especially when mixed with something appropriate to the ailment: used continuously as a bath it arrests ulcers that eat and corrode and spread: made into a warm fomentation with sulfur it benefits gout: plastered on with honey it resolves bruises. Mixed with rose oil and unwashed wool, or with sponges, it is good for inflammations of the head. The steam of the boiling vinegar benefits the dropsical, the deaf, and those with discharge from the ears, and distilled into the ear it kills the worms that breed there: a bath of it, tepid, resolves lumps, or applied over them with a sponge: it eases itching. Warmed and made into a bath it helps against the bites of those venomous animals that kill by their cold: but cold it serves in the same way against the bites of those that give a hot venom. Drunk warm and vomited up, it is good against all poisons, and especially against opium, hemlock, blood congealed in the stomach, poisonous mushrooms, curdled milk, ixia, and yew, taken together with salt. Drunk, it dislodges leeches swallowed in the throat: it eases a chronic cough, but irritates a fresh one. Drunk warm it is usefully taken for tightness of the chest and asthma: gargled it prevents inflammations of the throat, and is suited to quinsy and to a falling uvula, and kept warm in the mouth it relieves toothache.

C On Oxymel, Chapter 15.

Oxymel, which they call oximele, is made in the following way. Take five heminae of vinegar, one pound of common salt, ten heminae of honey, and five sextarii of water, and boil everything together until it has come to ten boils, and when it is cold, put it into its vessels. It is believed that drunk it purges thick humors, and that it benefits sciatica, epilepsy, and pains of the joints: it is useful for the bite of that kind of viper called sepa, against opium, and likewise against ixia, and it is beneficially gargled for quinsy.

On Acetous Brine, Chapter 16.

Acetous brine, which the Greeks call oxalme, is useful used as a wash against ulcers that spread and corrode, and likewise against putrid ones, against the bites of dogs, and against the stings of venomous animals. It stops the flow of blood caused by the incision made to extract bladder stones, if sprinkled hot immediately onto the wound: it reduces the prolapsed rectum. Enemas of it are used in dysentery, when the intestines are ulcerated by corrosive ulcers: but one must then immediately give an enema of milk: gargled or drunk it kills leeches that attach themselves to the throat while drinking: it cleanses dandruff and running ulcers of the head.

On Thymoxalme, Chapter 17.

Thymoxalme was used by the ancients, and they gave three or four cups of it diluted with warm water to those with weak stomachs, and likewise for ailments of the joints and for flatulence. It purges thick and dark humors. It is made in the following way. Take one acetabulum of ground thyme, the same amount of salt, of rue, of pennyroyal, of polenta, a little of each, and put it all together in a vessel, and then pour over it three sextarii of water and three cyathi of vinegar, cover the vessel with a cloth, and set it out in the open air.

BOOK FIVE. 387

On Scillitic Vinegar. Chapter 18.

Scillitic vinegar is made as follows. Take squill that is very white and clean, slice it, and thread the pieces on a string at a distance from one another so they do not touch; in this way they are dried in the shade for forty continuous days. Of these dried pieces, take one sira and steep them in twelve sextaries of good vinegar. Seal the vessel very tightly and leave it in the sun for seven continuous days. After that time, remove the squill, squeeze it well first with the hands, and discard it; then clarify the vinegar and store it. Some people make it by placing a single sira of squill in only five sextaries of vinegar. Others take fresh clean squill without drying it and place it with an equal weight of vinegar, leaving it to macerate for six months; this is truly more powerful for cutting and thinning thick humors. Scillitic vinegar dries up the superfluous moisture of putrid gums, stabilizes and firms loose teeth, removes decay from the mouth, and relieves heaviness of breath. Taken internally, it consolidates and hardens the throat, produces a clear and resonant voice. It is given for weakness of the stomach, to those who digest food poorly, to melancholics, to those with epilepsy, to those with vertigo, and to the mentally disturbed; to those with bladder stones; it helps with strangulations of the womb, enlargement of the spleen, and sciatica; it strengthens the weak, fortifies the body, and improves complexion; it sharpens the sight; instilled into the ears it helps deafness. In short, it is good for everything. However, it should not be used in ulcers of the internal organs, nor in headaches, nor in disorders and ailments of the nerves. It is drunk on an empty stomach, and at first only a small quantity is taken; but the dose is increased gradually each day, until at the end one drinks a cyathus per dose, though some give two cyathi per dose, and sometimes more.

On Scillitic Wine. Chapter 19.

Scillitic wine is made in the following manner. Take the sliced squill, dried in the sun as we have described above, pound it, and sift it finely. Then take a sira of this and tie it in a loose cloth, and submerge it in twenty sextaries of good, fresh must; leave it thus for three continuous months, then transfer it to another vessel and seal it well. Fresh squill may be used, doubling the weight, and slicing it as one slices turnips; but it must be kept in the sun for forty days and allowed to age. It is also made in another way: take three siras of sliced and well-cleaned squill and steep them in an Italian metreta of good must; leave it to macerate in a well-sealed vessel for six continuous months, after which time it is clarified and stored. It is useful for crudity and corruption of food, and likewise for vomiting of food, and for phlegm gathered in the stomach and intestines; it benefits those with spleen disorders, those with bad physical constitution, those with dropsy, with overflow of bile, with difficulty urinating, with pains in the bowels, with flatulence, with paralysis, with prolonged chills and shivering before fevers, with vertigo, and with spasms of the nerves; it provokes menstruation; it does not harm the nerves at all. It is better the older it gets. One should take care not to use it in fevers, nor where the internal organs are ulcerated.

On Wines Mixed with Sea Water. Chapter 20.

Aged wines are mixed with sea water in various ways: for there are those who add sea water immediately after the grapes are harvested. Some first dry the grapes on racks in the sun, then press them, adding salt water. Some macerate the already-dried grapes in barrels with salt water and then press out the wine; this becomes sweet. Those of this type that are austere are given in fevers when better ones cannot be found; they move the bowels; they benefit those who spit matter, and those who are costive. Those made from Aminean grapes cause headache, harm the stomach, and generate flatulence. But so that those who are most studious of this art may have—

388 BOOK

A We do not consider it truly useless to teach various compositions of wines in this copious history: not because their use is frequent and necessary, but to show that we have not neglected what is sought in such learning. There are some that are made with little effort and expense, being in everyday use, such as those made from quinces, pears, pods, and berries of the myrtle.

On Wine of Quinces. Chapter 21.

The wine of quinces, otherwise called Mesite, is customarily made in this way. The quinces are cut into pieces, as one cuts turnips, and having removed the seeds, they are steeped at a weight of twelve pounds in one measure of must, and for thirty days continuously they are left to macerate; the wine is then clarified and set aside. It is also made in another way. The quinces are crushed and their juice is pressed out, of which ten measures are combined with one measure of honey, and thus it is stored. This wine is astringent, benefits the stomach, dysentery, diseases of the liver, ailments of the kidneys, and difficulty of urination. Melomele, which is also called Cidonomele, is made in this way. First the quinces are cleaned of their seeds and placed in such a quantity of honey that they can be entirely submerged. It becomes good after one year, and comes to resemble honeyed wine, and is as valuable as the above-described composition.

On Hydromel. Chapter 22.

Hydromel is made from two measures of boiled water, kept in the sun during the dog days, and from one part of Melomele made from quinces, and it has the same virtue.

On Omphacomele. Chapter 23.

Omphacomele is made thus. Unripe grapes are taken and left in the sun for three days, and then their juice is pressed out, and one part of excellent skimmed honey is mixed with three parts of this juice, and having been transferred into other vessels it is placed in the sun. It has the virtue of repelling and cooling: it benefits relaxed stomachs and stomach fluxes. It is not used until after a year has passed.

On Apian Wine. Chapter 24.

The wine called Apian is made from pears, as is made that of quinces, but the pears must not be too ripe. It is similarly composed of pods, medlars, and sorb-apples. All of these are astringent and binding: they are useful to the stomach and stop all fluxes of the intestines.

On Oenanthine Wine. Chapter 25.

Oenanthine wine is made from the wild vine. The dried flowers of the wild grape are taken at a weight of two pounds, and placed for thirty days to infuse in a cask of must, and then it is strained and stored. It benefits weak stomachs, nausea from food, stomach fluxes, and dysentery.

On Wine of Pomegranates. Chapter 26.

The wine called Rhoite is made from ripe pomegranates that are seedless, by pressing the juice from the berries and cooking it down until it is reduced by a third, then storing it in vessels. It is effective against fluxes of the intestines and against fevers that begin with a flux of the body: it benefits the stomach, restrains the body, and promotes urination.

On Rose Wine. Chapter 27.

Rose wine is made thus. Take one pound of well-pounded dried roses tied in a cloth and submerge them in eight measures of must, and after three months it is clarified and transferred,

FIFTH BOOK. 389

it is set aside. Drunk after meals, it strengthens digestion. It is usefully taken against stomach pains where there is no fever; it is good for looseness of the bowels and dysentery. What they call Rhodomele is made from the juice of roses and honey, and is truly a suitable remedy for soothing the roughness of the throat.

On Wine Made from Myrtle Berries. Chapter 28.

The wine drawn from myrtle berries is made in the following way. Take the black myrtle berries, very well ripened, crush them, press out the wine through the press, and set it aside. There are those who dry the berries in the sun, then grind them to a powder, take one bushel of this powder, and steep it in three heminae of water along with an equal amount of old, austere wine, then press it and put it away. It powerfully astringes, is beneficial to the stomach, helps stomach fluxes, and likewise those of the body; it helps ulcers of the internal organs and female fluxes; it blackens the hair.

On Myrtle Wine. Chapter 29.

Myrtle wine is made thus. Take the branches of the black myrtle with their leaves and berries, crush them, place a weight of ten heminae to boil in three conzi of must until it reduces by a third, or indeed by half; then strain it and set it aside. It is good for dandruff, ulcers of the head that fester, the growth of scabs, for the gums, the uvula, and ears that discharge matter; it also prevents sweating.

On Wine of Mastic and Terebinth. Chapter 30.

The Mastic wine is prepared in the same way as the Myrtle wine, and likewise the Terebinth wine; and for this purpose one should choose branches that are laden with berries. Both have the same virtues: they are astringent and good for the stomach; they help fluxes of the internal organs, of the bladder, and of the stomach, and likewise of the blood. By making a wash of them they heal all ulcers caused by fluxes. Sitting in a bath of them is good for uterine fluxes and those of the seat.

On Wine of Dates. Chapter 31.

Date wine is made thus. Take the most common dates, well ripened, and put them in a vat that has a hole in the bottom, which hole is stopped with a pitched cane, and the hole of the cane stopped with linen; add over the dates forty sestarij and three conzi of water; if you do not want it too sweet, add five conzi; leave it thus for ten days, and on the eleventh draw out the linen from the spout and let the thick, sweet wine flow out, and set it aside. It is pleasant to the taste but harms the head; it is useful as an astringent for fluxes, looseness of the bowels, and fluxes of the stomach, and for spitting of blood. Some then add more water over the dates and press the wine again, repeating this three, four, and five times, but they do not go beyond this number, because what is made after the fifth pressing turns to vinegar.

On Wine Made from Dried Figs. Chapter 32.

Fig wine is made in Cyprus as date wine is, except that over the figs they pour water in which fresh grape marc, just pressed, has been soaked. They take the black dried figs called chelidonian, or Phoenician, and especially the black ones, and macerate them as described, and after ten days the liquid is drawn off; a second and third pressing is made with the same water in which the grape marc has stood; then after allowing a certain interval of time, a fourth and fifth pressing is made, but this comes out vinegary and is used in place of vinegar. It is thin, produces flatulence, is bad for the stomach, causes loss of appetite; nevertheless it moves the bowels and provokes—

390 BOOK

A it provokes urine: it stimulates menstruation, produces an abundance of milk, generates bad blood, and causes leprosy, as does also that drink called zitho. There are some who put ten sextaries of salt into six amphorae. Others add one amphora of brine, so that it does not spoil so easily, and they believe this moves the body more effectively. Others first put in a layer of fennel and thyme, and then a layer of figs: and so they make layer upon layer, until the vessel is full. It is also made in the same way with the figs of the Sycamore, but it turns into strong vinegar, because they do not have sufficient power to preserve the sweetness of their liquid for very long.

On Resinated Wine. Chapter 33.

Resinated wine is commonly made among ordinary people everywhere. It is produced in abundance in Galatia, because there, to prevent the cold from ripening the grapes, the new wine easily turns to vinegar unless pine resin is added to it. To make it, the resin is pounded with the bark of the pine tree, and half a sextary of resin is added per amphora of wine. Some, after it has boiled, strain it, thus separating the resin from the wine; others leave it in. These wines become sweeter as they age. They all cause headache and dizziness, but they aid the stomach in digestion; they stimulate urine; they help with catarrh and cough, and likewise with stomach fluxes, with dropsy, with dysentery, and with women's fluxes; they are applied to deep ulcers. Among these, those that are darker are more astringent than the white ones.

On Pine Wine. Chapter 34.

Pine wine is made by taking the pine cones whole with their bark, pounding them, and macerating them in must. It has the same effects as resinated wine. Furthermore, if one cooks the aforesaid pine cones in must, it makes a drink suitable for those who are consumptive.

C On Wine made from Cedar and from certain other trees. Chapter 35.

Wines are similarly made from Cedar, Juniper, Cypress, Laurel, Pine, and Fir. Branches of these trees are taken, freshly cut at the time they bear fruit, and while still fresh they are placed to sweat in the sun, or in a bath, or over a fire, and one pound of their liquid is added to each conzo of wine; after two months it is transferred to other vessels, and before being transferred it is left for some time in the sun. One should note that vessels containing wines mixed with other things must always be filled to the top, because if they are left partly empty, the wines tend to turn sour. It should also be known that all medicinal wines are not at all suitable for healthy people. All of these warm the body, stimulate urination, and cause constipation. Laurel wine, however, warms the body most powerfully. A wine is also made with the fruit of the greater Cedar, by adding half a pound of its pounded berries per conzo of must; it should then be kept in the sun for forty days, and afterward strained and transferred to other vessels. Similarly, a wine is made from the berries of the Juniper, as one makes Cedar wine, and it has the same virtues. Cedria, which is the proper liquor that distills from the Cedar,
D that wine called Cedrite, is made in this way. The Cedria is first washed with fresh water, and then each amphora is filled with a glass, and afterward filled with must. This has the virtue of warming and of thinning: it is useful for chronic cough where there is no fever, for pains of the chest and sides, for pains of the bowels, for ulcers of the internal organs, for spitting of pus, for suffocations of the womb, and for dropsy. It is beneficial for the extremities of the body, and for the chills that come before fevers; it helps with the bites of venomous animals; it kills serpents, and it heals pains of the ears when dripped into them.

On Pitched Wine. Chapter 36.

Pitched wine is made from must and liquid pitch. But one must first wash the pitch with brine or seawater until it turns white, and until the water

FIFTH BOOK. 391

The brine should run out clear, and after this wash it again with fresh water; then take one ounce of this, or two, in eight conzi of must, and after it has boiled well and settled, transfer it to other vessels. This warms, aids digestion, cleanses, and purges; it benefits pains of the chest, body, liver, spleen, and womb, provided no fever is present. It is good for chronic catarrhs, deep ulcers, coughs, tightness of the chest, weak digestion, varicose veins, and dislocations of the joints, especially when applied with unwashed wool.

On Wine of Wormwood. Chapter 37.

Wine of Wormwood is made in various ways. Some take forty-eight Italian amphora-sextarii, add one pound of Pontic Wormwood, and cook it until it is reduced by a third; then they add six more sextarii of vinegar and half a pound of Wormwood, mix everything together carefully, and put it into a vessel; once it has settled well, they strain and transfer it to other vessels. Others take a pound of pounded Wormwood wrapped in a cloth and steep it in a cask of must for two continuous months. Others take three or four ounces of Wormwood, of Spikenard of Syria, of cinnamon, of cassia, of squinant, of aromatic calamus, of palm bark, two ounces each, pound everything together, put it all into a measure of must, seal the vessel tightly, and leave it thus for two or three months, then strain it, transfer it to other vessels, and keep it for use. Others steep in a cask of must fourteen drams of Celtic spikenard and forty of wormwood, all tied in a cloth, and after forty days strain and transfer it. Others put in six sextarii of must one pound of wormwood and two ounces of dry pine resin, and after ten days strain and store the wine. This wine is beneficial to the stomach, provokes urine, accelerates digestion; it benefits those with liver ailments, overflow of bile, and the kidneys; it prevents nausea; it helps weak stomachs, old flatulence that puffs up the precordia, worms in the body, and promotes retained menstruation. Drunk in large quantities and vomited back up, it benefits anyone who has drunk the poison they call ixia.

On Wine of Hyssop. Chapter 38.

Among all others, the best is that made from Hyssop of Cilicia. It is made in the same way as the wine of wormwood: one takes a pound of pounded hyssop leaves and places them in an amphora of must, tied in a linen cloth together with some small stones so that the bundle of herb, made heavy, sinks to the bottom; the wine is then strained after forty days and transferred to other vessels. It is effective against ailments of the chest, the flanks, and the lungs, against chronic cough and tightness of the chest; it provokes urine; it benefits pains of the body, chills, and the shivering that comes at the onset of periodic fevers; and it promotes menstruation.

On Wines Made from Various Plants. Chapter 39.

The wine of Germander is made in much the same way as that of hyssop. It warms, resolves, and benefits those suffering from spasms, overflow of bile, flatulence of the womb, and stomachs that are slow to digest, and those in the early stages of dropsy. It improves with age. That of Stechas is made in the same manner, but putting one pound of stechas into six conzi of must. It dissolves thick humors, the viscosities of the flanks, nerve pains, and ailments caused by cold; it is usefully given in epilepsy, together with pyrethrum and sagapenum. A vinegar of stechas is also made for all these ailments, by steeping the herb in it as described, and it has the same virtues as the wine. To make that of Betony, the herb is taken when it is full of ripe seed, with its branches, to the weight of one pound, steeped in two conzi of wine, and racked off after seven months. It is as effective as the plant itself against many ailments of the internal organs. And speaking universally, it should be known that all medicated wines acquire the virtues of the things put into them; and therefore it will not be difficult for those who know the nature of the things steeped in them to recognize the virtues of the wines, which however should only be used when no fever is present.

392 BOOK

A One also makes a vinegar of Betony that is truly useful for all the aforesaid purposes. That of Tragorigano is made by steeping four drams of tragorigano wrapped in thin cloth in four sextaries of must, then decanting it after three months. It benefits bodily pains, spasms, hernias, side pains, tightness of breath, and stomachs that digest food poorly. That of Turnip is made by taking two drams of pounded turnip in four sextaries of must, and the rest is done as described above. It benefits weak stomachs and those fatigued by combat or long riding. That of Dittany is made by steeping four drams of it in eight sextaries of must. It is good for nausea and distaste of the stomach, promotes menstruation, and retained purgations after childbirth. That of Horehound is made by taking eight sextaries of its leaves, well ripened and ground, and steeping them in a metretes of must, then proceeding as described for the others. This is good for chest complaints and all ailments for which horehound is beneficial. To make that of Thyme, one takes a hundred ounces of pounded and sieved thyme, ties it in a cloth, and steeps it in an

B amphora of must. It is good for weakness of the digestive faculty, nausea, dysentery, nerve pains and pains of the chest, for the cold of winter, and for the bite of venomous animals, after which the body grows cold and the humor of the bite putrefies. Similarly one makes that of Savory, which resembles thyme in its virtues. That of Heraclean oregano, called Origanite, is made in the same way and has the same virtues. Wines of calamint, pennyroyal, and southernwood are also made in the same manner as that of thyme. They benefit weak stomachs, nausea, and overflow of bile, since they promote urination. Similarly one makes a wine of Fleabane, more effective against poisons and venomous animals than all the others.

On Aromatic Wine. Chapter 40.

C Aromatic wine is made as follows. Take palm, aspalathus, fragrant calamus, and Celtic spikenard, four sextaries of each; once you have reduced them to powder, knead them with raisin wine and form them into large lozenges; put these into twelve sextaries of dry must, seal the vessel well, and leave it to rest for forty days; once you have racked it off the sediment, store it away. It is also made in another way, as follows. Take one ounce of fragrant calamus, seven drams of valerian root, two drams of costus, six drams of Syrian nard, one ounce of cassia, four drams of saffron, five drams of amomum, four drams of asarum; pound all of these together, tie them in a cloth, and submerge everything in a cask of must; once the must has finished fermenting, decant it. It is good for pains of the chest, side, and lungs, for difficulty of urination, for the chills that come at the onset of fevers, for retention of menses, and for those who ride through cold places; it thins thick phlegm, gives good color, promotes sleep, relieves pains, and benefits ailments of the kidneys and bladder.

D On Wines Made from Various Aromatics. Chapter 41.

A wine is made for coughs, catarrhs, indigestion, flatulence, and stomach moisture. For this one takes two drams of myrrh, one of white pepper, six of iris, and three of anise; all of these are pounded together, placed in a cloth, and steeped in six sextaries of wine; the wine is then strained after three months and stored in another vessel. It is given after one has walked about a little, neat, in the measure of one cyathus. One makes that called Nettarite from the root of elecampane, taking five drams of the dried root, tying it in cloth, steeping it in six congi of must, and decanting it after three months. It is good for complaints of the stomach and chest and promotes urination. One also makes a wine of Syrian nard, and likewise of Celtic nard and of Malabathrum, in this way: take six ounces of each, steep them in two congi of must, strain after two months, and give one cyathus to drink mixed with three of water. This is valuable for ailments of the kidneys, complaints of the liver, overflow of bile, and difficulty of urination; it benefits

On Wines Made from Various Kinds of Herbs. Chapter 42.

The wine of Daucus is made as follows: take six drams of daucus roots well pounded, put them in an amphora of must, and let them infuse. It helps pains of the chest, the precordia, and the womb: it promotes menstruation, relieves belching, and provokes urination; it also helps with coughs, hernias, and spasms. To make Salviato wine, take one ounce of sage and steep it in an amphora of must. It is good against ailments of the kidneys, the bladder, and the sides; for spitting of blood, coughs, hernias, spasms, and retained menstruation. It helps with ruptures, spasms, bruises, and tightness of the chest; it reduces the spleen; it is beneficial for pains of the bowels and for sciatica; it strengthens digestion; it promotes menstruation and likewise aids delivery; and it is good for those with dropsy and for serpent bites. Wines of acorus and of sweet root are made in the same way, but eight ounces of each must be put in six congii of must, left to steep for three months, and then transferred to other vessels. They help with pains of the chest and sides, and promote urination. Celery wine is made by taking nine ounces of its ripe and fresh seed, pounded and sifted, wrapping it in a cloth, and placing it in an amphora of must. A wine of flower of salt is much more powerful as a purgative than wine mixed with sea water. It is harmful to the throat, bladder, kidneys, and stomach, and thus is of no benefit either in health or in illness. One is made to cause women to miscarry, in this way: hellebore, scammony, or wild cucumber is planted near the vines, so that the vines draw all of their virtue into themselves. The wine from these kills the fetus; when diluted with water it is given after fasting, before vomiting, in a measure of eight cyathi. To make the thimelea wine, take thirty drams of its branches along with the leaves and fruit, steep them in three congii of must, and cook at a slow fire until reduced by a third, then strain and set aside. The chamelea wine is made by gathering it in flower, together with its leaves, pounding them, then squeezing them out to a weight of ten drams, and placing them in one congio of must for two months, then transferring the wine to other vessels. It is beneficial for dropsies, liver ailments, wasting diseases, and for women who do not purge after childbirth. The chamepitys wine is made in the same manner and has the same virtues, and provokes urination. On all Metallic Stones, and first on Cadmia. Chapter 43.

The best Cadmia among all varieties is truly that from Cyprus, properly called Botrite, compact, moderately heavy, and inclining toward lightness, with a grape-cluster appearance, the color of spodium, and when broken is ash-colored and rusty. The second place in quality belongs to that which on the outside is sky-blue in color and whiter within, similar to onyx stone, and likewise those extracted from old metal mines. There is another Cadmia called Placodes, meaning crusty, which has certain spots on its surface like lines, and is therefore called Zonite. There is yet another kind called Ostracite, thin and for the most part black: but that which has the form of potsherds has collected much earth within itself. The white kind is considered inferior. Botrite and Onichite are useful in medicines for the eyes; and all the others for use in plasters and healing powders. That which comes from Cyprus is useful for all these purposes: but those brought from Macedonia, Thracia, and Spain are truly inferior. Cadmia has the virtue of constricting, of filling deep ulcers with flesh, of cleansing pus, of drying, of closing wounds, of removing superfluous flesh, of cicatrizing and healing those ulcers that consolidate with difficulty. Cadmia is generated from burning copper in furnaces, as its sparks cling and attach themselves to the walls of the furnace and likewise to its chambers. * Great iron rods, which the furnace workers call acestides, are fitted and fixed well into the tops of the chambers, so that the sparks rising from the copper may attach themselves to them and be retained there. These, then, clinging one upon another over time, finally form a mass:

A              On Pompholyx and Spodium,               Chapter 44.

Pompholyx differs from Spodium only in kind: for Spodium is darker, and most often heavier, full of chaff, hairs, and earth, and is almost a kind of superfluity that is swept from the vault of the furnaces where the copper ore is smelted; while Pompholyx is fatty, white, and so light that it can easily float away in the air. Of this there are two kinds, one of which tends toward the color of air, being somewhat fatty, and the other is very white and very light. White Pompholyx is made whenever craftsmen who work copper, wishing to make it excellent, scatter powdered cadmia copiously over the smelted ore: for all the very fine sparks that fly upward condense into pompholyx. Pompholyx is also made, beyond this, not only from the copper ore and the craft of the artisans, but also from cadmia that is evaporated by force of bellows. The way to make it is as follows. A house is built with two floors, with the furnace inside, the vault of which has a moderate opening at the top, that is, toward the floor above; the wall of the house where the furnace stands is pierced enough so that the pipe of the bellows can pass through. Beyond this, there should be a small door for the craftsman to enter and exit, and attached to this wall a small room where the bellows and the person who works them are kept. Then coals are lit in the furnace, and when they are lit, the craftsman scatters powdered cadmia finely over them, staying in the lower part, while his assistant does the same office by throwing it down into the fire from certain openings above in the vault, and so the craftsman goes on feeding the fire until all the cadmia they put in is consumed. This causes the light and fine part to rise up in smoke and fly to the upper floor, attaching itself to it, to the vault of the furnace, to the furnaces, and to the walls. This material, when it first begins to take body, resembles the bubbles that form on water, but as the material grows much more, it becomes like flakes of wool; the heavier parts falling back down return, some onto the furnace and some onto the floor of the house, and this is much inferior to the fine kind, because being earthy and when collected it brings with it much filth. There are some who believe that Spodium aforementioned can only be made in this way, of which the most praised is that which is brought from Cyprus, which when placed in vinegar breathes an odor of copper, is of a color almost like pitch, and of an odor of mud, and when it is not adulterated and placed on burning coals, it boils and melts, turning the color of air. And therefore one must be warned about all the signs described above, because some counterfeit it with hide glue, with sheep's or sea lung, or with burnt wild early figs and other similar things; but the fraud is easily detected, because on making the test none of the aforesaid signs are found. Pompholyx is commonly washed in this way. Tie it dry, or sprinkled with water, in a clean cloth of somewhat loose weave, and place it in a basin containing rainwater, and stir the cloth back and forth through the water. This causes the finest and best part to come out, while the coarser sediment remains in the cloth; then allow it to settle, and strain both the water and the pompholyx together through a strainer; pour more water over it again, mix it, and stir it all together again, and similarly strain it again, doing this as many times, refilling and straining, until no more sandy residue is found in it. Then finally strain the water alone, and dry the pompholyx, and so preserve it. Some others, taking it dry, dissolve it with their hands in water until it is as fluid as honey, and then placing a cloth over the mouth of the vessel where they wish to strain it, tied somewhat loosely, they strain it, and to help it pass more easily, they add water copiously over the cloth while stirring the sediment, and then they collect all the foamy strained part floating on top of the vessel with a ladle, and put it in a new earthen vessel; but that which settles they strain gently into another vessel, leaving however the sandy part at the bottom; again they let the sandy parts settle, and strain into another vessel, and this they do as many times until only pure ash without any trace of sand remains. Others soak it whole little by little in water, and reckoning that the small stones and sand, by their heaviness, will sink to the bottom, and that the straw and hairs, by their lightness, will remain on top, they separate only the middle part, and put it in a mortar, and then wash it as cadmia.
