Brasavola ought to have considered this much more carefully, when, being asked by his Apothecary what should be put in prescriptions in place of Spodium, he replied — if so ordered by some physician — that one should use Pompholyx, that is Tutia, as Galen did. In this, two very manifest errors are recognized: first, because without distinguishing whether one should do otherwise in medicines given by mouth, in which many physicians use Spodium, he concludes that one should use mineral Pompholyx both by mouth and externally. How appropriate this is, let those judge sincerely who better understand the nature of minerals. Second, by saying that Spodium's equivalent is Pompholyx, that is Tutia, he shows himself in the same error we mentioned above regarding Manardo: for if he had known that the common Tutia of the apothecaries was not Pompholyx, he would have corrected the error of his Apothecary, as is always his custom in every other matter. And from this arises not only the error of believing that true Pompholyx, made in the furnaces where copper is smelted, can be given by mouth, but it also shows how mistaken it is to believe that the common Tutia of the apothecaries is the Pompholyx of Galen, who, though he said that Pompholyx could conveniently replace Spodium, meant only in external medicines: for in his time it was not customary to put Antispodium in medicines given by mouth, as was later discovered by the Arabs. Galen wrote about Pompholyx and likewise about Spodium in the ninth book of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Pompholyx is found in the copper furnaces like cadmia, and also while cadmia is being burned in furnaces, as is done in Cyprus, where finding myself in the presence of the Master of the copper furnaces, who did not have the ore prepared, he ordered that some cadmia be prepared to make Pompholyx; having it placed in the furnace in small pieces, of which there was no small quantity on the ground near the bellows. The chamber of the furnace was vaulted and not perforated anywhere; being entirely closed, it received all the sparks rising from the cadmia, from which the Pompholyx was then collected. But that part which fell down to the floor is what they call Spodium, which is gathered abundantly where the copper ore is smelted. The substance called Antispodium seems to have virtues similar to Spodium. But I have never used Spodium, because I have always had a large supply of Pompholyx: and therefore it is not necessary for anyone to use Spodium when they have Pompholyx at hand, nor to use Antispodium. Pompholyx, when washed, is therefore a medicine far more effective than all others that dry without any bite: and is therefore suitable for cancerous ulcers and all malignant ones. For this reason it is put into collyria prepared for fluxes of the eyes, and in those that cure blisters and pustules that arise there. And beyond this it is a most perfect medicine for ulcers of the genital members and of the seat, because it dries without any harshness.

On Burnt Copper. Chapter 46.

The best burnt copper is that which is red, and when ground resembles cinnabar: for the black is more burnt than is needed. It is made from nails of broken ships, placed and arranged in a raw earthen vessel, sprinkling over them layer upon layer an equal weight of sulfur and salt: the vessel is then covered well and sealed with lute made of clay in a furnace, and left there until the vessel is baked through. Some use alum instead of sulfur and salt. Others, without sulfur and without salt, burn the vessel for many days. Others use sulfur alone: but this turns it black on account of the soot. Others, anointing the nails with scissile alum, vinegar and sulfur, then burn them in a raw earthen vessel. Others burn them in a copper vessel, first bathing the nails in vinegar, repeating this two or three times, and then setting them aside. The foremost place among all is held by that which is burnt at Memphis in Egypt, and the second is the Cyprian. It constricts, dries, staunches, refines, draws, and tempers, and cicatrizes ulcers: it benefits defects of the eyes: it consumes superfluities of the flesh. It consolidates corrosive ulcers, and drunk with honey-water causes vomiting, or licked with honey, or applied as a plaster externally. It is washed like cadmia, changing the water four times a day, until no shine appears in it. The foam of the washed copper used in the same manner has the same virtues, though considerably less effective.
It is perfectly clear what burnt copper is: although that which is found in the apothecaries' shops may be judged of little value, for being black, having been subjected to too much fire, and not red as Dioscorides said the finest should be. But this can easily be remedied whenever one takes the trouble to make it according to the teaching of Dioscorides, and whoever cannot obtain copper nails — which, being far more durable than iron ones, are used in the construction of ships — may take in their place some other old copper. Galen wrote about burnt copper at the end of the ninth book of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Burnt copper has something sharp and astringent. But when it is washed, it is truly a most excellent medicine for cicatrizing ulcers, though it may do this even before it is washed, and especially in hard flesh; but in soft flesh the washed form is much better.

FIFTH. 399
On the Flower of Copper. Chapter 47. A

The Flower of copper, which some of the ancients called filings of old nails, is truly excellent when it easily crumbles, turning red upon being ground, and has a form like millet grains, heavy, somewhat shining, astringent, and not mixed with copper filings, with which it is often adulterated. This is easily recognized when, upon biting it with the teeth, the filings spread out. It is made in furnaces when the molten copper is poured through channels suited to this purpose into its receptacle: for the workers prepared in this craft, wishing to purge it of dross and other impurities, immediately throw clear water over it to quench the heat, so that through the sudden condensation the aforementioned flower immediately comes forth. It is astringent and removes superfluities of the flesh; it clears the dimness of the eyes, but bites powerfully. Given by mouth at the weight of four oboli it purges gross humors; it resolves and corrodes the fleshy growths of the nose and of the seat; applied with wine it heals skin eruptions. The white variety, ground and blown with a cane into the B ears, is good against old deafness. The powder mixed with honey and applied repels the fluxes of the uvula and of the throat.

The true Flower of copper I have myself collected many times in the furnaces where it is smelted in the Trentino region, in this manner. As soon as the copper had been poured from the furnace into its receptacle, which had been prepared for it in the ground beforehand, as many as possible before it set on its own, I would throw over it a large bucket of clear and very fresh water. Whereupon there immediately rose from the copper with the greatest force a great smoke, and I immediately took a large iron shovel and held it firmly above the molten copper in the fury of that great vapor; and when it had ceased, I found the entire shovel covered with very fine red granules, of the color of copper, with some luster. And this came about because the vapor, carrying upward with it the finest part of the metal, then congealed owing to the coldness of the air into very fine granules, which upon falling back down settled on the iron shovel. And this I always keep by me, since in the apothecary shops throughout all Italy they use in its place only verdigris, which Dioscorides called rust, and not flower of copper. Galen wrote briefly about it at the end of the ninth book on the faculties of simples, saying thus: The Flower of copper is truly finer in its essence than burnt copper or the scale of copper, and therefore deservedly the collyriums made from it powerfully cleanse the roughness of the eyelashes.

On the Scale of Copper. Chapter 48. C

Of the Scale of copper beaten from the nails of the furnaces of Cyprus, that which is the best is the coarse kind, called Helite, that is, nail-scale. But that which is beaten from base and common copper, or from white copper, is truly harmful, being both thin and of little value. The coarse and red kind is most prized, especially that which, when moistened with vinegar, turns rusty. It has the virtue of binding, thinning, staunching, and corroding; it checks ulcers that eat the flesh; it consolidates ulcers. Drunk with honeyed water it purges the water of the body, for which reason some give it kneaded with flour and made into pills. It is used in medicines compounded for defects of the eyes; it removes the roughness of the eyelids and dries up the fluxes that flow into them. It is washed in the following manner. D
One puts half a pound of Scale, well dried and purified, into a stone mortar, and then pouring clear water over it, stirs everything together by hand until all the scale sinks to the bottom; then one draws off what sinks to the bottom and throws away the first water, and returns to washing with a measure of rainwater, and thus rubs the Scale in the mortar with an open hand, almost as if one wished to purge it; and when one feels it beginning to soften, one throws over it little by little up to six measures of water, and thus grinds it thoroughly, and moves it to one side of the mortar, where likewise it breaks apart; and having done this, one strains every humor squeezed out into a vessel of red copper. For this is like the flower of the Scale itself, most potent in its virtues and very efficacious for medicines of the eyes; while on the contrary the remainder is weak and inefficacious. One washes it until no stickiness is any longer felt in it, and then covers what has been strained with a cloth, and lets it rest thus for two days; then one decants the water gently, and dries what remains at the bottom, and stores it in a box. There are some who wash it like cadmia and store it accordingly.

On the Scale of Stomoma. Chapter 49.

The virtue of the Scale of Stomoma is the same as that of copper. Almost in the same manner, and it is stored similarly: but for loosening the body it is much less effective.

The Scale of Copper, which falls off when it is beaten, is ground up and a very well-known medicine: and furthermore, Dioscorides makes the method of washing it so clear that there is no need to write more by way of explanation. Galen wrote about the Scale of Copper in the ninth book on the faculties of simples, saying thus: The Scale of Copper is found to be a truly very useful medicine, as are those of iron and of Stomoma. All dry out powerfully; but they differ among themselves in nature, since one is more desiccative than another, and one is of coarser essence, another more subtle, and more or less astringent. That of copper, called Helite, is truly the most powerful for drying, being of a substance more subtle than all the others, having taken into itself something of verdigris. That of iron has a more powerfully astringent virtue, and even more so does that of Stomoma: and therefore these are more useful and more effective for stubborn and difficult-to-treat ulcers than that of copper. This of copper consumes and dissolves the flesh, and much more so does that of this species called Helite.
B They are all quite caustic. This makes it clear that the consistency of their essence is not too subtle but rather coarse. All this about the Scales Galen said. From this doctrine one can easily recognize that the Scale of Stomoma is not the Scale of copper, as the majority of modern writers believe to be true, and most especially Brasavola and Marcello Virgilio Fiorentino: because Galen's saying that the one called Helite of copper is truly the most powerful for drying, that iron has a more powerfully astringent virtue, and even more so does that of Stomoma, argues that the Scale of Stomoma is not a Scale of copper: because if it were of that more subtle part of copper, as Brasavola together with some moderns believes, it would be little or not at all different from the coarser one, proceeding as they do from the same metal, nor could Galen's statement stand, that the Scale of copper is more desiccative than all the others, and that of iron is more astringent than that of copper; but that much more astringent than that of iron is the Scale of Stomoma: for if that of iron is much more astringent than that of copper, it cannot in any way hold that, if the Scale of Stomoma were also a Scale of copper, it could nevertheless be more astringent than that of iron. Furthermore, Galen's statement at the beginning of the chapter, that one finds Scale of copper, of iron, and of Stomoma, demonstrates clearly that Stomoma is another material separate from copper: because if Galen had understood that Stomoma was a species of copper, he would have said: one finds Scale of copper, of Stomoma, and of iron, and not separated the species from their own species. But because he well knew that Stomoma was an iron-like material, he coupled it with iron and not with copper. This clearly demonstrates that all those who think that the Scale of Stomoma is a Scale of copper are in manifest error. Dioscorides likewise demonstrates this same thing: because if he had understood that the Scale of Stomoma was copper, he would not have made a separate chapter for it; but would have treated it in the preceding chapter, where he discussed the various species of the Scale of copper, and furthermore he would not have compared its virtues to those of the scale of copper, if it were itself the same thing as the Scale of copper. And let this suffice to prove that the Scale of Stomoma is quite a different thing from that of copper. But what Dioscorides, Galen, and the other ancient Greeks meant by the Scale of Stomoma cannot truly be proved except by conjecture: and therefore I say, that since the word stomoma signified the edge of swords and of all cutting ironwork, I believe one could easily say that the Scale of Stomoma was that very fine scale which the grindstone removes from steel tools when polishing them and giving them their edge, which is then found in the channel of the water running below: and therefore Galen rightly said that in this there was a more astringent virtue than in simple iron, because it is a scale of steel, which (as its hardness demonstrates) is more earthy and more astringent than iron, and therefore used in making the water for fluxes of the body. One might also reasonably say that since this verb stomoma means to quench, harden, and temper iron in water, the Scale of Stomoma might be that which scales off when tempering and quenching steel tools in water: and therefore I think it is nothing but a good opinion to believe that the Scale of Stomoma is a scale of steel, either made on the grindstone, or made in the quenching in water, or when it is struck with a hot hammer on the anvil.

On Scraped Verdigris. Chapter 50.

Scraped verdigris is made in this way. Place very strong vinegar in a barrel or other similar vessel, and cover it, placing over it an inverted concave copper vessel, or if not concave a flat one, and seal it around so that no air escapes from any side, and leave it thus for ten continuous days, and then uncover it and scrape off the verdigris that has formed on this covering. It is also made in another way as follows. Take small sheets of copper and suspend them in a vessel of vinegar, but so that they do not touch it, and after ten days scrape them. They are also placed in grape pomace that is not fresh but has begun to turn acidic — one or more sheets of copper — and then taken out and scraped. It is also made from

has been incorporated will turn entirely red: for by its nature writing ink turns red when burned.

On the Verdigris Called Scolecia. Chapter II.

That which they call Scolecia is of two kinds, one mineral and the other artificial,
made in this way. Into a mortar made of Cypriot copper one puts half a hemina
of strong white vinegar, and stirs it around with a pestle also of copper, until the
vinegar thickens like a liniment; at that point one adds a dram of round alum, with
an equal amount of transparent mineral salt, or very white sea salt, firm and solid, or an
equal weight of nitre, and all is ground together in the sun during the hottest days, when
the dog-star heats most powerfully, until it begins to look the color of verdigris and has
become thick and fat; then it is formed into small worm-like rolls similar to rhodiotti and
stored away. It becomes much more effective and acquires a much better color if two parts
of old urine are put into the mortar with one part of vinegar, and the rest done as described
above. There are some who take rasile verdigris, which does not come out well in the making,
and kneading it with gum sell it formed into little cakes: but this is condemned as a poor
product. There is also a verdigris made by goldsmiths for soldering gold, with the urine of
a young boy, worked likewise in a mortar of Cypriot copper with its pestle. All the
above-mentioned verdigris preparations correspond in their virtues to burnt copper, though
they are more potent in their operations. It should be known that the best verdigris to be
found is the mineral kind called Scolecia, and after that the rasile, and after the rasile that
which is made by art, even though this last is the most mordant and most strongly
constrictive. That of the goldsmiths corresponds to the rasile. All are constrictive,
attenuating, and warming: they remove scars from the eyes, cause tears, stop ulcers that eat
away the flesh, and prevent inflammation in ulcers; mixed with oil and wax they cicatrize
ulcers; boiled with honey and applied they remove calluses and cleanse foul ulcers. Mixed D
with ammoniac and applied as a collyrium they consume the callosities of fistulas; they are
useful for swellings of the gums; anointed with honey they powerfully thin the eyelids, but
afterward one must immediately foment them with a sponge soaked in warm water. Mixed
with resin of turpentine together with copper and nitre they expel and dry up the scab.
They are all burned by grinding them and placing them in an earthen pan over very hot
coals, stirring constantly, until they change to the color of ash; and when cold they are
stored for use. There are some who burn them in an unglazed earthen pot, as described:
but they do not always turn the same uniform color.

L. Verdigris, being of green color, is called by the Apothecaries and modern Physicians Verde rame (copper green),
of which there is abundance in every apothecary shop: though little of the genuine kind is to be found that is not
adulterated. Of this therefore

A It is found (according to Dioscorides) made in various ways, namely by nature in the hollow places of mines, and in various ways by art. The Mineral sort is no longer brought from Cyprus to Italy in our times; and since the best is lacking, we use the mediocre kind, which is made with vinegar and with gall-nuts: because the Scolecia is likewise no longer in use in our times. Some believe that Verdigris is the flower of copper, used daily in pharmacies in its place; but these people are truly in great error, for the reasons set forth at length above in the proper chapter on the Flower of Copper. Galen wrote about Verdigris in the ninth book of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Verdigris is truly sharp to the taste: it digests, draws, and liquefies not only tender flesh but also hard flesh. Besides this, it was said above that there are some who call these similar medicines cicatrizants, finding that when applied very finely with only the tip of a stylus in small quantity upon ulcers, by the next day they had contracted; yet such people should know that if a greater quantity were applied, they would find the ulcer not diminished but entirely corroded and consumed: and therefore they truly corrode and liquefy the flesh, while cicatrizing medicines draw in, compress, constrict, and harden like a callus; but Verdigris bites the taste perceptibly, let alone wounds and ulcers. It is indeed true that when a small amount is mixed with a great quantity of cerate, this mixture will truly cleanse without biting. Much has been said above about the nature of such medicines, and how many people err in such
B compositions, attributing to certain medicines virtues of flesh-regeneration and cicatrization, which those medicines do not possess at all. And so I say, that if these simple medicines cannot do it, the compounds made from them will do even less.

On the Rust of Iron. Chapter 52.

THE rust of iron is astringent. Applied, it stops the flows of women, and drunk does not allow them to become pregnant: made into a liniment with vinegar it heals erysipelas and blisters: it is most useful for roughness of the eyelids, for whitlows, and for superfluous flesh growing near the nails: it benefits swellings of the seat, firms the gums, eases gout, and causes hair to regrow. Wine, or likewise water, in which heated iron has been quenched, drunk benefits stomach fluxes, dysentery, those with spleen defects, choleric afflictions, and weak stomachs.

On the Slag of Iron. Chapter 53.

C THE slag of iron, which some call Scoria, has the same virtues as rust, but is not so powerful. Drunk with honeyed vinegar it benefits those who have taken aconite.

The rust of iron, and likewise the slag, which is also called Loppa, called Scoria of iron, are very well-known things. And therefore they need no further explanation. But so that no one be misled, the Scoria of iron,
L and likewise of copper, is not, as some believed, the same as the Scale, which we commonly call Scaglia: because this falls from iron while it is being hammered hot on the anvil, and can be gathered and turned back into iron. But the Scoria is that spongy superfluity that comes out of the furnace from the iron like a foam, which we call Spiuma, and others call Loppa, and this can no longer be returned to metal: because it is entirely superfluous and terrestrial matter. Galen wrote about it in the ninth book of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: All slags are a desiccating medicine; but more than all others, the one made from iron slag. I grind it most finely in the strongest vinegar, and then cook it, and thus use it as a most efficacious medicine for drying out ears that have long discharged matter, so that all those who see me prepare it in this way are amazed, not believing before the experience that ears could tolerate such a medicine. In addition to this, that of silver, which they call Helisima, is also put
D into certain desiccating plasters.

On the Wash of Lead, or Washed Lead. Chapter 54.

LEAD is washed in this manner. Put water in a lead mortar, and with a pestle of the same lead, stir it around so that the water becomes black, and thickens like mud, and becomes turbid, and then strain it through a linen cloth, adding more water from above so that all the dissolved matter can pass through; and you shall do this as many times as needed until you have enough: and when it has settled, drain off the first water, and add fresh water, and wash it as one does with cadmia, until no blackness remains in the water, and then make it into lozenges and store it. There are some who take lead filings and grind them in a stone mortar with a stone pestle, or who rub them by hand mixing water within—
the water

FIFTH BOOK. 403

the water little by little, until it turns black; and after the residue has settled to the bottom, they strain off the water and form it into lozenges: for when ground very finely it becomes similar to white lead. Some others add a little black lead powder to the lead filings, claiming that lead thus washed is much more efficacious. In its virtues it is refrigerant, astringent, filling, and emollient: it fills the hollows of ulcers, stops flows from the eyes, reduces proud flesh in ulcers, and stanches blood. Mixed with rose oil it is useful for ulcers, abscesses, and hemorrhoids of the seat, as well as for those ulcers that are difficult to consolidate. It has universally all the virtues of spodium, except that it does not produce scabs. Rubbed on in its pure form, it helps wounds from scorpion and sea-dragon stings.

On Burnt Lead. Chapter 55.

Lead is burnt in this way. Take lead rolled into thin sheets, and lay them in a new earthen vessel, and sprinkle powdered sulfur over them, continuing to add a layer of sheets and a layer of sulfur until the vessel is full. Then put it on the fire, and when the lead is well heated, stir it with an iron rod until the whole is converted to ash and no part remains unburnt; then remove it, stopping your nose very tightly, because the vapor is very harmful. It can also be made by putting lead filings together with sulfur in the vessel and burning them. There are others who put the lead sheets in an unfired earthen vessel, as described, and lute the lid over it, leaving a small air hole, and thus burn it in a furnace or fire. Some use white lead in place of sulfur, or barley. Others take only simple brands and burn them over a very hot fire, stirring continuously with a small iron rod until it becomes ash; but this last method is the most difficult, and if the burning is prolonged, it turns to a color like silver foam. Nevertheless, I prefer the first method of burning. Burnt lead is washed like cadmia and stored. It has the same virtues as washed lead, but in truth much more powerful.

On the Dross of Lead. Chapter 56.

The dross of lead, which they call Scoria, is truly the best kind: that which is dense, hard to break, resembling white lead, containing no part of lead, approaching red in color, and in its sheen resembling glass. It has the same virtues as burnt lead, but is in truth more astringent. It is washed in a mortar by pouring water over it and straining it off once it turns red, and this is done as many times as it takes to consume all the dross; and once the water has deposited its sediment, it is lightly strained off and formed into lozenges.

On Molybdoite, that is, Lead Stone. Chapter 57.

This stone is called Lead Stone because it resembles lead. It has the same virtue as the dross of lead, and is washed in the same manner.

The methods of making washed lead and burnt lead as described by Dioscorides are so clear and so plainly stated that no further commentary is needed for their explanation. But it is worth knowing that what Dioscorides calls Scoria, and we call Dross, and others call Slag, is in no way the black lead powder that always remains at the bottom of the vessel when lead is melted — for that is nothing other than lead beginning to calcine, and can easily be reduced back to pure lead, as is also done with litharge — but rather the foam that spits up on top when lead is melted in great mass from its ore in the furnace. And this is what is dense, hard, reddish in color, and shiny like glass, of which one can see, both in the Trentino region and in other parts of Germany, no small mountains thrown away outside the smelting houses by the craftsmen, as they also do with that from silver and copper, of which I have had in my hands on several occasions some pieces that appeared like the most beautiful enamel. Therefore it is truly necessary for whoever wishes to know clearly about such things not to look for them in apothecary shops, but in the places of mines and their smelting houses, where they originate and are also produced by art. But what stone today we would call that which Dioscorides names Molybdoite, that is Lead Stone, I cannot find anyone able to show me, unless it might be some sort of Marcasite,

406 BOOK

A The very large mountains of silver slag, which the smelters call Loppa, are to be seen at Perzene and at Laugio on the Trentino, where the ore is always smelted in various furnaces, as we mentioned above when speaking of lead. This closely resembles an artificial enamel made of glass, and is found in various colors. This occurs depending on how much of the other various metals are present alongside the silver in the ore being smelted; but for the most part it is black with some beautiful veins of azure and green, though some is found entirely azure and entirely green, truly shining like enamel. Writing of this in book nine of the Properties of Simple Medicines, Galen said that silver slag is properly called Helcisma, and it is used in certain drying plasters.

On Litharge, or Foam of Silver. Chapter 61.

B Litharge, that is foam of silver, is formed from a sand called piombaria, fired in furnaces until it becomes well red and glowing; another kind is made from silver, and the third from lead. The finest is that which comes from Athens; the second in quality is the Spanish, and after that the kind made at Dicearchia, that is at Pozzuoli, at Baia, in Campania, and in Sicily, and most of what is made in these places is made from sheets of lead placed in the fire. That which is golden in color and shining is called aureum, and this is the best of all. That which is made in Sicily is called argeteum on account of its whiteness, and that made from silver is called calaurite. Its virtue is to constrict, to soften, to fill cavities, to reduce proud flesh, to cicatrize, to cool, and to bind. Litharge is fired by breaking it into pieces the size of walnuts, placing them over lit coals and blowing until they glow well; then the impurities around it are removed, and thus it is stored. Others quench it when it is glowing three times in vinegar, or alternatively in wine, and then fire it again, and do as described above, and thus store it. It is washed like cadmia. White litharge is made thus: take what is called argenteum, or if this is lacking take the other kind, and divide it into pieces like spelt grains, until you have the measure of an Attic bushel, place it in a new earthenware pot with an equal measure of white grain, and tie together a handful of barley in a white, open-weave cloth and place it inside, attached on the outside by a cord to the handle of the vessel; fill it with water and let it cook until the barley dissolves, then pour everything into a basin with a wide mouth. Remove all the grain from it, then pour water into it and wash the litharge, rubbing it very well by hand; then dry it and grind it in a Theban mortar, pouring hot water over it until it is entirely dissolved; then strain the water and grind it all day, and in the evening pour hot water over it again and let it rest; strain it in the morning and pour fresh water over it, and thus strain it three times a day, and this is usually done for seven days continuously. Then add five drams of mineral salt for every mina of litharge, pour hot water over it, grind it three times a day, and strain it, always adding fresh water, and when it is properly white, pour hot water over it and wash it as many times as needed to remove all the saltiness. Finally dry it in the heat of the most ardent sun until all moisture is removed, and store it. But if one does not wish to do it this way, take a mina of silver litharge and grind it with three times its weight of mineral salt, place it in a new earthenware pot with enough water to cover it, mix it every evening and morning, and pour fresh water over it without ever draining away the first water, and do this for thirty days continuously; for if it is not stirred it will thicken and harden like a potsherd. Having done this, gently drain off the brine and grind the litharge in a Theban mortar, then place it in an earthenware vessel with water and mix it diligently by hand until all the saltiness is drawn out. Then take all the white portion that is found, place it in another vessel, and having made it into small cakes, store it in a little pot of lead. There are some others who divide it into fine pieces, place it in a raw pig's stomach, cook it in water until the stomach dissolves, then remove it, grind it with an equal weight of salt, and wash it as described above. Some others grind in the sun a pound of salt and one of litharge, continuously changing the water

FIFTH. 407

water, until it becomes white. It is also made in another way. Take as much litharge of silver as you like, wrap it first in white wool, and put it in a new pot with water and a handful of beans that are not old, well cleaned, and boil them over the fire: and when you see the beans cracking, and the wool turning black, remove the litharge, wrap it in fresh wool, and boil it again, always adding a cup of water and an equal amount of beans, doing everything as described above, up to the third time, and so long until the wool no longer turns black. Then put it in a mortar, and for every eighty Attic drams of litharge add one pound of mineral salt, and pound, grind, and mix it well together: then let it rest a while, and add forty-seven drams of the whitest nitre washed with water, and grind it again until you see it is quite white. Then put it in another wider-mouthed vessel, and pour a large amount of fresh water over it from above, and when the sediment has settled, pour off the water, and add fresh, mixing everything well by hand, and let it settle again, and pour it off: repeat this so many times until the water finally comes out pure, sweet, and without any saltiness: then filter it carefully, and put it in another vessel in the dog days of summer in the sun for forty continuous days, and when it is dry, store it and use it. For it seems that, washed in this way, it is very useful for medicines for the eyes, and likewise for removing ugly blemishes from scars, wrinkles from the face, bruises, and likewise spots.

Litharge, which is today used in apothecaries' shops, is made for the most part in furnaces where silver is refined, as I have seen many times in various places in the Trentino and in Germany, being reduced from pure lead by lengthy heating and by the vapors of other metals mixed with it during refining. For when craftsmen wish to refine large quantities of silver, they first make on the ash-bed a large bath of lead, in which, when it is well heated, they place the quantity of silver they wish to refine, which is for the most part mixed with lead and copper; and so in the course of the operation one sees on the surface of the bath, through the force of the fire kept continually burning by the bellows, the lead thinning like oil, which is finally driven by the bellows to the edge of the ash-bed, and this is copper and lead which the fire has converted into litharge, which the craftsmen drain off by cutting with an iron tool a little notch on the rim of the ash-bed, through which it flows out. Some of it is gold-colored, and some is more faintly colored, like a silvery color: and so one is called gold litharge and the other silver litharge, and apothecaries believe that the one is truly the foam of gold and the other the foam of silver. But they are clearly mistaken: for, as far as I have been able to tell by watching it being made carefully with my own eyes, and from what skilled craftsmen of this art have faithfully reported to me, if the silver being refined has a good deal of copper mixed with it, the litharge becomes more red, because the vapors rising from the copper are absorbed into the lead and color it gold; but if there is little or no copper, it remains white and without any reddish color. I therefore conclude that litharge is nothing other than lead mixed for the most part with copper, and sometimes also with silver, through the carelessness of the refiners. Which is why Dioscorides rightly said it was made from lead, lead-sand, and silver. Pliny also alludes to this entirely in chapter six of book thirty-three. Galen made mention of it in book nine of On the Properties of Simple Medicines, saying: litharge certainly desiccates, as all other metallic, mineral, and earthy medicines do; but it does this more moderately than all the others, and according to its other qualities and virtues it is almost temperate: for it does not heat, and does not manifestly cool, and has little astringent or constrictive virtue: and therefore it is less powerful than those medicines that promote new flesh, which we have shown to be slightly astringent, and likewise less potent than those that contract and constrict. But for chafing and heat-rash on the thighs, it is truly a useful medicine, because it mildly partakes of both the virtues mentioned above. Therefore it may rightly be said to be of middling value among the metals.

On Ceruse. Chapter 62.

Ceruse is made as follows. Put the strongest vinegar in a jar with a wide mouth, or in a thick earthenware basin, and over the mouth of the vessel place a piece of woven reed mat like a mat, and over this fix a sheet of lead, and cover it above with coverings so that it does not breathe or allow the vinegar to evaporate: and when the sheet has dissolved and fallen to the bottom, strain out all the clear vinegar, and put the thick, turbid part into another vessel, and dry it in the sun, then grind it on the grinding stone, or otherwise, and sieve it: then take what remains hard, and return it to the grinding stone, and sieve it again: and this is done up to three or four times. The best of all is that which is sieved the first time, and this should be put into medicines—
LL ii

408 BOOK

A those that are compounded for the eyes. The second in quality is likewise the second-sifted, and so on down the line for all the others. There are some others who fit small wooden sticks in the middle of the vessel, so that they do not touch the vinegar, and they lay a layer of lead over them; after which they cover the vessel and lute it all around, leaving it thus to stand; and after ten days have passed, they uncover it, look at it, and if the material has dissolved, they do as described above. To make pastilles of it, one kneads it with strong vinegar, shapes the pastilles, and dries them in the sun; but such work must be done in summer, because that is how it becomes white and effective. It can also be made in winter, however, by placing the vessels over furnaces, baths, or stoves, since the heat rising upward produces the same effect as the sun. The choicest is that made in Rhodes, in Corinth, and in Lacedaemon; the second-best is that from Pozzuoli. White lead is calcined in the following manner. The ground white lead is placed in a new earthen vessel, best of Attic clay, set over burning coals, and stirred continuously until it turns to ash, after which it is taken out, left to cool, and then used. It is also calcined in another way. It is ground and placed on burning coals in new earthen vessels and stirred continuously with a rod of fennel stalk, until it takes on the color of sandarach, and is then removed and kept for use. Some call this substance Sandyx. White lead is washed in the same manner as cadmia. Its virtue is to cool, to contract, to soften, to fill, and to refine; it gently dissolves superfluities of the flesh and promotes cicatrization. That which is made into pastilles is used in plasters and poultices called emollients; taken by mouth it is a mortal thing, being malignant and poisonous.

E White lead is a well-known and common medicine, and is made continuously in Venice and in other mercantile cities of Italy, not only for the use of medicine, but also for painters and other craftsmen; and therefore there is no need to discourse further upon it. Galen made mention of it at the end of the ninth book on the faculties of simples, saying thus: If white lead is dissolved in strong vinegar, it will not thereby be found sharp in taste, nor yet biting; but gentle and refrigerating, truly most unlike in all its faculties to verdigris, even though that too is made with vinegar dissolving copper. It is indeed true that from calcined white lead is made Sandyx, which is truly a medicament considerably more subtle than white lead itself, though not for that reason heating.

C On Chrysocolla. Chapter LXII.

The finest Chrysocolla is that from Armenia, leek-green in color throughout. The second in quality is the Macedonian, and the third the Cypriot. Of all these, that most praised is the purest, and that which is mixed with earth or with stones is condemned. It is washed in the following manner. It is ground and placed in a mortar, water is poured over it, it is rubbed with a hand suited to the mortar, and strained, until the sediment settles; then more water is poured over it, it is ground again and strained; and this is done so many times until it is seen to be pure and clean; after which it is dried in the sun and stored for use. But if one wishes to calcine it, one grinds as much as desired, places it in pans over coals, and proceeds as we have shown in other instances above. Chrysocolla purifies scars, removes superfluities of the flesh, contracts, cleanses, warms, and mildly corrodes, biting the flesh. Chrysocolla is one of those medicines that cause vomiting and that can kill.

D Chrysocolla (said Pliny, in the fifth chapter of the thirty-third book) is a liquid found in the caves of mines, which oozes out through the vein of gold, the slime condensing in the cold of winter until it hardens like pumice. The most esteemed is that found in the copper mines, and after that, that found in the silver mines. It is also found in lead mines, but of lesser quality than that from the gold mines. It is also made artificially in all these metal mines by lightly wetting the vein with water throughout the entire winter until June, when, drying out in June and July, it becomes Chrysocolla, which is nothing other than putrefied ore. The natural kind is truly different from the other, being much harder, yet it is counterfeited with the dye of the plant they call yellow, since Chrysocolla absorbs color as linen does, and likewise wool. All this concerning Chrysocolla was written by Pliny. In the apothecary shops in our time, Chrysocolla is called Borax, but little of the pure kind is found there that has the fine dark green color required; for the most part it is blackish, and yet quite a lot of the artificial kind is found, made of rock alum and ammoniac salt by means of fire, and this is what they call refined Borax. The greenest of all that I have seen in the mines and metal workings of Germany is that found in the copper veins; the black kind is that dug from the lead veins; and the whitish from those of silver. This has led me to believe that its color derives from the mine whence it is collected. Further on

On Lapis Lazuli (Caeruleum). Chapter 65.

The blue stone (Caeruleum) is found in Cyprus in the copper mine caves, but it is also found more abundantly in the sand along the shores, in certain caverns formed by the sea like grottos, and this latter kind is considered the best. The most select kind is the deepest in color. It is burned like chalcitis, and washed like cadmia. It has the virtue of repressing and somewhat eroding; it generates crusts and is ulcerative.

A    Following the words of the Arabs, the blue stone is commonly called throughout all Italy Lapis lazuli, and that kind is considered the best which has in itself certain glints of gold. Among the Arabs it is used, just as Armenian stone is, to purge melancholic humors, and therefore, on account of the affinity they recognized between these two stones, many have quite foolishly confused the one with the other. And because Avicenna said specifically that Lapis lazuli had in itself a putrefactive virtue, there are some among the Moderns who condemn its use, and likewise the use of its pills, which are commonly used in apothecaries to purge melancholic humors, as Fuchs openly does in his Paradoxes. But however incompletely the Arabs treated the subject, it is not reasonable to say that Lapis lazuli cannot benefit melancholic humors simply because this was not written by the ancient Greeks; for although Galen did not explicitly say it dissolved melancholy, he did say it was laxative, and with this as their basis, the Arabs discovered by experiment that its solvent action was upon the melancholic humor. For the Arabs were inventors of many things that were never written about or known by the Greeks, as we have truthfully treated in various places of this our volume. Indeed, as was said at length in the chapter just above, before Alexander of Tralles, no ancient person knew that Armenian stone had a virtue similar to white hellebore in purging melancholy without harm. Which clearly demonstrates that if until the time of Alexander the virtue of that stone had remained hidden, so too could that of Lapis lazuli have remained hidden and been discovered only afterward. For since these two stones are found together in the metal mines, one next to the other (as I myself have found in many places in Germany, and indeed sometimes both in one single piece), it led their discoverers to imagine that, not being very different in color, they would not be very different in virtue and value either. And indeed, when some people later wished to test this, knowing that Galen had given it a laxative virtue, they found in them equal virtue in dissolving the melancholic humor. And therefore the learned Manardo of Ferrara, in his censures on the simple laxatives of Mesue, said that he could in no way side with those who condemn Lapis lazuli as a deadly poison, since he had found by certain experience that when washed with diligence, it benefits marvelously with very little or no harm. In this opinion I believe every reasonable and not obstinate physician can canonically concur: for even though Avicenna said it was putrefactive, this does not prevent it from being able to purge the melancholic humor without harm. For its sharpness, which is the cause of its putrefactive action, is removed by washing and purging it as required. This likewise removes its power to ulcerate, which Dioscorides attributes to it. It is true that one should choose that which shines with gold; for the other, which apothecaries and those who make azure pigments in Germany are always supplied with, is by far not as valuable. I have already been in some silver mines where I found large quantities of both the blue stone and the Armenian stone piled together, but I found no piece that shone with golden glints; for this is only found in the true gold mines, while what is found in silver and copper mines is only found in those which contain some portion of gold. And therefore that azure called ultramarine, which is made from true Lapis lazuli from gold mines, is in the greatest esteem for surpassing in quality and color all other azures in the world. As for what is made from sea-shore sand, although Pliny and others spoke much of it, I have no knowledge of it yet. Galen wrote of it in book nine of On the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: the blue (celestial) stone is sharp and has a purgative and digestive virtue more powerful than cinnabar, and it also has some degree of astringency.

On Indigo. Chapter 66.

D    Indigo is of two kinds: one that grows naturally in India, issuing from certain reeds in the manner of a foam, and another that is made in dyeing workshops, which is a purple foam that floats on top in the vats, and which the craftsmen skim off and dry. The kind that most resembles azure blue, and which is smooth and succulent, is considered the best. Among medicines, indigo is counted among those that bind gently and that disperse inflammations and tumors; it cleanses ulcers and reduces superfluous flesh.

L    The indigo that is most commonly used by painters, although it is found in our times in apothecaries, is only that which is made in dyeing workshops, being made from woad, with which woolen cloth is dyed. The natural kind, which Dioscorides describes as rising like a foam on the reeds in India, is not found anywhere, nor was it known in Italy in the time of Pliny; for in the sixth chapter of book thirty-five he states that he had no knowledge of it, and shows that the manufactured kind of his times was made in dyeing workshops from the foam of purple dye, something quite different from woad, from which ours is made.

FIFTH BOOK. 411

On Ochre. Chapter 67.

The finest Ochre is that which is very light, entirely yellow, well-colored, not sandy, brittle, and of Attic origin. It is burned and washed like cadmia. It has astringent and corrosive properties: it resolves abscesses and skin eruptions, reduces flesh that grows too much, fills deep ulcers when combined with wax ointment, and breaks up stones that form in the joints.

The ochre of our times is that yellow earth which painters use as a pigment, and it is not from Athens as the finest quality: because up until the time of Vitruvius its use in Italy had already fallen off. This is an earth tinged yellow by the vapors of lead mines, in whose caves it is found.

On Cinnabar. Chapter 68.

All those who believe that cinnabar and minium are one and the same thing are clearly deceived. For minium is made in Spain from a certain stone mixed with a silvery sand, and otherwise it is not recognized. It produces a very brilliant and intense color in the furnaces; but in the mines it gives off a truly suffocating vapor, and so those who handle it cover their faces with wicker masks so they can see, and so that in breathing they do not draw in its malignant vapor. Painters use it for the most sumptuous ornamentation on the facades of walls. But cinnabar is brought from Africa, and it is very expensive, and so little of it is imported that painters can barely obtain enough to shade their paintings with various lines: it is deeply colored, and for this reason some thought it to be dragon's blood. Cinnabar has the same virtue as the stone called hematite, and is suitable in medicines for the eyes, in which use it is even more effective, being more astringent. Applied in a wax ointment it heals burns from fire and pustules.

In truth (as is the common opinion of all naturalists of our times) there is a very great difference between the cinnabar written about by Dioscorides and that which is presently in use in apothecary shops, and likewise among painters.
For ours (as will be made clear below) is found both in mineral and artificial forms, and is moreover poisonous and deadly; while that described by Dioscorides is brought from Africa in small quantities, and has the same virtues as the stone called Hematite, which he not only recommended applied externally for various ailments of the eyes, but also praised when taken internally for disorders of the urine, to stop women's fluxes, and likewise spitting of blood. Our common cinnabar in no way suits these purposes, being corrosive, ulcerative, poisonous, and an enemy of the eyes and internal organs. But what the cinnabar of Dioscorides actually was cannot truly be affirmed except by conjecture, since he does not describe what it is, nor how it is made or found in Africa. But before coming to the conjectures that truly demonstrate what the cinnabar of Dioscorides is in our times, one should know that Pliny, in chapter 7 of book 33, states affirmatively that cinnabar is nothing other than the blood of a dragon killed by the great weight of an elephant falling upon it, their blood mingling together, and that no other color better imitates in paintings the true color of blood. This same account is given by Julius Solinus in his Collectanea. Beyond this, one should also know that Dragon's Blood (though it is not such) is also the name given to a gum from an African tree of the most natural blood-red color, transparent and brittle, called today commonly Dragon's Blood in tears, distinguished from the sophisticated and worthless kind that is imported to us in cakes. And it may rightly be called "in tears," for (as Luigi Cadamosto relates in chapter 4 of his account of his voyage to Africa) this is a gummy, liquid tear that distills from a tree, and to obtain more of it the inhabitants score the bark with certain iron tools, and then collecting the liquid they cook it in cauldrons over fire, and call it Dragon's Blood. This leads us reasonably to conjecture that this gum is the cinnabar of Dioscorides: for, first, it is found that such liquid is brought to us from Africa in small quantities. It is used by painters for shading and outlining in light red. It sells at a high price on account of its rarity, and in its virtues it is similar to the stone hematite — indeed, as experience shows and as Dioscorides likewise affirms, this liquid is considerably more astringent — and therefore modern physicians use it for women's fluxes and dysentery, and likewise for spitting and fluxes of blood, with considerable success. Furthermore, since this liquid has been called Dragon's Blood from the time of Dioscorides onward, as it has continued to be called from age to age down to modern times, Dioscorides, knowing very well that it was not truly the blood of that so-named animal, said: "Cinnabar is deeply colored, and for this reason some thought it to be Dragon's Blood." This manner of speaking makes clear that Dioscorides wished to show that cinnabar was not Dragon's Blood, but truly another substance — even though it was called that by many at his time.
